essays.title: A shared national core serves every student

paragraphs.text: Where a child is born should not decide what that child has the chance to learn.
This principle supports the claim that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that the common curriculum sets a shared core of knowledge while leaving teachers room to adapt how it is taught.

A national curriculum promotes equal opportunity, it creates a shared foundation for citizens, and, although critics argue that it ignores local needs and stifles creativity, this risk can be managed.
First, a common curriculum promotes fairness because it guarantees that rural and poor students are taught the same essential content as wealthy urban students.
In Vietnam, a student in a mountain district and a student in central Hanoi follow the same national program, so both are prepared for the same university entrance examinations.
Without that shared standard, schools in poorer areas might quietly lower their expectations, leaving their students with a disadvantage they could never [[surmount|surmount]].
Similarly, a child whose family moves from one province to another can continue learning without gaps or repetition.
This continuity matters in a country where many families move to cities in search of work.
These cases show that a national curriculum makes education more [[equitable|equitable]], which is the strongest reason to require it for all students.
Equal content does not guarantee equal results, but it removes one important source of inequality.
Second, a shared curriculum gives citizens a common foundation of knowledge, which a nation needs in order to function as a community.
When every student learns the same basic biology, for instance, public health campaigns about vaccination or dengue prevention can build on knowledge that the whole population shares.
In my work on disease control, explaining risk is far easier when people already understand how infections spread.
Likewise, a common history course gives young people from different regions a shared story and a common vocabulary for discussing their country's future.
This shows that a national curriculum does more than transmit facts; it helps citizens from different backgrounds [[coalesce|coalesce]] into a society that can understand one another.
Such shared understanding is difficult to build if every school teaches entirely different content.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that a single curriculum may ignore local needs and limit creativity.
Finland, often admired for its schools, gives its highly trained teachers considerable freedom and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Nevertheless, this example shows the value of flexible teaching methods, not the danger of shared content, since Finland still sets national goals for what students should learn.
A national curriculum can likewise define core subjects while allowing schools to add local languages, crafts or electives.
This challenge therefore refines my position: the content of the core should be national, but the methods and the extras should remain local.
Shared goals and local freedom, in other words, are not opposites but partners.
In conclusion, I largely agree that all students should study the same national curriculum before college, as long as it defines a core rather than [[circumscribing|circumscribe]] every lesson.
A common curriculum promotes equal opportunity and a shared civic foundation, and flexibility in teaching can answer the concern about local needs.
Such a balance gives every child the same starting line without forcing every classroom into the same mold.

words.meaning_here: come together to form one whole

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (a single curriculum ignores local needs, as Finland's teacher freedom suggests), grants it, and answers it by separating national content from local methods.

essays.title: One curriculum cannot fit every student

paragraphs.text: Students form a [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] group, differing in talents, interests and goals as much as in height.
Yet the claim holds that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.

Although some shared standards are useful, I mostly disagree with this claim, because a single required curriculum ignores students' different needs and discourages the variety that drives better teaching.
A uniform curriculum fails students with different abilities and goals, it limits teachers' freedom to innovate, and, admittedly, common standards do help ensure fairness.
First, a single curriculum fails many students because it assumes that all of them need the same knowledge at the same pace.
Consider a sixteen-year-old in rural Vietnam who wants to become a mechanic or a farmer using modern techniques.
Requiring him to follow exactly the same academic program as a student preparing for medical school may leave him bored, unprepared for his chosen work and more likely to drop out.
Vocational programs in many countries keep such students engaged by linking lessons to real jobs.
Similarly, a student gifted in mathematics may lose interest when forced to [[dawdle|dawdle]] at the pace set for everyone else.
These cases show that uniformity, however well meant, can [[impede|impede]] the very students it claims to serve.
A curriculum that serves the average student well may serve the individual student poorly.
Second, a required national curriculum limits innovation by preventing schools and teachers from trying new approaches.
Finland, often admired for its schools, requires teachers to hold a master's degree and then trusts them with considerable freedom, relying far less on standardized testing than many countries.
This trust allows teachers to adjust lessons to the students in front of them rather than follow a script set by distant officials.

Likewise, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, learned through their own experiments with gliders and a homemade wind tunnel, a reminder that valuable learning often happens outside a fixed program.
This suggests that a nation benefits more from many experiments in teaching than from a single, [[ossified|ossify]] curriculum.
If one method fails, a nation with many methods can learn from the others; a nation with one method cannot.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that, without a common curriculum, schools in poor areas may offer weaker education, widening inequality.
In many countries, wealthy districts can afford richer programs, while poorer schools struggle to teach even basic subjects.
Wealthier families can also pay for private tutoring, which widens the gap further.
Nevertheless, this problem can be solved with national minimum standards in core subjects such as reading, mathematics and science, rather than with one curriculum for every subject and every year.
Vietnam, for example, could keep a national standard in core subjects while letting schools design vocational and advanced courses for different students.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the state should guarantee a floor of essential knowledge, but above that floor, students and schools should be free to choose their own paths.
Fairness requires a common minimum, not a common maximum.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that every student should follow the same national curriculum until college.
Such uniformity fails students with different goals and limits innovation, while the legitimate concern for fairness can be met by minimum standards.
A nation serves its young people best by setting a common foundation and then allowing many different paths to be built on it.

words.meaning_here: made up of very different parts

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (without a shared curriculum, poor schools fall behind), concedes it, and answers it with minimum standards instead of full uniformity.

essays.title: Require a semester abroad, and fund it

paragraphs.text: Some lessons cannot be learned from a textbook, only from living among people who see the world differently.
This is the main argument for the claim that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as universities provide financial support so that the requirement does not exclude poorer students.
Studying abroad builds the international outlook that modern problems demand, it develops independence and adaptability, and, although cost is a serious objection, it can be addressed.
First, a semester abroad is valuable because many of today's most important problems cross national borders.
The eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980, depended on a coordinated WHO campaign in which countries shared data and vaccine.
The people who led such efforts needed to understand other countries' health systems, languages and customs.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, also showed how much researchers from different countries can achieve together.

Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads today partly through the overuse and over-the-counter sale of antibiotics in many countries, including Vietnam, so tackling it requires professionals who can work across borders.
These cases show that global problems demand an international outlook, and a required semester abroad is one reliable way to [[engender|engender]] it.
Graduates who have lived abroad are better prepared to join such cooperation.
Second, living in a foreign country develops independence and adaptability that classroom learning rarely provides.
Consider a Vietnamese medical student who spends a semester at a hospital in another country.
She must work in an unfamiliar language, adapt to different routines and ask for help, and she returns with greater confidence and a broader view of how health care can be organized.
Likewise, a business student who spends a semester abroad learns firsthand that markets and customers differ, a lesson that no case study conveys as vividly.
In my experience, colleagues who trained abroad adapt quickly to new teams and unfamiliar problems.
Such experiences make students less [[insular|insular]] and more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]], qualities that employers and societies increasingly need.
These are skills that matter in every career, not only in international ones.
The most compelling challenge to this position is cost: travel, housing and tuition abroad can be [[prohibitive|prohibitive]] for students from poor families.
A student from a farming family in the Mekong Delta might be unable to pay for a semester in Europe, and a strict requirement could even prevent her from graduating.
Even with a partial scholarship, airfare and rent in a foreign city could exceed what her family can manage.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for funding the requirement, not for abandoning it.
Universities can offer scholarships, sign exchange agreements that keep tuition at home rates, and partner with nearby countries where living costs are lower.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the requirement is justified only when universities make it affordable for every student.
A requirement without funding would be unjust, but a funded requirement would open doors that many students could never open alone.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to study abroad for at least one semester, provided they make it financially possible for all.
Such a semester prepares graduates for global problems and builds independence, while scholarships and exchanges can answer the concern about cost.
A requirement backed by real support would turn a privilege of the few into an opportunity for everyone.

words.meaning_here: open to and familiar with many cultures
so high that it prevents action

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (cost excludes poor students), concedes it, and answers it by making funding a condition of the requirement.

essays.title: Encourage study abroad, but do not require it

paragraphs.text: An experience that transforms one student may be a heavy burden for another.
This is the main problem with the claim that colleges and universities should require all students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.

Although studying abroad can be valuable, I mostly disagree that it should be required, because a universal mandate would be unfair to many students and is unnecessary for gaining international understanding.
The requirement would exclude students with limited money or heavy responsibilities, its benefits can be achieved in other ways, and, admittedly, time abroad does offer real advantages.
First, a required semester abroad would be unfair because many students cannot afford it or cannot leave home.
Consider a student in Vietnam whose parents are farmers and who works part-time to pay her tuition; a semester in another country could cost more than her family earns in a year.
Other students care for sick relatives, have children of their own, or have disabilities that make travel difficult.
Similarly, students in demanding programs such as medicine may find that a semester abroad delays their clinical training and graduation.
A requirement that ignores these situations would force some students to choose between their families and their degrees.
For such students, the requirement would be not an opportunity but an [[onerous|onerous]] barrier, which [[undermines|undermine]] the claim that it should apply to everyone.
A rule that only some students can meet is not a fair graduation requirement.
Second, the benefits of studying abroad can often be achieved without leaving one's own country.
International collaboration increasingly happens online and in mixed teams at home.
Many of my own international collaborations in epidemiology, for instance, began with online meetings rather than travel.

The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, so a student almost anywhere can now take part in global science.
Likewise, universities can invite visiting professors, enroll international students and offer joint online courses, bringing foreign perspectives to students who stay home.
This suggests that a mandate is unnecessary, since the goal of a [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] education can be reached by many [[feasible|feasible]] paths.
Universities can therefore pursue international understanding without making travel compulsory.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that living abroad teaches lessons that no online course can, such as independence and the ability to adapt to an unfamiliar culture.
A medical student who spends a semester in a foreign hospital, for instance, must solve daily problems in another language and returns with a confidence that is hard to gain at home.
Nevertheless, recognizing these benefits supports encouraging and funding study abroad, not forcing it on every student.
Scholarships, exchange agreements and short summer programs can bring these experiences within reach of students who want them.

This challenge therefore shapes my position: universities should make study abroad widely available through scholarships and exchanges, while allowing students to choose it when it fits their circumstances.
Choice, not compulsion, is what makes such experiences meaningful.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that universities should require every student to study abroad.
Such a requirement would burden students with limited resources, and international understanding can also be gained at home, even though time abroad has real value.
Universities should therefore open the door to study abroad as widely as possible, without pushing every student through it.

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (living abroad builds independence that nothing else can), concedes it, and answers that this supports funding study abroad, not requiring it.

essays.title: Guiding students toward jobs helps everyone

paragraphs.text: Graduating with a degree but no job is one of the most discouraging experiences a young person can face.
To prevent it, some propose that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
I support this policy, as long as encouragement means giving students clear information and incentives rather than forbidding them to follow other interests.

The policy would reduce graduate unemployment, it would help societies meet urgent needs, and, although it might discourage some talented students from less practical fields, that consequence can be limited.
First, implementing the policy would likely reduce unemployment and wasted investment among graduates.
In Vietnam, many families make great sacrifices to send their children to university, yet some graduates in crowded fields struggle for years to find work related to their degree.
If schools showed students data on job prospects before they chose a major, more of them could enter fields where their effort would be rewarded.
Graduates with stable jobs can also repay their families' sacrifices, a responsibility many young Vietnamese take seriously.
Similarly, a student who learns early that demand for nurses or data analysts is high may choose a path that leads to stable employment and independence.
This consequence strongly shapes my support, because a policy that spares young people [[futile|futile]] years of searching for work is a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] form of care.
Students remain free to choose, but they choose with better knowledge.
Second, the policy would help societies meet their most [[pressing|pressing]] needs.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries with too few nurses, laboratory technicians and epidemiologists struggled to test and treat patients.
In my own work in public health, I have seen a shortage of trained staff delay a dengue response even when money and equipment were available.
When jobs go unfilled in such fields, patients wait longer and outbreaks spread further.
Likewise, as smartphones and digital services spread, societies need far more engineers and programmers than they once did.
This shows that guiding students toward fields with plentiful jobs serves not only individuals but also the public, since those jobs are plentiful precisely because the work is needed.
Encouraging students to fill such gaps is therefore a public good as well as a private benefit.

Admittedly, the policy could have a negative consequence: talented students might be discouraged from fields such as art, history or basic science, where jobs are scarce but contributions can be [[profound|profound]].
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
A policy that steered every young artist toward accounting might have cost the world such work.
Nevertheless, this risk arises only if encouragement becomes pressure, and a well-designed policy can avoid that.
Schools can provide job information and scholarships for high-demand fields while still supporting students who, fully informed, choose a different path.
This consequence therefore qualifies my support: the policy is beneficial as long as it informs students' choices rather than dictating them.
Information widens choices; only coercion would narrow them.
In conclusion, I support encouraging students to choose fields with plentiful jobs, provided the encouragement respects their freedom.
Such a policy would reduce graduate unemployment and help meet urgent social needs, and its risks to less practical fields can be limited.
Clear information, offered early, allows students to follow their interests with open eyes rather than discover the job market too late.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace positive consequences of implementing the policy; Body 3 weighs a negative consequence (lost talent in arts and basic science) and explains how it limits the support.

essays.title: Steering students toward jobs can backfire

paragraphs.text: The job market of today is rarely the job market of tomorrow.
This uncertainty raises doubts about the policy that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.

Although students deserve accurate information about careers, I oppose this policy, because steering them toward currently popular fields would likely create future surpluses, waste individual talent and neglect work whose value appears only later.
Job markets change faster than degrees can be completed, students do their best work in fields that suit them, and, admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment.
First, implementing the policy could backfire because today's plentiful jobs may become tomorrow's crowded fields.

If every school pushed students toward a profession that is in demand today, large numbers of graduates might enter the market at the same time several years later, when demand may already have fallen.
Students who chose a field for its job prospects alone would then face the very unemployment that the policy was meant to prevent.
In my own field, for instance, the demand for epidemiologists rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic and then eased once the emergency passed.
Kodak's story shows how quickly an industry can change: its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet the company clung to film and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
These consequences suggest that the policy rests on a [[myopic|myopic]] view of the job market, which is one reason I oppose it.
Guidance based on today's vacancies may simply move unemployment a few years into the future.
Second, the policy would likely waste talent, because students perform best in fields that match their abilities and interests.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, a career few advisers would have called a safe choice.
Her achievements came from [[ardent|ardent]] commitment to her subject, not from a calculation about available jobs.
Likewise, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed mRNA research, work that later made rapid COVID-19 vaccines possible and won the 2023 Nobel Prize.
This consequence shapes my opposition: a policy that pushes students away from their interests would [[sap|sap]] the motivation that produces excellence.
Societies need such people, and they rarely appear on lists of plentiful jobs.
Admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment and help students avoid degrees that lead nowhere.
In Vietnam, some families invest heavily in degrees that leave graduates searching for work for years, and clearer guidance might prevent such losses.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be achieved by giving students honest information about job prospects rather than actively steering them.
A university that publishes employment rates for each program and offers career counseling respects students' choices while still protecting them from uninformed decisions.
This consequence therefore refines my position: institutions should inform students, but they should not encourage them to [[abdicate|abdicate]] their own judgment in favor of the latest job report.
Honest information protects students; active steering replaces their judgment with someone else's.
In conclusion, I oppose the policy of actively encouraging students to choose fields in which jobs are plentiful.
It could create future surpluses, waste talent and neglect fields whose value emerges slowly, while its benefits can be gained through honest career information.
Schools serve students best by informing their choices, not by making those choices for them.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace harmful consequences of implementing the policy (future gluts, lost talent); Body 3 weighs a benefit (less short-term unemployment) and explains how it shapes the position toward information rather than steering.

essays.title: Circumstances shape most of what we do

paragraphs.text: Few people like to think of themselves as puppets, yet much of what we do each day follows [[pervasive|pervasive]] patterns we never chose.
Our habits, our work and even our health decisions are shaped by laws, markets and social norms long before we act.
I therefore largely agree that people's behavior is determined by forces not of their own making, although some individuals do manage to resist those forces.
This view is supported by the power of laws and incentives and by the influence of economic systems, and it survives even the strongest examples of individual resistance.
First, behavior largely follows the rules and incentives that surround people, because most people adapt to their environment rather than reshape it.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets offers a clear case.
Before the law, helmet use was low, even though the danger of head injury was well known; within months of the law, helmet use rose to over 90%, and head injuries and deaths fell.

Similarly, in my work on antibiotic resistance, I see patients buy antibiotics over the counter not because they misunderstand medicine, but because [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]] pharmacies sell them freely.
Doctors, too, prescribe more freely when patients demand antibiotics and no rules discourage the practice.
These cases show that the same people behave very differently once the forces around them change, which suggests that those forces, not personal will, largely determine behavior.
A rider who refused a helmet in 2006 was not necessarily more reckless than one who wore it in 2008; the rule had simply changed.
Second, economic systems, which no single person designs, shape how people work and what they produce.
Before 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning, and the country faced food shortages despite having millions of hardworking farmers.
After the Doi Moi reforms introduced market incentives, the same country became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.

Likewise, Kodak was slow to embrace digital photography, even though its own engineer Steven Sasson had invented the digital camera in 1975, because the company was protecting its profitable film business.
The farmers did not suddenly become different people, and Kodak's managers were simply responding to the rewards of their business; in each case, a system [[elicited|elicit]] the behavior.
Behavior, in other words, is often a response to structures that individuals inherit rather than create.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that some individuals plainly overcome the forces around them.
Marie Curie, for instance, won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Nevertheless, such achievements are remembered precisely because they are rare.
Even a bold thinker like Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to [[recant|recant]] his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
If someone of Galileo's standing could not withstand such pressure, ordinary people are far more likely to follow the forces around them.
For every Curie, countless talented women of her era never had the chance to enter a laboratory at all.
Curie's success therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] my position rather than overturning it: individuals can rise above their circumstances, but only occasionally.
In conclusion, while people are not mere puppets, most of their behavior is shaped by forces they did not create.
Laws and incentives, economic systems, and the rarity of genuine resistance all point to this conclusion.
Recognizing this fact should make us slower to blame individuals and more willing to change the conditions that guide their choices.

essays.title: People make choices, and choices remake forces

paragraphs.text: Every society tells its members how to behave, but history is also full of people who refused to listen.
The real question is whether outside pressures, from laws to culture, truly decide what people do.
I mostly disagree with the claim that behavior is largely determined by forces not of our own making, because people regularly choose against their circumstances and can even reshape those forces.
This essay discusses individual choices made under pressure and collective choices that change society, and then it addresses the strong evidence that environments influence behavior.
First, individuals often act on their own judgment even when the norms around them push the other way.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide was given to pregnant women in Europe, where it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, and the country then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Similarly, Ignaz Semmelweis kept urging doctors to wash their hands in chlorinated lime, although most of his colleagues rejected his idea.
His choice went unrewarded in his lifetime, since germ theory vindicated his idea only years after his death.
Neither Kelsey nor Semmelweis was simply following the habits of the time; each made a deliberate choice.
If behavior were largely determined by outside forces, both would simply have followed the practice of their peers.
Such cases show that personal conviction can [[supersede|supersede]] the expectations that surround a person.
Moreover, the "forces" that seem to control people are themselves created by human choices, so people are often their authors rather than their victims.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
Their [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] protest helped end bus segregation in that city, changing the very rules that had governed their daily lives.
Likewise, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 only because many countries chose to cooperate in a global WHO vaccination campaign, sharing data and vaccine.
No law of nature forced these nations to work together; they decided to do so because they shared a goal.
In both cases, people did not passively accept the forces around them; they deliberately replaced them.
Thus, the claim treats as fixed what is in fact the product of human action.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is the evidence that environments strongly shape what most people do.
After Vietnam's 2007 helmet law, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, which suggests that the law, not personal choice, changed behavior.
Similarly, in many countries, including Vietnam, antibiotics are overused and sold over the counter, which suggests that easy access, more than individual judgment, drives what patients do.
Nevertheless, such forces set the options that people face rather than determining their choices completely.
A law makes wearing a helmet the expected choice, but each rider still decides to wear it; indeed, the law itself was a decision made by people.
Laws, markets and technologies are powerful, but they work through human decisions rather than around them.
This evidence therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] my position, reminding me that most people [[adhere|adhere]] to the rules around them, but it does not [[negate|negate]] the role of choice.
In conclusion, outside forces clearly influence behavior, but they do not largely determine it.
Individuals make deliberate choices under pressure, groups reshape the forces that bind them, and even strong environmental effects leave room for choice.
For this reason, we should hold people responsible for their actions while also building environments that make good choices easier.

essays.title: Study abroad pays off if funded

paragraphs.text: Many of today's most serious problems, from pandemics to climate change, do not stop at national borders.
It is therefore reasonable to ask whether universities should require every student to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I support this policy, provided that universities help students pay for it, because its likely consequences for students and society outweigh its costs.
Requiring study abroad would prepare students to work across cultures and would build their independence, although its financial burden must be addressed.
First, one likely consequence of the policy is that graduates would be better prepared to solve problems that cross borders.
Smallpox, for example, was declared eradicated in 1980 only after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign in which countries shared data and vaccine.
Such cooperation depended on professionals who could understand colleagues from very different systems and cultures.
Today's challenges, from antibiotic resistance to dengue, demand the same kind of cross-border teamwork.
In my own research collaborations with partners abroad, I have noticed that colleagues who once studied overseas handle cultural differences with far more ease.
A semester abroad cannot turn every student into a diplomat, but it gives each one direct experience of another system.
Graduates who have lived abroad are more likely to see foreign partners as colleagues rather than strangers.
This consequence alone makes the policy advantageous for an increasingly [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] workforce.
Second, the policy would likely make students more independent and adaptable, qualities that classroom learning rarely builds.
Consider a Vietnamese engineering student who spends a semester in Japan.
She must find housing, manage a budget and study in an unfamiliar language, so she quickly learns to solve problems without relying on her family.
By the end of the semester, she has gained a confidence that no lecture on independence could provide.
Similarly, a student from a small town who studies in a large foreign city learns to adjust to new customs and new people.
These experiences [[inure|inure]] students to discomfort and teach them to adapt, which employers value highly.
In my experience supervising young researchers, those who have lived abroad tend to take initiative more readily.
Thus, a required semester abroad would give every student, not only the most [[audacious|audacious]], a chance to develop this kind of maturity.
Admittedly, the most serious consequence on the other side is cost, since a semester abroad can be [[prohibitive|prohibitive]] for students from poor families.

In Vietnam, for instance, a semester in Europe or the United States would be far beyond the means of many rural families, so an unfunded rule would exclude exactly the students who could benefit most.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for funding the policy, not for abandoning it.
Universities can offer scholarships to students in need, favor lower-cost destinations nearby, and arrange exchange agreements in which students pay only home tuition.
A Vietnamese student, for instance, could spend a semester in Thailand or Malaysia for far less than a semester in Europe would cost.
Such measures would turn the policy's greatest weakness into a reason for universities to invest in fairness.
Without such support, the policy would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality rather than broaden minds.
This consequence therefore shapes my position: I support the requirement only when it comes with real financial support.
In conclusion, requiring students to study abroad for a semester would be a wise policy, as long as universities make it affordable.
It would prepare graduates for international problems and build their independence, while its main drawback, cost, can be addressed through careful planning.
A university that adopts this policy should treat funding as part of the requirement itself, not as an afterthought.

essays.title: A mandatory semester abroad does more harm

paragraphs.text: Good intentions do not always make good rules.
Studying abroad can be a valuable experience, but requiring every college student to spend a semester in a foreign country is a different matter.

I oppose this policy as a universal requirement, because its likely consequences for poorer students and for demanding programs outweigh its benefits, although universities should still encourage voluntary study abroad.
A mandatory semester abroad would burden low-income students and disrupt tightly structured programs, even though its benefits for those who choose it are real.
First, the most likely consequence of the policy would be to place an [[onerous|onerous]] financial demand on students with little money.
Consider a first-generation student from a rural province in Vietnam who already works part-time to pay her tuition.
A required semester in another country would force her family to borrow money for flights, housing and living costs, or it would force her to leave the university altogether.
Even a semester in a nearby country would require money that her family does not have.
Similarly, students who care for younger siblings or sick parents could not simply leave home for several months.
For these students, the policy would turn a privilege into a barrier.
Even generous scholarships rarely cover lost wages, family duties and the stress of living far from home.
A rule that [[exacerbates|exacerbate]] inequality in this way cannot be justified by benefits that mainly reach students who are already comfortable.
Second, the policy would disrupt programs whose courses must follow a strict sequence.
Medical students in Vietnam, for instance, move through basic sciences, clinical rotations and licensing requirements that are tied to local hospitals and local law.
A semester abroad might not count toward these requirements, so many students would have to delay graduation.
Likewise, engineering and nursing programs often depend on accredited courses and supervised practice that a foreign university may not offer.
A nursing student in her final year, for example, may need many supervised hours in local hospitals before she can be licensed.
Universities could try to design matching courses abroad, but doing so for every program would be costly and slow.
Delays of this kind have real costs, from extra tuition to fewer doctors and nurses entering the workforce.
Thus, the policy would be most [[deleterious|deleterious]] in exactly the fields that society needs most.
Admittedly, study abroad has genuine benefits, and a policy that spread them widely would have some appeal.
Students who live in another country often become more independent and better at working across cultures, which matters in a world where epidemics cross borders.
Smallpox, for instance, was declared eradicated in 1980 only after countries shared data and vaccine in a coordinated WHO campaign.
Nevertheless, these benefits can be achieved without forcing every student to travel.
Universities can offer scholarships for voluntary exchanges, invite international students to their campuses, and build joint online projects with partner schools.
A Vietnamese public health student, for example, could join an online research project with a partner school in Japan and learn a great deal about working across cultures.
These alternatives would keep most of the benefits while avoiding the harmful consequences described above.
The real advantages of study abroad therefore shape my position toward encouragement rather than requirement.
In conclusion, universities should support study abroad but should not make it a condition of graduation.
A mandatory semester would burden poorer students and delay demanding programs, and its real benefits can be gained through voluntary options.
A [[judicious|judicious]] university would therefore expand opportunities for international experience while leaving the final choice to each student.

essays.task_note: As a policy task, Bodies 1-2 trace two harmful consequences of the requirement and Body 3 weighs its benefits, which shape the position toward voluntary study abroad.

essays.title: Classroom technology often distracts from learning

paragraphs.text: As laptops and tablets become [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]] in schools, a classroom full of screens can look like the future of education.
Yet the statement claims that video, computers and the Internet, despite their promise, all too often distract students from real learning.

I largely agree with this statement, because these technologies are frequently used in ways that weaken attention and replace good teaching, although they can support learning when teachers use them with a clear purpose.
Technology distracts by fragmenting attention and by replacing skilled teaching, but it can still help in carefully designed lessons.
First, the statement holds true because digital devices compete constantly for students' attention.
Consider a lecture hall where every student has a laptop open to take notes.
Within minutes, many screens show messages, social media or online shopping, and the students leave having copied slides without understanding them.
I have seen the same pattern in my own lectures, where students who type every word often remember the least.

Moreover, the same smartphones and social media that helped activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011 also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so students who rely on them may absorb false claims as facts.
Real learning requires sustained focus and careful judgment, and these tools often [[undermine|undermine]] both.
A student who checks a phone every few minutes may sit through an hour of class yet learn almost nothing.
In such settings, technology does more than fail to help; it actively distracts.
Second, the statement holds true when schools treat technology as a substitute for skilled teaching.

Finland offers a useful contrast: it requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Its approach places trust in well-trained people rather than in devices.
By contrast, imagine a school that spends its budget on tablets while its teachers receive little training; students may watch videos all day yet rarely discuss or question what they see.
Children in such a school may become skilled at using devices but remain weak at reading closely and arguing logically.
These cases suggest that the quality of teaching, not the number of screens, drives learning.
Screens are cheaper to buy than good teachers are to train, which makes this substitution tempting for school boards.
When technology [[supplants|supplant]] teachers instead of supporting them, the statement is clearly true.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true when technology is used with a clear purpose.
When I teach epidemiology, for example, students analyze real outbreak data with statistical software, a task that would be impossible with paper alone.
Likewise, the Human Genome Project made the human DNA sequence freely available, so students today can explore genetic data online.
In such lessons, technology is a tool for answering questions, not a source of entertainment.
Nevertheless, these benefits depend on a teacher who designs the task and guides the analysis.
Without such guidance, the same software becomes a toy and the same database merely a [[plethora|plethora]] of unread files.
This consideration qualifies my position: technology is not harmful in itself, but it distracts more often than it helps when it is used without purpose.
In conclusion, I largely agree that classroom technology all too often distracts from real learning.
Devices fragment attention and can replace skilled teaching, although well-designed lessons show that technology can also serve learning.
The lesson for schools is not to [[eschew|eschew]] technology but to invest first in teachers who know when, and when not, to use it.

essays.task_note: As a statement task, Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (attention, replacing teachers) and Body 3 shows where it does not (purposeful use), which shapes a qualified agreement.

essays.title: The tool is not the problem

paragraphs.text: Every new teaching tool, from the printed book to the calculator, has been accused of making students lazy.
Today the same charge is aimed at video, computers and the Internet, which the statement says all too often distract from real learning.

I mostly disagree with this statement, because these technologies have greatly expanded what students can learn, and the distraction usually comes from poor teaching rather than from the tools themselves.
Technology widens access to knowledge and allows more active learning, although it can distract when schools use it carelessly.
First, the statement does not hold true for the many students to whom technology gives access to knowledge they could never reach before.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, and a student in a remote village can now read it on a phone.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
A biology student in Hanoi can therefore explore the same genetic data as a researcher at a famous university abroad.
None of this was possible for an ordinary student a generation ago.
Far from distracting from learning, such tools make education more [[egalitarian|egalitarian]], because access no longer depends on a school's library or a family's wealth.
For students in rural Vietnam, where school libraries are often small, this access can decide whether a curious child keeps learning.
Second, technology often makes learning more active and therefore deeper.
When I teach epidemiology, students no longer just memorize formulas; they use statistical software to analyze real data on dengue outbreaks, find errors and defend their conclusions.
Students who once found statistics [[arcane|arcane]] begin to see how numbers can guide public health decisions.
Likewise, a short video of a surgical procedure can show medical students what a textbook diagram cannot.
A nursing student who can replay a procedure many times learns at her own pace instead of relying on a single demonstration.
Simulation software lets engineering students test a design, watch it fail, and try again without wasting materials.
In these cases, technology does not compete with real learning; it is the means of it.
Used in this way, technology moves students from passive listening to active problem solving.
What matters is whether the teacher designs a task that requires thinking.
Admittedly, the statement does hold true in some settings, especially when devices are used without guidance.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, and a student scrolling through social media during class is clearly not learning.
Nevertheless, this problem points to a weakness in teaching, not in technology itself.

Finland, for instance, requires its schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a selective profession, which reflects the view that a teacher's judgment matters more than any single tool.
Well-trained teachers can set rules for devices and teach students to check sources, turning the [[pernicious|pernicious]] spread of misinformation into a lesson in judgment.
Banning devices would only hide the problem, since students will meet the same distractions outside school.
Thus, the risk of distraction qualifies my position but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, video, computers and the Internet distract from learning far less often than the statement suggests.
They open access to knowledge and support active learning, and the distraction they sometimes cause reflects how they are used.
Schools should therefore [[bolster|bolster]] teacher training rather than blame the tools, since a skilled teacher can turn almost any technology into a path to real learning.

essays.title: Breadth makes better specialists

paragraphs.text: Many important problems sit at the boundaries between fields rather than inside any single one.
For this reason, some universities require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study.
I support this policy, provided the requirement is modest, because its main consequences, more creative problem solving and better ethical judgment, outweigh its cost in time.
Required breadth helps students connect ideas across fields and prepares them to make sound ethical decisions, although it does take time from specialized training.
First, one important consequence of the policy is that students learn to connect ideas from different fields, which often leads to new solutions.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Their success came after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, which shows how skills from one field can transfer to another.
Similarly, in my own field, epidemiology, the best studies of dengue control draw on biology, statistics, economics and an understanding of how communities behave.
Students who have taken courses outside their major are more likely to recognize such connections.
A history major who has studied statistics, for example, can read evidence more critically than one who has not.
Thus, the policy would [[engender|engender]] the kind of flexible thinking that specialized training alone rarely provides.
Second, the policy would help students in technical fields develop the ethical judgment their work requires.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
The researchers were trained scientists, yet their training did not stop them from causing grave harm, and public outrage later led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
By contrast, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Kelsey's caution shows the kind of careful judgment that a broad education can help to build.
Courses in ethics, history or philosophy cannot guarantee good behavior, but they give future scientists a language for questioning their own work.
Such courses also help students avoid a [[myopic|myopic]] focus on results alone, which makes required breadth especially valuable in fields where mistakes harm people.
Admittedly, a breadth requirement has a real cost: it takes time away from training in the student's own field.
Medical and engineering students already face [[onerous|onerous]] schedules, and a few extra courses in art or literature might delay their graduation or reduce their practical training.
For a future doctor, every extra course competes with time spent learning at the bedside.
Nevertheless, this cost can be controlled through careful design rather than by abandoning the policy.
A university could require only a few courses and let students choose ones related to their goals, such as health economics for a nursing student or statistics for a history major.
With such limits, the policy keeps its main benefits while avoiding its worst consequence.
Students who choose their outside courses are also more likely to take them seriously.
This consideration therefore shapes my position: I support the requirement, but only in a modest and flexible form.
In conclusion, universities are right to require students to take a variety of courses outside their major.
Such courses help students connect ideas and judge the ethics of their work, and their cost in time can be limited by thoughtful design.
A graduate who understands more than one field is not a weaker specialist but a more [[adroit|adroit]] one.

essays.title: Required breadth wastes students' limited time

paragraphs.text: Time is the scarcest resource in any student's education.
Requiring every university student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field would spend a large share of that time on subjects the student did not choose.

I oppose this policy as a strict requirement, because its likely consequences, weaker training in the major and box-checking rather than real learning, outweigh its benefits, although breadth should remain available to those who want it.
Required breadth would dilute specialized training and encourage half-hearted study, even though exposure to other fields can be valuable.
First, the policy would likely [[attenuate|attenuate]] training in fields that demand intense preparation.
Finland, for instance, requires its schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, a sign that some professions need long, focused preparation before practice.
Medicine is similar: a future doctor must master anatomy, pharmacology and clinical skills, and every semester spent on unrelated courses is a semester not spent on these.
A medical student required to take music and art history may enjoy them, but they will not help her treat a patient with severe dengue.

When training time is limited, a policy that diverts it to subjects not [[germane|germane]] to the student's work risks producing graduates who know a little about many things but not enough about their own field.
In a profession where mistakes can cost lives, such shallow preparation is a serious risk.
Second, a breadth requirement often produces box-checking rather than genuine learning.
Consider an engineering student who must take three humanities courses to graduate.
Instead of choosing what interests him, he picks the easiest courses that fit his schedule, attends lectures with [[apathy|apathy]], and forgets the material soon after the exam.
His transcript shows that he completed the requirement, but his thinking has not changed at all.
Meanwhile, the time he spent on these courses could have gone to an advanced design project in his own field.
Similarly, many students treat required courses as obstacles and approach them in a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] way.
Learning depends on curiosity, and curiosity cannot be required.
A rule that forces students into courses they do not value may therefore teach them only how to satisfy requirements.
Worse, such courses can teach students that learning is a set of hoops rather than a source of insight.
Admittedly, exposure to other fields can lead to creativity, and this is the strongest consequence in the policy's favor.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903, which shows that knowledge from one area can transfer to another.
Similarly, my own field of epidemiology draws on biology, statistics and economics.
Nevertheless, the Wright brothers were not required to study flight; they pursued it out of their own interest, through years of experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their breadth came from curiosity, and no university rule could have produced it.
Their story supports voluntary breadth, not mandatory breadth.

Universities can achieve this benefit by offering attractive electives and joint projects while letting students decide, so this consequence shapes my position toward flexibility rather than requirement.
Students who want breadth can still choose it, and they will likely learn more because they chose it.
In conclusion, universities should encourage breadth but should not require every student to take a variety of courses outside the major.
A strict requirement would weaken specialized training and invite box-checking, while the creative benefits of breadth can be gained through choice.
The best policy is one that trusts students to follow their curiosity, because genuine interest, not a mandate, is what makes learning last.

essays.title: Great ideas start with ordinary things

paragraphs.text: Most people walk past ordinary things every day without a second look.
The statement claims that the best ideas come from people who look at such commonplace things with passionate interest.

I largely agree with this statement, because many great discoveries began with careful attention to everyday events, although some important ideas also come from abstract research that seems far from daily life.
Passionate attention to commonplace things has produced breakthroughs in medicine and in technology, even though some major ideas arise in a different way.
First, the statement holds true in medicine, where several landmark ideas came from close attention to ordinary events.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate.
His interest was not in grand theory but in what had happened to one ordinary culture plate in his laboratory.
Many scientists would have thrown the plate away as a spoiled experiment, but his curiosity about this [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] accident started the path to penicillin.
Similarly, Ignaz Semmelweis focused on something as simple as handwashing, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
In both cases, the key insight lay in something ordinary that others had overlooked.
Many people had seen spoiled plates and unwashed hands before, but few had asked why they mattered.
Passionate interest, not rare materials, turned these [[mundane|mundane]] observations into ideas that saved lives.
Second, the statement also holds true in technology and public health, where ordinary objects have inspired lasting solutions.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers who worked daily with simple machines, and their [[assiduous|assiduous]] experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves led to the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Likewise, in my work on dengue control, I have watched researchers study the ordinary mosquito in great detail.
Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
The method has also been tested in Vietnam, which shows how an insight about a familiar insect can travel across countries.
These examples show that the best ideas often come from people who care deeply about familiar things that others take for granted.
The mosquito, after all, is one of the most commonplace creatures in tropical life, yet passionate study turned it into a tool against disease.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for every great idea, since some arise from abstract research far from everyday life.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, for instance, were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Their work dealt with molecules, not with commonplace objects.
Likewise, the Human Genome Project, an international effort completed in 2003, was organized around a scientific goal rather than an everyday observation.
Nevertheless, even the mRNA case supports half of the statement, because it was passionate interest that sustained Karikó and Weissman's research for so long.
Such research shows that great ideas can also grow from questions that ordinary people never think to ask.
This consideration qualifies my position: passion appears necessary for the best ideas, while commonplace things are a frequent, but not universal, source.
The statement is therefore largely, rather than [[unequivocally|unequivocal]], true.
In conclusion, many of the best ideas do arise from passionate interest in commonplace things.
Discoveries in medicine and technology often began with ordinary observations, although abstract research shows that the source can also be less familiar.
The practical lesson is to pay close attention to the everyday, because [[latent|latent]] insights often hide in plain sight.

essays.title: The best ideas need deep expertise

paragraphs.text: It is tempting to believe that genius begins with a casual look at an ordinary object.
The statement reflects this belief, claiming that the best ideas arise from a passionate interest in commonplace things.

I mostly disagree, because many of the most valuable ideas come from specialized research and organized effort rather than from everyday objects, although ordinary observations sometimes spark important work.
The best ideas often depend on specialized knowledge and large-scale cooperation, even though a few famous discoveries did begin with commonplace things.
First, the statement does not hold true for many great ideas that grew out of specialized and abstract research.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Their work concerned molecules that few people outside the laboratory had ever heard of.
Their success depended on knowledge that took decades to build.
Similarly, Marie Curie, an [[erudite|erudite]] scientist, won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry for research that required specialized training rather than casual curiosity.
These ideas did not come from commonplace things; they came from years of [[esoteric|esoteric]] work that only trained specialists could do.
A passion for commonplace things would not have led anyone to such discoveries.
Expertise, not everyday interest, drove them.
Second, some of the most valuable ideas are not individual insights at all but the product of organized effort.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
The key idea was not a sudden observation but a strategy that required planning across many nations.
Likewise, the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Researchers around the world could then build on that sequence instead of starting from scratch.
Such achievements show that the best ideas often emerge from institutions and teamwork, with many people working toward a shared plan over many years.
No single person's passionate interest in an everyday object could have coordinated vaccine supplies across so many countries or sequenced the human genome.
Admittedly, the statement does hold true in some well-known cases.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, an ordinary accident that eventually led to penicillin.
His curiosity about a spoiled plate is often told as proof that great ideas begin with ordinary things.
Nevertheless, penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
Fleming noticed the mold, but turning that observation into a medicine required the skills of an entire research team.
Fleming's observation was a valuable start, but the idea became important only through specialized work that had little to do with commonplace things.
This case therefore qualifies rather than reverses my position: ordinary observations can [[kindle|kindle]] an idea, but expertise and organization usually turn it into something useful.
In conclusion, the best ideas arise far more often from specialized knowledge and collective effort than from passionate interest in commonplace things.
Basic research and organized campaigns have produced many of the greatest advances, while famous ordinary observations, such as Fleming's, needed expert work to matter.
Rather than [[lionizing|lionize]] the lucky glance, societies should invest in the patient, specialized work that turns observations into real progress.

words.meaning_here: having or showing deep, scholarly knowledge
understood only by a small group of specialists
treating as a celebrity; praising too highly

essays.task_note: As a statement task, Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (mRNA, smallpox) and Body 3 admits where it holds (Fleming's mold), which keeps the disagreement qualified.

essays.title: Public trust requires ethical leaders

paragraphs.text: A government can pass any law it wants, but it cannot force citizens to trust it.
This is why many people believe that, to be an effective leader, a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards.
I largely agree with this claim, because effective leadership depends on public trust and on protecting people from harm, although leaders must sometimes make practical compromises.
High ethical standards build the trust that policies need and guard the public against harm, even though the challenge of political compromise must be taken seriously.
First, ethical standards are essential because public officials can lead effectively only when citizens trust them.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
When the public learned of it, the outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards, and such a betrayal can make people suspicious of health authorities for a long time.
In my work in public health, I have seen that vaccination and dengue campaigns succeed only when communities believe that officials are honest with them.
An official who lies or abuses power may gain in the short term, but he loses the cooperation that every public program requires.
Thus, high ethical standards are not a luxury; they are a condition of effective leadership.
Second, officials with strong ethical standards protect the public from harms that others might accept.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve the drug, and the United States then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
A leader willing to cut corners might have approved the drug to please its makers or to save time.

Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, which raised helmet use to over 90% within months, reflected a commitment to protecting lives even when the rule was inconvenient for many riders.
Such decisions require officials to accept criticism today for the sake of lives saved tomorrow.
In both cases, the officials' [[probity|probity]] and sense of duty produced concrete benefits for the public.
Effective leadership, then, is measured not only by what officials achieve but also by the harms they [[forestall|forestall]].

Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that politics often requires compromise, and leaders who insist on moral purity may become [[sanctimonious|sanctimonious]] and achieve little.
Abraham Lincoln, for example, appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Such [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] decisions suggest that effectiveness depends on judgment, not on purity alone.
Leaders who refuse every deal with opponents may keep their principles but fail to pass any law.
Nevertheless, Lincoln's decision was itself principled: he placed the nation's needs above his personal pride.
In fact, choosing able critics over loyal followers required the humility that high ethical standards demand.
Compromise of this kind differs from corruption or dishonesty: Lincoln compromised on methods, not on his basic honesty or his duty to the country.
This challenge therefore qualifies my position: the highest standards do not mean refusing every compromise, but they do mean never betraying the public's trust.
In conclusion, I largely agree that effective public officials must hold themselves to the highest ethical and moral standards.
Such standards build public trust and protect citizens from harm, and the need for compromise does not justify abandoning them.
Leaders who remember that their power is borrowed from the public are the ones most likely to use it well.

essays.title: Effective leaders need integrity, not perfection

paragraphs.text: Voters often say they want saints in public office, yet they also want their problems solved.
The claim insists that, to be an effective leader, a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards.
I mostly disagree, because effective leadership requires practical judgment and compromise more than moral perfection, although basic honesty remains essential.
Effective officials often succeed through pragmatism and flexibility, and strict moral purity can block progress, even though serious ethical failures destroy public trust.
First, many effective leaders have succeeded by making practical choices rather than by keeping their hands perfectly clean.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
This was a calculated political move rather than an act of moral virtue, yet it gave his government talent it would otherwise have lacked.

Similarly, Vietnam's leaders launched the Doi Moi reforms in 1986, replacing central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Achieving this required leaders to abandon policies they had once defended as morally right.
These leaders were effective because they were [[pragmatic|pragmatic]], willing to set aside loyalty or ideology to achieve results.
Neither choice would satisfy a strict moralist, but both served the public well.
Rigid devotion to principle would likely have prevented both successes.
Second, insisting on the highest moral standards can actually make officials less effective.
Consider a health minister who refuses to work with any company that has ever broken a rule.
If the only firms able to produce a needed vaccine fall into that category, her moral purity could leave millions of children unprotected.
Likewise, an [[intransigent|intransigent]] official who never compromises with opponents may watch every reform fail in the legislature.
In public health, officials often must work with imperfect partners to reach people quickly during an outbreak.
In such cases, rigid standards [[stymie|stymie]] the very goals that ethics is meant to serve.
Effective leadership often means choosing the lesser of two imperfect options, not waiting for a perfect one.
Moral perfection is a luxury that officials facing urgent problems rarely have.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that serious ethical failures can destroy the public trust that leaders need.

In the Tuskegee syphilis study, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent from 1932 to 1972, and the public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Such betrayals can make communities suspicious of public institutions for many years.
Nevertheless, this example shows the need for basic integrity, not for the highest moral standards.
Avoiding [[unconscionable|unconscionable]] acts such as cruelty and deception is a minimum that every official must meet, but it is very different from moral perfection.
Voters can forgive a compromise far more easily than a lie.
This challenge therefore refines my position: leaders must never cross certain ethical lines, yet within those lines they need room for compromise.
In conclusion, effective public officials need honesty and decency, but they do not need to maintain the highest ethical and moral standards in every decision.
Practical judgment has guided many successful leaders, strict purity can block progress, and only serious ethical failures truly undermine leadership.
Citizens should therefore judge officials by both their integrity and their results, rather than demanding a perfection that no effective leader has ever achieved.

essays.title: Imagination outweighs experience in progress

paragraphs.text: Every invention we now take for granted was once only an idea in someone's mind.

The claim states that imagination is a more valuable asset than experience, and the reason given is that people without experience can imagine freely, without the constraints of established habits and attitudes.
I largely agree with the claim and partly agree with its reason, because imagination drives progress and established habits often limit it, although experience remains necessary to test new ideas.
I will first evaluate the claim, then examine the reason, and finally consider the strongest case for experience.
First, the claim is largely correct, because imagination produces the new ideas that experience alone cannot.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001, relied on unpaid volunteers rather than professional editors, a plan that experienced publishers might easily have [[dismissed|dismiss]].
Yet it grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, imagined powered flight and achieved it in 1903.
Their lack of formal training did not stop them; it may even have freed them from assumptions that experts held.
Imagination set their goal, and experience came later, through practice.
In both cases, the decisive asset was the ability to picture something that did not yet exist.
Without imagination, the world would still rely on encyclopedias written by a few experts.
Experience can improve an idea, but it rarely creates a [[novel|novel]] one, which is why imagination is the more valuable of the two.
Second, the reason is partly true, since established habits and attitudes do often block new ideas.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
The company had decades of experience, yet that experience made it [[complacent|complacent]].
Likewise, most of Ignaz Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his idea of handwashing, which clashed with their established practice.
Their years of practice made them confident, and that confidence kept them from seeing what was happening on his ward.
However, the reason goes too far in suggesting that only inexperienced people can imagine freely.
Sasson himself was a Kodak insider, so the real obstacle was not experience itself but an organization's attachment to its old success.
Thus, the reason captures a real danger, but it misplaces the cause.
Admittedly, the strongest point on the other side is that experience prevents imaginative ideas from causing harm.
Around 1960, thalidomide was given to pregnant women in Europe and caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA, applying careful professional judgment, refused to approve it.
Her experience allowed her to see risks that an eager innovator might ignore.
Nevertheless, experience in this case served as a filter for ideas, not as their source.
Kelsey did not create a new drug; she judged whether someone else's product was safe.
Society needs both, but imagination generates the options that experience then evaluates.
Without imagination, experience would have nothing new to [[winnow|winnow]]; therefore, the claim remains largely true, even if its reason must be [[qualified|qualify]].
In conclusion, imagination is generally a more valuable asset than experience, although the reason offered for the claim is only partly convincing.
Imagination creates new possibilities, established habits can indeed limit them, and experience is best seen as a check on imagination rather than a rival to it.
The most effective people and organizations, therefore, value fresh ideas while using experience to decide which ones deserve to survive.

essays.title: Experience makes imagination useful

paragraphs.text: A bold idea can change the world, but only if someone knows how to make it work.
The claim holds that imagination is a more valuable asset than experience, because inexperienced people are free to imagine without the constraints of established habits and attitudes.

I disagree with both the claim and its reason, since experience usually turns imagination into results and inexperience does not by itself free the mind, although established habits can sometimes block new ideas.
This essay first evaluates the claim, then questions the reason, and finally addresses the strongest point in their favor.
First, the claim is mistaken, because imagination without experience rarely produces anything of value.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, but penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
The imaginative leap mattered, yet experienced scientists were needed to turn it into medicine.

Similarly, in my clinical work, I have seen that a young doctor may imagine many possible diagnoses for a feverish patient, but only experience reveals which warning signs of severe dengue require urgent action.
Without that experience, a creative but untrained doctor could miss a dangerous case.
These examples show that experience is not merely useful; it is what makes imagination practical and safe.
An inexperienced dreamer could have seen the same mold and never known what to do with it.
In most fields, then, experience is the more valuable asset.
Second, the reason behind the claim is weak, because inexperience does not automatically free people to imagine.

The idea of releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, came from researchers who knew mosquito biology well, and it cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had spent decades on earlier basic research on mRNA.
Their long familiarity with the molecule allowed them to imagine uses that newcomers could not have foreseen.
The reason assumes that imagination and experience are [[antithetical|antithetical]], but these cases suggest the opposite.
A person with no experience may imagine freely, but often imagines things that cannot work or have already been tried.
Experience often supplies the material from which imagination builds, so the reason fails to support the claim.
Admittedly, the strongest point in favor of the claim and its reason is that established habits sometimes do block new ideas.
Most of Ignaz Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his idea that doctors should wash their hands, and germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.
Similarly, Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
Nevertheless, the problem in these cases was not experience itself but rigid [[dogma|dogma]] and [[complacent|complacent]] attitudes.
Semmelweis was himself a trained physician, and his idea came from careful observation on his own ward.
The cure for such habits is open-mindedness, which experienced people can possess as fully as beginners.
Therefore, this point [[qualifies|qualify]] my position, since habits can be harmful, but it does not show that inexperience is an advantage.
In conclusion, experience is generally a more valuable asset than imagination, and the reason offered for the opposite claim does not hold up.
Experience turns ideas into results, it often fuels rather than limits imagination, and the real enemy of new ideas is rigid habit, not knowledge.
The ideal, therefore, is not an inexperienced dreamer but an experienced person who remains willing to imagine.
