essays.title: Imagination separates great work from good

paragraphs.text: Knowledge tells us what is; imagination asks what could be.
The statement claims that in most professions and academic fields, imagination is more important than knowledge.

I largely agree, because imagination is what allows professionals to solve new problems and to see new uses for what they know, although some fields demand a firm base of knowledge before imagination can be trusted.
Imagination drives breakthroughs in research and success in business, while the need for knowledge in high-risk professions limits how far the statement holds.
First, the statement holds true in scientific research, where knowledge alone rarely produces breakthroughs.
Dengue researchers had long known how mosquitoes spread the virus, but someone had to imagine fighting mosquitoes with other mosquitoes.

Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Knowledge of mosquito biology was necessary, but imagination turned that knowledge into a solution.
Similarly, Galileo embraced the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, a view so contrary to accepted belief that the Church forced him to [[recant|recant]] his support for it in 1633.
Many scholars of his time knew the accepted view thoroughly, but that knowledge kept them from imagining an alternative.
In both cases, existing knowledge described the world, but imagination changed how people understood it.
This is why imagination, more than the accumulation of facts, defines [[landmark|landmark]] research.
Second, the statement holds true in business and technology, where success depends on imagining new uses for existing knowledge.
GPS was built by the US military, but once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
The engineers who built it had the knowledge, but others had the imagination to see what ordinary people could do with it.

By contrast, Kodak had the knowledge to lead digital photography, since its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet it was slow to embrace the new technology and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Kodak's experts knew a great deal about photography, yet that knowledge did not save the company.
Kodak shows that knowledge without imagination can leave even a leading company [[obsolete|obsolete]].
Thus, in fields that change quickly, imagination is the more important asset.
In business, the winners are often those who imagine a new use, not those who know the most.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in professions where errors can cause serious harm, such as medicine, engineering and teaching.
Finland, for example, requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a selective profession, which reflects how much it values deep knowledge in those who teach.
Similarly, an engineer who imagines a daring bridge without understanding materials could endanger many lives.
Nevertheless, even in these fields, knowledge is the foundation while imagination determines who advances the field.
A physician must know the standard treatments for an infection, but the doctors who improve care are those who imagine better ways to deliver it.
This consideration qualifies my position: knowledge is a [[cardinal|cardinal]] requirement in high-risk professions.
In these professions, imagination must work within limits that knowledge sets.
Yet imagination is what distinguishes excellent work from merely competent work.
In conclusion, imagination is more important than knowledge in most professions and academic fields, although not in all of them.
It drives breakthroughs in research and success in business, while high-risk professions show that knowledge must come first.
The most valuable professionals, therefore, are those who master their field's knowledge and then dare to imagine beyond it.

essays.title: Knowledge matters more in most fields

paragraphs.text: A surgeon with a vivid imagination but little training is not someone most patients would choose.
Yet the statement claims that in most professions and academic fields, imagination is more important than knowledge.

I mostly disagree, because the daily work of most professions depends on accurate knowledge, and imagination without knowledge often produces error, although imagination does matter at moments of breakthrough.
Knowledge guides routine professional decisions and keeps imaginative ideas honest, even though some famous advances began with imaginative leaps.
First, the statement does not hold true for the daily work of most professions, which relies on knowledge more than on imagination.
As a physician, I know that treating a patient with dengue depends on recognizing specific warning signs and managing fluids correctly, not on inventing new approaches at the bedside.
Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads partly because antibiotics are overused and sold over the counter, so prescribing well requires knowing when not to use them.
Likewise, an engineer designing a bridge must apply known principles of load and material strength rather than imagine untested ones.
Teachers, accountants and pilots, too, spend most of their working hours applying what they know.
In these fields, most of the value professionals create comes from applying knowledge reliably.
A doctor who improvises without knowledge does not innovate; she endangers her patients.
Imagination is [[peripheral|peripheral]] to most of this work, while knowledge is central.
Moreover, imagination without solid knowledge often leads to error, which shows that knowledge is the more important of the two.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, revealing how often single findings mislead.
Interesting ideas alone, without rigorous testing, did not make those findings reliable.
Imaginative hypotheses are easy to produce; knowing whether they are true is far harder.
Similarly, imagine a hospital that adopts an exciting new treatment because it seems logical, before any trial has tested it.
If the treatment proves harmful, patients pay the price for imagination unchecked by knowledge.
These cases show that knowledge, not imagination, protects the public from [[specious|specious]] ideas, because only [[empirical|empirical]] testing separates good ideas from bad ones.
Admittedly, the statement does hold true at certain moments of breakthrough, when imagination opens doors that knowledge alone could not.
Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria to block dengue transmission was an imaginative idea, and it cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
Nevertheless, this idea rested on detailed knowledge about mosquitoes, bacteria and the dengue virus.
Researchers needed to understand how Wolbachia affects the virus before anyone could test the idea in a city.
Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Their decades of quiet work supplied the knowledge that made a rapid, imaginative response possible.
Breakthroughs, then, do not prove that imagination outranks knowledge; they show that imagination is productive only when it grows from deep knowledge.
Imagination may light the spark, but knowledge supplies the fuel.
This consideration qualifies my position without reversing it.
In conclusion, knowledge is more important than imagination in most professions and academic fields.
It guides the routine decisions that make up most professional work, it protects people from attractive but false ideas, and it even underlies the breakthroughs that seem to prove the opposite.
Students and professionals should therefore build deep knowledge first, since imagination is most [[efficacious|efficacious]] when it has something solid to build on.

essays.title: Public trust requires ethical public conduct

paragraphs.text: Few things erode a community's trust faster than discovering that the people who make its rules quietly break them.
This is why many people believe that a public official, more than any private citizen, must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards to be an effective leader.
I largely agree that strong ethics are essential to effective public leadership, as long as "the highest standards" means honesty and fairness in public duties rather than a flawless private life.
Ethical conduct earns the trust that officials need, it protects citizens from harmful decisions, and although some flawed leaders have succeeded, their success rarely lasts without integrity.
First, high ethical standards make a public official effective because citizens follow rules more willingly when they trust the people who make them.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets is a useful case. Within months, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90%, and head injuries and deaths fell.
Such rapid compliance was possible partly because people could see the rule as a fair measure for their own safety rather than a scheme to enrich officials.
Similarly, in my work on dengue control, I have seen households open their homes to inspection teams far more readily when local health officials are known for their [[probity|probity]].
This shows that integrity is not a decorative virtue; it is a practical tool that turns a leader's orders into public action.
Without that trust, even well-designed laws are ignored or quietly resisted.
Second, high ethical standards matter because officials who cut moral corners can seriously harm the very people they serve.

The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent. The officials who [[condoned|condone]] it may have believed they were advancing science, but the public outrage it caused led the US to require ethics review boards for research on people.

In contrast, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and her firm standards protected American families.
These cases suggest that when public power is involved, an ethical lapse is not a private matter but a public danger, which is exactly why the statement holds true in this area.
An honest official, by contrast, earns the authority to make hard decisions, because citizens believe those decisions serve them.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every case, since some officials with [[pronounced|pronounced]] moral flaws have still accomplished a great deal.

History offers leaders who made questionable deals yet built roads, won wars or reformed economies, and a purely [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] voter might conclude that results, not virtue, define effective leadership.
Nevertheless, such achievements usually come at a cost that appears later, when hidden corruption is exposed and public trust collapses.
A single scandal can [[undermine|undermine]] years of good policy, because citizens begin to doubt every decision the official has made.

At the same time, demanding a saintly private life would shrink the pool of capable candidates, which is why I limit the standard to honesty and fairness in public duties; in this qualified form, the requirement remains both realistic and essential.
In conclusion, I largely agree that effective public leaders must hold themselves to high ethical standards, provided those standards focus on their public conduct.
Integrity earns the trust that makes policies work, prevents officials from harming the people they serve, and protects achievements that scandal would otherwise destroy.
Citizens should therefore judge leaders not by perfect personal records but by whether they can be trusted with public power.

words.meaning_here: accepted or allowed something morally wrong
focused on practical results rather than principles

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (trust, preventing harm), and Body 3 names where it does not (flawed but successful leaders) and explains how that narrows the position to public conduct.

essays.title: Competence matters more than moral perfection

paragraphs.text: Voters often say they want saints in office, yet they rarely elect them.
This gap raises the question of whether a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards in order to lead effectively.
I mostly disagree with this statement: basic honesty in public duties is necessary, but the highest moral standards are neither required for effective leadership nor a guarantee of it.
Effectiveness depends chiefly on competence and judgment, morally rigid leaders can fail in a world that requires compromise, and only a basic ethical floor is truly essential.
First, the statement overstates the role of morality because effective leadership depends mainly on competence and sound judgment.

Abraham Lincoln is widely admired, but his effectiveness came from political skill as much as from virtue. He appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, and that [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] decision strengthened his government.

Similarly, Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 succeeded because leaders recognized that central planning was failing and replaced it with market incentives, turning a country that had faced food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This shows that the outcomes citizens care about most, such as stability and prosperity, flow from skill and judgment, which a person of ordinary morals can possess.
In other words, the statement confuses being good with being good at governing, two qualities that often appear together but are not the same.
Second, an official who insists on the highest moral standards in every decision may actually accomplish less, because public life requires compromise.

Consider a health minister who refuses to negotiate with a tobacco-friendly faction in parliament because she finds its position morally offensive. Her stance is admirable, but if she cannot secure those votes, a tax that would reduce smoking never passes, and many preventable deaths follow.
Likewise, many reform laws in democracies pass only after leaders trade support on unrelated issues, a practice that a [[doctrinaire|doctrinaire]] moralist might [[deride|deride]] as unprincipled.
In such settings, moral purity can become an obstacle to helping people, so the highest standards may reduce rather than increase a leader's effectiveness.
A leader who refuses every imperfect bargain may keep a clean conscience, but the public pays for that purity.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in one important respect: some ethical lapses are so [[egregious|egregious]] that they destroy public trust.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, caused public outrage and led the US to require ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, this case shows the need for a firm ethical floor, not for the highest possible standards.
Officials must not lie to the public, steal public funds or harm citizens, but they need not be models of personal virtue in every respect.

Separating this basic floor from an idealized ceiling lets us demand integrity where it matters without excluding capable leaders for mere [[peccadilloes|peccadillo]], and this distinction is what shapes my position.
Honesty, then, is required, but moral perfection is not.
In conclusion, effective public leadership requires basic honesty, but not the highest ethical and moral standards that the statement demands.
Competence and judgment drive results, rigid moralism can block useful compromise, and only serious violations of public trust truly disqualify a leader.
Voters would be wiser to ask whether an official is capable and honest in public duties than whether he or she is morally flawless.

words.meaning_here: rigidly applying a theory without considering practical effects

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (competence and compromise matter more), and Body 3 names where it holds (egregious lapses) and explains how that leads to a basic ethical floor rather than the highest standards.

essays.title: Specialized work needs expert critics

paragraphs.text: Every day, people offer confident opinions on work they barely understand, from films to vaccines.
This habit raises the question of whether critical judgment of work in a field has any real value unless it comes from an expert in that field.

I largely agree that, in technical and specialized fields, critical judgment is valuable mainly when it comes from experts, although non-experts can still offer useful feedback on how a work affects them.
Experts can detect hidden flaws that others miss, their judgment carries the credibility needed to stop harmful work, and ordinary users contribute only within a narrower range.
First, expert judgment is valuable because only trained critics can detect the hidden flaws in complex work.

In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them. Many [[credulous|credulous]] readers had accepted those findings without question, but [[discerning|discerning]] experts who understood sampling and statistics were able to test them and reveal how often single findings mislead.
Similarly, when I review a manuscript on antibiotic resistance, I look for flaws such as a biased study design or poorly handled missing data, which a [[layperson|layperson]] would never notice.
This shows that in specialized fields the most important errors are often invisible to non-experts, so their criticism, however sincere, has limited value.
A general reader may notice that a conclusion sounds surprising, but only a specialist can explain why it is wrong and how to fix it.
Second, expert criticism matters because it carries the [[credibility|credibility]] needed to stop harmful work.

Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe. Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and her refusal was taken seriously precisely because she was a trained reviewer.
The US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Likewise, in a hospital, a pharmacist who questions a doctor's prescription is heard because pharmacists are trained to spot dangerous drug interactions.
In both cases, the critic's expertise is what turns an opinion into a judgment that institutions are willing to act on, which supports the statement.
Without such authority, a warning from a non-expert is easy to dismiss, even when it happens to be correct.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for every kind of work, since non-experts sometimes judge certain aspects better than specialists do.
Patients, for example, cannot evaluate the pharmacology of a treatment, yet they are the best judges of whether a clinic's instructions are clear and its waiting times reasonable.
Nevertheless, this kind of feedback concerns the user's experience of a work, not the quality of its technical substance.
A patient can rightly complain that a drug causes nausea, but only a [[circumspect|circumspect]] clinician can decide whether that side effect is an acceptable price for a cure.
Thus, non-expert criticism qualifies rather than overturns my position: it has real value, but within a narrower range than expert judgment.
In short, users can tell us whether a work serves them, while experts tell us whether it is sound.
In conclusion, I largely agree that criticism in specialized fields gains most of its value from expertise.
Experts can uncover hidden flaws and command the credibility to change practice, while non-experts contribute mainly by reporting how a work affects its users.
The wisest approach, therefore, is to let experts judge substance while still listening carefully to the people the work is meant to serve.

words.meaning_here: too ready to believe things without evidence
a person without specialized training in a field
the quality of being trusted and believed
careful to consider all risks before acting

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (hidden flaws, credibility), and Body 3 shows where it does not (patients judging their own experience) and explains how that limits the agreement to technical substance.

essays.title: Non-experts often judge work well

paragraphs.text: History is full of valuable work that experts dismissed and ordinary people eventually embraced.
This pattern challenges the statement that critical judgment of work in any field has little value unless it comes from an expert in that field.
I mostly disagree: expertise often improves criticism, but non-expert judgment can be highly valuable, especially when experts share the same blind spots or when a work is meant for the public.
Experts can be wrong as a group, the users of a work often judge it best, and although technical fields do require expert review, that review is not the only judgment that counts.
First, expert judgment deserves less automatic [[deference|deference]] than the statement implies, because experts often share the same blind spots.

In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply. Yet most of his colleagues rejected the idea, and germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.
Similarly, in 1633 Galileo was forced by the Church, then the [[arbiter|arbiter]] of learned opinion, to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
The Church's authorities were confident, yet they were wrong.

These cases show that expert consensus can [[ossify|ossify]] into [[dogma|dogma]]; the critics who proved right stood outside that consensus, so judgment from beyond the established circle can be a necessary correction rather than worthless noise.
An outsider who asks a simple question, such as why a ward with handwashing has fewer deaths, may see what trained eyes refuse to see.
Second, non-experts are often the best judges of work that is created for them.

Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history. The judgment of his own era's market proved wrong, while the response of later viewers, most of whom were not specialists, proved far more accurate.
Likewise, in my clinical work, patients' complaints about confusing discharge instructions have improved our hospital's care more than several expert audits.
In such cases, the user's response is not a weak substitute for expert opinion; it is the very measure of whether the work succeeds.
A painting exists to move its viewers, and a discharge note exists to be understood by patients, so their reactions are central evidence of quality.
Admittedly, in highly technical fields, the statement comes close to the truth.
A [[layperson|layperson]] cannot meaningfully evaluate the design of a vaccine trial or the safety of a bridge, and confident but uninformed criticism can mislead the public.
Nevertheless, even in these fields, non-expert judgment keeps its value when it addresses consequences rather than technical details.
Residents who live near a new bridge can report cracks, and patients in a trial can report side effects that researchers did not anticipate.
Therefore, expertise determines which questions a critic can answer well, but it does not decide whether a critic's judgment has value at all.
In medicine, patients' reports of unexpected symptoms are a valued source of safety information, which is why careful health systems collect them.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that criticism has little value unless it comes from an expert.
Experts can collectively err, ordinary users are often the best judges of work made for them, and even technical fields benefit from observations by non-specialists.
A healthy field, then, values expert review highly but never treats it as the only voice worth hearing, because good ideas and serious flaws can be spotted from anywhere.

words.meaning_here: respectful acceptance of someone else's judgment
a person or body with authority to settle questions
become rigid and unable to change
beliefs accepted as true without question

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (experts' shared blind spots, users as judges), and Body 3 shows where it nearly holds (technical fields) and explains how that refines the position to what non-experts can judge.

essays.title: Science has mainly deepened our understanding

paragraphs.text: A century ago, a child with a bacterial infection could die within days, and no one could fully explain why some patients survived.
Today we understand such diseases far better, which raises the question of whether science has mainly clarified the world or mainly revealed how complex it is.
I side with the first view: although science has exposed new layers of complexity, its main effect has been to give us a much better understanding of the world around us.

Discoveries have explained phenomena that once seemed mysterious, this understanding lets us predict and control nature, and even the complexity stressed by the second view is itself a form of deeper understanding.
First, I favor the first view because scientific discoveries have turned many [[enigmas|enigma]] into explained phenomena.

In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet no one at the time could explain why. Germ theory later solved the mystery by showing that invisible microbes travel from patient to patient.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, giving science a map of the instructions that build the human body.
These examples show that science does not merely add puzzles; it [[elucidates|elucidate]] what once seemed baffling, which is exactly what the first view claims.
Before these discoveries, people relied on guesses about bad air or fate; afterward, they had explanations they could test.
Second, the first view is closer to the truth because our understanding is proven by our growing ability to predict and control the world.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, which was possible only because decades of earlier research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had explained how mRNA could be used in the body.
In my own field, a clearer understanding of dengue transmission now helps health officials anticipate outbreaks and plan mosquito control.
Likewise, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign; no one could defeat a disease so completely without understanding how it spreads.
If science had revealed only bewildering complexity, such [[efficacious|efficacious]] interventions would be impossible, so their success is strong evidence of real understanding.
Engineers cannot build a bridge from a mystery, and doctors cannot design a vaccine from confusion.
Admittedly, the second view captures something important: each discovery tends to raise new questions, and some systems are more complex than scientists once assumed.
The genome, for instance, did not explain disease as simply as many people hoped, because most conditions arise from the [[interplay|interplay]] of many genes and the environment.
Nevertheless, recognizing this complexity is itself a gain in understanding, not a loss of it.
A doctor who knows that a disease has many interacting causes understands it better than one who wrongly believes it has a single cause.
Similarly, learning that many diseases have several causes has led to better prevention programs, not to despair.
Thus, the complexity highlighted by the second view does not contradict the first view; it shows that our understanding has become more accurate and more attentive to [[nuance|nuance]].
In conclusion, while science has certainly shown that the world is more complex than we once believed, its greater achievement has been to deepen our understanding of it.
Discoveries have explained old mysteries, enabled us to predict and control nature, and even turned complexity into knowledge.
The second view describes the road that science travels, but the first view better describes where that road has taken us.

words.meaning_here: mysterious things that are difficult to understand
successful in producing the intended result
the way two or more things affect each other

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 fairly grants what the second view gets right (new complexity) before explaining why the first view is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Science keeps revealing deeper complexity

paragraphs.text: Every answer in science seems to arrive with a new set of questions attached.

This experience lies behind a debate between those who believe that scientific discoveries have given us a much better understanding of the world and those who believe science has revealed a world far more complex than we realized.
Although the first view is partly right, my own position aligns more closely with the second: the deeper science looks, the more complexity it uncovers.

Triumphant discoveries have revealed unexpected complications, apparently solid findings often prove fragile, and while science has undeniably improved our understanding, that understanding mostly shows us how much remains unknown.
First, I side with the second view because even triumphant discoveries have exposed complications that no one anticipated.

When Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, penicillin seemed to promise victory over infection. Yet in his 1945 Nobel lecture, Fleming himself warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria, and today overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
In my own work on antimicrobial resistance, each new study reveals another route by which resistant bacteria [[proliferate|proliferate]] across hospitals, farms and communities.
Antibiotics, in other words, did not simplify our picture of bacteria; they revealed an [[inexorable|inexorable]] evolutionary contest more complex than anyone imagined.
Each solution, in short, became the starting point for a harder problem.
Second, the second view is more convincing because many findings that seem to explain the world later prove fragile.

In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them. Explanations of human behavior that had appeared settled turned out to be far less certain.

Similarly, releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, but whether that result holds in other cities, including those in Vietnam where the method has been tested, still requires careful study.
Such cases show that human behavior and ecosystems involve so many interacting factors that our explanations often remain [[tenuous|tenuous]].
If even well-designed studies cannot settle such questions, the world they describe must be far more intricate than early scientists believed.
Admittedly, the first view rightly points out that science has given us real and useful understanding.
We now know that a virus causes dengue and that mosquitoes transmit it, knowledge that guides every control program I have worked on.
Nevertheless, this understanding works best as a starting point that reveals how much we still do not know.
Knowing how dengue spreads has not explained why outbreaks rise and fall from year to year, a pattern shaped by climate, immunity and urban growth that still [[confounds|confound]] researchers.
Therefore, the gains stressed by the first view are real, but they are better described as clearer maps of a vast and complicated territory than as a complete understanding of it.
This is why the second view, rather than the first, better captures what science has taught us.
In conclusion, while scientific discoveries have certainly improved our knowledge, their most [[profound|profound]] lesson is that the world is more complex than we ever realized.
Triumphs such as penicillin have created new problems, influential findings have proven fragile, and even our best knowledge points toward further unknowns.
Recognizing this complexity is not a reason for despair but a reason for humility in how we use what science tells us.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the second view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 grants what the first view gets right (real understanding) before explaining why the second view is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Valuable criticism rests on expert knowledge

paragraphs.text: In the age of social media, everyone has become a critic.
Because judgments now flood in from every direction, it is worth asking whether criticism of work in a field has little value unless it comes from an expert in that field.
I largely agree with this claim for fields that require specialized knowledge, although I recognize that collective non-expert judgment can sometimes add value.

Experts know the standards by which work should be judged, uninformed criticism can cause real harm, and the strongest challenge to my view, the success of volunteer projects, ultimately depends on expert standards.
First, expert criticism is valuable because only experts know the standards by which work in a field should be judged.

Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Only specialists in trial design could judge the [[credibility|credibility]] of that result by checking how the trial was randomized and how cases were counted.
They could also ask whether the trial lasted long enough to show a lasting effect.
Similarly, when I review epidemiological papers, I can tell whether a reported association has been [[confounded|confound]] by age or income, a judgment that requires years of training.
This shows that the value of criticism depends on whether the critic understands what makes work in that field good or bad.
A non-expert might praise the trial because the number is impressive, but praise without understanding adds nothing to our knowledge.
Second, the claim is persuasive because uninformed criticism can do real harm.

Smartphones and social media helped activists organize during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow. When non-experts loudly [[disparage|disparage]] a safe vaccine, parents may refuse protection for their children, and outbreaks can follow.
Likewise, patients who believe that antibiotics cure every cold may judge a doctor harshly for refusing to prescribe them, even though overuse helps resistant bacteria spread.
A pharmacist who gives in to similar demands from customers protects her sales but harms public health.
In such cases, non-expert criticism is not merely of little value; it actively [[impairs|impair]] good decisions.
The louder such criticism becomes, the harder it is for experts to protect the public from avoidable harm.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that groups of non-experts sometimes produce excellent work and criticism.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, and its volunteers constantly correct one another's errors.
Similarly, online patient forums sometimes notice the side effects of a new drug before official reports describe them.
Nevertheless, Wikipedia's quality depends on rules borrowed from expert practice, such as citing reliable published sources, and forum reports become useful only after experts investigate them.
A forum post claiming that a drug causes a rare illness may be correct or may be coincidence, and only a trained investigator can tell the difference.
Thus, the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my view rather than refuting it: non-experts add value when their judgment is anchored to standards that experts have established.
Volunteer criticism, in other words, works best as a supplement to expert judgment, not as a replacement for it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that criticism in a field has limited value unless it reflects expert knowledge.
Experts understand the standards that define good work, uninformed criticism can cause harm, and even successful volunteer efforts rely on expert sources.
The goal, then, is not to silence non-experts but to ensure that their judgments are grounded in the knowledge experts provide, so that public debate improves work rather than distorts it.

words.meaning_here: the quality of being believable and trustworthy
distorted by a third factor linked to both variables
speak of something as having little worth

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (Wikipedia and patient forums show non-experts can judge well) fairly and then answers it by showing that such judgment depends on expert standards.

essays.title: Good criticism depends on reasoning, not credentials

paragraphs.text: The most useful criticism often comes from people who see a problem from outside it.
This possibility challenges the claim that critical judgment of work in any field has little value unless it comes from an expert in that field.
I mostly disagree with this claim: expertise strengthens criticism in technical matters, but non-experts frequently offer judgments that are just as valuable, and sometimes more so.

Experts can be blinded by their investment in existing practice, the users of a work are often its most relevant judges, and although uninformed criticism can be dangerous, that danger does not justify dismissing non-expert judgment.
First, non-expert judgment is valuable because experts are sometimes too invested in existing methods to judge new work fairly.

Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012. The company's specialists knew more about photography than anyone, yet ordinary consumers judged the value of the new technology more accurately.

Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments, showing that sound judgment about which designs work can come from patient testing rather than from credentials.
These cases show that expertise can bring a vested interest or a [[myopic|myopic]] view, which an outsider's judgment can correct.
Insiders often measure new ideas against old standards, while outsiders judge them by whether they actually work.
Second, the claim overlooks the fact that the people who use a work are often its most relevant critics.

In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, our health leaflets were reviewed by epidemiologists, but it was mothers in community meetings who told us that the leaflets were too technical to follow. Their criticism, not the experts', led us to [[revamp|revamp]] the materials.
The revised leaflets, with simpler words and pictures, were far easier for families to use.
Likewise, Wikipedia, written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history partly because readers without credentials could flag and fix errors.
In such cases, the value of criticism comes from the critic's experience of the work, not from a professional title.
No expert review would have caught the problem with our leaflets, because the experts already understood the technical terms.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that uninformed criticism can be dangerous, especially in medicine.

Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, and confident non-experts who [[impugn|impugn]] vaccine safety can persuade parents to refuse protection for their children.
Nevertheless, the problem in such cases is not that the critics lack credentials but that they ignore evidence.
A non-expert who reads trial data carefully and asks a sharp question about side effects adds value, while an expert who [[equivocates|equivocate]] to protect a sponsor does not.
Therefore, the true test of criticism is the quality of its reasoning and evidence, a standard that experts often meet but do not own.
Credentials can help us guess who is likely to reason well, but they cannot replace the reasoning itself.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that criticism has little value unless it comes from an expert.
Experts can be blinded by their own interests, users often judge work most relevantly, and the danger of misinformation calls for better reasoning rather than for silencing non-experts.
Any field that becomes [[insular|insular]], listening only to its own experts, risks missing the very flaws that outsiders see most clearly.

words.meaning_here: speaks vaguely to avoid committing to the truth

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (dangerous misinformation from non-experts) fairly and then answers it by shifting the test of criticism from credentials to evidence.

essays.title: Fixed terms keep organizations fresh and accountable

paragraphs.text: Power, like a medicine, can do great good in the right dose and serious harm when taken for too long.
This concern explains the claim that, in any profession, those in power should step down after five years.
I largely agree that leaders should step down after a fixed period such as five years, as long as the rule allows planned transitions in fields where continuity is essential.

Regular turnover brings fresh ideas into organizations, it prevents the abuse that comes with unchecked power, and although losing experienced leaders is the strongest objection, that cost can be managed.
First, regular turnover benefits organizations because new leaders bring fresh ideas that long-serving leaders tend to resist.

Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012. Leaders who had built their careers on film found it hard to [[jettison|jettison]] the model that had made them successful.
Similarly, in one university department I know, a newly appointed head finally updated an outdated curriculum, because she was not attached to the courses her predecessor had designed.
This shows that a five-year limit can protect organizations from leaders who grow [[complacent|complacent]] with the [[status quo|status quo]].
A new leader, who has no personal stake in past decisions, can ask whether the old way still makes sense.
Second, the claim is persuasive because limits on tenure prevent the abuse that grows when power goes unchecked.

Consider a hospital director who has served for twenty years. Staff may hesitate to report errors because promotions depend on his favor, and a small [[coterie|coterie]] of loyal deputies may control every key decision.
The same pattern can appear in schools, companies and research institutes.
In politics, this danger is even clearer, which is why many democracies limit how long a president may serve.
A fixed term reminds leaders that they will one day return to the [[ranks|ranks]] and answer to their successors, which encourages honesty and accountability.
Knowing that power is temporary also makes leaders more willing to share decisions and train others.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to this claim is that forcing leaders out after five years may waste experience that takes many years to build.
A research director who has spent a decade building partnerships with funders and governments may be hard to replace, and a large project could stall if she had to leave midway.
Funders, too, may hesitate to support a project whose leader is about to change.
Nevertheless, this risk can be reduced through planned succession and by allowing departing leaders to remain as advisers.
A director who steps down after five years can still mentor her successor, so her experience continues to guide the organization without her holding power indefinitely.
Thus, the challenge argues for flexibility in how the rule is applied, not for abandoning the principle of limited terms.
A good leader should build an organization that can thrive without her, and a five-year term encourages exactly that.
In conclusion, I largely agree that those in power should step down after a fixed period such as five years.
Regular turnover brings fresh ideas, checks the abuse of entrenched power and, with careful succession planning, need not waste valuable experience.
The exact number of years matters less than the principle that no one should hold power so long that an organization cannot imagine life without them.

uncritically satisfied with the current situation
a small, exclusive group of people
ordinary members of an organization, not its leaders

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (loss of hard-won experience) fairly and answers it with planned succession, showing it calls for flexibility rather than rejecting the claim.

essays.title: Judge leaders by results, not years

paragraphs.text: Arbitrary rules are attractive because they are simple, but simplicity is not the same as wisdom.
The claim that those in power, in any profession, should step down after five years is a good example of this tension.
I mostly disagree with this claim: leaders should face regular and rigorous review, but a fixed five-year limit applied to every profession would remove effective leaders for no good reason.

Important projects often take longer than five years, different professions need different kinds of leadership, and although entrenched power is a real danger, accountability addresses it better than an arbitrary deadline.
First, a five-year limit is unwise because many of the most valuable achievements require sustained leadership over a longer period.

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine. A campaign of that scale depends on long-term relationships and trust, which a constant rotation of leaders could easily disrupt.
Changing its leadership every five years would have forced newcomers to rebuild relationships again and again.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, needed steady coordination among many countries and laboratories.
Forcing leaders out at an arbitrary point would put such [[arduous|arduous]] long-term efforts at risk precisely when experience matters most.
Five years may be enough to start such an effort, but it is rarely enough to finish it.
Second, the claim fails because it treats every profession as if it needed the same kind of leadership.

Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession. In such a system, a principal who has built trust with teachers and families over many years is an asset, not a threat.

In my own field, a laboratory head who has spent a decade training a research team may be the reason the team produces reliable work, and replacing her by rule would [[undermine|undermine]] that progress.
A limit that may suit political office becomes [[counterproductive|counterproductive]] when applied blindly to schools, laboratories and businesses.
What works for a president, who commands armies and budgets, may not suit a teacher or a scientist whose influence is far narrower.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that leaders who stay too long often become complacent or abuse their power.

Kodak's leaders, protecting a profitable film business, were slow to embrace the digital camera that their own engineer, Steven Sasson, had invented in 1975, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure came from poor strategy, not simply from the length of anyone's tenure, and a new leader who shared the same assumptions might well have made the same mistake.
Many organizations have struggled under new leaders, and many have thrived under long-serving ones.

The better remedy is regular performance review, strong boards and open criticism, which can remove ineffective leaders at any point while allowing [[estimable|estimable]] ones to continue their work.
These tools address the real problem, which is unaccountable power, rather than its rough [[proxy|proxy]], which is time in office.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that those in power should step down after exactly five years.
Major achievements often require long leadership, professions differ in what they need, and the danger of entrenched power is better met by accountability than by a calendar.
Organizations would be more [[judicious|judicious]] to judge leaders by their results and integrity than by how many years they have served.

words.meaning_here: having the opposite of the intended effect
a substitute measure standing in for the real thing

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (long-serving leaders grow complacent, as at Kodak) fairly and answers it by showing that accountability, not a fixed deadline, is the better remedy.

essays.title: Well-designed breadth makes students truly educated

paragraphs.text: A doctor who understands only the body may still fail the patient who sits in front of her.
This idea lies behind the statement that requiring university students to take a variety of courses outside their major is the best way to ensure that they become truly educated.
I largely agree with this statement, provided that the required courses are well designed and connected to students' broader goals rather than chosen at random.
Broad coursework helps students solve problems that cross disciplines, it prepares them for careers that change, and although poorly designed requirements can waste time, that weakness can be fixed.
First, a variety of courses makes students truly educated because real problems rarely respect the boundaries of a single discipline.

Antibiotic resistance is a good example: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread. Solving it requires not only microbiology but also economics, psychology and law, since pharmacists, patients and regulators all shape the problem.
Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry, showing how command of more than one field can produce outstanding work.
This shows that students trained across fields can [[amalgamate|amalgamate]] ideas in ways that narrow specialists cannot, which is a [[hallmark|hallmark]] of a truly educated person.
A student who has studied only microbiology may understand how resistance develops but not why people keep buying antibiotics they do not need.
Second, broad requirements are valuable because careers change in ways that no student can predict.

GPS was built by the US military, but once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps. The people who turned it into new industries had to see far beyond its original military purpose.
In my own career, a statistics course I once took outside clinical medicine later became the foundation of my work as an epidemiologist.
Breadth gave me tools that my medical training alone did not provide.
A curriculum that requires breadth makes students [[adroit|adroit]] at learning unfamiliar subjects, a skill that matters more than any single body of facts.
Since many graduates will work in jobs that do not yet exist, the ability to learn across fields is a form of insurance.
Admittedly, the statement may not hold true when breadth requirements are poorly designed.
Many students take unrelated courses only to meet a requirement, study them in a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] way and forget the material soon after the final exam.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for better requirements, not for abandoning them.
Courses that connect to students' interests, such as ethics for engineers or economics for medical students, can engage students who would ignore a random elective.
When students see how a course relates to their future work, they are far more likely to take it seriously.
This consideration qualifies my position: breadth is the best route to a true education only when it is planned with care.
In other words, the question is not whether breadth helps, but how universities should require it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that requiring a variety of courses outside the major is the best way to make students truly educated, as long as those courses are thoughtfully chosen.
Such breadth prepares students for problems that cross disciplines and for careers that change, and its weaknesses can be fixed through better design.
Universities should therefore treat breadth not as a box to check but as a central part of what it means to be educated.

words.meaning_here: done with minimal effort, only as a routine

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (cross-disciplinary problems, changing careers), and Body 3 shows where it does not (badly designed requirements) and explains how that qualifies the agreement.

essays.title: Depth and practice matter more than breadth

paragraphs.text: A university degree is supposed to mark the moment a person becomes educated, but the path to that moment can take many forms.
The statement claims that requiring students to take a variety of courses outside their major is the best way to ensure that they become truly educated.
I mostly disagree: some breadth is valuable, but required courses outside the major are not the best way to produce truly educated people, because depth, practice and curiosity matter more.
True education depends on deep mastery of a field, much of it comes from experience and self-directed learning, and although breadth has real benefits, students can gain them in better ways.
First, required breadth is not the best path because a truly educated person needs deep mastery, which takes time that scattered courses consume.

Finland, for example, requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, reflecting the belief that teaching well demands deep, specialized training. It also makes teaching a respected and selective profession, so its teachers are expected to master their field before they lead a classroom.
Breadth requirements that take time from such training may weaken the very expertise that makes a teacher valuable.
Similarly, a medical student who spends many hours on unrelated electives may graduate with only a [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] grasp of how to manage a critically ill patient.
This shows that breadth gained at the expense of depth can leave students knowing a little about everything but not enough about anything.
Depth is not narrowness; it is the foundation that allows a person to judge new information critically.
Second, the statement overlooks the fact that many people become truly educated through experience and curiosity rather than through required courses.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves. Their education came from disciplined practice, not from a university's course requirements.
Likewise, my own understanding of health economics came not from an elective but from working on real budget problems in Vietnamese hospitals.
In such cases, curiosity and practice produced a kind of understanding that no required course could [[supplant|supplant]].
A university that values curiosity can encourage such learning without forcing every student through the same list of courses.
Admittedly, the statement holds true to some degree, since students who never look beyond their major can become narrow thinkers.
An engineer with no exposure to ethics may build a product without considering its harm, and a doctor with no training in communication may struggle to explain a diagnosis.
Nevertheless, these gaps are better filled by building ethics and communication into the major itself than by requiring unrelated courses.
Teaching medical ethics through real clinical cases, for instance, is more [[efficacious|efficacious]] than a general philosophy course that students take only to fulfill a requirement.
Thus, breadth matters, but the requirement the statement describes is not the best way to achieve it, and this distinction shapes my position.
Breadth that grows out of the major is also more likely to be remembered and used.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that required courses outside the major are the best way to ensure that students become truly educated.
Deep mastery, practical experience and personal curiosity contribute more to a true education, and the benefits of breadth can be gained within the major.
Universities should therefore [[eschew|eschew]] rigid requirements and focus on teaching students how to keep learning for life, both inside and beyond their chosen fields.

words.meaning_here: replace or take the place of
effective in producing the desired result

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (depth, practice), and Body 3 shows where it holds (narrow graduates) and explains how that leads to building breadth into the major rather than requiring outside courses.

essays.title: Shared welfare is the truest measure of greatness

paragraphs.text: Tourists admire a nation's monuments, but citizens live in its hospitals, schools and homes.

This contrast underlies the claim that the surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists, and the reason that the true indicator is the welfare of all its people.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, as long as welfare is understood broadly to include health, education and freedom, not income alone.

The claim is sound because elite achievements can coexist with widespread suffering, the reason is persuasive because broad welfare reveals how well a nation's institutions serve everyone, and although elite achievements often improve welfare, they remain a less reliable indicator.
First, the claim is convincing because the achievements of a few can [[belie|belie]] the hardship of the many.

The Tuskegee syphilis study took place in the United States from 1932 to 1972, a period of great scientific progress, yet researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent. A nation's laboratories may lead the world while some of its citizens are denied basic care.
Similarly, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, a reminder that a society later celebrated for its art may neglect the people who create it.
This shows that achievements at the top cannot by themselves prove that a nation is great, which is exactly what the claim asserts.
Greatness measured only by a nation's stars would ignore the many citizens who never share in their success.
Second, the reason is persuasive because the welfare of all people reveals how well a nation's institutions actually work.

After the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, Vietnam, a country that had faced food shortages, became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades. As a Vietnamese physician, I see this broad rise in welfare as a more meaningful sign of national progress than any monument or prize.
Likewise, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Such [[egalitarian|egalitarian]] outcomes require effective policy, honest administration and economic strength together, so they offer a [[cogent|cogent]] summary of a nation's greatness.
Admittedly, those who disagree have a strong point: the achievements of rulers, artists and scientists often create the very welfare that the reason values.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 only after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign built on scientific achievement, and that success protected ordinary people everywhere.
Nevertheless, this connection supports rather than weakens the reason, because such achievements matter most when they improve the lives of ordinary people.
Vaccines that reached only the wealthy, by contrast, would not make a nation great.
Scientific excellence that never reaches clinics, or artistic glory enjoyed only by a [[coterie|coterie]] of the wealthy, would say little about a nation's true greatness.
Achievement, in other words, earns its place in a nation's greatness through its effect on welfare.
In conclusion, I largely agree with both the claim and the reason: a nation's greatness is measured best by the welfare of all its people rather than by the achievements of its elites.
Elite success can hide widespread suffering, broad welfare reflects the quality of a nation's institutions, and even great achievements matter most when they improve ordinary lives.
A nation that wants to be great should therefore ask not only what its leaders have built, but whom that work has served.

words.meaning_here: hide or give a false impression of
based on the principle that all people deserve equal benefits

essays.task_note: Body 1 explicitly evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason (true and supportive of the claim), and Body 3 concedes that elite achievements often create welfare before showing this supports the reason.

essays.title: Greatness combines achievement and shared welfare

paragraphs.text: When people describe a great nation, they often name its scientists, its artists or the leaders who shaped its history.
The claim rejects this habit, arguing that such achievements are not the surest indicator of greatness, and it rests on the reason that the welfare of all the people is the truer measure.

I mostly disagree with the claim and only partly accept the reason: welfare is essential, but a nation's achievements in leadership, art and science are equally important signs of greatness, partly because they make lasting welfare possible.

The claim ignores how elite achievements benefit humanity beyond a nation's borders, the reason treats welfare as separate from achievement when it is often a result of it, and although welfare must matter, it cannot stand alone.
First, the claim is flawed because the achievements of a nation's scientists and leaders often benefit people far beyond its own population.

The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers. Its value lies not only in the welfare of the participating countries but in the knowledge it gave every nation.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military, yet once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps around the world.
A definition of greatness that ignores such contributions would overlook one of the most [[salutary|salutary]] things a nation can do: improve the lives of people everywhere.
Greatness, in this sense, is measured not only at home but also by what a nation gives to the world.
Second, the reason is weaker than it seems because the welfare of a nation's people is usually the result of achievements by its leaders and scientists.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters as poverty fell dramatically. That rise in welfare was not separate from leadership; it [[stemmed|stem]] from a bold decision by the country's rulers.
Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, developed in under a year thanks to decades of basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, protected the health of ordinary people in many countries.
Therefore, the reason creates a false [[dichotomy|dichotomy]] between achievement and welfare, when in practice the first often produces the second.
Admittedly, supporters of the claim are right that elite achievements can coexist with injustice.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, took place in a country with advanced science.
Nevertheless, this case shows that welfare is a necessary part of greatness, not that it is the surest or only indicator.
A small nation with comfortable citizens but no contribution to science, art or the solution of global problems would be fortunate, even [[laudable|laudable]], yet few people would call it great.
Thus, welfare and achievement must be judged together, and neither alone deserves to be called the surest indicator; each tells us something important, and the strongest nations combine both.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree with the claim and only partly accept the reason on which it is based.
Achievements in science and leadership benefit people far beyond one nation, they often produce the very welfare the reason values, and broad welfare, though necessary, is not sufficient on its own.
The surest sign of a great nation is the combination of remarkable achievement and widely shared well-being, each reinforcing the other.

words.meaning_here: a division into two opposed parts
