essays.title: Lasting results require steady leadership

paragraphs.text: Public opinion can change as quickly as the weather, especially in the age of social media.
This volatility supports the statement that any leader who is quickly and easily influenced by shifts in popular opinion will accomplish little.
I largely agree with this statement, although I believe that leaders should still listen carefully to the public when its concerns are deep and lasting.
Major achievements require consistency over time, many valuable reforms are unpopular at first, and while responding to public opinion can be wise, it differs from being easily swayed.
First, a leader who shifts with every change in opinion accomplishes little because important goals require years of consistent effort.

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine. Such a campaign could succeed only because its leaders kept to the plan for years rather than abandoning it whenever public enthusiasm faded.
Similarly, in dengue control, a district that clears mosquito breeding sites only when outbreaks make the news never sustains the year-round prevention that actually reduces cases.
Each year the outbreak returns, and each year the response starts from the beginning.
This shows that a [[mercurial|mercurial]] leader, however popular, cannot finish the long projects that produce lasting results.
Long projects always pass through periods of public fatigue, and a leader who gives up at those moments wastes everything invested before.
Second, the statement holds true because many valuable reforms are unpopular when they are introduced.

Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets is a clear example. The rule was unlikely to please riders who were used to riding without helmets, yet the government enforced it, and helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months while head injuries and deaths fell.

Likewise, most of Ignaz Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his handwashing practice even though it had sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever, so a leader guided by their opinion would have [[squelched|squelch]] a life-saving idea.
Leaders who [[vacillate|vacillate]] under pressure tend to abandon such reforms before their benefits appear, and they therefore accomplish little.
In public health especially, benefits often arrive only after the complaints have faded.
Admittedly, the statement may not hold true in every case, because shifts in popular opinion are sometimes right and leaders should follow them.

The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helped end bus segregation in that city; on that issue, the public's demand was plainly right.
Leaders who ignored such a demand would have stood on the wrong side of history.
Nevertheless, the boycott was not a quick or easy shift in opinion but a sustained, principled movement.
Its participants held their position for over a year, so a leader who heeded the boycott would have been following a stable public demand, not a passing mood.
Responding to deep and lasting public demands is wise leadership, whereas being swayed by every passing mood is not, so this consideration refines rather than reverses my position.
In conclusion, I largely agree that leaders who are quickly and easily swayed by popular opinion accomplish little.
Lasting achievements demand consistency, valuable reforms are often unpopular at first, and even responsiveness to the public must separate sustained demands from [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] moods.
The most effective leaders listen to everyone but change course only when the evidence, not the noise, requires it; that steadiness is what allows them to accomplish great things.

words.meaning_here: changing mood or mind suddenly and unpredictably

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (consistency, unpopular reforms), and Body 3 shows where it does not (the Montgomery boycott) and explains how that refines the position to sustained versus passing opinion.

essays.title: Responsive leaders often accomplish more

paragraphs.text: In a democracy, the people are supposed to be the leader's boss.
Yet the statement claims that any leader who is quickly and easily influenced by shifts in popular opinion will accomplish little.

I mostly disagree: while leaders should not follow every passing mood, those who respond quickly to public opinion often accomplish more than those who ignore it, especially when that opinion reflects real needs.

Responsive leaders can turn public demands into lasting change, they avoid the failures that come from stubbornly ignoring reality, and although constant shifting can paralyze a leader, flexibility itself is not the problem.
First, leaders who respond quickly to popular opinion can accomplish a great deal because public demands often point to real problems.

The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helped end bus segregation in that city. The demand was just, and leaders who listened to it early could have spared the city a long and painful conflict.
Here, the public saw an injustice more clearly than many of those in power.

Similarly, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, which shows how fast public demands can now form; leaders who listen early can address them before they become crises.
This shows that being easily influenced by the public can be a strength, since it lets leaders act while problems are still manageable.
Listening early is not weakness; it is a way of gathering information that no expert report can fully provide.
Second, leaders who remain [[intransigent|intransigent]] as opinion changes often accomplish less, because they cling to failing policies.

Before 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning even as the country faced food shortages. Once its leaders adopted the Doi Moi reforms, which introduced market incentives, Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Likewise, Kodak's leaders, protecting a profitable film business, were slow to embrace digital photography even as consumers' preferences shifted, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
In both cases, the danger came not from flexibility but from an [[obdurate|obdurate]] refusal to move in the direction that opinion and evidence were already pointing.
A leader who had responded sooner to rising discontent might have spared citizens or employees years of hardship.
Admittedly, the statement contains some truth, since a leader who changes direction with every poll may never finish anything.
Consider a health minister who announces a tobacco tax, withdraws it after one week of complaints and then proposes it again; such [[dithering|dither]] wastes time and confuses the public.
Nevertheless, the problem in this case is a lack of judgment, not responsiveness itself.
Such a minister accomplishes little not because she listens, but because she has no plan to defend.
A capable leader can listen closely to the public while keeping a clear goal, adjusting the methods without abandoning the purpose.
Thus, the statement holds only for leaders who lack direction, and it overlooks the many leaders whose sensitivity to opinion is the source of their success.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that leaders who are quickly influenced by popular opinion will accomplish little.
Responsive leaders can turn public demands into reform and avoid the failures of stubbornness, and the real danger lies in poor judgment rather than in flexibility.
Leaders should therefore be [[pliant|pliant]] in their methods but firm in their goals, because that combination turns public opinion into an engine of progress rather than a source of confusion.

words.meaning_here: being indecisive; repeatedly changing one's mind

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (responsiveness enables reform, stubbornness fails), and Body 3 shows where it holds (leaders who shift with every poll) and explains how that limits it to leaders lacking direction.

essays.title: Officials should lead with accountable judgment

paragraphs.text: Every democracy faces a quiet tension between what citizens want today and what will serve them best tomorrow.
This tension becomes sharpest for government officials, who must decide whether to follow public opinion or their own expert judgment.
I largely agree that officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people, as long as that judgment remains open to public scrutiny.
Officials often hold knowledge that the public lacks, popular wishes can conflict with long-term welfare, and yet unchecked judgment carries real dangers that must be limited.
First, officials should trust their own judgment because their positions often give them knowledge and evidence that ordinary citizens do not have.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide was given to pregnant women in Europe, where it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, relying on her own [[circumspect|circumspect]] review of the evidence.
Her decision spared American families that tragedy, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Similarly, a district health officer who sees rising dengue cases in surveillance data may order spraying before residents notice any danger.
This shows that officials who act on expert evidence can protect the people they serve, even before those people know what to ask for.
Expertise, in other words, is part of what citizens entrust to the people they elect or appoint.
Second, officials must sometimes resist the popular will because what citizens want in the moment can [[undermine|undermine]] their own long-term welfare.
Antibiotic resistance offers a clear case: in many countries, including Vietnam, people are used to buying antibiotics over the counter, and this overuse helps resistant bacteria spread.
As a result, drugs that once cured infections now often fail, so a health official who restricts such sales is serving the public even if the rule is unpopular.
Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 helmet law imposed a duty that many riders would not have chosen for themselves, yet helmet use rose to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
In both cases, officials who followed short-term public preference would have failed the very people whose will they claimed to honor.
A [[salutary|salutary]] rule may be resented at first and appreciated only later.
Admittedly, officials who ignore the public can become arrogant, and their judgment can be badly wrong.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, a decision that no independent body was required to review.
When the study became public, outrage over this [[egregious|egregious]] abuse led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, this case argues for checking official judgment, not for replacing it with whatever the majority demands at a given moment.
The Tuskegee researchers failed because no one reviewed their choices, whereas Kelsey made her decision inside a system that could question and correct her.
Thus, the danger of abuse qualifies my position: judgment should guide officials, but it must be exercised openly and remain accountable to the public.
In conclusion, government officials should generally act on their own informed judgment instead of simply obeying the people's current wishes.
Their access to evidence and their duty to long-term welfare justify this independence, while cases of abuse show why it needs firm limits.
The best officials, therefore, listen carefully to the public but are willing to [[demur|demur]] when the evidence points elsewhere, and they explain their reasons openly.

words.meaning_here: careful to consider all risks before acting
beneficial, even if unwelcome at first
politely object or decline to agree

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (expert evidence, long-term welfare), and Body 3 names where it fails (Tuskegee) and explains how that limits the position to accountable judgment.

essays.title: Officials should mainly serve the public's will

paragraphs.text: History offers many examples of leaders who were certain they knew better than the people they governed.
The statement asks whether government officials should act on such confidence or carry out the will of the citizens who placed them in office.
I mostly disagree with the statement: in most matters, officials should faithfully carry out the public's will, using their own judgment mainly to decide how, not whether, to act.
Officials' judgment is often less reliable than they believe, public pressure frequently corrects injustice, and only in narrow technical emergencies should private judgment prevail.
First, officials should not place their own judgment above the people's will, because that judgment is often narrower than it appears.
Before 1986, Vietnam's leaders ran the economy through central planning, deciding from above what should be produced, and the country faced food shortages.
When the Doi Moi reforms replaced this system with market incentives, ordinary households were finally free to act on their own choices, and Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Similarly, a city planner who ignores residents' complaints about a new road may overlook local knowledge that no map can show.
Residents know which streets flood, which corners are dangerous and which markets their livelihoods depend on.
This shows that the people's will often contains practical wisdom that officials, however [[erudite|erudite]], cannot see from their offices.
Planners in distant offices rarely feel the consequences of their errors as directly as the families who live with them.
Second, public pressure has repeatedly forced officials to correct injustices that their own judgment had [[condoned|condone]] for years.
In the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
Local officials had defended segregation as normal, but the [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] protest of ordinary citizens helped end bus segregation in that city.

Likewise, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent from 1932 to 1972, and the public outrage it caused led to US rules requiring ethics review boards.
In both cases, the will of the people was not a passing mood but a moral correction that officials should have heeded far sooner.
The officials who relied on their own judgment were the problem, not the solution.
Admittedly, there are moments when the public's wishes would lead to harm and an official must stand firm.
Around 1960, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Her expert caution protected American families, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Nevertheless, such cases are narrow: they involve technical questions in which evidence, not values, decides the right answer.
In my own field, a health officer may rightly close a market during an outbreak even if traders object.
Neither Kelsey nor that officer is overriding the people's will; each is protecting exactly what the people want, namely safety.
Therefore, this concession refines rather than reverses my position, since expert judgment should govern methods while the public sets the goals.
In conclusion, officials should, for the most part, carry out the will of the people rather than substitute their own preferences for it.

Their judgment is often less reliable than they assume, and public pressure has corrected injustices that officials once [[countenanced|countenance]], although technical emergencies may require independent expertise.
A healthy government, then, lets citizens choose the destination and asks officials to use their skill in charting the route.

words.meaning_here: accepted or allowed something morally wrong

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (central planning, Montgomery, Tuskegee), and Body 3 names where it holds (Kelsey, outbreak control) and explains how that narrows the position to technical questions.

essays.title: A common core promotes fairness

paragraphs.text: What a child learns at school often depends less on talent than on the place where that child happens to be born.
One way to reduce this inequality is the proposal that every student in a nation should study the same national curriculum until college.
I largely agree with this statement, provided that the common curriculum sets core content while leaving teachers free to choose how to teach it.
A national curriculum promotes equal opportunity and builds a shared civic foundation, and its main weakness, rigidity, can be reduced through flexible teaching.
First, a common curriculum promotes fairness because it guarantees that poor and remote students are taught the same essential content as wealthy urban students.
Consider a village school in a mountain province of Vietnam where teachers are scarce and families cannot pay for extra classes.
Without national standards, that school might quietly drop chemistry or advanced mathematics, leaving its graduates unable to compete for university places with students from Hanoi.
With a national curriculum, by contrast, the gap in content is visible, and authorities can be pressed to [[redress|redress]] it with teachers and materials.
Similarly, when I was a student, classmates who moved between provinces could continue their studies without repeating or skipping entire subjects.
This shows that a single curriculum turns equal opportunity from an abstract ideal into a standard that schools can be held to.
Moreover, a shared curriculum gives all citizens a common foundation of knowledge, which a nation needs in order to solve problems together.
During a dengue outbreak, for instance, public health messages work only if most people already understand basic biology, such as how mosquitoes breed in standing water.
In my work on dengue control, I have found that communities with stronger basic science education respond to such messages with greater [[alacrity|alacrity]].
Likewise, a shared knowledge of national history allows citizens from different regions to debate public questions using the same basic facts.
Consider, too, a voter deciding whether to support a vaccination program; without basic science, such a choice becomes guesswork.
Without this shared ground, public debate becomes a [[cacophony|cacophony]] of voices that cannot even agree on the facts.
In this way, a common curriculum is not merely an educational tool but a [[buttress|buttress]] for informed citizenship.
Admittedly, a uniform curriculum can become rigid, forcing every student into the same mold regardless of talent or interest.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their success suggests that some of the most creative learning happens outside any official syllabus.
Nevertheless, the problem lies in rigid teaching and testing, not in a common curriculum itself.
Finland, for example, requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, trusting skilled teachers to adapt lessons to their students.
A national curriculum can therefore define what every student should learn while allowing teachers to decide how to teach it, which leaves room for curious minds like the Wrights'.
In conclusion, I largely support requiring a common national curriculum before college, as long as it defines core content rather than every classroom method.
Such a curriculum promotes fairness and a shared civic foundation, and its risk of rigidity can be managed by trusting well-trained teachers.
The goal should be a common floor for every student, not a ceiling on any student's curiosity.

words.meaning_here: correct or remedy an unfair situation
a confused, clashing mix of noisy voices

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (equal opportunity, shared civic knowledge), and Body 3 names where it fails (rigid teaching, the Wright brothers) and explains how that limits the curriculum to core content.

essays.title: One curriculum cannot fit every student

paragraphs.text: No two students arrive at school with the same talents, interests or ambitions.
Yet the statement proposes that a nation should require every student to study the same national curriculum until entering college.
I mostly disagree: although every student needs a shared core of basic skills, requiring one identical curriculum until college wastes talent and discourages good teaching.
Students' abilities differ widely, local communities have different needs, and a limited common core, rather than a full national curriculum, can secure fairness.
First, a single curriculum ignores the [[disparate|disparate]] talents of students, many of whom learn best by pursuing their own interests.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
They succeeded through years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, a practical education that no national syllabus would have prescribed.
Similarly, a teenager with a gift for programming may spend hours memorizing historical dates she will never use while her real talent lies [[dormant|dormant]].
This shows that a uniform curriculum, by treating all students alike, may hold back exactly those students whose different paths a nation most needs.
A system with room for electives and vocational tracks would let such students grow without abandoning basic education.
Second, an identical national curriculum prevents schools and teachers from adapting lessons to local needs.

Finland offers a useful model: it requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
This approach treats teachers as trained professionals who can shape lessons to their students rather than as clerks following orders from a central office.
Likewise, a school in Vietnam's Mekong Delta might reasonably teach more about agriculture and flood management than a school in central Hanoi.
A student who learns to measure rising water in her own village may grasp scientific method better than one who memorizes a distant textbook example.
Such flexibility is not a luxury; it keeps education [[germane|germane]] to students' lives, which a single program imposed from above cannot achieve.
Teachers who know their communities are better placed than a distant ministry to decide which examples will make a lesson meaningful.
Admittedly, a nation without any common standards risks deepening inequality between rich and poor regions.
Consider a remote mountain school that, without national requirements, might quietly drop chemistry because it lacks a qualified teacher, leaving its students unable to compete for university places.
Nevertheless, this risk justifies a limited common core in reading, mathematics and science, not a complete national curriculum governing every subject until college.
Indeed, a uniform syllabus alone cannot place a chemistry teacher in that remote school; only funding and training can.
A country can set minimum standards and support weak schools to meet them while still allowing electives, vocational tracks and local content above that floor.
In other words, the concern about fairness qualifies my position but does not overturn it, since equity depends on adequate resources more than on identical lessons.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that every student should follow the same national curriculum until entering college.
Students' differing talents and communities' differing needs call for flexibility, while fairness can be protected by a modest common core.
A nation should therefore guarantee that every student learns the basics, but then let schools adapt the rest to the [[multifarious|multifarious]] talents of their students.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (differing talents, local needs), and Body 3 names where it holds (fairness for remote schools) and explains how that leads to a limited common core rather than a full national curriculum.

essays.title: Cities are where traditions meet and endure

paragraphs.text: Walk through any old capital city, and you will see centuries of a nation's culture in its streets, temples and theaters.
Such scenes lead many people to believe, as the statement claims, that it is primarily in cities that a nation's cultural traditions are generated and preserved.
I largely agree with this view, although I recognize that rural communities remain essential keepers of many traditions.
Cities bring diverse people together to create new culture, they hold the institutions that preserve it, and their limits appear mainly in the living customs of the countryside.
First, cities generate cultural traditions because they bring together people from many regions and backgrounds, whose ideas mix and produce something new.
Consider Ho Chi Minh City, where migrants from every province of Vietnam live side by side, sharing food, music and customs.
Over time, dishes and styles that began in one region [[coalesce|coalesce]] into a new urban culture that later [[permeates|permeate]] the provinces through television and social media.
Similarly, a young musician who moves from a small town to the capital meets teachers, audiences and fellow artists who push her work in directions her hometown could not.
Many of the songs and fashions that people now call national traditions began in exactly this kind of urban mixing.
This shows that the density and diversity of cities act as a [[catalyst|catalyst]] for cultural creation, supporting the statement's claim that traditions are generated there.
Second, cities preserve traditions because they contain the institutions that record, protect and teach a nation's culture.
National museums, libraries, universities and theaters are concentrated in capitals, where they keep [[artifacts|artifact]] and performances that might otherwise disappear.
In Hanoi, for instance, a visitor can study ancient ceramics in a museum in the morning and watch a traditional opera performance in the evening.
Likewise, when an old village craft declines, it is often an urban museum or university that documents its techniques before the last masters die.
Universities in large cities also train the scholars, curators and performers who carry these traditions into the next generation.
Without such institutions, many traditions would survive only in fading memories, which is why cities serve as a nation's long-term memory.
In this sense, cities do not merely store culture; they actively keep it alive by teaching it.
Admittedly, many of a nation's most cherished customs are practiced and kept alive in the countryside rather than in cities.
In Vietnam, many city families return to their home villages for the Lunar New Year, because the ancestral altars, family graves and village festivals are there.
Similarly, traditional crafts such as weaving or pottery survive in small villages, not as [[vestiges|vestige]] of the past but as living work.
Nevertheless, these rural traditions increasingly depend on cities for their survival, since city buyers support village crafts and city media keep village festivals visible.
The countryside, therefore, is a vital partner in preserving culture, but cities remain the main place where traditions are renewed, recorded and passed to a wider public.
This concession refines my position: the statement holds largely true, but not exclusively.
In conclusion, I largely agree that cities are the primary places where a nation's cultural traditions are generated and preserved.
Their diversity sparks new culture and their institutions protect old culture, even though villages remain important keepers of living customs.
A wise nation, then, will invest in its urban cultural institutions while making sure they stay connected to the rural communities from which many traditions first came.

words.meaning_here: come together to form one whole
something that speeds up or sparks change
objects made by people, with historical value
small remaining traces of something that has mostly disappeared

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (cities mix people and house cultural institutions), and Body 3 names where it does not (village festivals and crafts) and explains why the statement is largely but not exclusively true.

essays.title: The countryside creates and keeps tradition

paragraphs.text: Ask people where their traditions come from, and many will name a village, a grandmother or a festival, not a city.
This common answer challenges the statement that a nation's cultural traditions are primarily generated and preserved in cities.
I mostly disagree with the statement: while cities display and record culture, the traditions themselves are more often created and kept alive in rural communities.
Many traditions grow from rural life, cities often weaken inherited customs, and the real strength of cities lies in archiving and spreading culture rather than generating it.
First, many of a nation's traditions are generated in the countryside because they grow directly out of farming, seasons and village life.
In Vietnam, the Lunar New Year, harvest festivals and ancestor worship are all tied to the rhythm of rice farming and to the family home in the village.
The foods eaten during these festivals, such as sticky rice cakes, also come from the fields rather than from the city.
Even after the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 turned a country that had faced food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters, rice farming has remained at the center of many customs.
Similarly, a craft village that has made pottery for generations develops its own designs and rituals, which urban shops later sell as "traditional" goods.
This shows that cities often consume and display traditions that were generated elsewhere, contrary to the statement's claim.
Second, cities frequently weaken inherited traditions rather than preserving them, because urban life is fast, mobile and commercial.
In my work in Hanoi, I meet many young families who live far from their relatives, work long hours and have little time for the rituals their parents observed.
Their children may know global brands better than local folk songs, and customs that seemed [[immutable|immutable]] in the village begin to fade within one generation.
Likewise, when old neighborhoods are replaced by shopping malls, the street markets and small temples that held a community's memory often disappear.
Cities, in short, tend to [[supplant|supplant]] local culture with a [[homogeneous|homogeneous]] global one, which makes them unreliable guardians of national traditions.
It is often in the countryside, by contrast, that elders still teach these customs to the young.
Admittedly, cities do play an important role in preserving culture through their museums, universities and archives.
A national museum in the capital can protect ancient [[artifacts|artifact]], and a university can record the techniques of a dying craft before its last masters pass away.
Similarly, city-based television and radio can bring a regional folk opera to a national audience.
Such work is valuable, and without it some traditions would be forgotten entirely.
Nevertheless, recording a tradition is not the same as keeping it alive; a song stored in an archive is a record, while a song sung at a village festival is a living practice.
Thus, the work of cities is [[complementary|complementary]] to that of villages: cities archive culture, but they are not its primary source.
This concession qualifies my position without reversing it, since the statement holds true only for the narrower task of documenting traditions.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that cultural traditions are primarily generated and preserved in cities.
Many traditions grow from rural life and survive there, while cities often weaken them, even though urban institutions help to document and share them.
If a nation wants its traditions to endure, it should support the villages where they are lived, not only the museums where they are displayed.

words.meaning_here: adding to something else so that together they are complete

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (traditions grow from rural life; cities erode them), and Body 3 names where it holds (urban archives and media) and explains why that role is documenting, not generating or keeping alive.

essays.title: Shared goals make deep learning possible

paragraphs.text: Most real learning happens not in a single moment of argument but over years of patient work.
The statement claims that we can learn much more from people whose views we share than from those whose views contradict our own.
I largely agree, provided that "shared views" means shared goals and basic assumptions, not identical opinions on every question.
Shared views allow deep, sustained collaboration, they create the trust needed to accept correction, and although opponents can expose our errors, their lessons are usually narrower.
First, we learn more from like-minded people because shared assumptions allow long, deep collaboration instead of endless debate about first principles.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on basic research on mRNA, work that received little notice for many years.

Because they shared a belief in the idea, they could [[corroborate|corroborate]] and extend each other's results, and their research later allowed the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines to be developed in under a year and earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, worked side by side for years on gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves before their first powered flight in 1903.
In my own field, the most productive research teams I know are built around a shared question rather than constant dispute.
This shows that shared views do not produce lazy agreement; they free partners to spend their energy learning rather than arguing.
Second, people who share our views are often the ones whose criticism we actually accept, so they teach us more in practice.

The case of Ignaz Semmelweis is [[apposite|apposite]] here: when he had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.
Because those colleagues did not share his views, they learned almost nothing from him, and germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.
By contrast, in my own research team, a colleague who shares my methods can offer [[candid|candid]] criticism of my analysis, and I can fix the flaw within a day.
In other words, learning depends not only on the content of a message but on our willingness to receive it, and shared views supply that willingness.
Admittedly, people who disagree with us can reveal errors that like-minded colleagues are [[predisposed|predisposed]] to miss.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, showing how often single findings mislead.
Without researchers willing to test accepted results, these errors might have remained unchallenged.
Nevertheless, such correction teaches us mainly what is wrong, while like-minded collaborators teach us how to build something right.
Moreover, that replication effort was itself carried out by researchers who shared a commitment to rigorous science.
This concession qualifies my position: we should seek critics, but we should not expect most of our learning to come from them.
Critics are like a fire alarm: essential in an emergency, but of little use in designing and building the house.
In conclusion, I largely agree that we learn more from people whose views we share, as long as those shared views involve common goals rather than blind agreement.
Shared views support deep collaboration and make us open to correction, while opponents, though useful, mainly expose flaws.
The wisest learners, therefore, build their work among allies while inviting the occasional [[skeptic|skeptic]] to test it.

words.meaning_here: a person who questions accepted claims

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (sustained collaboration, openness to correction), and Body 3 names where it does not (critics exposing errors) and explains how that limits rather than reverses the position.

essays.title: Opponents teach what allies cannot

paragraphs.text: It is comfortable to spend time with people who agree with us, but comfort rarely teaches us much.
The statement nevertheless claims that we learn much more from people whose views we share than from those whose views contradict our own.
I mostly disagree: although like-minded people help us develop ideas, those who contradict us are more likely to expose our errors and widen our thinking.
Opponents reveal mistakes we cannot see, they introduce perspectives we would never consider, and while allies do help us build on ideas, that learning is narrower.
First, people who disagree with us teach more because they are willing to expose the errors that like-minded people overlook.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Many of those findings had been accepted by researchers who shared the same assumptions, and it took [[skeptics|skeptic]] willing to test them to reveal how often single findings mislead.
Agreement had allowed weak results to [[proliferate|proliferate]] in textbooks and lectures.
Similarly, in my own work, the reviewer who rejects my manuscript usually teaches me more than the colleague who praises it.
Such critics are not enemies of science; they are its most demanding teachers.
This shows that disagreement, though uncomfortable, is often the most direct path to learning what we have gotten wrong.
Second, people with opposing views widen our thinking by introducing perspectives we would never consider on our own.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
By surrounding himself with people who might [[gainsay|gainsay]] him, Lincoln made sure his decisions were tested from several angles before he acted.
Likewise, a public health team that includes economists and community leaders will design a better dengue program than a team made up only of epidemiologists like me.
Each of these outside views would expose assumptions that epidemiologists, trained alike, tend to share without noticing.
Such diversity of views does not slow learning; it enriches it, because each disagreement forces us to defend, refine or abandon our ideas.
A circle of allies, by contrast, can become an echo chamber in which no idea is ever seriously challenged.
Admittedly, people who share our views can help us learn in depth, especially when a project requires years of steady work.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA, and their shared commitment later made it possible to develop the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines in under a year.
Their partnership shows that allies can sustain an unpopular idea through years of neglect.
Nevertheless, even their success depended on finally reaching a scientific community that had long been [[indifferent|indifferent]] to their idea.
Shared views helped them develop the idea, but convincing others required answering the doubts of people who did not yet agree.
Thus, like-minded allies help us go deeper, whereas opponents help us see further, and the second kind of learning is usually broader.
This concession qualifies my position but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree with the statement, because those who contradict us often teach us more than those who agree.
Opponents reveal our errors and widen our perspectives, while allies, though valuable, mainly help us deepen ideas we already hold.
We should therefore seek out thoughtful critics rather than avoid them, since an unchallenged belief is rarely a well-understood one.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (critics expose errors and widen thinking), and Body 3 names where it holds (Karikó and Weissman's partnership) and explains why that depth does not outweigh the breadth opponents provide.

essays.title: Modern needs usually outweigh old buildings

paragraphs.text: Cities are living places, and every generation must decide what to keep from the past and what to build for the future.
This choice becomes especially difficult when old buildings stand on land that modern planners believe could better serve the needs of today's residents.
I largely agree that modern development should generally take precedence in such cases, except when a building has exceptional historic value that cannot be preserved in any other way.
Growing populations need housing, modern facilities can protect health and safety, and only truly irreplaceable landmarks deserve to block development.
First, development should usually take precedence because growing cities urgently need housing, and land in city centers is limited.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Such a program would be impossible in a crowded country if every old structure were treated as [[sacrosanct|sacrosanct]], since land for new housing must come from somewhere.
Similarly, in Hanoi, where many families live in cramped rooms, a row of decaying old warehouses might be replaced by apartments for hundreds of households.
This shows that when the choice is between preserving old walls and housing living people, the needs of the living should usually prevail.
Housing, after all, is not a luxury but a basic condition for health, education and work.
A city that refuses to change risks becoming a museum that its own residents can no longer afford to live in.
Second, modern development deserves priority when the new use directly protects health and safety.
Consider a district hospital in Vietnam that cannot expand its emergency department because an old administrative building occupies the only available land.
During each dengue season, patients wait in crowded corridors, so replacing that building with a modern ward could [[alleviate|alleviate]] suffering and save lives.
In my own work, I have seen how a lack of space, more than a lack of skill, often limits the care that hospitals can give.
Likewise, an old market hall with weak foundations may pose a real danger to the people who use it every day.
In such circumstances, insisting on preservation would place the [[aesthetic|aesthetic]] value of a building above the welfare of the people it is supposed to serve.
Admittedly, some historic buildings are so important that no modern purpose could justify destroying them.
A temple that has stood for centuries or a building tied to a nation's founding carries a meaning that cannot be rebuilt once it is gone.
Destroying a thousand-year-old pagoda to build a car park, for instance, would be a loss that no economic gain could justify.
Once destroyed, such a building is lost forever, while a new apartment block could be built elsewhere.
Nevertheless, such landmarks are relatively few, and their protection should be a carefully defined exception rather than a general rule.
Planners can also [[incorporate|incorporate]] an old facade into a new building, keeping a [[vestige|vestige]] of history while still using the land for modern needs.
This consideration qualifies my position: development should usually win, but only after experts have identified the buildings that are truly irreplaceable.
In conclusion, I largely agree that modern development should take precedence over historic buildings when land is badly needed for modern purposes.
Housing shortages and public safety justify this priority, although a small number of exceptional landmarks deserve lasting protection.
The best planners, then, will build boldly for the present while carefully protecting the few places that make a city's past visible.

words.meaning_here: too sacred to be changed or touched
include as part of a whole
a small remaining trace of the past

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (housing shortages, health and safety), and Body 3 names where it does not (irreplaceable landmarks) and explains how that makes preservation a selective exception.

essays.title: Historic buildings deserve priority in most cases

paragraphs.text: A new office tower can be built in two years, but a building that has stood for two centuries can never be replaced.
This simple fact lies at the heart of the debate over whether modern development should take precedence over the preservation of historic buildings.
I mostly disagree with the statement: preservation should usually come first, and development should replace historic buildings only when a pressing public need cannot be met elsewhere.
Historic buildings are irreplaceable records of identity, they often bring more lasting economic value than new construction, and only urgent needs such as housing can justify an exception.
First, historic buildings should usually be preserved because they are irreplaceable records of a community's history and identity.
Consider Hanoi's Old Quarter, whose narrow streets and old shop houses show how merchants lived and traded long ago.
If planners replaced these blocks with glass towers, the city would gain office space but lose a living link to its past that no textbook could restore.
Visitors and residents alike sense this history when they walk its streets, even if they never read a word about it.
Similarly, an old hospital in a provincial town reminds residents of how medicine and public health developed in their region.

This shows that historic buildings are not merely old structures but [[artifacts|artifact]] of collective memory, and destroying them for short-term convenience is a loss that cannot be [[redressed|redress]].
Once demolished, such places can be copied but never truly restored.
Second, preservation often serves a city's economy better than new development, because historic districts attract visitors and give a city its character.
Tourists rarely travel across the world to see ordinary office blocks, but they will pay to walk through well-kept old streets, temples and markets.
In a mid-sized Vietnamese city, for instance, a restored old quarter can support many small family businesses, from cafes to craft shops.
By contrast, a modern shopping mall may bring quick profit to one developer while making the city look like every other city.
Planners who favor development often take a [[myopic|myopic]] view of value, counting the immediate return on new buildings but ignoring the long-term income that heritage provides.
Preserving old buildings, then, is frequently the more [[prudent|prudent]] economic choice as well as the more respectful one.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which a pressing human need should outweigh preservation.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats, and such a program requires large amounts of urban land.
Likewise, a hospital that must expand to treat patients during a dengue epidemic may have no choice but to replace an old building next door.
Nevertheless, these cases should be treated as exceptions that require strong evidence, not as a general rule that gives development automatic precedence.
In many cities, planners can build new housing on empty or industrial land and leave historic districts intact, so the conflict is often less [[stark|stark]] than the statement assumes.
This concession shapes my position by limiting it, not by reversing it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that modern development should be given precedence over historic buildings.
Such buildings preserve identity and often produce lasting economic value, while urgent needs such as housing or health care justify only occasional exceptions.
Before demolishing the past, a city should ask whether the future it wants could be built somewhere else, and the answer is often yes.

words.meaning_here: objects made by people that carry historical meaning
wise and careful about the future

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement fails (identity, long-term economic value), and Body 3 names where it holds (urgent housing or hospital needs) and explains how that limits the position to rare, evidence-based exceptions.

essays.title: Great achievements usually lift ordinary lives

paragraphs.text: When people think of a great nation, they often picture its famous leaders, painters and scientists.
The claim states that such achievements are the surest indicator of national greatness, and the reason given is that they ensure a good life for most of the nation's people.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, although I believe the reason holds only when the benefits of these achievements are widely shared.

The claim is persuasive because great achievements reveal a nation's capacity, the reason is largely true because such achievements often raise living standards, and the main objection concerns benefits that are unequally shared.
First, the claim is largely convincing because the achievements of a nation's leaders and scientists reveal its capacity to solve problems that matter.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, for example, replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This [[landmark|landmark]] decision by the country's leaders revealed a capacity for self-correction that few other indicators could capture.

Similarly, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign, an achievement that revealed the scientific and organizational strength of the countries that shared data and vaccine.
Such achievements are visible, measurable and lasting, which is why the claim reasonably treats them as a strong indicator of a great nation.
Second, the reason on which the claim rests is largely true, because great achievements by leaders and scientists frequently improve the lives of ordinary people.

Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, for instance, raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, so a decision by a few leaders protected ordinary riders across the country.

Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, and those vaccines then protected ordinary people around the world.
As a physician, I see the legacy of such discoveries every day in patients who survive diseases that once would have killed them.
These cases show that the reason is [[cogent|cogent]]: great achievements do not stay at the top of society but often reach the majority.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that great achievements do not automatically ensure a good life for most people.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, yet his art did little to feed or heal the people of his time.
A great painting may enrich a nation's culture for centuries without changing whether its poorest citizens have enough to eat.
Similarly, in his 1945 Nobel lecture Alexander Fleming warned that misuse of penicillin would breed resistant bacteria, and today overuse means that drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Nevertheless, these examples show that achievements must be well managed and widely shared, not that they are irrelevant to national greatness.
This objection therefore qualifies my agreement: achievements indicate greatness most reliably when a nation also ensures that their benefits [[permeate|permeate]] society.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the achievements of rulers, artists and scientists are a strong sign of a great nation and that they often improve ordinary lives.
Reforms such as Doi Moi and discoveries such as mRNA vaccines support both the claim and the reason, although unequal or poorly managed benefits limit them.
A nation's achievements, then, prove its greatness only when they [[redound|redound]] to the benefit of its people as a whole.

words.meaning_here: historically important; marking a turning point

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason (whether achievements really ensure a good life for most people), and Body 3 concedes the strongest objection (van Gogh, antibiotic misuse) before qualifying both.

essays.title: Achievements alone do not guarantee good lives

paragraphs.text: A nation can produce brilliant scientists and celebrated artists while many of its citizens still struggle to find clean water or a decent job.
This contrast raises doubts about the claim that the surest indicator of a great nation is the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason on which it rests, although I accept that some achievements do improve ordinary lives.
The claim confuses a few people's success with national greatness, the reason assumes too much, and the strongest opposing cases depend on benefits being widely shared.
First, the claim is flawed because the achievements of a small elite reveal little about how a nation treats most of its people.
The United States produced remarkable scientists in the twentieth century, yet from 1932 to 1972 the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
A nation that could perform world-class research while committing such an [[egregious|egregious]] abuse cannot be judged great by its scientific record alone.
The study's existence did not erase American scientific achievements, but it shows that those achievements said little about how Black citizens were treated.
Similarly, a ruler who builds a [[palatial|palatial]] capital may win praise abroad while rural families at home lack doctors and schools.
This shows that achievements at the top can coexist with neglect below, so they cannot be the surest indicator of national greatness.
Second, the reason is unconvincing because great achievements do not automatically ensure a good life for the majority.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria, and penicillin became a usable drug during World War II, yet in his 1945 Nobel lecture he warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.

His warning proved [[prescient|prescient]]: today, overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, mean that drugs which once cured infections now often fail.
Likewise, Vincent van Gogh, now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and his genius did little to improve the lives of his neighbors.
Whether an achievement improves ordinary lives depends on how a society manages and shares it, which the reason simply ignores.
Admittedly, the strongest challenge to my position is that some achievements by rulers and scientists have clearly improved the lives of millions.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign, and Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 were followed by a dramatic fall in poverty over the next decades.
Nevertheless, these successes mattered because they reached ordinary people, through vaccines delivered to whole populations and incentives open to ordinary households.
Without such broad distribution, the same achievements would have remained [[nominal|nominal]] triumphs with little effect on daily life.
In other words, it is the general welfare that results from achievements, not the achievements themselves, that marks a great nation.
This concession therefore supports a revised claim rather than the original one.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that the achievements of rulers, artists or scientists are the surest indicator of a great nation.
Elite success can hide neglect, and achievements improve ordinary lives only when they are wisely managed and widely shared, as the cases of smallpox and Doi Moi show.
A better test of greatness is how well a nation turns the brilliance of a few into a good life for the many.

words.meaning_here: grand and luxurious, like a palace
in name only; having little real effect

essays.task_note: Body 1 rejects the claim (elite success can hide neglect), Body 2 rejects the reason (achievements do not automatically reach the majority), and Body 3 concedes the strongest opposing cases (smallpox, Doi Moi) and shows they depend on welfare.

essays.title: Achievements reveal a nation's greatness best

paragraphs.text: Centuries from now, people will remember nations less for their average incomes than for what they discovered, created and built.

Some people therefore claim that national greatness is best judged by the achievements of rulers, artists or scientists, while others argue that the surest indicator is the general welfare of all the people.
My position aligns more closely with the first view, provided that we count achievements that serve humanity rather than mere displays of power.
Achievements reveal a nation's deeper capacities, they often create the welfare that the second view values, and although welfare matters greatly, it is a less distinctive measure of greatness.
First, I side with the first view because great achievements reveal capacities, such as creativity, organization and courage, that welfare statistics cannot show.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911 despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Her achievement reflected an [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] persistence that later generations of scientists, especially women, have tried to [[emulate|emulate]].
No welfare statistic could have predicted or measured such persistence.

Similarly, the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, displayed the ambition and generosity of the nations behind it by making the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Such [[landmarks|landmark]] capture the qualities that make a nation great in a way that average incomes or life expectancy never could.
Second, achievements by leaders and scientists often create the very welfare that the second view treats as the true measure.

In 1986, Vietnam's leaders launched the Doi Moi reforms, replacing central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Poverty then fell dramatically over the following decades, so the general welfare was not a separate achievement but the result of a decision at the top.
Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Those vaccines then protected the health of ordinary people across the world, again showing achievement turning into welfare.
Since welfare so often follows from achievement, looking at achievements lets us see the cause rather than only the effect.
Admittedly, the second view is right that achievements mean little if most people live in poverty or fear.
Consider a country that builds a famous space program while its rural hospitals lack basic medicines.
Few people would call such a nation great; its achievements would seem [[ostentatious|ostentatious]] rather than admirable.
Nevertheless, welfare alone is an incomplete measure, because a comfortable nation can enjoy high living standards without contributing anything that the rest of the world remembers or uses.
Welfare is therefore a necessary condition for greatness, but achievement is what distinguishes a great nation from a merely comfortable one.
In fact, the two views often point in the same direction, since great achievements usually spread their benefits over time.
This is why I accept the second view's warning but not its conclusion.
In conclusion, I side with the view that a nation's greatness is best judged by the achievements of its rulers, artists and scientists, as long as those achievements serve people.
Achievements reveal deep national capacities and often produce welfare, while the welfare view, though important, describes a minimum rather than greatness itself.
A great nation must care for its people, but it is remembered for what it gives the world.

words.meaning_here: try to equal or copy someone admired
major achievements that mark a turning point

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 treats the welfare view fairly (what it gets right) before explaining why achievement remains the closer measure; both views are named explicitly.

essays.title: General welfare is the surest test

paragraphs.text: A nation can win Nobel Prizes and build grand monuments while many of its children still go to bed hungry.
This contrast divides those who judge a nation by the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists from those who judge it by the general welfare of all its people.
My own position aligns more closely with the second view, because the well-being of ordinary citizens is a fuller and more [[equitable|equitable]] measure of greatness.
Welfare reflects how a nation treats everyone rather than a gifted few, it depends on the effort of the whole society, and although achievements matter, they count most when they improve welfare.
First, I side with the second view because general welfare shows how a nation treats all of its people, not just a celebrated few.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
This quiet achievement of public policy may never win a prize, yet it shapes the daily security of most Singaporean families more than any famous building could.
Similarly, Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession, so ordinary children are taught by highly trained professionals.
Such policies reveal a nation's character more truly than its elite triumphs, because they show what the nation provides to the [[layperson|layperson]] rather than to the exceptional.
Second, welfare is a more reliable indicator because it reflects sustained, broad effort rather than the [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] appearance of a genius.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
No single hero produced this result; it came from a policy and the cooperation of millions of ordinary riders.
In my work on dengue control, I have likewise seen that cases fall when whole communities clear standing water, not when one expert publishes a brilliant paper.
Because welfare depends on the efforts of an entire society, it measures the nation itself rather than a few exceptional individuals within it.
A genius may be born anywhere, but a healthy, educated population must be built.
Admittedly, the first view is right that the achievements of rulers and scientists can transform a nation and even the world.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign, an achievement of science and leadership that protected people everywhere.
Nevertheless, such achievements earn praise precisely because they improve general welfare, which shows that welfare remains the deeper standard.

Moreover, a nation can produce great minds without deserving credit for them: Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to [[recant|recant]] his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
Achievements, therefore, are best seen as means to welfare, and they reflect a nation's greatness only when they serve its people.
The first view captures part of the truth, but it does not identify the surest indicator.
In conclusion, the view that a nation's greatness lies in the general welfare of its people aligns more closely with my own than the view that celebrates its rulers, artists and scientists.
Welfare reflects how everyone is treated and depends on the effort of the whole society, while achievements matter mainly when they serve that welfare.
The surest sign of a great nation, then, is not a list of famous names but the ordinary lives of its citizens.

words.meaning_here: an ordinary person without special expertise or status
publicly take back a belief or statement

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the second view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 treats the achievement view fairly (smallpox) before explaining why welfare remains the deeper standard; both views are named explicitly.

essays.title: A society's heroes mirror its values

paragraphs.text: The statues in a city square often say more about the people who built them than about the figures they portray.
This idea underlies the claim that the best way to understand the character of a society is to examine the men and women it chooses as heroes or role models.
I largely agree with this claim, since a society's choice of heroes reveals its values, although those choices must be read alongside how the society actually behaves.

Heroes show what a society admires, changes in its heroes reveal how its values change, and the strongest challenge, that heroes reflect ideals rather than reality, refines but does not defeat the claim.
First, the claim holds because the heroes a society honors reveal the qualities it most admires.

In the United States, Abraham Lincoln is celebrated not only for leading the nation but also for appointing political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
That Americans [[venerate|venerate]] a leader partly for this choice suggests a society that values open debate and competence over personal loyalty.
A society that honored only wealthy or powerful figures, by contrast, would reveal very different priorities.
Similarly, in Vietnam, doctors who served poor rural communities are often held up as [[paragons|paragon]] for medical students, which reflects a cultural respect for service and sacrifice.
This shows that a society's heroes act as a mirror of its ideals, which supports the claim directly.
Second, changes in a society's heroes reveal how its character evolves over time.
Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.
Only after germ theory vindicated him, years after his death, did the medical world begin to [[lionize|lionize]] him, a shift that marked a new respect for evidence over tradition.
Likewise, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime but is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, which shows how artistic values have changed.
By tracing whom a society once ignored and now celebrates, we can follow the evolution of its character more clearly than through laws or statistics.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that heroes often represent what a society wishes to be, not what it actually is.
The United States celebrated scientific progress during the very decades when the Tuskegee syphilis study, from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
A visitor who studied only American scientific heroes would have missed this [[iniquity|iniquity]] entirely.
Nevertheless, this challenge shows that heroes must be interpreted carefully, not that they are irrelevant to understanding a society.
The gap between a society's heroes and its conduct is itself revealing, because it shows where the society falls short of its own ideals.
This challenge therefore qualifies my position: heroes are the best starting point for understanding a society, but they must be checked against how it treats its weakest members.
In conclusion, I largely agree that examining a society's heroes and role models is the best way to understand its character.
Heroes reveal what a society admires and how its values change, even though the gap between ideals and behavior requires careful interpretation.
To know a people, we should ask whom they honor, and then ask whether they live up to those heroes.

words.meaning_here: models of excellence to be imitated
treat as a celebrity or hero

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 support the claim, and Body 3 states the most compelling challenge (heroes show ideals, not conduct, as Tuskegee reveals) fairly and then answers it.

essays.title: How a society treats the weak reveals more

paragraphs.text: Every society praises its heroes, but praise costs little compared with the daily choices a society makes about how to live.
The claim nevertheless holds that the best way to understand a society's character is to examine the men and women it chooses as heroes or role models.
I mostly disagree: heroes reveal a society's ideals, but its true character is better shown by how it treats ordinary and vulnerable people.
Heroes often reflect flattering self-images, actual conduct toward the weak is more revealing, and while heroes do offer real clues, they are only a starting point.
First, heroes are an unreliable guide because societies often honor people whose values they fail to practice.
Ignaz Semmelweis, who in 1847 had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, saw deaths from childbed fever on his ward fall sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.
Today medicine honors him as a pioneer, yet in hospitals I have visited, busy staff still [[flout|flout]] his lesson by skipping hand washing between patients.
Honoring Semmelweis, in other words, has proved far easier than following him.
Similarly, a nation may celebrate famous acts of [[philanthropy|philanthropy]] while leaving its poorest citizens without basic care.
This shows that heroes reveal what a society claims to value, which can differ sharply from its real character.
Admiring a hero, after all, requires no sacrifice.
Second, a society's character is better revealed by how it treats its most vulnerable members.
From 1932 to 1972, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, a fact that no list of American heroes would reveal.
Yet the public outrage that followed, which led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people, also shows a society capable of correcting itself.

Likewise, the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, revealed both the injustice of segregation and the courage of ordinary citizens.
In my own work, I judge a health system less by its famous hospitals than by the care it gives to poor patients in remote districts.
Such episodes offer [[unequivocal|unequivocal]] evidence of a society's character in action, revealing both its failures and its capacity for reform.
Admittedly, the strongest challenge to my view is that heroes do reveal something real, because societies choose them deliberately.
In the United States, Abraham Lincoln is admired partly for appointing political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
This admiration suggests that many Americans value competence and open debate, which is useful information about their society.
Nevertheless, such admiration reveals ideals, and ideals are only half of character; the other half is conduct, which must be observed directly.
Heroes, therefore, are a helpful starting point, but they cannot be the best way to understand a society, since a society may [[venerate|venerate]] virtues it rarely practices.
To know whether a society truly lives by those ideals, we must look at its laws, its hospitals and its treatment of minorities.
This challenge qualifies my position without changing its direction.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that examining a society's heroes is the best way to understand its character.
Heroes often reflect flattering self-images, while a society's treatment of vulnerable people reveals its true values, even though heroes still offer useful clues.
To understand a society, we should look past its statues and examine its hospitals, schools and buses.

words.meaning_here: openly ignore a rule or principle

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 support the position, and Body 3 states the most compelling challenge (societies choose heroes deliberately, as Lincoln's reputation shows) fairly and then answers it.

essays.title: A semester abroad benefits nearly every student

paragraphs.text: Many of the most important lessons people learn come not from textbooks but from finding themselves in unfamiliar places.
For university students, a semester abroad is one of the few structured chances to have this experience before careers and families make long trips difficult.

I largely agree that all college students would benefit from spending at least one semester studying in a foreign country, as long as universities make such programs affordable and academically serious.

A semester abroad broadens students' professional perspective and builds the independence that every field requires, and although it is not right for every student at every moment, its benefits outweigh its costs for most.
First, studying abroad benefits students because it shows them that the methods they learned at home are only one way of solving a problem.
During my medical training in Vietnam, I assumed that the antibiotic habits I saw in local pharmacies were normal, since over-the-counter sales were common everywhere around me.

Only when I studied abroad alongside colleagues from countries with strict prescription rules did I fully understand that overuse helps resistant bacteria spread and that the [[status quo|status quo]] at home was a choice, not a law of nature.
Similarly, an engineering student who spends a semester in Japan or Germany may return with new ideas about quality control that no lecture at home had made vivid.
This shows that time abroad does more than add a line to a résumé; it allows students to compare systems, which is the first step toward correcting a [[myopic|myopic]] view of their own system.
Second, a semester in a foreign country benefits students because it forces them to become independent and adaptable.
Consider a student from a small town who has never managed her own budget, rented a room, or spoken a second language every day.
Abroad, she must solve these problems alone, and by the end of the term she has gained a confidence that is difficult to teach in a classroom.

Likewise, a business student who completes a group project with classmates from four countries learns to work across [[disparate|disparate]] habits and expectations, a skill that modern international teams demand.

Therefore, the benefit of studying abroad is not limited to language students or future diplomats; adaptability is useful to nurses, accountants and scientists alike, which supports the statement's claim that "all" students would gain.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for every student at every moment, since some face financial, family or academic constraints that make a semester abroad [[prohibitive|prohibitive]].
A medical student in the middle of required clinical rotations, or a working parent studying part-time, may lose more than he or she gains by leaving for four months.
Nevertheless, these cases argue for better program design rather than against the value of the experience itself.
Universities can offer scholarships, shorter summer terms, or partnerships that allow credits to transfer, so that the most constrained students are not excluded.

Thus, the exceptions [[qualify|qualify]] my position rather than overturn it: nearly every student would benefit, but whether each one actually can go depends on how well institutions remove the barriers.
In conclusion, a semester abroad is valuable for almost every university student, provided that cost and scheduling do not make it an unfair burden.
It broadens professional perspective and builds independence, and its main drawbacks can be reduced through thoughtful policy.
Universities that wish to prepare graduates for an interconnected world should therefore treat study abroad not as a luxury for the few but as an opportunity open to all.

so costly or difficult that it prevents action
