essays.title: Study abroad helps many, but not all

paragraphs.text: Travel is often described as the best teacher, and few people would deny that living abroad can change a young person's outlook.
Yet the claim that every college and university student would benefit from a semester in a foreign country goes much further than this familiar idea.
I mostly disagree with the statement, because the benefits of studying abroad depend heavily on a student's field, finances and goals, although the experience is clearly valuable for many.
The cost is too high for some students and comparable learning is often available at home; moreover, while study abroad clearly helps students in certain fields, this does not justify the word "all."
First, the statement fails to hold for many students because the cost of a semester abroad can outweigh its benefits.
Consider a first-generation student from a rural province in Vietnam whose family has borrowed money to pay her tuition.

For her, a semester in Australia or France would mean extra debt, lost income from a part-time job, and perhaps a delayed graduation, and the stress could [[undermine|undermine]] her academic performance.
Similarly, a nursing student who must complete a fixed sequence of supervised clinical hours may find that foreign courses do not count toward a license at home.
These cases show that the benefit is not automatic; for students with [[scant|scant]] resources or rigid programs, the costs may be greater than the gains.
A universal expectation to go abroad would therefore burden exactly the students who can least afford it.
Moreover, many of the advantages attributed to studying abroad can be gained without leaving one's country.
In my work as an epidemiologist, I have learned a great deal from international collaborators through joint projects, online meetings and conferences, without ever enrolling in a foreign university.
Students today can similarly join global research teams, take online courses offered by foreign universities, or work with international classmates on their own campus.
Likewise, a Vietnamese pharmacy student can learn how other countries regulate antibiotic sales through an international online course or a visiting lecturer, without paying for a semester overseas.

Therefore, a semester abroad is one useful route to a broad education, but it is far from the only one; for a student who already gains that perspective at home, a semester abroad may add little beyond expense, so the claim that all students would benefit is [[tenuous|tenuous]].
Admittedly, for students in some fields, the statement holds true, and a semester abroad is almost essential.
A student of French literature or international relations gains fluency and cultural understanding abroad that no classroom can fully replace.
Likewise, a future diplomat needs direct exposure to other political systems.
Nevertheless, the success of study abroad in these fields does not mean it will produce the same results for a chemistry major or a future accountant.

These examples [[qualify|qualify]] my position: study abroad should be strongly encouraged where it is clearly relevant, but the word "all" in the statement turns a good option into an [[onerous|onerous]] expectation for students whose needs lie elsewhere.
In conclusion, while studying abroad can be a valuable experience, it is not something from which every university student would benefit.
For many students the financial and academic costs are too high, similar learning is available at home, and the clear benefits in some fields cannot be generalized to all.
Universities should therefore offer study abroad as a well-supported choice rather than present it as a universal good.

words.meaning_here: burdensome and difficult to carry out

essays.title: Preserve wilderness; develop only at the edges

paragraphs.text: Once a forest is cut down or a river is dammed, it may take centuries to recover, if it recovers at all.
This simple fact lies at the heart of the debate over whether governments should preserve wilderness areas in their natural state or develop them for potential economic gain.
I side largely with the first view, that wilderness should generally be preserved, although I accept that limited development can be justified when it clearly serves people's basic needs.

Preservation protects benefits that markets fail to value and keeps options open for future generations, and although the second view rightly stresses economic needs, these needs can usually be met in other ways.
First, governments should preserve wilderness because natural areas provide services that are essential but rarely appear in economic calculations.
Forests filter water, store carbon, and control floods, yet a logging company counts only the value of the timber it sells.

When upland forests are cleared, communities downstream often face worse floods and landslides, and the government may later have to pay for repairs that exceed the [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] profits of the logging.
Similarly, as an epidemiologist I know that clearing forests can bring people into closer contact with wild animals and the diseases they carry.
This shows that the second view, applied without limits, is [[myopic|myopic]]: it counts the profits of development but ignores its hidden costs.
A government that overlooks these costs is not creating wealth but simply passing the bill to its citizens.
Second, preservation is the wiser choice because development is usually irreversible, whereas preservation keeps future options open.
Consider the history of medicine: many important drugs, from antibiotics to cancer treatments, were first found in molds, plants and soil microbes that live in nature.
A rainforest that is destroyed today may contain compounds that future scientists will never have the chance to study.
Likewise, a protected national park can always be opened to careful use later, but a mine or a highway cannot easily be undone.
Therefore, when the value of an area is uncertain, the [[prudent|prudent]] policy is to preserve it, since only preservation allows a future government to choose differently.
Admittedly, the second view gets something important right: people living near wilderness areas need jobs, roads and income, and strict preservation can leave them in poverty.

Vietnam's own history shows how economic growth can transform lives, since the Doi Moi reforms helped a country that had faced food shortages become one of the world's largest rice exporters and reduced poverty dramatically.
Nevertheless, that growth came mainly from market incentives for farmers and businesses, not from destroying the country's last wild places.
Moreover, protected areas can themselves generate income through tourism and research, often for the same communities that live nearby.

Thus, the economic concerns of the second view are legitimate, but they [[militate|militate]] for careful, limited development at the edges of wilderness rather than for opening it entirely to profit.
In conclusion, I believe governments should, as a rule, keep wilderness areas in their natural state, while allowing limited development where the need is real and the damage is small.
Natural areas provide hidden but essential services, their loss is usually permanent, and the economic benefits stressed by the second view can be gained in less destructive ways.
A nation that sells its wilderness for short-term profit may find that it has [[forfeited|forfeit]] something no amount of money can buy back.

words.meaning_here: careful and wise about future risks
serve as a strong reason (for or against something)
lost as a consequence of one's own action

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Bodies 1-2 support preservation, and Body 3 fairly credits the second view's economic concerns before explaining why preservation is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Careful development serves people and nature

paragraphs.text: For millions of families in developing countries, the most pressing question is not how to protect nature but how to earn a stable living.
This reality complicates the debate over whether a government should preserve its wilderness areas in their natural state or develop them for economic gain.
I side more closely with the second view, that wilderness areas may be developed for economic gain, provided that development is planned carefully and the most valuable ecosystems are protected.

Responsible development can lift people out of poverty and can even fund the protection that preservation requires, and although the first view rightly warns against irreversible damage, a strict ban on development is rarely the best answer.
First, developing some wilderness areas is justified because economic growth is one of the most powerful ways to improve people's lives.

After Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms in 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Growth on that scale inevitably requires land for farms, roads and ports, and some of that land must come from areas that were once wild.
Similarly, a poor mountain district that builds a road through a forest may give farmers access to markets and children access to schools and clinics.

These cases show that the economic gain stressed by the second view is not mere [[avarice|avarice]]; for poor nations, it often means food, health and education, and denying it in the name of preservation would be unfair.
Second, carefully managed development can actually pay for conservation, whereas untouched wilderness often lacks the money to protect itself.
Consider a national park in a low-income country that has no budget for rangers, so illegal logging and hunting continue and the area is "preserved" only on paper.
If part of the land is opened to eco-tourism, the fees can pay for patrols and give local people a reason to [[champion|champion]] protection rather than resist it.
Likewise, revenue from a regulated mine or dam can be used to restore damaged land elsewhere.
Therefore, the choice is not simply between preservation and destruction; [[judicious|judicious]] development can produce the resources that make real preservation [[feasible|feasible]].
Preservation that exists only on paper protects nothing.
Admittedly, the first view is right that some development causes damage that can never be reversed, and governments have often underestimated these costs.
Clearing forests can bring people into closer contact with wild animals and the diseases they carry, and an ancient forest, once gone, cannot be replaced within a single lifetime.
Nevertheless, this danger argues for careful selection and strict rules, not for treating every wild area as untouchable.
A government can fully protect watersheds and rare habitats while allowing development on land of lower ecological value.

Thus, the warning of the first view [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: development is justified only where its benefits clearly outweigh its permanent costs, and the most valuable areas must stay untouched.
In conclusion, I believe that wilderness areas can and often should be developed for economic gain, so long as governments protect the ecosystems that matter most.
Development can reduce poverty, generate money for conservation, and, when guided by the legitimate concerns of the first view, avoid the worst forms of damage.
The goal should not be to keep nature untouched at any human cost, but to use it wisely so that both people and ecosystems benefit.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the second view, Bodies 1-2 support careful development, and Body 3 credits the first view's warning about irreversible damage before explaining why development remains closer to the author's position.

essays.title: Imagination turns knowledge into progress

paragraphs.text: Every major advance begins with someone asking a question that no one else thought to ask.
This observation is central to the claim that, in most professions and academic fields, imagination matters more than knowledge.

I largely agree with the claim, because knowledge becomes valuable mainly when imagination puts it to new use, although imagination without a solid base of knowledge is often useless or even dangerous.

Imagination drives discovery and solves problems that existing knowledge cannot, and while the strongest challenge to my view is that some fields reward accuracy above originality, even those fields depend on imaginative leaps.
First, imagination is more important than knowledge because it is the source of new discoveries, while knowledge alone only records what is already known.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis imagined that doctors' own hands might be spreading childbed fever, and he had them wash their hands in chlorinated lime.
Deaths on his ward fell sharply, yet most of his colleagues, who possessed the standard medical knowledge of the time, [[dismissed|dismiss]] his idea.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 while many better-educated people doubted that such flight was possible.
These cases show that knowledge can even become an obstacle when it hardens into [[dogma|dogma]], and that imagination is what allows a person to see beyond it.
In both cases, the people with the most knowledge were not the ones who moved their fields forward.
Second, in everyday professional work, imagination allows people to solve problems for which no textbook provides an answer.
In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, the standard approach is to spray insecticide and remove standing water, yet outbreaks return every year.

Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, required researchers to imagine fighting mosquitoes with mosquitoes, and a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, showed that the method cut dengue cases by 77%.
Likewise, a teacher who invents a game to explain fractions often reaches students whom a perfectly accurate lecture had left behind.
Thus, in fields from public health to education, knowledge defines the problem, but imagination produces the [[novel|novel]] solution.
Without that imaginative leap, the standard knowledge would simply have produced more of the same results.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that in fields such as surgery, accounting or engineering, an imaginative professional who lacks knowledge can cause serious harm.
A pilot who improvises instead of following checklists, or a pharmacist who guesses at doses, puts lives at risk, and no one wants a creative bridge that collapses.
Nevertheless, this challenge shows that knowledge is necessary, not that it is more important.
A surgeon, for example, needs [[meticulous|meticulous]] knowledge of anatomy, but the surgeons who develop safer operations are those who imagine new ways to use that knowledge.
Therefore, knowledge is the foundation every professional must build, while imagination decides what is built on it; in that sense, imagination remains the scarcer and more decisive quality.
In conclusion, I largely agree that imagination is more important than knowledge in most fields, as long as it is grounded in [[empirical|empirical]] understanding.
Imagination drives discovery, it solves problems that standard knowledge cannot, and even in fields that demand precision, it decides how knowledge is used.
Schools and employers that reward only memorization therefore risk producing experts who know a great deal but rarely create anything new.

essays.title: Knowledge makes imagination useful and safe

paragraphs.text: Popular culture likes to [[lionize|lionize]] the lone genius whose sudden flash of inspiration changes the world.
This image lies behind the claim that, in most professions and academic fields, imagination is more important than knowledge.
I disagree with the claim, because in most fields knowledge is what makes imagination useful and safe, although imagination plays a vital role at the frontiers of a discipline.

Most professional work depends on reliable knowledge, and even celebrated acts of imagination grew out of deep expertise; while the strongest challenge to my view comes from famous breakthroughs, these are exceptions rather than the rule.
First, knowledge is more important than imagination because most professional work requires the accurate application of what is already known.

When a patient arrives at a district hospital with severe dengue, the physician does not need a creative new treatment; she needs to recognize the warning signs, give fluids at the right rate, and monitor the patient closely.
In this setting, an imaginative but poorly informed doctor would be dangerous, while a knowledgeable one saves lives every day.

Similarly, when the sedative thalidomide caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, it was the expert caution of Frances Kelsey of the US FDA that kept the drug from being approved in the United States.
These cases show that in medicine, engineering, law and many other professions, knowledge is not a [[pedestrian|pedestrian]] substitute for imagination but the core of competence.
Second, even the achievements usually [[ascribed|ascribe]] to imagination depend on deep knowledge.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, which may look like a stroke of inspiration, but they were possible only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Their insight was imaginative, but it became useful only through long and careful experimental work.
Without that patient accumulation of knowledge, no amount of imagination could have produced a vaccine so quickly.
Likewise, Marie Curie's Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry rested on [[assiduous|assiduous]] laboratory work, not on intuition alone.
Thus, imagination is most productive in a mind already [[steeped|steeped]] in its field; knowledge comes first and makes meaningful imagination possible.
Imagination, in other words, works with the material that knowledge supplies.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that some breakthroughs came from people who imagined what experts considered impossible.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903, and Ignaz Semmelweis's idea of handwashing was rejected by colleagues who relied on established medical knowledge.
Nevertheless, these examples are less damaging to my view than they first appear.
The Wright brothers succeeded only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, which means they created new knowledge rather than ignoring it.
Such cases show that imagination matters at rare turning points, but they do not show that it outweighs knowledge in the daily work of "most professions," which is what the claim asserts.
In conclusion, while imagination has a real place in every field, knowledge is the more important quality in most professions and academic disciplines.
Most work demands accurate knowledge, celebrated breakthroughs rest on long study, and even the famous counterexamples reveal the value of careful learning.
Students who hope to be creative should therefore begin by mastering their field, because imagination without knowledge is merely guessing.

showing great care and persistent effort

essays.title: Greatness shows in how ordinary people live

paragraphs.text: Visitors to a capital city often admire its monuments, museums and universities, but they rarely see how ordinary families live a few miles away.
This gap explains why some argue that the surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists, but the general well-being of all its people.
I largely agree with the claim, because a nation's greatness should be judged by how it treats most of its citizens, although remarkable achievements often contribute to that well-being.

Widespread well-being reflects the quality of a nation's institutions, and the achievements of a few can hide the hardship of many; while the strongest challenge is that great achievements benefit everyone, their value is best measured by that very benefit.
First, the general well-being of a people is the best indicator of greatness because it reflects choices a nation makes for everyone, not only for an elite.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms in 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters while poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
This change was not the work of one brilliant leader or scientist but of policies that allowed millions of ordinary farmers and workers to improve their lives.
Similarly, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.

These cases show that broad well-being results from institutions that serve citizens in a fairly [[egalitarian|egalitarian]] way, and such institutions, more than individual stars, are what make a nation great.
Second, the achievements of rulers, artists and scientists can be a misleading measure, since they may coexist with widespread suffering.

Throughout history, empires have built [[lavish|lavish]] palaces and funded great art while many of their subjects lived in poverty, paying heavy taxes to support the splendor that later visitors admire.
Such monuments tell us about the ambitions of rulers but very little about the lives of the people who built them.

Likewise, a country may produce famous scientists while its rural clinics lack basic medicines, a [[discrepancy|discrepancy]] that anyone working in public health in a developing country will recognize.
Therefore, judging a nation only by its achievements risks praising an [[ostentatious|ostentatious]] surface while ignoring the reality beneath it.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that great achievements often create the conditions for general well-being.
When smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign, the work of scientists and health leaders improved the lives of ordinary people everywhere.
Nevertheless, this example actually supports my view, since we honor such achievements precisely because they improved the lives of ordinary people.
By contrast, a grand stadium or a prestige project that does nothing for health or education may impress foreign observers while the population gains little.

In other words, achievements matter, but their value is best measured by how widely their benefits are shared, which makes general well-being the more reliable indicator, and indeed the "surest" one, as the claim states.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the general well-being of a nation's people is the surest sign of its greatness.

Well-being reflects the quality of national institutions, achievements can hide widespread hardship, and even the greatest achievements earn their value through the benefits they bring to ordinary citizens.
A nation that wishes to be great should therefore measure its success not only in medals and monuments but in the health, education and security of its people.

words.meaning_here: a gap between two things that should match

essays.task_note: Body 3 addresses the most compelling challenge, that great achievements produce well-being, and turns it into support by arguing such achievements are valued for their shared benefits.

essays.title: Well-being is a foundation, not the measure

paragraphs.text: When people think of ancient Greece or Renaissance Italy, they remember philosophers, painters and scientists, not the average income of farmers.
This fact challenges the claim that the surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists, but the general well-being of all its people.

I mostly disagree with the claim, because general well-being, though essential, is a foundation of greatness rather than its surest indicator, and greatness is better revealed by achievements that benefit people far beyond a nation's borders.

Well-being alone cannot distinguish great nations from merely comfortable ones, and achievements often produce benefits for the whole world; while the strongest challenge is that achievements built on suffering are hollow, this concern does not make well-being the surest indicator.
First, the well-being of a population, by itself, does not distinguish a great nation from one that is merely comfortable.
Several small, wealthy countries offer their citizens excellent health care and high incomes, yet they rarely shape the course of science, politics or culture beyond their borders.
Their success is [[laudable|laudable]], but we would hesitate to call every prosperous nation "great" in the historical sense.
Similarly, a person may be healthy and secure without having done anything remarkable; we admire her good fortune, but we do not call her great.
This shows that well-being is a necessary condition of a good society, but greatness implies something more: a contribution that others recognize and [[emulate|emulate]].
Second, the achievements of a nation's scientists and leaders can benefit humanity far more than the comfort of its own citizens.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, so its value reaches laboratories everywhere.
Likewise, GPS was built by the US military, and once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
In Vietnam, where I work, millions of motorbike riders and delivery drivers now depend on this technology every day.
Therefore, such achievements reveal a nation's greatness more clearly than its average living standards, because their benefits are not confined to its own people.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that achievements built on the suffering of ordinary people do not deserve to be called great.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent from 1932 to 1972, shows how scientific ambition can ignore human dignity.
Nevertheless, this concern shows that achievements must be judged by ethical standards, not that general well-being is the surest measure of greatness.
Indeed, the public outrage over Tuskegee led to US rules requiring ethics review boards, so that research could continue while protecting the people who take part in it.
A nation that pursues ambitious science while protecting its citizens displays greatness in both senses, so well-being [[qualifies|qualify]] the value of achievement rather than replacing it.
In conclusion, although the well-being of all citizens is a vital goal, I do not believe it is the surest indicator of national greatness.
Comfort alone does not set a nation apart, achievements can benefit all of humanity, and the danger of unethical ambition calls for limits on achievement rather than its dismissal.
The greatest nations, in my view, are those that care for their own people while also creating knowledge and tools from which the whole world can [[reap|reap]] benefits.

words.meaning_here: imitate in order to match or surpass
receive as a result of others' effort

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (achievements built on suffering, as at Tuskegee) and answers that it calls for ethical limits on achievement, not for making well-being the surest measure.

essays.title: Leaders must compete, and cooperate to win

paragraphs.text: Few people reach the top of any field without wanting very badly to win.

This observation supports one side of the debate over whether successful leaders in government, industry and other fields must be highly competitive or must instead be willing and able to cooperate with others.

I side more closely with the first view, that successful leaders must be highly competitive, although the best leaders aim that competitiveness at rivals and goals rather than at their own colleagues.

Competitiveness drives leaders to outperform rivals and pushes organizations to keep improving, and while the second view rightly stresses cooperation, cooperation usually serves as a tool of competitive leaders rather than a replacement for their drive.
First, leaders must be competitive because in most fields success is measured against rivals.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Its leaders were too comfortable with their position to compete hard in the new market that their own company had helped create.
Similarly, a laboratory director who does not compete hard for grants may watch a less talented but more [[ardent|ardent]] rival win both the funding and the best young scientists.
These cases show that a leader who lacks competitive drive can lead even a strong organization into decline, which supports the first view.
In a market or a grant competition, good intentions cannot replace the will to win.
Second, competitive leaders push their organizations to keep improving instead of settling for the [[status quo|status quo]].
In public health, provincial programs often improve their vaccination coverage once their results are compared publicly with those of neighboring provinces.
A director who wants to rank first will push staff to find missed children and fix weak clinics, while a less competitive peer may accept modest results year after year.
Likewise, companies whose leaders fear falling behind tend to invest in new products before competitors force them to.
Thus, competitiveness is not merely a personal trait; it [[galvanizes|galvanize]] whole teams and creates the pressure that drives progress.
A leader without this drive may keep an organization stable, but rarely makes it better.
Admittedly, the second view is right that no leader can succeed alone, and a leader who treats colleagues as rivals may destroy the trust an organization needs.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, and this cooperation strengthened his government.
Nevertheless, Lincoln's choice was itself a competitive strategy, since he gathered the most capable people available in order to succeed at the hardest tasks of his presidency.
Similarly, a business leader who forms a partnership with a rival company usually does so to defeat a larger competitor, not out of kindness.

This example shows that the best leaders cooperate in order to compete more effectively; cooperation is a means, but the drive to win remains the [[cardinal|cardinal]] quality that the first view identifies.
In conclusion, I believe successful leaders must be highly competitive, provided that their competitiveness is aimed at rivals and goals rather than at their own teams.
Competitiveness helps organizations outperform rivals and keeps them improving, and, as Lincoln's example suggests, even cooperation is often a competitive tool.
Organizations choosing leaders should therefore look for people who hate to lose but know that they cannot win alone.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the competitive view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 credits the cooperation view through Lincoln before arguing that cooperation serves competition.

essays.title: Cooperation is the core of leadership

paragraphs.text: The image of a leader as a lone hero who defeats every rival is attractive, but it rarely matches how great things are actually achieved.
This tension lies at the center of the debate over whether successful leaders must be highly competitive or must be willing and able to cooperate with others.
I side more closely with the second view, that cooperation is essential to successful leadership, although I accept that some competitive drive helps leaders set ambitious goals.

Cooperation allows leaders to solve problems that no single group can solve and builds the trust that keeps organizations strong, and while the first view rightly notes that leaders face real rivals, competition works best within a framework of cooperation.
First, cooperation is essential because the largest problems leaders face cannot be solved by any one organization or nation alone.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Had each nation's health leaders competed for prestige or kept supplies for themselves, the virus could have survived in the gaps between them.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
These cases show that, in government and science, the leaders who achieve the most are those who can unite [[disparate|disparate]] partners around a shared goal, as the second view claims.
Second, leaders who cooperate earn the trust and loyalty that allow their organizations to endure.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Rather than treating them as enemies, he drew on their talents, turning potential opponents into partners in government.
Likewise, in the research teams I have worked with, the investigators who share credit generously tend to keep their best staff, while [[pugnacious|pugnacious]] leaders lose them to other groups.
Thus, cooperation is not a sign of weakness but a source of strength, because it turns talented people into allies instead of rivals.
A leader who cannot cooperate may win individual contests but will struggle to keep the people needed to win the next one.
Admittedly, the first view captures something real: leaders in business and politics face genuine rivals, and a leader without competitive drive may let an organization fall behind.

Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography even though its own engineer, Steven Sasson, had invented the digital camera, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure came less from a lack of competitiveness than from an [[intransigent|intransigent]] attachment to its old business and a failure to listen to its own engineer.
A more cooperative leadership, open to ideas from within, might have recognized the value of Sasson's invention much earlier.
Therefore, competitiveness is useful, but it succeeds only when it rests on cooperation inside an organization, which is why the second view more closely matches my own.
In conclusion, while a competitive spirit has its place, I believe that the ability to cooperate is the more essential quality of a successful leader.
Cooperation solves problems too large for any one group, earns lasting loyalty, and even makes competition effective, as the failure of Kodak suggests.
Leaders who see colleagues and even rivals as potential partners are therefore more likely to reach goals that [[outstrip|outstrip]] what any competitor could achieve alone.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the cooperation view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 fairly credits the competitive view through Kodak before explaining why cooperation is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Job prospects should guide most students' choices

paragraphs.text: A university degree is one of the largest investments that many young people and their families will ever make.
For this reason, some argue that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.

I largely agree with this recommendation, since job prospects deserve a central place in that choice, although they should be weighed alongside a student's abilities and interests rather than considered alone.

Adopting the recommendation is advantageous when students face financial pressure and when a field's job market is clearly shrinking, but it is less advantageous for a student with exceptional talent in a field with few openings.
First, basing a field of study on job availability is clearly advantageous when students and their families face financial pressure.
Consider a student from a low-income family in rural Vietnam whose parents have borrowed money to pay her tuition.

If she chooses nursing or information technology, fields with steady demand, she can repay the loan and support her family within a few years, whereas a degree in a crowded field might leave her unemployed and in debt.
Similarly, in countries where student loans are large, graduates in fields with few jobs often spend years in work unrelated to their degrees.

In such circumstances, following the job market is not a betrayal of one's interests but a [[prudent|prudent]] response to real constraints, which supports the recommendation, at least for students in her position.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous when a field's job market is clearly shrinking, because students who ignore such signals may train for careers that are becoming [[obsolete|obsolete]].
Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
A student who trained for a career in film processing during those years would have found that her skills had little value by graduation.
By contrast, students who chose fields linked to growing technologies, such as data analysis, found their skills in high demand.
In this circumstance, paying attention to job availability helps students avoid investing years in knowledge that is quickly turning into an [[anachronism|anachronism]].
Choosing a field without checking its future is like investing in a company without reading its accounts.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous for every student, particularly one with exceptional talent in a field with few jobs.

Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history; a strict focus on job prospects might have [[squelched|squelch]] such talent.
Nevertheless, such cases are rare, and most students cannot know in advance whether they possess unusual gifts.
Moreover, a student who loves a field with few openings can still combine it with practical skills, for example by pairing painting with graphic design.
These exceptions [[qualify|qualify]] my position: job availability should be the main, but not the only, factor, especially for students without financial security.
In conclusion, I largely agree that college students should base their choice of field on job availability, while still considering their talents and interests.
This approach is clearly advantageous for students under financial pressure and for those facing shrinking fields, though it may hold back the rare student whose gifts lie in a field with few jobs.
Students should therefore ask not only what they love, but also whether that love can support the life they hope to build.

words.meaning_here: wise and careful about the future
something belonging to an earlier time

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 describe circumstances where adopting the recommendation is advantageous (financial pressure, shrinking fields) and Body 3 a circumstance where it is not (exceptional talent), explaining how each shapes the position.

essays.title: Choose by ability, not this year's job list

paragraphs.text: Many students choose their majors by reading lists of the "best jobs of the year," hoping to secure a comfortable future.
This habit reflects the recommendation that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.

I largely disagree with this recommendation, because job markets change too quickly to predict and students perform best in fields that suit their abilities, although job prospects deserve some weight when finances are tight.

Following job availability is disadvantageous when the market changes before students graduate and when it pushes students into fields that do not match their strengths; still, it can help students with heavy financial obligations.
First, adopting the recommendation would be disadvantageous whenever job markets shift faster than students can complete a degree.

Consider a student who enters a four-year program because a particular field is booming, only to find at graduation that many others have made the same choice and employers are [[inundated|inundate]] with applicants.
The "available" jobs that guided her decision have vanished, and she has spent years on a subject she never enjoyed.

Similarly, when GPS was built by the US military, no student could have predicted that it would later support ride-hailing and delivery apps, creating whole categories of jobs that did not exist before.
These examples show that today's job market is a poor guide to tomorrow's, so basing a lifelong choice on it is a [[precarious|precarious]] strategy.
Second, the recommendation would be disadvantageous when it pushes students away from fields where their talents and interests lie.

In medical school in Vietnam, I knew classmates who had chosen medicine mainly because their families saw it as a secure career, and some of them were [[listless|listless]] and unhappy in clinical work.
Meanwhile, classmates who were genuinely curious about disease went on to research and public health careers they had not even known existed when they enrolled.
Likewise, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, pursued their fascination with flight long before anyone could have called it a career.
Thus, interest and ability often create opportunities, whereas a field chosen only for its jobs may produce a competent but uninspired worker, a poor outcome for both the student and the employer.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which following job availability is advantageous, especially for students whose families depend on their income soon after graduation.
A student from a poor rural family who has borrowed heavily for tuition may reasonably choose nursing over philosophy, since nursing offers steady demand and a quicker path to repaying the debt.
Nevertheless, even in this case, the student would be wise to choose, among several employable fields, the one that best fits her abilities rather than simply the one with the most openings.
For instance, she might choose among nursing, pharmacy and public health according to which one best matches her strengths and temperament.
This circumstance [[qualifies|qualify]] my view: job prospects may [[delimit|delimit]] the range of choices, but they should not decide the final choice on their own.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that students should base their choice of field mainly on job availability.
Job markets change too quickly to predict, and students thrive in fields that suit them, though financial pressure can justify giving job prospects greater weight.
The wiser approach is to choose a field one can do well and enjoy, and then to build the practical skills that make any field employable.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 describe circumstances where adopting the recommendation is disadvantageous (shifting markets, mismatched talents) and Body 3 a circumstance where it helps (financial pressure), explaining how it shapes the position.

essays.title: Companies owe society more than profit

paragraphs.text: A factory may obey every law and still leave a river polluted, a town unhealthy, and its workers exhausted.

This possibility is at the heart of the debate over whether corporations have a responsibility to promote the well-being of their societies and environments, or whether their only responsibility, within the law, is to make as much money as possible.
I side more closely with the first view, that corporations have responsibilities beyond profit, although I agree with the second view that profit remains their primary purpose.

Laws cannot anticipate every harm a company may cause, and corporations depend on healthy societies; while the second view rightly warns that social goals can distract a business, responsible conduct usually serves long-term profit as well.
First, corporations must look beyond profit because the law alone cannot prevent all the harm they can cause.

Antibiotic resistance is a clear case: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
A pharmacy chain that pushes antibiotic sales as far as local law allows may earn more money, but it [[exacerbates|exacerbate]] a crisis that will harm millions.
Similarly, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe before stricter drug-testing rules existed.
These cases show that laws often follow harm rather than prevent it, so a company that recognizes only legal duties may cause [[grievous|grievous]] damage before society can respond.
Second, corporations have a responsibility to society because their own success depends on a healthy population and a stable environment.
A company cannot find skilled workers if local schools are poor, and it cannot sell products to customers who are sick or impoverished.
Firms that support training programs, safe working conditions and clean water are therefore investing in the conditions that make their business possible.
Likewise, a garment factory that provides safe conditions and reasonable working hours tends to keep experienced workers longer, which lowers its training costs and protects its own operations.
Thus, promoting social well-being is not charity [[antithetical|antithetical]] to business but part of a [[sound|sound]] long-term strategy.
Companies that ignore this connection may profit for a few years, but they weaken the society that sustains them.
Admittedly, the second view has a point: a corporation is not a government, and managers who pursue social causes may waste shareholders' money on projects they are not qualified to run.
A company that donates heavily to [[modish|modish]] causes while its products decline in quality may end up helping no one, including the employees who lose their jobs when it fails.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for focused responsibility, not for abandoning responsibility altogether.
A pharmaceutical firm need not build schools, but it should avoid encouraging the misuse of its drugs.
Therefore, the second view correctly reminds us that profit is necessary, but it fails to recognize that a company's duties extend at least to the harms connected to its own products and operations.
In conclusion, I believe corporations do have a responsibility to promote the well-being of their societies and environments, even though making a profit remains central to their purpose.
Laws cannot prevent every harm, companies depend on healthy communities, and the second view's warning about distraction calls for focus rather than indifference.
The most admirable companies, therefore, are those that make money in ways that leave their communities stronger rather than weaker.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Bodies 1-2 support corporate social responsibility, and Body 3 credits the second view's warning about distraction before explaining why the first view is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Profit within strong laws serves society best

paragraphs.text: When a company announces a new charity campaign, customers often applaud, but they rarely ask who pays for it.

This question is central to the debate over whether corporations have a responsibility to promote the well-being of society and the environment, or whether their only responsibility, within the law, is to make as much money as possible.

I side more closely with the second view, that a corporation's main responsibility is to make money within the law, although the law itself must be strong enough to protect society and the environment.

Profit-seeking firms already benefit society by creating jobs and products, and social goals are better set by elected governments than by managers; while the first view rightly notes that laws can lag behind harm, the answer is better laws rather than vague corporate duties.
First, corporations serve society best by doing what they do well: producing goods and services that people want and earning a profit.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms in 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters while poverty fell dramatically.
This progress came largely from farmers and firms pursuing profit, not from businesses trying to act as social agencies.
Similarly, once GPS was opened to civilians, private companies built navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps that created jobs and convenience for millions of people.
These cases show that the pursuit of profit, within fair rules, often promotes social well-being as a natural result, which [[belies|belie]] the idea that profit and the public good are opposed.
Second, decisions about society's priorities belong to elected governments, not to corporate managers who answer to no voters.
When managers spend company money on causes they personally favor, they are in effect taxing shareholders, employees and customers without their consent.
One executive may support environmental programs, another a political cause that many employees [[abhor|abhor]], and neither has any public mandate.

By contrast, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, because the rule applied to everyone at once.
Thus, clear laws applied equally to all firms and citizens protect the public more effectively and more fairly than a [[hodgepodge|hodgepodge]] of corporate good intentions.
Admittedly, the first view is right that laws often lag behind harm, and companies can cause great damage before the rules catch up.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe before the US passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Nevertheless, this tragedy shows the need for stronger regulation rather than for vague moral duties that each company can interpret however it wishes.
Indeed, it was a regulator, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA, who refused to approve the drug, and the law then changed to protect everyone.

Therefore, the first view identifies a real problem, but the solution lies in vigilant governments, a point that [[qualifies|qualify]] my position only by making the phrase "within the law" more demanding.
In conclusion, I believe that a corporation's chief responsibility is to make money within the law, provided that the law is strong and up to date.

Profit-seeking firms already create widespread benefits, social priorities belong to accountable governments, and the risk that laws will lag behind harm calls for better regulation rather than corporate moralizing.
Citizens who want responsible companies should therefore focus less on corporate promises and more on the laws that hold all companies to the same standard.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the profit view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 fairly grants the first view's point that laws lag behind harm before arguing that stronger laws, not vague duties, are the answer.

essays.title: Basic research pays off in unexpected ways

paragraphs.text: Some of the most useful discoveries in history were made by people who were looking for something else.

This pattern supports the claim that researchers should not limit their investigations to areas in which they expect an immediate, practical application, as well as the reason offered for it: that the outcome of research cannot be predicted with any certainty.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, although the reason is slightly overstated and some research should still be directed toward urgent practical needs.

The claim is supported by the long-term value of basic research and the reason is largely true because research outcomes are often unpredictable; while the strongest objection is that limited funds should address pressing problems, a balance of both kinds of research serves society best.
First, the claim is sound, because research without an obvious immediate use often produces the most valuable results in the long run.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Had funders supported only projects with obvious applications, that work might never have been done, and the world would have faced the pandemic without its fastest vaccines.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, creating a resource whose uses extend far beyond what its planners could list.

These cases show that limiting research to immediate applications would be [[myopic|myopic]] and even [[counterproductive|counterproductive]], since the most important applications often appear only decades later.
Second, the reason on which the claim is based is largely true, since the outcome of research is often impossible to foresee.

In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, a discovery he had not set out to make, and penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
Neither the original observation nor its eventual use could have been planned in advance.
Likewise, GPS was built by the US military, yet its greatest everyday impact came only after it was opened to civilians and became the basis of navigation and delivery apps.
Thus, the reason [[buttresses|buttress]] the claim well: if outcomes cannot be foreseen, then restricting research to predictable applications means losing many unexpected ones.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that funding is limited and that urgent problems, such as drug-resistant infections, demand research aimed at practical results.

As an epidemiologist, I know that antibiotic resistance is spreading, partly because of overuse and over-the-counter sales in countries such as Vietnam, and patients cannot wait decades for basic science to pay off.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for a balance, not for limiting all research to immediate applications.

Moreover, the reason should be qualified slightly: the results of some studies, such as a well-designed drug trial, can be anticipated with reasonable confidence, which is why applied research also deserves support.
Therefore, I agree with the claim and largely with its reason, while recognizing that a [[judicious|judicious]] research system funds both curiosity-driven and problem-driven work.

In conclusion, I agree that researchers should not restrict themselves to areas with immediate, practical applications, and I accept, with minor reservations, the reason that research outcomes are hard to predict.
Basic research has produced some of the most valuable advances, its results are often unforeseeable, and urgent needs justify applied work without justifying a ban on everything else.
Governments and universities should therefore protect a meaningful share of funding for research whose value cannot yet be seen.

words.meaning_here: producing the opposite of the intended result

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason and whether it supports the claim, and Body 3 concedes the strongest opposing point while noting that the reason is slightly overstated.

essays.title: Most public research should target foreseeable needs

paragraphs.text: Every year, public research budgets must be divided among thousands of projects, and every grant given to one idea is a grant denied to another.

This reality complicates the claim that researchers should not limit their investigations to areas in which they expect an immediate, practical application, and the reason given for it, that the outcome of research can never be predicted with certainty.

I partly disagree with the claim and largely disagree with the reason, because most publicly funded research should focus on foreseeable needs, although a smaller share of curiosity-driven work is valuable.

The claim overlooks the urgency of practical problems and the reason exaggerates the unpredictability of research; although the strongest point of the other side is that basic science has produced unexpected breakthroughs, these cases do not justify unlimited freedom.
First, the claim is weak because many urgent problems require research aimed directly at practical solutions.
Dengue strikes many communities in Vietnam every year, and in my own work I have seen how much depends on testing control methods quickly.
The randomized trial of Wolbachia mosquitoes in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, which cut dengue cases by 77%, was designed with a clear practical goal, and its results could be applied almost at once.
Similarly, research on antibiotic resistance must focus on practical results, because overuse of antibiotics has helped resistant bacteria spread and drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
These examples show that when lives are at stake, directing research toward immediate applications is not a narrow choice but a responsible one, a point the claim [[slights|slight]].
Second, the reason on which the claim rests is overstated, since the outcomes of many lines of research can be predicted with reasonable confidence.
A team testing whether a drug lowers blood pressure, or whether a new helmet design reduces head injuries, can estimate in advance what kinds of results are possible and how they would be used.
Such applied studies are planned precisely because their likely uses are known before they begin.
Similarly, when Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, he tested a specific practical idea, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.

Thus, uncertainty exists in all research, but it is a matter of degree, and the reason's claim that outcomes cannot be predicted "with any certainty" is [[hyperbole|hyperbole]] that supports the claim less strongly than it seems.
Admittedly, the strongest point of the other side is that basic research has sometimes produced breakthroughs no one expected.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Nevertheless, such successes are memorable precisely because they are rare, and many open-ended projects never produce results anyone can use.
A wise funding system can therefore reserve a modest share of its budget for curiosity-driven research while directing most resources toward clear needs.
This concession [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: some freedom for curiosity is justified, but in public funding it should be the exception, not the [[paradigm|paradigm]].
In conclusion, I partly disagree with the claim and largely disagree with its reason, since most research can and should be guided by expected practical benefits.
Urgent problems demand applied work, research outcomes are often more predictable than the reason admits, and the rare breakthroughs of basic science justify only a limited share of funding.
Researchers who spend public money therefore owe the public a clear account of how their work is likely to help, even if they cannot promise certainty.

words.meaning_here: the standard model or typical pattern

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 tests whether the reason is true and supports the claim, and Body 3 concedes the strongest opposing point (unexpected breakthroughs) before limiting it.

essays.title: Technology often crowds out real human contact

paragraphs.text: Walk into any café in Hanoi today, and you will likely see friends sitting together while each one stares at a separate phone.
This familiar scene raises a real question about whether technology brings people closer or quietly pushes them apart.

Although technology offers useful new ways to communicate, I side more closely with the first view: our growing reliance on it significantly reduces our opportunities for genuine, face-to-face interaction.

Technology replaces direct contact with thinner exchanges and fills the moments in which relationships form; the second view rightly stresses its reach, but that benefit rarely makes up for what is lost.
First, technology tends to replace direct human contact with communication that is faster but far thinner.
During my clinical training in Vietnam, I watched many doctors spend most of a consultation typing into an electronic record rather than looking at the patient in front of them.
Patients noticed this, and several told me afterward that they felt processed rather than heard, even though the visit was technically efficient.
One elderly woman put it simply: the doctor had looked at the screen more often than at her face.
Similarly, a manager who sends ten short messages a day may feel connected to her team, yet the team rarely learns how she actually thinks or what worries her.
These cases show that technology often converts rich interaction into a stream of brief exchanges, and the sheer volume of contact can hide how little real connection is taking place.
In medicine, where trust depends on being seen and heard, this loss is not a minor inconvenience but a threat to care itself.
Moreover, technology reduces our opportunities for interaction by filling the small, unplanned moments in which relationships used to form.
Consider a family dinner: twenty years ago, waiting for food meant talking, but now each person can retreat into a screen the moment conversation slows.
Because smartphones are [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]], the same pattern appears in waiting rooms, buses and lecture halls, where strangers once struck up conversations and colleagues once traded ideas.
Likewise, many students now text a classmate sitting a few meters away instead of simply turning around to speak.
This shows that the loss lies not only in the hours we spend online but in the casual encounters that technology quietly [[supplants|supplant]].
Such moments seem trivial, yet they are often where trust, friendship and collaboration begin.
Admittedly, the second view captures something important: technology does create new ways to connect, especially across distance.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, and today video calls allow migrant workers from Vietnam to see their children every evening.
Nevertheless, these benefits mostly link people who are already apart; they do little to restore the interaction lost among people who are physically together.

Indeed, a migrant worker who video-calls his children every evening may still spend his lunch break scrolling alone beside coworkers, as his phone [[undermines|undermine]] the friendships he could build at work.
Therefore, the second view is right about reach but [[myopic|myopic]] about depth, since a wider network of contacts is not the same as better human relationships.
A thousand online followers cannot replace one friend who notices, across the table, that something is wrong.
In conclusion, while technology offers real tools for connecting distant people, I believe the first view is closer to the truth because our growing use of it erodes everyday human interaction.
It replaces rich conversation with thinner exchanges, fills the casual moments in which bonds form, and offers benefits that rarely [[offset|offset]] these losses.
The practical lesson is not to reject technology but to use it [[judiciously|judicious]], protecting the face-to-face time that no screen can replace.

words.meaning_here: shortsighted; failing to see the wider picture

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Body 1-2 support it, and Body 3 fairly grants what the second view gets right before explaining why the first is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Technology widens and deepens human connection

paragraphs.text: A century ago, a letter from a son working abroad could take weeks to reach his mother, if it arrived at all.
Today, the same message arrives in seconds, which is why people now debate whether technology reduces our opportunities for human interaction or provides new and better ways to connect.
Although technology can distract us from the people beside us, I side with the second view, because it greatly expands both the reach and the purpose of human connection.

Technology keeps distant relationships alive, it allows strangers to collaborate on a scale never seen before, and while the first view rightly warns about distraction, that problem lies in how we use technology rather than in technology itself.
First, technology provides better ways to connect because it keeps relationships alive across great distances.
In my research on infectious diseases, I work with colleagues in Vietnam and in Sub-Saharan Africa, and weekly video calls let us discuss data, argue about methods and become genuine friends.
We have co-authored papers and planned studies together, often long before meeting in person.
Twenty years ago, such a partnership would have depended on rare conferences and slow email, and many of these relationships would never have formed.
Similarly, many Vietnamese families with relatives working abroad now share meals over video calls instead of waiting months for a visit.
These cases show that technology does not merely replace interaction; it creates contact that would otherwise not exist at all.
For many migrant families in particular, a daily video call is the main thread that holds a household together across borders.
Moreover, technology enables cooperation among strangers on a scale that was once impossible.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, built through countless conversations, edits and debates among people who never met.
Likewise, during the Arab Spring of 2011, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly and [[galvanized|galvanize]] citizens who had previously felt isolated.
Similarly, once GPS was opened to civilians, it became the basis of ride-hailing and delivery apps that connect drivers, customers and small businesses every day.
This shows that technology can turn scattered individuals into communities with a shared purpose, a form of connection that is new rather than [[ersatz|ersatz]].
In such cases, the interaction is not thinner than before but often more meaningful.
Admittedly, the first view captures a real problem: screens can pull attention away from the people who are physically present.
Many parents have watched a family dinner fall silent as each person checks a phone, and students often text a classmate sitting a few meters away instead of simply turning to speak.
Nevertheless, these harms stem from [[lax|lax]] habits rather than from technology itself.
A family that keeps phones away from the dinner table can enjoy face-to-face conversation and still video-call grandparents afterward.
Similarly, a team that agrees to keep laptops closed during meetings recovers the attention that devices can steal.
Thus, the first view correctly identifies a risk, but it mistakes a problem of use for a flaw in the tools, so it does not overturn my position.
The remedy is better habits, not less connection.
In conclusion, I side with the view that technology provides new and better ways to communicate, even though it can distract us when used carelessly.
It sustains relationships across distance, enables cooperation among strangers, and causes harm mainly when habits, rather than tools, are at fault.
The challenge is to use these tools [[judiciously|judicious]], so that they [[augment|augment]] rather than replace the conversations around us.

words.meaning_here: shock or excite someone into taking action
artificial; a poor substitute for the real thing

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the second view, Body 1-2 support it, and Body 3 fairly grants what the first view gets right before explaining why the second is closer to the truth.

essays.title: The past guides less than we assume

paragraphs.text: People often say that those who forget history are doomed to repeat it, as if the past were a reliable instruction manual.

The claim that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today challenges this familiar belief, and it rests on the reason that today's world is far more complex than it was even in the recent past.
I largely agree with the claim when it concerns specific decisions, and I accept much of the reason, although I would qualify both by admitting that history still offers broad principles.
Past success often misleads decision makers, today's complexity makes old solutions unreliable, and historical principles, while still valid, are too general to settle concrete choices.
First, the claim is persuasive because lessons drawn from the past frequently lead decision makers in the wrong direction.
Kodak offers a clear case: its own engineer, Steven Sasson, invented the digital camera in 1975, but the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography.
The shift to digital images was a change that no record of the film era could have prepared its leaders for.
Those leaders trusted what had worked before, and in 2012 Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
Similarly, military historians often observe that generals tend to prepare for the last war rather than the next one.
These cases show that knowledge of the past can make leaders [[complacent|complacent]], so the claim is right that history often fails to help, and sometimes even harms, important decisions.
A leader who studies the past too closely may simply learn to repeat old successes in a world that no longer rewards them.
Second, the reason behind the claim is largely accurate: the world today is significantly more complex than it was even a few decades ago.
In my work on antibiotic resistance, I see this directly: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in Vietnam and many other countries, help resistant bacteria spread.
As a result, drugs that once cured infections now often fail, and the doctors who first used penicillin faced far less of this problem, so their experience offers little guidance today.
Likewise, a new virus can now cross continents within a day because of air travel, a speed that earlier epidemics never reached.
Because conditions have changed so much, [[extrapolating|extrapolate]] from the past is risky, and the reason therefore gives real support to the claim.
In such a world, the experience of earlier generations is often not merely incomplete but actively misleading.
Admittedly, knowing about the past is not useless, because some principles remain true across centuries.

When Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, and hand hygiene remains central to infection control today.
Nevertheless, such lessons are general principles rather than answers to specific decisions.
Knowing that clean hands save lives does not tell anyone how to stop resistant bacteria from spreading through a modern hospital network.
History can remind a hospital director to insist on hand washing, but it cannot tell her which antibiotic policy to adopt next year; for concrete choices, current data deserve [[primacy|primacy]].
Thus, the concession narrows my agreement without overturning it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that knowing about the past offers little help with today's important decisions, and that the world's growing complexity explains why.
Past success can mislead, modern problems often lack any [[analogous|analogous]] precedent, and history's lasting principles are too general to settle specific choices.
A [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] decision maker should therefore treat history as a source of humility rather than a set of instructions.

essays.title: History remains an essential guide

paragraphs.text: Every hospital I have worked in follows rules that were written after something went badly wrong.

Such rules suggest that the past teaches lessons, yet some claim that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today because the world is now far more complex than it once was.
I disagree with both the claim and its reason: although modern problems are more complicated, knowledge of the past remains one of the most reliable guides for important decisions.

Past failures have directly shaped wise modern policies, the reason confuses greater complexity with a change in human nature, and even problems that seem entirely new are solved with lessons from history.
First, the claim is mistaken because many of today's most important decisions are guided directly by lessons from the past.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve the drug, and the United States then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, rules whose successors still shape how new medicines are approved.

Similarly, the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to rules requiring ethics review boards, and I still submit every research protocol to such a board.
Painful as they were, these lessons proved [[salutary|salutary]], and they are now built into the very institutions that [[inform|inform]] important decisions today.
Without that history, regulators today would be deciding blindly, and patients would pay the price.

Second, the reason does not support the claim: although the world is certainly more complex, with global trade, instant communication and new technologies, human motives such as fear, greed and hope have changed very little.
When Vietnam launched the Doi Moi reforms in 1986, its leaders replaced central planning, which had left the country facing food shortages, with market incentives.
A country that had struggled to feed itself became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Leaders who ignored that history would have repeated a costly experiment; leaders who studied it chose a better path.

This case shows that complexity changes the details of a problem, not the basic forces that drive it; history helps leaders [[distill|distill]] which incentives actually work, because people respond to incentives much as they always have.
Admittedly, some problems today have no clear precedent, and here the reason has real force.
The COVID-19 pandemic demanded vaccines faster than any earlier vaccine had been developed.

Nevertheless, even this [[unprecedented|unprecedented]] success depended on the past: the mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Moreover, the smallpox campaign, which ended in eradication in 1980 because countries shared data and vaccine, remains a model for global cooperation against disease.
Thus, even when a problem looks entirely new, the knowledge needed to solve it usually comes from the past.
History did not supply the vaccine itself, but it supplied the science and the habits of cooperation that made a rapid response possible.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that knowing about the past cannot help with important decisions, and I find its reason too weak to support it.
Past disasters shape present rules, human motives remain largely constant despite greater complexity, and even novel crises are solved with older knowledge.
The real danger lies not in a complex present but in a society that forgets what its past has already taught it.
