essays.title: Distance sharpens our view of history

paragraphs.text: A painting seen from a few centimeters away looks like a confusion of colors; only from across the room does the image appear.
The claim that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today rests on a similar idea: we cannot connect current events to past events until we have some distance from both.
I largely agree with the reason, and I therefore accept a qualified version of the claim: history helps decision makers far less in the moment than we expect.

People facing a decision often cannot see which past lessons apply, early judgments are often corrected only by time, and although some lessons are clear immediately, they are the exception rather than the rule.
First, the claim holds in many important cases because people facing a decision often cannot see which past lessons apply.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected the idea, and only germ theory, years after his death, showed that he had been right.
Those doctors had plenty of medical history to draw on, but it did not help them recognize a new truth in front of them.
Similarly, in 1633 the Church, drawing on centuries of accepted teaching, forced Galileo to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
This suggests that knowledge of the past can fail precisely when a decision matters most, because the meaning of the present is still [[ambiguous|ambiguous]].
Second, the reason itself is largely sound: accurate connections between events usually appear only after time has passed.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
His contemporaries were too close to his work to see how it related to the art that came before and after it.
Science shows the same pattern: in 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Findings that looked solid when they appeared turned out to be [[ephemeral|ephemeral]], which [[corroborates|corroborate]] the reason: only distance reveals which connections are real.
In my own field, epidemiologists learn to wait for several confirming studies before changing clinical guidelines, precisely because the first result is often wrong.
Admittedly, some connections between past and present are clear immediately, and in such cases history helps without delay.

When Vietnam passed its 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell, so policymakers could learn from it at once.
Nevertheless, such cases are relatively rare: the helmet law offered a clear lesson only because it produced a simple, measurable result almost at once.
By contrast, the full effects of Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, which reduced poverty dramatically, became clear only over the following decades.
Most important decisions involve slower and more [[convoluted|convoluted]] chains of cause and effect, such as economic reforms or new scientific ideas.
This concession therefore limits the claim to complex situations without overturning the reason.
In conclusion, I largely accept the reason that clear connections between past and present require distance, and I therefore agree that the past helps less with urgent decisions than people assume.
Decision makers often misread the present, early judgments frequently prove wrong, and only simple cases offer immediate lessons.
The [[prudent|prudent]] response is not to ignore history but to hold our present conclusions loosely until time can test them.

essays.title: We learn from history in real time

paragraphs.text: Doctors do not wait ten years to learn from a patient's death; they review the case the following week.
Yet some claim that knowing about the past cannot help people make important decisions today, because we cannot connect current and past events until we have distance from both.
I disagree with the claim and largely reject its reason, since careful people regularly link present events to the past while those events are still unfolding.

Societies have acted quickly and wisely on fresh lessons, modern data allow connections to be made almost in real time, and although distance improves some judgments, it is not required for useful knowledge.
First, the claim is contradicted by cases in which knowledge of the recent past directly shaped important decisions.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA had refused to approve the drug, and in 1962 the United States passed stricter drug-testing rules.
Lawmakers did not wait decades for perspective; they connected a recent disaster to weak testing practices and acted within a few years.

Similarly, public outrage over the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
No historian's distance was needed to see that a drug causing birth defects should never have been sold without careful testing.
These cases show that knowledge of the past, even the very recent past, can [[galvanize|galvanize]] [[timely|timely]] decisions that protect millions of people.
Second, the reason underestimates how well modern data connect current events with past ones without waiting for distance.
In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, we compare this week's case counts with the same weeks in earlier years, and an unusual rise prompts mosquito control before an outbreak peaks.
Last season's data, only months old, tell us which districts to target first and which control methods failed.

Likewise, a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, found that releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77%, and Vietnam has already tested the method.
Similarly, after Vietnam's 2007 helmet law, officials could see within months that helmet use had risen to over 90% and that head injuries and deaths had fallen.
These examples show that connections between past and present are not [[inscrutable|inscrutable]] until time passes; with systematic records, they become visible almost at once.
The reason therefore rests on an [[erroneous|erroneous]] assumption about how knowledge is produced.
Admittedly, distance does improve some judgments, especially about art and ideas whose value is not yet clear.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Nevertheless, this shows only that distance refines our understanding, not that we are unable to make connections without it.
Even the lesson of Van Gogh, that new art is often undervalued, is one that museums and critics can apply today when they judge unknown artists.
In other words, distance can deepen knowledge, but the claim goes too far when it treats distance as a requirement for any useful lesson.
Waiting for distance before learning from Van Gogh's story would only repeat the mistake his contemporaries made.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that knowing about the past cannot help with present decisions, and I find its reason only partly true.
Societies have acted quickly on fresh lessons, modern data link present and past almost in real time, and distance improves understanding without being required for it.
We should revisit our conclusions as time passes, but waiting for perfect perspective before acting would make decision makers dangerously [[dilatory|dilatory]].

essays.title: Steer students toward secure careers, gently

paragraphs.text: In Vietnam, many families spend a large share of their savings to send one child to university.
For such families, the question of whether schools should actively encourage students to choose fields of study that lead to lucrative careers is not abstract; it is a matter of financial survival.
I support this policy as long as schools encourage rather than force, because its likely consequences for students, families and society are largely positive.
The policy would protect students from financial hardship and help direct talent toward fields that society needs, and although it could undervalue less profitable fields, that risk can be managed.
First, implementing this policy would protect many students from years of financial hardship after graduation.
Consider a student from a rural province who chooses a field with few well-paid jobs simply because no adviser explained the job market to her.
After graduating, she may take an unrelated low-wage job while her family struggles to repay the money borrowed for her tuition.
Her parents, who expected the degree to lift the whole family, may feel that their sacrifice was wasted.
Similarly, a classmate who received good career advice might enter accounting or nursing and begin supporting her parents within a few years.
This shows that when schools give honest guidance about earnings, they [[mitigate|mitigate]] a real risk of [[penury|penury]], especially for students who cannot afford a costly mistake.
Encouragement of this kind is not greed; it recognizes that financial security is the foundation on which many young people build the rest of their lives.
Moreover, the policy would help channel talent toward the skilled fields that drive a country's development.
When Vietnam adopted the Doi Moi reforms in 1986, replacing central planning with market incentives, the economy began to reward skills in trade, engineering and management.
As poverty fell dramatically over the following decades, demand for such skills grew, and well-paid careers often signaled where the economy most needed workers.
In public health, for instance, well-paid posts in data analysis and laboratory science exist precisely because hospitals and ministries urgently need such skills.
Because high salaries usually reflect real demand, encouraging students to follow them can align individual ambition with national needs.
In this sense, lucrative careers are not only private rewards but also useful signals of where society's needs are most [[pressing|pressing]].
Admittedly, one consequence of the policy could be to [[marginalize|marginalize]] fields that pay little but matter a great deal, such as art, basic science and teaching.

Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and the early mRNA research of Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman went little noticed for decades, yet both produced work of enormous value.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for limiting the policy, not rejecting it.
Schools can present earnings data alongside information on purpose and aptitude, and they can still offer scholarships to students with an [[ardent|ardent]] interest in less lucrative fields.
As long as encouragement remains advice rather than pressure, the policy's benefits outweigh this cost.
In fact, a student who first secures a stable income may later have more freedom to pursue art, research or public service.
In conclusion, I support encouraging students to consider lucrative careers, provided that schools inform rather than dictate.
Such guidance protects students from hardship, directs talent toward pressing needs, and need not crowd out valuable but modest fields if it is applied with care.
The likely consequences of the policy, therefore, make it worth adopting in a [[qualified|qualified]] form.

essays.title: Money is a poor guide to vocation

paragraphs.text: Ask a room of successful scientists why they chose their field, and very few will mention salary.
Even so, some argue that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study that will prepare them for lucrative careers.
Although schools should certainly share honest information about earnings, I oppose this policy because its likely consequences would harm both students and society.
The policy would push students into careers that do not suit them, it would draw talent away from important but modest fields, and its financial benefits could be achieved without it.
First, a likely consequence of the policy is that many students would enter careers that fit the job market but not their own abilities or [[intrinsic|intrinsic]] interests.
In Vietnam, medicine is widely seen as a secure and respected path, and I have met medical students who chose it mainly for that reason.
Several of them found clinical work exhausting and joyless, and their lack of interest showed in how they treated patients.
Similarly, a talented writer pushed into finance may become a [[lackluster|lackluster]] analyst instead of a gifted journalist.
This shows that steering students by income can produce graduates who are well paid but [[listless|listless]], which serves neither them nor the people who depend on their work.
Over a career of forty years, a mismatch between person and profession is a heavy price to pay for a higher starting salary.
Second, the policy would draw talent away from fields that pay modestly but create enormous public value.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman had spent decades on little-noticed basic research, work that offered no obvious path to wealth.
Their work later earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Likewise, Finland requires teachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession, showing that respect and high standards, not only salary, can attract strong candidates.
Similarly, Wikipedia, written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, a reminder of how much value people create without financial reward.
If schools [[exhort|exhort]] their best students to chase high salaries, the next generation of basic scientists and teachers may simply never appear.
The result would be a [[myopic|myopic]] society, rich in consultants but poor in discoveries.
Admittedly, the policy would bring real benefits to some students, especially those from poor families who cannot afford to fail financially.
For a student whose parents borrowed to pay tuition, a stable, well-paid job may matter more than personal fulfillment.
Nevertheless, this goal can be met by giving every student clear information about job prospects and earnings rather than by actively steering them.
A school can publish salary data and offer career counseling while still respecting each student's choice.
Students who understand the trade-offs can then choose a lucrative path freely, while those drawn to teaching or research can proceed with open eyes.
Thus, the financial benefit is real, but it does not require the policy itself, and it does not outweigh the costs described above.
Information empowers students, whereas active steering quietly replaces their judgment with the institution's.
In conclusion, I oppose actively encouraging students to pursue lucrative fields, although I support honest guidance about earnings.
The policy would create mismatches between students and careers, divert talent from vital but modest fields, and offer financial gains that information alone could provide.
Schools serve students best when they help them find work they can do well and sustain, not merely work that pays well.

essays.title: Guide students toward fields that need workers

paragraphs.text: A degree is one of the largest investments most young people will ever make.
It therefore seems reasonable to ask whether educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that schools encourage rather than pressure, because guiding students toward available jobs protects them and meets real social needs.
Such guidance reduces the risk of unemployment and helps fill shortages in essential services, and although job markets can change quickly, this challenge calls for better advice rather than none.
First, schools should encourage students toward fields with plentiful jobs because unemployment after graduation can be costly and lasting.
Consider two graduates from the same Vietnamese university: one studied nursing, where hospitals are hiring, while the other chose a popular field with few openings.
The nurse begins earning and gaining experience at once, whereas the other graduate may spend years in unrelated temporary work while the skills he learned slowly fade.
Similarly, students who learn about job prospects early can plan internships and courses that lead directly to employment.
This shows that guidance toward plentiful jobs is not a [[trifling|trifling]] matter; it can shape the first decade of a student's working life.
For students from modest backgrounds, that difference can decide whether a degree becomes a ladder out of poverty or a source of lasting debt.
Moreover, encouraging students toward fields with many openings helps societies meet [[pressing|pressing]] needs.
In my work in public health, I have seen district hospitals in Vietnam struggle to recruit enough trained staff, and the shortage directly affects patients.
During dengue season, wards fill quickly, and a few extra trained nurses can make a visible difference in care.
Similarly, a district that lacks laboratory technicians must send samples elsewhere and wait days for results, a delay that each newly trained technician helps shorten.
When universities [[advocate|advocate]] careers in nursing, laboratory science or epidemiology, they help close such gaps.
Plentiful jobs usually signal unmet demand, so steering students toward them serves both the graduate and the public.
In this sense, the needs of the job market and the needs of society often point in the same direction.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that job markets change quickly, so a field with plentiful jobs today may offer few tomorrow.

Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012, leaving workers trained for film with shrinking options.
Nevertheless, this challenge argues for better guidance, not for none.
Schools can encourage fields with broad, durable demand, such as health care, and teach transferable skills such as statistics and writing.
Health care is a good case: populations are aging and infections such as dengue remain common, so demand for nurses and doctors is unlikely to vanish.
In this way, the [[volatile|volatile]] nature of job markets qualifies my position without overturning it.
A student trained in a field with lasting demand and flexible skills is far better protected than one left to guess alone.
In conclusion, I largely agree that schools should encourage students to consider fields with plentiful jobs, as long as that encouragement is flexible and well informed.
Such guidance protects graduates from unemployment and helps fill shortages in vital services, while changing markets call for broad skills rather than an end to advice.
The [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] goal is to help students choose work that is both available and lasting.

essays.title: Interest and adaptability outlast job trends

paragraphs.text: Every few years, a new field is announced as the safest path to employment.
In response, some argue that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
I mostly disagree with this claim: schools should share labor-market information, but actively steering students toward today's plentiful jobs is often unwise.

Job markets shift faster than degrees, students perform best in fields that suit them, and although graduates in crowded fields do face real risks, those risks are better addressed by teaching adaptable skills.
First, steering students toward plentiful jobs is risky because job markets change faster than a four-year degree.
Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace the digital camera that its own engineer had invented in 1975, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Students advised to train for the film industry when its jobs seemed plentiful would later have found that demand had [[plummeted|plummet]].
[[Conversely|conversely]], GPS, built by the US military, later became the basis of ride-hailing and delivery apps, creating jobs that few career counselors could have predicted.
These cases show that today's plentiful jobs are an [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] guide, so schools that follow them risk preparing students for yesterday's economy.
Advice that is accurate today may be harmful in ten years, and schools have no reliable way to tell which.
Second, students tend to excel in fields that match their interests and abilities, not merely in fields with many openings.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves led to the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Their achievement grew from [[assiduous|assiduous]] work on a problem that fascinated them, not from a crowded job market.
Likewise, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he kept painting and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Similarly, I moved from clinical medicine into epidemiology because its questions interested me, and that interest has sustained me through long, demanding projects.
This shows that genuine interest produces the persistence that careers require, while a field chosen only for its openings may lead to [[lackluster|lackluster]] work.
Students who love their work also tend to keep learning, which makes them more employable over time, not less.
The most compelling challenge to my view is that graduates in crowded fields may struggle to find work, a serious risk for students from poor families.
A Vietnamese student whose family borrowed to pay tuition cannot afford several years of unemployment after graduation.
Nevertheless, the better response is to give such students clear information and adaptable skills, not to push them into whatever field is currently hiring.
Statistics, writing and problem solving remain useful across many careers, and they protect graduates when particular markets decline.
In my own field, colleagues who combined medicine with statistics found work in hospitals, universities and international agencies when other options narrowed.
Thus, the challenge is real, but it supports honest advice and broad training rather than the claim itself.
Schools can prepare students for an uncertain market without deciding their field for them.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that schools should actively encourage students to choose fields with plentiful jobs.
Job markets change unpredictably, students succeed in fields that suit them, and the risk of unemployment is better reduced by adaptable skills than by steering.
Schools should inform students about the job market and then trust them to make a choice they can sustain for decades.

essays.title: Honest discouragement can be a kindness

paragraphs.text: The kindest advice is not always the most pleasant to hear.
This is especially true in education, where some argue that institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.

I largely agree with this statement when schools base their advice on clear evidence and leave the final choice to the student, but it does not hold when predictions rest on weak signals or prejudice.

Honest discouragement protects students from costly failure, it protects the people who depend on competent professionals, and yet it becomes harmful when schools mistake early struggle or social bias for lack of ability.
First, the statement holds true because honest discouragement can save students years of time and money.
Consider a medical student who repeatedly fails anatomy and clinical examinations despite tutoring and extra time.
If the school says nothing, the student may spend six or more years and much of the family's savings before failing the final licensing exam.
A [[candid|candid]] conversation in the second year, by contrast, would allow the student to move into a related field, such as public health or pharmacy, where her strengths may fit better.
Such a change would preserve her years, her savings and her confidence.
In such cases, dissuading a student is not cruel but responsible, because silence only prolongs a [[futile|futile]] effort.
Honest advice also gives the student the information she needs to make her own choice.
Moreover, the statement holds true when a student's failure would harm other people.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve the drug, and her [[meticulous|meticulous]] judgment protected American families.
Similarly, in my own work, I have seen how one careless laboratory error in a disease survey can mislead an entire district's response.
Fields such as medicine, pharmacology and engineering need people with that level of skill, so schools owe a duty not only to students but also to future patients and clients.
When evidence shows that a student cannot reach the required standard, discouraging that student serves the public interest.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when schools judge potential too early or on biased grounds.
Marie Curie faced the barriers that women in science encountered at the time, yet she won Nobel Prizes in both physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.
Had her teachers dissuaded her on the basis of [[ingrained|ingrained]] assumptions about women, science would have lost one of its greatest minds.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, would have seemed poor candidates to solve the problem of flight, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Nevertheless, these cases argue for better evidence, not for silence.
Schools should discourage students only after sustained, fairly measured poor performance, and they should present their advice as guidance that the student may reject.
In practice, this means looking at several years of results, not a single failed exam, and listening to the student's own view of her goals.
In conclusion, I largely agree that schools should dissuade students from fields in which they are unlikely to succeed, provided their judgment rests on solid evidence.
Such advice protects students from costly failure and the public from incompetent professionals, but it turns harmful when based on early or biased predictions.
The responsibility, then, is not to close doors but to give students an honest, [[impartial|impartial]] view of what lies behind them.

essays.title: Schools are poor predictors of success

paragraphs.text: History is full of people who were told they would never succeed.
Even so, some argue that educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.

I mostly disagree with this statement, because schools predict success poorly and discouragement often does more harm than good, although the statement does hold true in fields where safety is at stake.
Predictions of success are often wrong, discouragement tends to fall hardest on students who already face barriers, and only in high-stakes professions does the statement clearly hold.
First, the statement assumes that schools can tell who will succeed, yet such predictions are often wrong.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, and few experts would have picked them to solve the problem of flight.
Through years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Similarly, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.

These cases show that early signs of success are [[tenuous|tenuous]] evidence, so a school that discourages students on that basis may [[stymie|stymie]] exactly the people who would have achieved the most.
Many of the most important advances in history came from people whom experts would have quietly advised to choose something safer.
Second, discouragement tends to fall hardest on students who already face unfair barriers.
Marie Curie faced the barriers women in science encountered at the time, yet she won Nobel Prizes in both physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.
In her era, many advisers might have judged a woman unlikely to succeed in physics, not because of her ability but because of prejudice.
Likewise, in Vietnam, students from rural schools often enter university with weaker preparation, and early low grades can make them look less capable than they are.
I have taught some of these students, and several who struggled in their first year became among the strongest researchers I know.
When schools act on such signals, they risk turning social disadvantage into a self-fulfilling prophecy, which [[exacerbates|exacerbate]] inequality rather than reducing it.
Schools should instead offer extra support, which helps students reveal abilities that early grades conceal.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in fields where a person's failure would endanger others, such as surgery or aviation.
A surgical trainee who repeatedly makes dangerous errors despite extra supervision should be guided toward another specialty, because patients' lives are at stake.
Likewise, a pilot trainee who cannot master emergency procedures should not be allowed to fly passengers, however enthusiastic he may be.
Nevertheless, even here the school's duty is to set clear standards and give honest feedback, not to discourage students before they have had a fair chance.
A trainee who fails a fair assessment can be redirected; a student who is merely predicted to fail should not be.
This distinction narrows the statement to a small set of high-stakes cases and leaves my broader position intact.
In medicine, for example, objective clinical assessments already serve this purpose well.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that schools have a responsibility to dissuade students from fields in which they seem unlikely to succeed.
Predictions of success are unreliable, discouragement often reinforces existing barriers, and only fields that affect public safety justify firm redirection.
Schools should [[inform|inform]] students honestly about their performance and then respect the [[resolve|resolve]] of those who choose to persist.

essays.task_note: Body 1-2 show where the statement does not hold, and Body 3 names the high-stakes fields where it does hold and explains how that narrows the position.

essays.title: Healthy competition pushes students to excel

paragraphs.text: Few people run their fastest when they run alone.

The same may be true in the classroom, where some believe that competition for high grades motivates students to excel, while others argue that such competition seriously limits the quality of real learning.
I side mainly with the first view: when it is fair and moderate, competition for grades motivates students to work harder and learn more.

Competition gives students clear goals, it pushes them beyond the minimum, and although the second view rightly warns about stress and shallow learning, these problems come from excessive competition rather than competition itself.
First, competition for high grades motivates students by giving them clear, measurable goals.
In Vietnam, where grades and entrance examinations largely decide university places, many students study with remarkable discipline throughout secondary school.
I remember classmates who rarely opened a textbook until a class ranking was posted, after which they studied every evening.
One friend who had been content with average marks began solving extra problems each night once he saw his name below a rival's.
Similarly, medical students preparing for competitive residency places often master far more material than the minimum required to pass.
These examples show that a [[salient|salient]] standard of comparison turns vague effort into concrete targets, which [[galvanizes|galvanize]] students who might otherwise drift.
Without a ranking, many students would set lower goals simply because they would not know what was possible.
Moreover, competition pushes students to go beyond the minimum, and that extra effort often produces real learning.
When students compete for top marks in mathematics, they must solve harder problems than the ones they find comfortable, and this struggle deepens their understanding.
Likewise, a student aiming for the top of an epidemiology class must understand why a method works, not just memorize formulas, because questions at that level demand [[nuance|nuance]].
Similarly, in research, competition for grants pushes scientists to sharpen their questions and test their methods more carefully before they submit.
This shows that competition, far from limiting real learning, often forces students to engage with material more deeply than they would on their own.
Over time, it can also [[inculcate|inculcate]] habits of discipline that last well beyond school.
Competition, in short, raises the ceiling of what students expect of themselves.
Admittedly, the second view captures a real danger: intense competition can encourage memorization, anxiety and even cheating.

Finland, which relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, makes teaching a selective profession requiring a master's degree, showing that strong education does not depend on constant ranking.
In Vietnam, some students attend extra classes late into the night, and the strain can damage both health and curiosity.
Nevertheless, these problems arise mainly when competition becomes extreme and grades become the only measure of worth.
A class that rewards top grades while also valuing projects and discussion keeps the motivating effect while limiting the harm.
Thus, the second view is correct about excessive competition, but it does not show that competition for grades itself undermines learning.
Removing competition entirely would throw away a powerful source of motivation in order to cure a problem of degree.
In conclusion, I agree more with the view that competition for high grades motivates students to excel, provided the competition remains fair and balanced.
It provides clear goals, pushes students beyond the minimum, and causes harm mainly when taken to extremes.
Schools should therefore not abolish competition but [[mitigate|mitigate]] its excesses, so that the drive to win serves the goal of learning.

a subtle difference in meaning or understanding
instill an idea or habit by persistent instruction

essays.title: Grade competition narrows real learning

paragraphs.text: A student can earn a perfect score and still understand very little.
This gap lies at the heart of a debate about whether competition for high grades motivates students to excel or seriously limits the quality of real learning.
Although competition can spur effort in the short term, I side with the second view, because competing for grades often replaces [[intrinsic|intrinsic]] curiosity with a narrow pursuit of marks.

Grade competition rewards memorization over understanding, it discourages collaboration and risk taking, and while the first view is right that it motivates some students, that motivation is often shallow.
First, competition for grades limits real learning because it rewards students for memorizing answers rather than understanding ideas.
In my medical training in Vietnam, many classmates memorized lists of drug doses to top the class, yet some could not explain why a drug worked or when it might harm a patient.
Their grades were excellent, but their knowledge was fragile and faded soon after the examinations.
I was one of those students for a time, and I relearned much of pharmacology later at the bedside.
Similarly, students preparing for competitive entrance exams often practice the same question types for months, learning to spot patterns rather than to think.
These cases show that when the goal is to outscore others, learning becomes a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] exercise in recall rather than a search for understanding.
A future doctor who cannot reason from principles is more dangerous than one with modest grades who truly understands.
Second, competition discourages the collaboration and risk taking on which real learning depends.
In a class graded on a curve, a student who explains a hard concept to a classmate may lower her own rank, so many students quietly stop helping one another.
Finland takes a different path: it relies far less on standardized testing than many countries and requires teachers to hold a master's degree, placing its trust in teachers rather than in rankings.
Its approach suggests that a school system can value deep learning without making students compete constantly for marks.
When students see classmates as rivals, they share less, avoid difficult courses that might lower their averages, and [[eschew|eschew]] the risky questions that produce real insight.
Such habits [[undermine|undermine]] exactly the kind of learning that schools claim to value.
Collaboration, by contrast, lets students test ideas aloud and learn from one another's mistakes.
Admittedly, the first view is correct that competition motivates some students, especially those who are already strong.
A student near the top of a class ranking may work harder simply to stay there.
I knew classmates who studied hardest in the weeks just before a ranking was posted.
Nevertheless, this motivation is often shallow, and it rarely reaches the many students who know they cannot win.
For a student ranked in the middle, a posted ranking may bring only discouragement and [[apathy|apathy]].
Thus, competition may raise effort among a few students while lowering the quality of learning for most, which is why the second view is closer to the truth.
Real learning, in contrast, depends on curiosity that every student can share, regardless of rank.
In conclusion, I agree more with the view that competition for high grades seriously limits real learning, even though it can push some students to work harder.
It rewards memorization, discourages collaboration and risk taking, and motivates mainly those who already excel.
Schools would serve students better by measuring understanding rather than ranking students against one another.

words.meaning_here: coming from within a person; natural
done as a routine, with little care or interest

essays.title: Experts should lead on complex policy

paragraphs.text: Few passengers would want to vote on how the pilot should land the plane.

A similar logic underlies the claim that major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and other government experts, because they are more informed and thus have better judgment than the general public.
I largely agree with the claim and its reason, especially for technical policies, although the word "always" goes too far, since experts need public oversight.
Experts can adopt necessary but unpopular measures, their greater knowledge often does produce better judgment, and while expert failures are real, they call for oversight rather than public control.
First, the claim is largely sound because leaving major policies to experts allows governments to adopt measures that are wise but initially unpopular.
Consider Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, a rule that many riders likely found inconvenient at first.
Within months, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90%, and head injuries and deaths fell.
A referendum held in the first week might well have rejected the helmet law.
Similarly, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives and turned a country facing food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters.
These cases show that decisive, expert-led policy can produce benefits that public opinion, focused on short-term costs, might have blocked.
Officials and their advisers can also accept short-term criticism in pursuit of long-term gains.
Second, the reason is largely true: specialists usually understand complex problems better than the general public does.

Around 1960, thalidomide caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, but Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve the drug, relying on her expertise rather than on public demand.

Likewise, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, a task that required expert planning across many nations.
In my own work, decisions about releasing Wolbachia mosquitoes, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, depend on technical evidence few citizens could evaluate.
In each case, better information led to better judgment, which [[substantiates|substantiate]] the reason behind the claim.
Laypeople rarely have the time or training to weigh such evidence, so [[deference|deference]] to experts on technical matters is [[warranted|warranted]].
Admittedly, government experts can abuse their authority, and this is the strongest argument against the word "always."
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
The study continued for four decades, showing that expertise without accountability can lead to grave injustice.
Nevertheless, the response to that scandal was not to hand research decisions to the public but to create ethics review boards that check experts' work.
Under that system, experts still design and run studies, but independent reviewers check their work before it begins.
This shows that experts should lead major policy decisions within a system of oversight, so I accept the claim in [[qualified|qualified]] form rather than as an absolute rule.
In conclusion, I largely agree that major policy decisions should be left to politicians and government experts, and that their greater knowledge usually gives them better judgment.
Experts can adopt beneficial but unpopular measures, their information improves their decisions, and their failures call for oversight rather than replacement.
The best system, therefore, lets experts decide while ensuring that independent bodies can [[censure|censure]] them when they err.

essays.title: Good policy needs the public's voice

paragraphs.text: Some of history's worst decisions were made by well-informed people who listened to no one.

That fact challenges the claim that major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and other government experts, on the grounds that they are more informed and therefore have better judgment than the public.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason: experts should advise and often lead, but excluding the public from major decisions invites error and abuse.

Experts without public scrutiny can cause serious harm, being informed does not guarantee good judgment, and although technical decisions do require expertise, they still benefit from public accountability.
First, the claim is dangerous because experts who answer to no one can commit serious wrongs.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
It was public outrage, not expert self-correction, that led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Similarly, during the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and their action helped end bus segregation in that city.
These cases show that the public is often the [[catalyst|catalyst]] for correcting policies that officials have long [[condoned|condone]].
Accountability to the public is therefore not an obstacle to good policy but one of its main safeguards.
Second, the reason is flawed because being more informed does not always mean having better judgment.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his expert colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
Likewise, in 1633 the Church, the leading authority of its day, forced Galileo to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
By contrast, Abraham Lincoln appointed political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
The authorities in the first two cases possessed more information than ordinary people, yet their judgment proved wrong, whereas Lincoln deliberately invited challenge.

Expert communities can become [[insular|insular]] and resist evidence that threatens their [[dogma|dogma]], so knowledge alone does not guarantee sound judgment; public debate supplies the outside challenge they need.
Admittedly, some major decisions are so technical that the public cannot reasonably make them.
When thalidomide caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe around 1960, it was Frances Kelsey, an FDA expert, rather than public opinion that kept the drug off the US market.
Few members of the public could have evaluated the drug's safety data on their own.
Nevertheless, the stricter drug-testing rules that followed in 1962 were passed by elected lawmakers answerable to the public, not by experts alone.
This suggests that the best model combines expert advice with public accountability rather than leaving decisions to experts in every case.
I therefore accept an important role for expertise without accepting the claim's absolute wording.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and government experts, and I doubt that their knowledge reliably ensures better judgment.
Unchecked experts have caused grave harm, informed communities have often resisted the truth, and even technical decisions gain legitimacy from public involvement.
Good policy needs both expert knowledge and a public willing to [[impugn|impugn]] decisions that seem wrong.

accept or allow behavior that is wrong
firmly held beliefs not open to question

essays.title: Breadth requirements make graduates better professionals

paragraphs.text: Few people end up doing exactly the job they imagined at eighteen.

This uncertainty lies behind a familiar debate: should universities require students to take a variety of courses outside their field, or should they offer only the courses that prepare students for jobs in their chosen fields?
I largely side with the first view, since a set of required courses outside one's field serves students better than a narrow, job-focused program, as long as those courses are chosen with care.

Breadth helps graduates solve real problems and prepares them for careers that change, and although the second view raises a fair concern about cost, that concern argues for better courses rather than fewer.
First, the problems that graduates face at work rarely respect the borders between academic fields, so narrow training often leaves them unprepared.
In my own work as a physician and epidemiologist in Vietnam, the hardest questions about dengue control were not purely medical.

Deciding whether a district should pay for mosquito control required some knowledge of economics, and persuading families to clear standing water required an understanding of how people actually make choices.
A graduate who has studied nothing beyond medicine may know what should be done but not how to make it happen.

Similarly, the Wolbachia method, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, depended on biologists, statisticians and community workers who could understand one another's work.
This shows that courses outside one's field are not a luxury; they are often the very tools that make specialized knowledge useful in the real world.
Second, required breadth protects students in a job market that changes faster than any curriculum.

Kodak offers a clear warning: although its own engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, the company protected its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography, and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Workers whose skills were tied only to film suddenly found those skills [[obsolete|obsolete]].
Likewise, a student who studies only the software tools that employers want today may see them replaced before she reaches mid-career.

Courses in writing, statistics or history cannot predict the future, but they build flexible habits of thought that outlast any single technology, which is exactly what a [[myopic|myopic]] focus on a first job cannot promise.
Admittedly, the second view makes a fair point about cost and focus.

In Vietnam, many students pay tuition with family savings or loans, and a [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] general-education lecture delivered to hundreds of students can feel like money and time taken away from their real goals.
Nevertheless, the remedy for poorly taught breadth courses is to teach them better, not to abolish them.
Universities can let students choose among several options outside their major, so that a future engineer might take public health or economics rather than a course with no link to her interests.
This concern therefore qualifies my position rather than overturning it: breadth requirements are worth keeping only when they are flexible and [[judiciously|judicious]] designed.
Students should be able to see why each required course matters to the life they hope to lead.
In conclusion, universities are wiser to require some study outside a student's field than to train students only for their first job.

Broad courses [[bolster|bolster]] graduates' ability to solve complex problems and to adapt to changing careers, and the legitimate worry about wasted time can be answered through better course design.
A degree should prepare students not only for their first position but also for the unexpected questions they will face across a working life.

words.meaning_here: no longer useful because something newer has replaced it
focused only on the near term and unable to see wider needs
done routinely and with little care or interest
with good judgment and careful thought

essays.title: Let students choose their own breadth

paragraphs.text: For many families, a university degree is one of the largest investments they will ever make.

Given this cost, people disagree about whether universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside his or her field or should require only the courses that prepare students for jobs in their chosen fields.

I mostly side with the second, more [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] view: universities should not force students into unrelated courses, although they should make such courses easy to choose for those who want them.
Required breadth wastes scarce time and money, focused training builds real expertise, and while the first view is right that other fields have value, that value is best pursued by choice.
First, mandatory courses outside the major impose a real cost on the students who can least afford it.
Consider a nursing student in Vietnam whose parents have borrowed money to pay her tuition.
If one semester of her program is filled with required courses that she did not choose and that do not bring her closer to a license, her family pays for months of study with little return.

Similarly, students who work part-time to support themselves often find these extra requirements [[onerous|onerous]], since every additional course [[impedes|impede]] their progress toward graduation.
This shows that forcing breadth on everyone is not a neutral choice; it shifts costs onto students for whom a job-focused degree is the most direct path out of financial hardship.
A university that ignores this reality serves wealthy students well and poorer students badly.
Second, deep and focused training is what allows people to make serious contributions in their fields.

Medicine is an obvious case: a surgeon needs years of [[assiduous|assiduous]] practice in anatomy and technique, and her patients gain little if that training is diluted by courses unrelated to her work.
History offers a similar lesson.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 not through a broad education but through years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.

Their success suggests that sustained focus on one problem, rather than a sampling of many subjects, is often what produces real progress, which supports the view that universities should let students concentrate on preparing for their chosen work.
Admittedly, supporters of the first view are right that knowledge from other fields can be valuable.
The Wolbachia method of dengue control, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, required biology, statistics and community work, not medicine alone.
Nevertheless, this value does not justify forcing every student into the same set of unrelated courses.
In my experience, many researchers learn the other disciplines they need later in their careers, when a concrete problem gives them a reason to do so.
A physician who later needs economics for a cost study, for example, will study it far more seriously than an undergraduate forced to sit through it.

Breadth, in other words, is most useful when it is chosen with a purpose; when it is imposed, students often complete it [[perfunctorily|perfunctory]], so the benefit that the first view promises rarely appears.
In conclusion, universities should prepare students for their chosen careers and treat courses outside the major as an option rather than an obligation.
Required breadth burdens students financially, focused study builds genuine expertise, and the real benefits of other fields come most readily when learners seek them out.
A university that respects students' time and choices is more likely to produce graduates who are both skilled and curious.

words.meaning_here: practical and focused on real results rather than ideals
with little effort or genuine interest

essays.task_note: The essay states in the thesis that it sides with the second view, supports it in two body paragraphs, and grants what the first view gets right before explaining why the second view is closer to the truth.

essays.title: Abandoning sound principles usually costs more

paragraphs.text: Most people can recall a moment when holding to a principle would have been costly and giving way would have been easy.
The statement claims that, in such moments, it is more harmful to compromise one's own beliefs than to [[adhere|adhere]] to them.
I largely agree, as long as "beliefs" refers to principles that a person has examined carefully rather than to untested habits or opinions.
Holding to sound principles protects other people and preserves trust, although clinging to mistaken beliefs can cause harm of its own, which is why the statement needs this qualification.
First, compromising one's beliefs is especially harmful when other people depend on those beliefs for their safety.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, and the country then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Had she given way, many American families might have suffered the same tragedy.

In the same way, a physician in Vietnam who believes that antibiotics should not be given for viral fevers protects patients when she refuses demands for them, because overuse helps resistant bacteria spread.
These cases show that a professional who compromises a well-founded belief does not merely betray herself; she may expose many others to harm.
In such cases, the cost of holding firm falls on one person, while the cost of giving way falls on many.
Moreover, compromising core principles can damage the trust on which whole institutions depend.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, setting aside medicine's most basic duty to patients.
The public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
The damage lasted for decades, since many people came to distrust medical research itself.

By contrast, during the Montgomery bus boycott, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses rather than [[acquiesce|acquiesce]] in injustice, and their persistence helped end bus segregation in that city.
Together, these examples suggest that abandoning a principle spreads a [[pernicious|pernicious]] loss of trust, whereas holding firm can build the credibility needed for change.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when the belief itself is wrong.

Kodak's leaders believed so firmly in their profitable film business that the company was slow to embrace digital photography, even though its own engineer had invented the digital camera, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, this case shows the danger of refusing to examine a belief, not the virtue of giving up principles under pressure.
A [[principled|principled]] person changes her mind when evidence shows she is wrong, but she does not abandon a sound belief simply because it is inconvenient.
Kodak's real failure was not loyalty to a principle but a refusal to test a business assumption against new facts.
This distinction shapes my position: the statement holds for carefully examined principles, but it fails for [[obstinate|obstinate]] attachment to beliefs that evidence has already undermined.
In conclusion, giving up well-founded beliefs is generally more harmful than holding to them, both for the individual and for the people who rely on her.
Firm principles protect people who depend on us and preserve the trust that institutions need, while the Kodak case reminds us that beliefs must remain open to evidence.
The real lesson, then, is to examine our beliefs honestly and, once they survive that examination, to hold them even when doing so is costly.

essays.title: Rigid adherence often does more harm

paragraphs.text: History remembers its heroes of conviction, but it rarely counts the damage done by people who were certain and wrong.
The statement holds that it is more harmful to compromise one's beliefs than to adhere to them, yet this claim overlooks how often firm beliefs turn out to be mistaken.
I mostly disagree: in many situations, a willingness to compromise does less harm than rigid adherence, although a small set of core ethical principles should not be compromised.
Adhering to mistaken beliefs can be disastrous, compromise makes cooperation and progress possible, and only fundamental moral duties justify refusing to bend.
First, adhering to a belief is harmful when the belief is wrong, and people are often wrong.
In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues clung to their existing beliefs and rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
Similarly, Kodak's faith in its profitable film business made the company slow to embrace digital photography, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Its leaders were loyal to their belief, and that loyalty cost the company its future.
These cases show that when a belief hardens into [[dogma|dogma]], holding to it can cost lives and livelihoods, so the statement fails exactly where certainty is least justified.
Firm conviction is valuable only when the belief behind it is correct.
Second, compromise is often what allows people with different beliefs to work together and achieve progress.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, a major departure from earlier policy.
As a result, a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Abraham Lincoln made a similar choice when he appointed political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, preferring able critics to loyal followers.
Lincoln gave up the comfort of a loyal team, but he gained advisers who could test his decisions.
An [[intransigent|intransigent]] leader in either case might have kept his beliefs intact, but a more [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] willingness to bend produced far greater benefits.
Compromise, in these cases, was not a betrayal of principle but a recognition that the old approach had failed.
I must [[concede|concede]], however, that the statement holds for certain core ethical principles.

In the Tuskegee syphilis study, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and the public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, such cases involve basic duties, such as not harming others, rather than the ordinary beliefs about policy, science or strategy that people hold every day.
A doctor must never compromise on honesty with patients, but she should readily change her view about the best treatment when new evidence appears.
In medicine, refusing to update a belief about treatment can harm patients as surely as abandoning a moral duty.
This distinction shapes my position: a few moral principles deserve firm adherence, but most beliefs should remain [[malleable|malleable]] enough to change.
In conclusion, compromising one's beliefs is not generally more harmful than holding to them; often the reverse is true.
Mistaken beliefs held too firmly can do great damage, compromise enables cooperation and reform, and only a narrow set of ethical duties should be treated as fixed.
The wiser course is to hold our deepest moral principles firmly while treating our other beliefs as open to revision.

words.meaning_here: a belief accepted as true without question
refusing to change one's views or to agree
