essays.title: Fixed curricula give students needed direction

paragraphs.text: A first-year student facing a catalog of several hundred courses can easily feel lost.

For this reason, some argue that colleges and universities should specify all required courses and eliminate elective courses in order to provide clear guidance, because college students, like people in general, prefer to follow directions rather than make their own decisions.
I largely agree with the claim, especially for professional programs, and I partly agree with the reason, although neither is true for every student.
A fixed curriculum ensures coherent training, many students do welcome direction, and the value of electives, while real, can be kept without leaving students to choose alone.
First, the claim is sound because a fully specified curriculum ensures that students learn what their field actually requires.
Medical education in Vietnam is a clear case: students follow a largely fixed sequence in which anatomy and physiology come before clinical rotations.
No patient would want a doctor who skipped pharmacology because she preferred a more interesting elective.
Similarly, a student who builds a [[desultory|desultory]] schedule of unrelated electives may reach the final year without the courses needed to graduate.
Without a clear map, such a student may spend an extra year and extra tuition fixing mistakes that a fixed curriculum would have prevented.
This shows that clear requirements protect students from gaps in their training, which is precisely the guidance the claim says they need.
In fields where every course builds on the last, removing electives removes confusion rather than opportunity.
Second, the reason is partly true: many students do prefer to follow directions, at least when they begin college.
As a teaching assistant, I often met first-year students who asked not "What interests me?" but "What should I take?"
Faced with an [[exhaustive|exhaustive]] list of options, these students tended to [[dither|dither]], postpone their decision, or simply copy their friends' choices.
Several told me later that they would have been grateful if the university had simply decided for them.
The same pattern appears outside education, since many people accept the default option on a form rather than compare the alternatives.
This tendency supports the reason, although the phrase "people in general" goes too far; the reason is true for many students, not for all, so it strengthens the claim without fully proving it.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that electives allow students to discover interests that no required list could anticipate.
A biology student who takes an elective in statistics, for instance, may find a lifelong career in epidemiology.
Without that elective, she might never have discovered the field at all.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be preserved within a fixed curriculum.
A university can require one course in statistics, one in ethics and one in economics for every student, so that discovery is built into the program instead of left to chance.
Students would still meet new subjects, but they would meet them through a plan rather than by accident.
This approach keeps the guidance the claim values while recognizing that students who are given no direction often make choices they later regret.
Discovery and direction, in other words, are not opposites.
In conclusion, it is [[prudent|prudent]] for colleges to specify their courses clearly, even if the reason offered for doing so is somewhat overstated.
A fixed curriculum ensures complete training, many students genuinely welcome direction, and the discoveries that electives allow can be designed into the required program.
A well-planned curriculum is also more [[equitable|equitable]], because students without family guidance are not left to navigate the catalog alone.

words.meaning_here: lacking a plan or purpose; random
be unable to make a decision
wise and careful about future consequences

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason that students prefer directions, and Body 3 concedes the strongest point against both before limiting it.

essays.title: Choice is part of a college education

paragraphs.text: Learning to make good decisions is one of the main things young adults must do in college.

The claim that colleges and universities should specify all required courses and eliminate electives would remove much of that practice, and it rests on the reason that college students, like people in general, prefer to follow directions rather than make their own decisions.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and its reason, although I accept that many students need more guidance than they currently receive.
Eliminating electives would harm students' development, the reason is both doubtful and a poor basis for policy, and the real need for guidance can be met without abolishing choice.
First, the claim is mistaken because electives often shape careers in ways that no fixed list of courses could plan.
My own path is a modest example: an elective in biostatistics during my medical training led me toward epidemiology, a field my required courses barely mentioned.
Without that choice, I would probably have followed a narrower clinical path and never found the research I now find most rewarding.
Similarly, a computer science student who takes an elective in linguistics may discover an interest in language software that no required list of courses would ever have pointed her toward.
A curriculum with no electives would make such [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] discoveries far rarer, so the "clear guidance" it promises would come at a high price.
Remove that flexibility, and students lose the chance to find the work they are best suited to do.
Second, the reason is weak, both because it is doubtful and because it would not support the claim even if it were true.
Many people clearly enjoy making their own decisions: Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers who chose their own topics, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Moreover, even students who prefer directions at eighteen will soon face jobs in which no one tells them exactly what to do.
A college that makes every decision for them denies them the practice they need to become [[autonomous|autonomous]] adults.
The reason is therefore [[specious|specious]]: it sounds plausible, but a preference for being directed is a weakness to correct, not a principle on which to design a curriculum.
I must [[concede|concede]], however, that some students are overwhelmed by choice and make poor decisions.
A first-generation student with no family experience of college may choose courses at random and graduate late as a result.
For such a student, a long list of electives can feel like a maze rather than an opportunity.
Nevertheless, the solution is better guidance, not the elimination of choice.
Universities can offer academic advisers, recommended course sequences and a small number of core requirements, while still leaving room for electives.
A single meeting with a good adviser can often prevent the poor choices that critics of electives worry about.
This approach gives anxious students the direction they need without removing the opportunity for others to explore, so the concession refines my position rather than reversing it.
In conclusion, colleges should not eliminate electives, and the assumption that students prefer to be told what to do is both overstated and beside the point.
Electives allow discoveries that fixed lists cannot plan, many people clearly prefer to make their own choices, and students who struggle can be helped through advising.
The goal of a college is not only to give clear directions but to prepare students for a life in which they must choose for themselves.

words.meaning_here: able to act and decide independently

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason that people prefer directions, and Body 3 concedes the strongest point for the other side before limiting it.

essays.title: Major advances borrow from other fields

paragraphs.text: Fields of study are human inventions, but the problems they try to solve do not follow those boundaries.
This is why the statement argues that no field of study can advance significantly unless it incorporates knowledge and experience from outside that field.
I largely agree, because the greatest advances usually come where fields meet, although a single discovery can begin within one discipline before outside help turns it into real progress.
Outside tools transform a field's methods, outside experience brings new ways of seeing problems, and even discoveries made inside one field usually need outsiders to reach their full significance.
First, fields often advance significantly when they borrow tools developed elsewhere.
Dengue control is a good case: traditional mosquito control has often struggled to stop outbreaks.

Then scientists borrowed knowledge from microbiology, releasing mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, and the method cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
The method has also been tested in Vietnam, where dengue remains a serious public health problem.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military, but once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
In both cases, outside knowledge served as a [[catalyst|catalyst]] for progress that the receiving field had not achieved on its own.
Public health did not need to abandon its own expertise; it needed to combine that expertise with knowledge from another discipline.
Second, people who bring experience from outside a field often see solutions that insiders miss.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their practical experience with machines gave them an approach that more [[insular|insular]] experts lacked.
Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
Their work came from basic research rather than vaccine development, yet it transformed vaccines and earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
These examples show that progress often depends on [[disparate|disparate]] kinds of knowledge that [[converge|converge]] on a single problem.
A field that listens only to its own members risks repeating the same assumptions.
Admittedly, some important discoveries begin within a single field.
Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, an observation made entirely within his own laboratory work.
Nevertheless, his discovery remained a [[nascent|nascent]] idea until Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed penicillin into a usable drug during World War II.
The Human Genome Project shows the same pattern on a larger scale, since this international effort made the human DNA sequence freely available to researchers in many fields.
Researchers in medicine, public health and other fields could then build on it in ways no single discipline had planned.

Such cases suggest that a first insight may arise inside a field, but significant advancement usually requires knowledge and effort from beyond it, which is why my agreement is strong but not absolute.
In conclusion, the statement is largely correct: significant progress in a field usually depends on knowledge and experience from outside it.
Borrowed tools, outsiders' perspectives and the development of discoveries by broader teams all show how fields grow by drawing on one another.
Universities and research funders should therefore encourage collaboration across disciplines rather than allowing each field to work in isolation.

words.meaning_here: something that causes or speeds up important change
isolated and uninterested in outside ideas

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement holds (imported tools and borrowed knowledge) and then examines a case where an advance began inside one field, explaining how that case qualifies the word "significantly."

essays.title: Many advances come from within

paragraphs.text: It has become fashionable to say that all innovation happens at the boundaries between disciplines.

The statement takes this idea to an extreme, claiming that no field of study can advance significantly unless it incorporates knowledge and experience from outside that field, as if expertise alone were never enough.
I mostly disagree, because many major advances have come from deep and careful work inside a single field, even though outside knowledge often helps.
Careful observation within a field can produce breakthroughs, fields can advance by correcting their own methods, and the useful role of outside knowledge does not make it a requirement.
First, significant advances often come from close observation by experts working within their own field.
In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis, working on his own hospital ward, had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime.
Deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, a change produced by [[meticulous|meticulous]] clinical observation rather than by ideas imported from another discipline.
He did not need economics or engineering; he needed careful attention to what was happening on his own ward.
Similarly, Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, which led to the discovery of penicillin.
That observation came from a scientist working with familiar tools in his own laboratory.
These cases show that deep familiarity with one field can itself be the source of breakthroughs, which contradicts the statement's claim that progress requires outside knowledge.
Expertise, rather than borrowing, was the decisive ingredient.
Second, fields can advance by examining and improving their own methods.
In 2015, a large collaboration of psychologists tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
This finding, produced by psychologists studying their own field, revealed how often single findings mislead and pushed researchers toward more careful, [[empirical|empirical]] standards.
Medicine offers a parallel: a hospital that regularly reviews its own deaths and complications can find and correct the errors in its own practice.
Such reviews draw on doctors' hard-won clinical experience, not on ideas borrowed from another discipline.
Such self-correction [[underscores|underscore]] that a field's own experience, including its failures, can drive significant advances without help from outside.
A field that can honestly measure its own errors already has a powerful engine of progress.
Admittedly, outside knowledge has sometimes been essential.
The Wolbachia method of dengue control, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, relied on microbiology to solve a public health problem.
Without microbiology, public health might still be relying only on traditional mosquito control.
Nevertheless, showing that outside knowledge often helps is different from showing that no field can advance without it.
The statement's word "unless" turns a common pattern into a strict rule, and the Semmelweis and replication examples are enough to show that the rule does not hold.

Thus the strongest [[tenable|tenable]] version of the statement is that outside knowledge frequently speeds progress, a claim the evidence does [[corroborate|corroborate]], but not that it is always necessary.
In conclusion, while outside knowledge can be valuable, fields of study can and do advance significantly from within.
Careful observation, honest self-examination and the lessons of a field's own failures have all produced major progress, and cases of borrowed knowledge show only that outside help is useful.
Researchers should welcome ideas from other fields, but they should not underestimate the power of mastering their own discipline deeply.

words.meaning_here: based on observation and experiment rather than theory
emphasizes or shows the importance of
able to be defended as reasonable

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement fails (careful observation and self-correction within a field) and then grants a case where outside knowledge was essential, explaining why that case does not prove the word "unless."

essays.title: Success means reaching your own goals

paragraphs.text: In many families, success is measured by a familiar list: a good salary, a respected title and a comfortable home.
The statement offers a different measure, claiming that true success can be measured primarily in terms of the goals one sets for oneself, rather than by the standards that others impose.
I largely agree, provided that the goals are worthwhile and demanding, because external measures often miss what makes a life or a career truly successful.
Self-set goals capture achievements that outside judgments overlook, they give work a meaning that rewards cannot, and only goals that are trivial or harmful weaken the statement.
First, judging success by one's own goals captures achievements that public judgments often miss.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and would have looked like a failure by the standards of his own day.
Yet he kept working toward his own artistic aims, and he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Similarly, Ignaz Semmelweis was rejected by most of his colleagues, but his idea that hand-washing could prevent childbed fever was vindicated by germ theory years after his death.
These [[posthumous|posthumous]] reversals show that outside judgments can be badly wrong, while measuring success by self-set goals captures what these people actually achieved.
Had they measured success by public approval, both men might have abandoned work that later proved important.
Second, goals that people set for themselves give their work an [[intrinsic|intrinsic]] meaning that external rewards cannot provide.
In my own field, a young epidemiologist might aim to answer one question well, such as why dengue returns to the same districts each year, even if the answer never appears in a famous journal.
Reaching that goal through [[arduous|arduous]] fieldwork may matter more to her, and to the districts she serves, than a prize would.
Likewise, the Wright brothers spent years on careful experiments with gliders before achieving the first powered flight in 1903.
They were not chasing fame; they were trying to solve a problem they had chosen for themselves.
Because their success came from goals they set themselves, it remained real even before others noticed, which is exactly what the statement claims.
Admittedly, the statement fails when the goals themselves are trivial or harmful.

A business executive whose goal is simply to protect this year's profits may succeed on his own terms while leading his company toward ruin, much as Kodak protected its film business and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, this weakness shows that goals must be judged, not that self-set goals are a poor measure of success.
A person who sets a [[laudable|laudable]] goal, such as improving patient care or mastering a craft, can reasonably judge success by how close she comes to it.
Such goals contain their own standard of value, so meeting them is a meaningful achievement.
This consideration shapes my position by adding a condition: self-set goals are the primary measure of success only when they are worthy ones.
In other words, the statement is right about who should set the measure, but the measure itself must be sound.
In conclusion, true success is best measured mainly by the worthwhile goals that people set for themselves.
Self-set goals capture achievements that others overlook and give work a deeper meaning that prizes and salaries cannot supply, although they must be worthy to count.
Public praise may be pleasant to [[garner|garner]], but lasting satisfaction comes from reaching goals that one has chosen carefully.

words.meaning_here: belonging to something itself, not from outside
very difficult and demanding much effort
gather or collect, often praise or support

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement holds (lasting value and personal meaning) and then examines a case where it does not, unworthy goals, and uses it to add a condition to the position.

essays.title: Success must be judged by impact

paragraphs.text: A student who sets out to pass an exam and passes it has met her goal, but few would call that, by itself, true success.
The statement nevertheless claims that true success can be measured primarily in terms of the goals one sets for oneself.
I mostly disagree, because self-set goals can be too low, too narrow or too selfish, so success must also be judged by its effects on other people.
People often set goals that are too modest or [[myopic|myopic]], real success is measured by what it does for others, and personal goals matter mainly for private satisfaction.
First, self-set goals are an unreliable measure because people often set the wrong goals.
Kodak's leaders set the goal of protecting their profitable film business, and for years they met it.
Yet the company was slow to embrace digital photography, even though its own engineer had invented the digital camera in 1975, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
On a smaller scale, a [[complacent|complacent]] employee who aims only to keep her job may reach that goal and still waste her abilities.
This shows that a measure based on one's own goals is too [[subjective|subjective]]: it rewards whoever sets the lowest or narrowest target.
A measure that gives Kodak's leaders full marks for reaching their goal is clearly missing something important.
Second, true success is better measured by its effects on others than by private goals.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
No single vaccinator could claim that success alone, yet together they ended a disease that had killed people for centuries.
The success of that campaign lies in the lives it saved, not in whether each participant reached a personal target.
Similarly, Alexander Fleming's discovery that mold killed bacteria became truly successful only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed penicillin into a usable drug during World War II.
In both cases, the most [[salient|salient]] measure of success was the benefit to many people, a standard that the statement ignores.
Success, in this sense, is something that other people can see and share, not only something one feels.
Admittedly, the statement holds true when we speak of personal satisfaction.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he kept pursuing his own artistic aims and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Nevertheless, his case actually supports my view, since we call him successful today because of the value his work has had for others, not because he met private goals.
His own goals may have given him purpose, but they do not explain why the world now honors him.
Self-set goals can [[mitigate|mitigate]] the pain of being ignored, but they are a measure of motivation rather than of success, so this concession limits rather than reverses my position.
A meaningful life may include private goals, but a successful one should also leave something of value for others.
In conclusion, self-set goals are not the primary measure of true success, even though they play a real role in motivating people.
Such goals may be too low or too narrow, real success is shown by its effects on others, and personal aims matter mainly as a source of motivation.
A better measure combines both standards: setting ambitious goals and asking whether reaching them has made other people's lives better.

words.meaning_here: focused on the short term and unable to see wider consequences
too satisfied with oneself to try harder
based on personal feelings rather than facts

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement fails (goals can be too low or too narrow, and impact on others matters) and then grants a case where it holds, personal satisfaction, explaining how this limits the position.

essays.title: Ordinary lives reveal a nation's greatness

paragraphs.text: Tourists remember a nation by its palaces, museums and monuments, and history books often do the same.
Yet the claim asks a deeper question: is the general welfare of a nation's people a better indication of that nation's greatness than the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists?
I largely agree, because a nation exists for its people, although great achievements matter most when they improve ordinary lives.

A nation's welfare shows how well it serves the many rather than the few, it reflects the choices of the whole society, and the strongest challenge, the lasting fame of great achievements, refines rather than defeats this view.
First, general welfare is a better indication of greatness because it measures how a nation treats all its people, not only its most famous citizens.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives.
As a result, a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Similarly, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.

No single hero may be [[lionized|lionize]] for these achievements, but they reveal national greatness in the most meaningful sense: millions of people rose out of [[penury|penury]] and gained secure homes.
A ruler's palace benefits a few, but a secure home benefits a family for generations.
Moreover, general welfare reflects the efforts of an entire society rather than a few individuals.
When Vietnam passed its 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
The law succeeded because police, health workers and ordinary riders all changed their behavior.
Likewise, Finland's schools reflect a national commitment: teachers must hold a master's degree, and teaching is a respected and selective profession.
Such a system depends on thousands of teachers, not on a single famous educator.
The [[aggregate|aggregate]] welfare of a people is therefore a portrait of the whole nation, while the achievements of a few rulers or artists show only a small part of it.
No single leader, artist or scientist could produce such results alone.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that great achievements, not ordinary welfare, are what the world remembers.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry, and the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.

Nevertheless, such achievements are great largely because they [[ameliorate|ameliorate]] people's living conditions, and a nation whose people are poor and sick has little claim to greatness however famous its scientists are.
A monument built while citizens go hungry impresses visitors but does not reveal a great nation.
Greatness built on hunger is not greatness that its own citizens would recognize.
This challenge therefore refines my position rather than defeating it: achievements contribute to greatness when they serve people's welfare, but they cannot replace it.
The question is not whether achievements matter, but whether they matter more than the lives of the people who make them possible.
In conclusion, the general welfare of a nation's people is a better sign of its greatness than the achievements of its elites, however impressive those achievements may be.
Welfare shows how a nation treats all its citizens, it reflects the work of the whole society, and even celebrated achievements matter most for the welfare they create.
Fame may be [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] or misleading, but a healthy, secure and educated population is lasting evidence of a great nation.

words.meaning_here: treated as a celebrity or hero
total, formed by combining many individual parts

essays.task_note: The essay supports the claim with two examples of national welfare and then states the strongest challenge, the lasting fame of great achievements, before answering it.

essays.title: Achievements show greatness beyond borders

paragraphs.text: Few people today can describe the daily lives of ordinary citizens in Renaissance Florence, yet many can name its painters.
This contrast raises the question of whether the general welfare of a nation's people is a better indication of that nation's greatness than the achievements of its rulers, artists or scientists.
I mostly disagree: welfare is necessary for a good nation, but greatness is shown more clearly by achievements that benefit people far beyond a nation's borders and generations.

Achievements extend benefits to all of humanity, welfare often depends on luck and can be [[transitory|transitory]], and although welfare reflects how a nation treats its own people, it cannot alone define greatness.
First, the achievements of scientists and leaders can benefit people everywhere, which is a sign of greatness that welfare alone cannot show.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Researchers in Vietnam, Africa and Europe now use that knowledge, so the project's benefits reach far beyond the countries that paid for it.
Similarly, GPS was built by the US military, yet once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of navigation and delivery apps used worldwide.
Such [[munificent|munificent]] contributions to humanity, rather than the comfort of one nation's citizens, are what we usually mean by greatness.
A nation that gives knowledge freely to the world shows a generosity that no measure of domestic comfort can capture.
Second, general welfare often depends on luck and can change quickly, which makes it a weak sign of lasting greatness.
A small nation with rich natural resources may enjoy high incomes for a generation without producing any lasting achievement in science, art or government.
Its welfare is real, but it is partly [[fortuitous|fortuitous]] rather than the result of national excellence.
By contrast, the work of scientists such as Marie Curie, who won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry, is still honored more than a century later.
Because welfare can rise and fall with circumstances while great achievements endure, judging greatness by welfare alone would be [[myopic|myopic]].
Lasting achievements, rather than passing prosperity, are the better evidence.
Admittedly, the strongest challenge to my view is that welfare reflects how a nation treats all its people, while achievements may reflect only a privileged few.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms, for instance, helped a country that had faced food shortages become one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Nevertheless, this example supports a balanced view rather than the claim, since the reform was itself an achievement of the nation's leaders.
Welfare, in other words, is often produced by the very achievements that the claim ranks below it.
Without the reformers' decisions, the later gains in welfare would not have occurred.
This challenge shapes my position: a nation that neglects its people cannot be great, but the nations we [[venerate|venerate]] most are those whose achievements improved lives at home and abroad.
In conclusion, general welfare is not a better indication of greatness than the achievements of a nation's leaders, artists and scientists.
Achievements spread benefits across borders and generations, welfare can rest on luck, and the welfare that does reflect greatness usually comes from achievements.
Greatness, therefore, is best judged by asking what a nation has given both to its own people and to the world, and how long those gifts endure.

words.meaning_here: happening by luck rather than design

essays.task_note: The essay argues that achievements are an equal or better sign of greatness and then states the strongest challenge, that welfare reflects how a nation treats all its people, before answering it.

essays.title: Persuading skeptics is the hardest test

paragraphs.text: It is easy to win an argument with people who already agree with you, but such victories prove very little.
For this reason, the statement holds that the best test of an argument is its ability to convince someone with an opposing viewpoint.
I largely agree, as long as the opponent is open to evidence, because persuading a fair-minded critic requires an argument to be both logically sound and well supported.

Opponents expose weaknesses that supporters ignore, convincing skeptics demands strong evidence, and although some opponents will reject even correct arguments, this limitation only qualifies the statement.
First, opponents are the best test because they find weaknesses that supporters overlook.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
By doing so, he ensured that his arguments would be tested by people who were eager to find their flaws.
Lincoln could not rely on loyalty to win these debates; he had to persuade.
In my own research, the most useful peer reviewers are often the ones who doubt my conclusions, since their [[candid|candid]] objections show me which parts of an analysis are weak.
An argument that survives such scrutiny is far more trustworthy than one that has only been praised by friends, which is exactly what the statement suggests.
Praise from allies feels good, but it rarely improves an argument.
Second, the need to convince skeptics forces arguments to rest on strong evidence rather than on assumptions.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Findings that had convinced sympathetic readers failed when skeptical researchers tested them again.
By contrast, the Wolbachia method rests on a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, which showed that it cut dengue cases by 77%, the kind of evidence that can persuade even doubters.
Such results speak even to readers who began as critics.
These cases show that a [[cogent|cogent]] argument is one that can win over people who begin by disagreeing.
Persuading a skeptic is difficult precisely because it requires evidence strong enough to overcome doubt.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when opponents are not open to evidence.
In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis showed that hand-washing in chlorinated lime sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever, yet most of his [[obdurate|obdurate]] colleagues rejected his idea.
Nevertheless, his argument eventually passed the test, since germ theory [[corroborated|corroborate]] it years after his death and convinced the medical world.
Galileo's case is similar: in 1633 the Church forced him to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, but that idea later won universal acceptance.
His opponents were not persuaded in his lifetime, but later generations were.
These cases qualify my position: the best test is an argument's ability to convince [[dispassionate|dispassionate]] opponents over time, not every opponent at once.
The statement remains valuable, then, as long as we give fair opponents enough time to weigh the evidence.
In conclusion, the ability to convince someone with an opposing view is generally the best test of an argument, provided that the opponent is willing to judge it fairly.
Opponents reveal hidden weaknesses and demand strong evidence, while the examples of Semmelweis and Galileo show that the test works best with fair critics and enough time.
We should therefore seek out thoughtful critics rather than avoid them, because their doubts make our arguments stronger.

words.meaning_here: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion
not influenced by strong emotion; fair

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement holds (critics expose weaknesses and fair skeptics require strong evidence) and then examines a case where it does not, correct ideas rejected by biased opponents, and explains how that case qualifies the position.

essays.title: Evidence matters more than persuasion

paragraphs.text: In an age of social media, the most persuasive messages are not always the most accurate ones, and the most accurate are not always persuasive.
This problem casts doubt on the statement that the best test of an argument is its ability to convince someone with an opposing viewpoint.
I mostly disagree, because whether an argument convinces people depends on its audience as much as on its quality; the best test is whether its logic and evidence hold up.
Sound arguments are often rejected by opponents, weak arguments often succeed, and while convincing a fair critic is useful, it is a sign of quality rather than the test itself.
First, many sound arguments have failed to convince their opponents, at least for many years.
In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
Similarly, in 1633 the Church forced Galileo to [[recant|recant]] his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
Yet his view, like that of Semmelweis, was later accepted as correct.
If the statement were correct, both arguments would have failed the test, even though they were right; their opponents were simply [[intransigent|intransigent]].
The fault lay with the audience, not with the arguments.
Second, weak or false arguments sometimes convince people easily, which shows that persuasion is a poor measure of quality.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so false claims often reach and persuade millions before the truth catches up.
In medicine, I often meet patients who are convinced that antibiotics will cure a viral cold, even though overuse of these drugs helps resistant bacteria spread.
Because antibiotics are often sold over the counter in Vietnam, this belief easily turns into harmful practice.
The argument persuades because it is simple and familiar, not because it is true.
These cases show that [[credulous|credulous]] audiences can make [[specious|specious]] reasoning seem strong, so the ability to convince does not prove an argument's [[veracity|veracity]].
Popularity measures how well an argument fits what people already believe, not whether it is true.
Admittedly, convincing a thoughtful opponent can be a valuable check on an argument.
Abraham Lincoln appointed political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers so that his ideas would face real challenge.
Seward and the others were able men who could challenge Lincoln's reasoning on its merits.
Nevertheless, the value of Lincoln's approach came from the quality of the critics, not from the simple fact that they disagreed.
An opponent who examines the evidence fairly is useful; an opponent who refuses to listen tells us nothing about the argument.
This consideration shapes my position: persuading fair-minded critics is a helpful sign of quality, but the fundamental test remains logic and evidence.
A critic's judgment is only as good as the critic's willingness to weigh evidence.
In conclusion, the ability to convince opponents is not the best test of an argument, although it can be a useful sign.
Correct arguments are often rejected, false arguments often spread, and even the value of persuading critics depends on whether those critics judge the evidence fairly.
An argument should be judged first by its reasoning and evidence, and only then by how many people it convinces.

words.meaning_here: publicly withdraw a belief one held
seeming true or reasonable but actually false

essays.task_note: The essay shows two ways the statement fails (sound arguments rejected and weak arguments accepted) and then grants a case where convincing opponents is a useful test, explaining how this shapes the position.

essays.title: Citizens' well-being reveals effective leadership

paragraphs.text: Political leaders are often judged by their speeches, their popularity or the grand projects that carry their names, yet none of these shows whether ordinary people are better off.
The statement proposes a more practical standard: the effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by examining the well-being of that country's citizens.
I largely agree, as long as well-being is measured over time and with attention to forces beyond leaders' control.

Well-being shows whether policies actually work, it reflects how leaders treat all citizens rather than a favored few, and although outside events can distort it, careful comparison can address that problem.
First, citizens' well-being is the clearest evidence of whether leaders' policies actually work.
When Vietnam's leaders passed a law in 2007 requiring motorbike helmets, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months.
Head injuries and deaths fell, giving citizens and observers a direct measure of the policy's [[efficacy|efficacy]].
Similarly, Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats, a result that any citizen can see.
Such results are difficult to fake, because citizens experience them in their daily lives.
These cases show that well-being turns abstract promises into measurable outcomes, which makes it a better test of leadership than [[ostentatious|ostentatious]] projects or speeches.
A leader who promises safer roads can be judged by whether fewer people die on them.
Second, measuring well-being reveals whether leaders serve all citizens rather than only the powerful.
Finland's leaders, for example, require schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and have made teaching a respected and selective profession, which benefits children in every community.
In contrast, a government that builds impressive airports while rural clinics lack basic medicines may appear successful in photographs but fails most of its people.
In my work in Vietnam, the clearest signs of good health policy appear in district hospitals, not in national ceremonies.
A leader's effectiveness shows in whether a farmer's child can see a doctor, not in how many ribbons are cut in the capital.
Examining the [[equitable|equitable]] spread of well-being, rather than averages or headlines alone, therefore tells us whether leaders are effective for the whole country.
Averages can hide neglected groups, so effectiveness must be judged by how widely well-being is shared.
Admittedly, the statement does not fully hold when well-being changes for reasons beyond leaders' control.
During a global pandemic or recession, citizens may suffer even under capable leaders, while a fortunate country may prosper under weak ones because of rich natural resources.
Nevertheless, leaders can still be judged by how well they [[mitigate|mitigate]] such shocks compared with similar countries.
Comparing countries that faced the same crisis allows us to separate bad luck from bad leadership.
If two neighboring countries face the same storm or epidemic and one recovers faster, the difference says something about their leaders.

This consideration shapes my position: well-being is the best measure of leadership only when it is examined over time and in context, rather than used to [[extrapolate|extrapolate]] from a single good or bad year.
In conclusion, the well-being of citizens is generally the best measure of how effective a country's leaders are, provided it is judged fairly.
It shows whether policies work, reveals whether leaders serve everyone, and, when outside shocks are considered, offers a fair basis for comparison.
Citizens should therefore judge their leaders less by what they promise and more by how people's lives change under their leadership.

designed to impress or attract notice
draw a broader conclusion from known facts

essays.title: Judge leaders by decisions, not outcomes alone

paragraphs.text: When citizens are healthy and prosperous, it is tempting to give their leaders the credit, and when citizens suffer, it is just as tempting to blame them.
The statement turns this habit into a rule, claiming that the effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by examining the well-being of that country's citizens.
I mostly disagree, because well-being is shaped by many forces besides leadership, so it should be one measure among several rather than the best one.
The effects of good leadership often take decades to appear, well-being depends heavily on outside forces, and only in some cases does it reflect leaders' choices directly.
First, the results of effective leadership often appear long after the leaders' decisions, so current well-being can mislead.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
A judgment based only on citizens' well-being in the late 1980s would have missed how [[prescient|prescient]] those reforms were.

Similarly, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, so the value of supporting such research became visible only much later.
This shows that well-being measured at one moment may reward or punish the wrong leaders.
Leaders whose reforms pay off slowly may be judged harshly, while those who inherit good times may be praised unfairly.
Second, citizens' well-being depends heavily on [[extraneous|extraneous]] factors that leaders cannot control.
A country rich in natural resources may enjoy high incomes even under weak leaders, while a poor country may struggle despite capable ones.
Likewise, a pandemic or global recession can harm citizens everywhere, regardless of how wisely their governments act.
In such cases, falling well-being says more about the crisis than about the people trying to manage it.
Leaders may even raise well-being in an [[expedient|expedient]] way, for example by borrowing heavily, leaving the economy in a [[precarious|precarious]] position for their successors.
A better measure of effectiveness is the quality of leaders' decisions given the circumstances they faced, not simply the outcomes that followed.
Judging leaders by outcomes alone would reward luck and punish courage.
Admittedly, there are cases in which citizens' well-being does reflect leadership quite directly, and in such cases the statement holds.
When Vietnam passed its 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
Nevertheless, such clear links are the exception, since most national outcomes have many causes and long delays.
The helmet law was a single, simple policy with fast results, unlike economic or educational reforms.
Few other policies show their effects so quickly or so clearly.
This case shapes my position: well-being is a useful measure for specific, short-term policies, but it cannot be the best general test of leadership.
For most decisions, we must look at the choices themselves and ask whether they were wise given what leaders knew at the time.
In conclusion, citizens' well-being is an important but imperfect measure of how effective a country's leaders are, and it should never be used alone.
The benefits of good decisions often appear only after many years, outside forces strongly shape well-being, and direct links like the helmet law are uncommon.
Leaders are best judged by examining both the decisions they made and the conditions in which they made them.

convenient in the short term but not wise

essays.title: Protect wilderness by law, but flexibly

paragraphs.text: Every year, roads, farms and cities push a little further into land that has never been developed.
Because such land cannot easily be restored once it is cleared, the question of whether nations should protect it by law is more [[pressing|pressing]] than ever.
I largely agree that nations should pass laws to preserve their remaining wilderness areas in a natural state, as long as those laws leave room for limited, carefully managed local use.
Wilderness protects human health, and its loss is nearly impossible to undo; although a rigid ban can impose real costs on poor communities, this concern calls for flexible laws rather than none.
First, preserving wilderness serves a nation's own interest because intact ecosystems protect human health.
In my work as an epidemiologist in Vietnam, I have seen how clearing forests and draining wetlands bring people, livestock and mosquitoes into close and constant contact.
When natural habitats are broken up, infections that once circulated only among wild animals gain new chances to reach humans, and outbreaks become harder to predict and control.
Similarly, coastal mangrove forests act as a natural [[buffer|buffer]] against storms, so villages that cut them down for shrimp ponds are often left more exposed to flooding.
This shows that wilderness is not a luxury for hikers but a form of protection that benefits everyone, which is why its preservation deserves the force of law.
Voluntary pledges by companies or local officials are too easily broken when profits are at stake, so only a law can make this protection reliable.
Second, laws are needed because the loss of wilderness is largely permanent, whereas the economic gains from developing it are often [[ephemeral|ephemeral]].
Consider a province that allows an old forest to be logged to pay for a new road.
The timber is sold within a few years, but the forest, with its soil, rivers and wildlife, may take centuries to recover, if it recovers at all.
Likewise, once a species disappears, no amount of later investment can bring it back.

When one choice can be reversed and the other cannot, a [[prudent|prudent]] nation should protect the option it cannot recreate, and a binding law is the most reliable way to keep that option open for future generations.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that strict preservation can slow development in countries that still need to reduce poverty.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters while poverty fell dramatically.
Growth of this kind depends on land and resources, and a law that locked away every remaining forest could deny farming families similar opportunities.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for well-designed laws, not for having no laws at all.
A preservation law can allow local residents to collect forest products, guide visitors or work as rangers, while still forbidding large-scale logging and mining.
In this way, the concession refines my position rather than overturning it: wilderness should remain largely natural, but the people who live beside it should share in its benefits.
In conclusion, I largely agree that nations should protect their remaining wilderness by law, provided that such laws are flexible enough to support nearby communities.
Intact ecosystems safeguard public health, their destruction is difficult to reverse, and the genuine costs to the poor can be [[mitigated|mitigate]] through careful design.
A nation that sacrifices its last wild places for quick gains will find that some losses are permanent, which is precisely why the law should act before the bulldozers do.

essays.title: Manage wilderness, do not freeze it

paragraphs.text: Few people would argue that a nation should destroy its last forests, rivers and mountains for short-term profit.
Yet the claim that nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness in its natural state goes much further, because it treats every wild area the same and rules out almost all human use.
I mostly disagree with this claim; wilderness deserves strong protection, but rigid, all-or-nothing laws are less effective than flexible management based on evidence and local needs.
Blanket preservation ignores the people who live in or near wild areas, and it prevents active management that some ecosystems require, although a few unique places do warrant strict protection.
First, laws that preserve every wild area untouched often harm the communities that depend on that land.
In rural Vietnam, many families gather firewood, medicinal plants and food from nearby forests, and their incomes are small and [[precarious|precarious]].
If a national law suddenly banned all such use, these households would lose part of their livelihood, and they might come to see conservation as an enemy rather than a shared goal.
Similarly, a community excluded from a protected area has little reason to report illegal logging or to help fight a forest fire.
By contrast, residents who are allowed to use a forest carefully often become its most [[assiduous|assiduous]] guardians, because its health is tied to their own.
This shows that a law requiring "any" wilderness to stay in its natural state can [[alienate|alienate]] the very people whose cooperation conservation needs most.
Second, a strict "natural state" rule is often impractical because many ecosystems already depend on human management.
Consider a national park where invasive plants are spreading or where a disease is killing native animals.
Leaving such an area completely alone does not preserve it; it allows the damage to continue, whereas careful intervention, such as removing invasive species, can restore balance.

Public health offers a useful parallel: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a trial in Indonesia, showing that thoughtful intervention in nature can be [[salutary|salutary]].
The goal of policy, therefore, should be healthy ecosystems, and achieving that goal sometimes requires active management rather than a legal command to leave everything untouched.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is that some wilderness areas are so rare and fragile that any human use would damage them permanently.
An ancient forest with species found nowhere else, for example, cannot be replaced once it is logged or fragmented by roads.
Nevertheless, this argument supports strict protection for specific places that scientists identify as irreplaceable, not a uniform rule for every wild area in a nation.
A country can fully protect its most unique habitats while allowing regulated, sustainable use of larger forests that already support local communities.
Accepting this point therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] my position without reversing it: protection should be graded by value and risk rather than applied in the same way everywhere.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that nations should legally preserve all remaining wilderness exactly as it is.
Such laws can harm and alienate local communities and can block the active management that damaged ecosystems need, even though a small number of irreplaceable places deserve strict protection.
Wise conservation law should be [[discriminating|discriminating]], protecting what is unique absolutely and managing the rest with both nature and the needs of local people in mind.

essays.title: Five-year limits keep power accountable

paragraphs.text: Power has a way of protecting itself, even when the people who hold it mean well.
For this reason, some argue that anyone in power, whether in business, politics, education or government, should be required to step down after five years.

I largely support this policy for positions of significant power, because the fresher thinking and better-prepared successors it would likely produce outweigh the cost of losing some experienced leaders.
A five-year limit would prevent leaders from clinging to outdated ideas and would develop a deeper pool of successors, although it could sometimes remove an effective leader too early.
First, a mandatory limit would make organizations less likely to become trapped by the views of a leader who has stayed too long.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Leaders who had built their careers on film had little reason to [[champion|champion]] a technology that threatened it.
Similarly, when Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand washing reduced deaths from childbed fever, most established colleagues rejected his idea.
These cases show that long tenure can make leaders defend the [[status quo|status quo]] instead of questioning it, and a five-year limit would regularly bring in people with less to protect.
Fresh leaders are not always wiser, but they are less likely to [[harbor|harbor]] an attachment to yesterday's decisions.
Second, the policy would force institutions to train successors, which makes them stronger over time.
Consider a provincial hospital whose director has held the post for twenty years, long after the original reforms have been completed.
Because everyone expects the director to stay, younger doctors rarely gain management experience, and when the director finally retires, no one is ready to lead.
A five-year rule would change this pattern, since the organization would know from the start that it must prepare the next leader.
In my own field of public health research, projects led by teams that share responsibility tend to survive changes in staff far better than those built around one person.
The consequence of the policy, therefore, is not only new leadership but a culture of planning that keeps organizations strong after any single leader leaves.
Rather than depending on one indispensable person, the institution learns to depend on its own systems.
Admittedly, the policy could sometimes remove a skilled leader in the middle of important work.

A school principal who is halfway through a successful reform might be forced to leave just as results begin to appear, and the new principal might [[jettison|jettison]] good programs simply to make a personal mark.
Nevertheless, five years is long enough to set a clear direction, and a capable leader can stay on as an adviser while the successor continues the work.

This cost is real, but it is smaller and more manageable than the cost of leaders who stay so long that they become [[complacent|complacent]], so it shapes how I would apply the policy rather than whether I support it.
In conclusion, I largely support requiring those in significant positions of power to step down after five years.
Such a rule would protect organizations from outdated thinking and would build a reliable supply of new leaders, while the risk of losing good leaders early can be reduced through advisory roles.
Limiting how long anyone holds power is a [[modest|modest]] price for keeping institutions open to change.

essays.title: A fixed five-year exit is too blunt

paragraphs.text: Good leadership is hard to find, and it often takes years to develop.
The proposal that anyone in power, in any field, must step down after five years therefore deserves careful scrutiny.

I oppose this policy as a universal rule, because its likely consequences, lost expertise and short-term thinking, would outweigh its benefits, although term limits make sense for some high political offices.
Forcing every leader out after five years would waste hard-won experience and would discourage long-term projects, even though the policy would reduce the danger of leaders becoming entrenched.
First, a five-year limit would throw away experience precisely when it becomes most valuable.
Consider a district health director in Vietnam who spends her first years learning the budget, building trust with village health workers and fixing weak reporting systems.
By her fifth year, she finally understands which programs work, yet the policy would force her to hand everything to a newcomer who must start again.
Similarly, the founder of a small business who is forced to leave the company she built would lose her income, and the firm would lose its most knowledgeable person.
These examples show that the policy would treat experience as a danger rather than an asset, an approach that is [[counterproductive|counterproductive]] in fields where skill grows slowly.
In medicine, research and teaching, the most valuable judgment often appears only after many years, so a fixed exit date would remove leaders at the moment they reach their [[acme|acme]].
Second, the policy would encourage leaders to favor quick results over work that pays off only in the long run.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Achievements like this require patient, consistent leadership, because the benefits arrive long after the first decisions are made.
A leader who knows she must leave in five years may avoid such [[arduous|arduous]] commitments and choose visible, short-term projects that make her own record look good.
Her successor, facing the same deadline, would have the same incentive, so the pattern would repeat every five years.
The consequence would be organizations that [[husband|husband]] their energy for easy wins while neglecting the difficult goals that matter most.
Admittedly, leaders who stay too long can block new ideas, and this is the strongest argument for the policy.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure was a failure of judgment, and a rule removing all leaders after five years would not have guaranteed better judgment from their replacements.
Better remedies already exist: boards can replace weak executives, voters can remove politicians, and schools can review principals regularly.
This consequence therefore shapes my position only partly; it justifies term limits for offices where power is hard to check, such as a presidency, but not a single rule for every field.
A blunt rule applied to a village school, a family company and a national government alike would cause more harm than the problem it is meant to solve.
In conclusion, I oppose requiring all people in power to step down after five years.
The policy would waste valuable experience and push leaders toward short-term thinking, while the real problem it targets, entrenched leaders, can be solved with more [[judicious|judicious]] tools.
Rather than replacing everyone on a fixed schedule, institutions should judge leaders by their results and remove them when those results fail.

essays.title: Ideals set the direction for politics

paragraphs.text: Every major reform in history began as an idea that most people once considered unrealistic.
This raises a basic question about politics: should its goal be the pursuit of an ideal, or should it be finding common ground and reaching reasonable consensus?
My position aligns more closely with the first view, because an ideal gives politics its direction, although consensus is often the practical means of moving toward it, not the goal itself.

Ideals push societies to correct injustices that comfortable majorities would accept, and they motivate long-term efforts that compromise alone cannot sustain; still, the second view rightly stresses that ideals must be negotiated into law.
First, the pursuit of an ideal is essential because consensus can easily preserve injustice.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and their action helped end bus segregation in that city.

A search for common ground with defenders of segregation would likely have produced only small changes, because the injustice itself was the [[status quo|status quo]], and its defenders had little reason to [[relent|relent]].

Similarly, public outrage over the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
These cases show that when the existing arrangement is unjust, politics must be guided by a principle rather than by whatever the majority already accepts.
Second, an ideal motivates the long, [[arduous|arduous]] effort that ambitious public goals require.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
The goal of removing a disease from the entire planet must have seemed [[quixotic|quixotic]] at first, yet it gave governments a shared purpose that justified sustained cooperation.
In my own work on dengue control in Vietnam, I have seen that programs with a clear, ambitious target keep their funding and staff far longer than programs that only aim to satisfy every stakeholder.
An ideal, therefore, is not the enemy of practical politics; it supplies the energy and focus that practical work needs.
Without a guiding ideal, consensus tends to settle on whatever is easiest, and difficult goals are quietly abandoned.
Admittedly, the second view is right that ideals pursued without compromise can divide a society and achieve nothing.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, a choice that helped him govern a deeply divided nation.
Nevertheless, Lincoln compromised on methods and people, not on his central purpose of preserving the Union.
Consensus was his tool, while the ideal remained his goal.
Had he treated agreement with his rivals as the purpose of politics, he might have accepted the division of the country as a reasonable compromise.
This example clarifies rather than weakens my position: reasonable consensus is valuable, but its value depends on the direction an ideal provides, so the ideal should remain the goal of politics.
In conclusion, I side with those who believe that politics should pursue an ideal, while recognizing that consensus is usually how ideals become reality.

Ideals expose injustices that majorities tolerate and sustain long efforts like the eradication of smallpox, and even the most skilled consensus builders, such as Lincoln, used compromise to advance a principle.
A politics of consensus alone might be efficient but [[desultory|desultory]], so the ideal must come first and agreement second.

lacking a clear plan or purpose

essays.title: Politics works through consensus

paragraphs.text: In a society of millions of people with different values, almost no political decision pleases everyone.
For this reason, people disagree about whether politics should pursue an ideal or should aim to find common ground and reach reasonable consensus.
My position aligns more closely with the second view, because consensus produces policies that last and can actually be implemented, although ideals remain important as a source of moral direction.

Consensus makes reforms durable, and it allows leaders to respond [[pragmatically|pragmatic]] to evidence; at the same time, the first view rightly reminds us that some injustices cannot be bargained away.
First, the goal of consensus matters because policies built on broad agreement survive and work in practice.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
As a physician, I see this law as a public health success because enforcement was feasible only once most citizens, police and businesses accepted the rule as reasonable.
By contrast, a policy imposed in pursuit of an ideal that the public rejects is often ignored, reversed or enforced only at great cost.
This shows that political success is measured by results people accept, which is why consensus, not purity, should be the goal.
An ideal that is never implemented helps no one, however noble it sounds.
Second, the pursuit of consensus encourages practical, evidence-based choices instead of rigid [[dogma|dogma]].

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters while poverty fell dramatically.
The reforms succeeded because leaders were willing to [[jettison|jettison]] parts of an earlier ideal when the evidence showed it was failing.
Similarly, Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Rather than surrounding himself with people who shared every view, he gained advisers who could warn him when his plans were weak.
In both cases, leaders gained strength by listening to opponents and adjusting, which is the essence of reasonable consensus.
Admittedly, the first view is right that some issues are matters of principle, and consensus can become an excuse for accepting injustice.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and their firm stand helped end bus segregation in that city.
Their cause was just, and no amount of polite negotiation would have made segregation acceptable.
Nevertheless, even this victory became lasting only when the change was accepted by courts, officials and, gradually, the wider public.
Ideals can start a movement and give it [[inexorable|inexorable]] moral force, but consensus is what turns it into stable policy, so this example refines my position rather than reversing it.
The ideal view explains why change begins, but the consensus view explains why change lasts, and lasting results are what politics must ultimately deliver.
In conclusion, I believe that finding common ground and reaching reasonable consensus should be the main goal of politics, with ideals serving as a moral compass rather than the destination.
Consensus produces durable laws like Vietnam's helmet rule and supports practical reforms like Doi Moi, while even idealistic movements ultimately depend on broad acceptance.
A politics that seeks agreement is less dramatic than one that chases an ideal, and its victories are often gradual, but it is far more likely to improve people's lives.

essays.task_note: It names the consensus view as its position in the thesis, supports it in two body paragraphs, and credits the ideal view through the Montgomery boycott before explaining why consensus still matters more.

essays.title: Strict trash limits change behavior fastest

paragraphs.text: Most people throw things away without thinking about where their trash goes.

Because household waste fills landfills and pollutes rivers, some argue that the best way to solve this problem is for towns and cities to impose strict limits on the amount of trash they accept from each household.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as the limits are combined with convenient recycling and composting services that give households a realistic alternative.
Strict limits change behavior directly at the source and make the cost of waste visible to every family, although critics rightly worry about illegal dumping and fairness.
First, strict limits work because they change behavior where waste is actually created, in the household.
Public health experience shows that clear, enforced rules can change daily habits quickly.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Earlier campaigns that merely [[exhorted|exhort]] people to wear helmets had achieved far less, because voluntary appeals are easy to ignore.
Similarly, a family that knows only one bag of trash will be collected each week quickly learns to buy fewer packaged goods and to separate recyclable materials.
This shows that a firm limit, unlike a poster asking people to "reduce waste," turns a vague goal into a concrete daily decision.
Polite requests alone rarely change [[ingrained|ingrained]] habits, but a rule that affects every household every week does.
Second, limits make the hidden cost of waste visible, which encourages lasting changes in consumption.
Consider a city where trash collection is unlimited and paid for through general taxes.
Residents in such a city have no reason to notice how much they discard, so waste grows with income year after year.
Once the city sets a limit, however, each extra bag requires effort or payment, and households begin to scrutinize what they buy.
Over time, stores also respond by offering products with less packaging, because customers start to prefer them.
A limit therefore creates a chain of [[salutary|salutary]] effects, from household habits to retail practices, that broad education campaigns rarely achieve.
In my experience with public health programs in Vietnam, people respond far more to a change in what is convenient or costly than to advice about what is good for them.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that strict limits might lead some residents to dump trash illegally or might burden large and poor families unfairly.
A household with several children produces more waste than a single person, and a family without a car may find it hard to reach a recycling center.
Nevertheless, these problems call for better design, not for abandoning limits.
Cities can set limits by household size, collect recycling and food waste for free at the curb, and fine illegal dumping heavily as a [[deterrent|deterrent]].
With these measures, the limit becomes both fair and [[feasible|feasible]], so the challenge refines my position rather than defeating it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that strict household trash limits are the best way to reduce consumer waste, provided that cities make the alternatives easy and fair.
Such limits change behavior at the source and reveal the real cost of waste, while the risks of illegal dumping and unfairness can be managed through careful policy.
When throwing things away stops being free and unlimited, people quickly discover how much they never needed to buy.

words.meaning_here: possible and practical to carry out
deeply fixed and hard to change
