essays.title: Fix waste at its source, not the curb

paragraphs.text: When a sink overflows, mopping the floor is less useful than turning off the tap.
The same logic applies to the claim that the best way to solve problems caused by consumer waste is for towns and cities to impose strict limits on the trash they accept from each household.
I mostly disagree with this claim, because household limits address waste too late in its life and can create new problems, although they can play a [[modest|modest]] supporting role.
The main sources of waste lie with producers rather than households, and strict limits can encourage illegal dumping and unfairness, even though limits do succeed in changing some household habits.
First, household limits are not the best solution because much consumer waste is decided before a product ever reaches the home.
A family buying instant noodles, bottled water or a new phone has little control over the plastic wrapping, the bottle or the packaging that comes with them.

Rules that require companies to use less packaging, or to take back used products, would reduce waste for every household at once, without requiring millions of families to change their routines or pay new fees.

In public health, we learned long ago that preventing a problem is more effective than dealing with its consequences one case at a time; smallpox was eradicated by a global vaccination campaign, not by treating each patient.
This shows that targeting producers, the source of the problem, is likely to be more [[efficacious|efficacious]] than penalizing the families at the end of the chain.
Second, strict limits can backfire by encouraging illegal dumping and by placing an unfair burden on poorer households.
Consider a town that suddenly accepts only one bag of trash per week from each home.
A large family that cannot afford extra fees may begin burning waste in the yard or leaving it by a river at night, and the town's environmental problem simply moves somewhere less visible.
In parts of Vietnam where waste collection is already limited, open burning is a common practice that harms air quality and health.
A policy that worsens pollution while burdening the poor can hardly be the best way to protect the environment, so the claim overstates what limits can achieve.
Admittedly, the strongest challenge to my view is that limits do change household behavior quickly and visibly.
Firm rules often succeed where voluntary appeals fail: Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months.
Nevertheless, a helmet protects the person who wears it, whereas limiting trash collection does not remove the packaging that producers keep making.
A household under a strict limit may [[pare|pare]] its waste somewhat, but it still cannot buy products that companies do not offer.
Limits can therefore support a broader strategy, but they cannot be the best or main solution.
To treat them as the primary answer would [[relegate|relegate]] producers, who design the packaging, to the edge of a problem they largely create.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that strict household trash limits are the best way to solve consumer waste problems.
Waste is largely determined by producers, and strict limits risk illegal dumping and unfair costs, even though they can modestly improve household habits.
Cities should still encourage recycling and composting at home, but the [[pressing|pressing]] task is to turn off the tap by making producers responsible for the waste they create.

words.meaning_here: effective in producing the desired result
move to a less important position

essays.task_note: It challenges "the best way" in the claim and uses the fourth paragraph to give the strongest opposing reason, that limits quickly change habits, before explaining why it is insufficient.

essays.title: Struggle teaches more than success

paragraphs.text: Success feels good, but it rarely forces us to ask why things worked.
Perhaps this is why many people believe that we learn our most valuable lessons from struggling with our limitations rather than from enjoying our successes.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that people reflect on their struggles instead of simply enduring them, since hardship without reflection teaches very little.
Struggle forces us to understand problems deeply and builds the persistence that later success requires, although success can also teach valuable lessons when we study it carefully.
First, struggling with limitations teaches more because it forces us to understand a problem rather than merely solve it once.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their lack of formal training and funding meant they could not rely on others' answers, so each failed glider taught them something precise about lift and control.
Similarly, when I first analyzed dengue surveillance data, my early models failed repeatedly, and those failures taught me more about the data's weaknesses than any successful model did.
This shows that limitations push us to examine why something does not work, and that kind of understanding is the most valuable lesson of all.
Success can hide our weaknesses, whereas a limitation exposes them and forces us to deal with them directly, a process that is uncomfortable but deeply [[edifying|edify]].
Second, struggle builds the persistence and resilience that are necessary for later achievements.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911 despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Overcoming those barriers required a [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] commitment that easy success could never have taught her.
Likewise, a medical student who fails an exam and must study again often develops habits of discipline that serve her for the rest of her career.
The struggle, in these cases, does more than produce one success; it shapes a character that can [[surmount|surmount]] future obstacles.
Someone who has never struggled may [[buckle|buckle]] at the first serious setback, while someone who has struggled knows that obstacles can be overcome with time and effort.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that success can also teach important lessons, especially about what works.

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, and that success showed the world how global cooperation can defeat a disease.
Nevertheless, success teaches best when people study the difficulties that came before it, rather than simply enjoying the result.
The lessons of smallpox lie largely in how the campaign overcame shortages, distrust and logistical problems along the way.
Students of public health learn less from the final announcement of victory than from the many problems that had to be solved before it.
This challenge, therefore, [[qualifies|qualify]] my view instead of overturning it: success is instructive, but mostly because of the struggles hidden inside it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that our most valuable lessons come from struggling with our limitations rather than from enjoying our successes.
Struggle forces deep understanding, as the Wright brothers showed, and builds persistence, as Marie Curie's career showed, while even great successes teach mainly through the obstacles they overcame.
The lesson for any learner is not to avoid difficulty but to examine it, since our limitations are often our best teachers.

essays.title: Success teaches as much as struggle

paragraphs.text: Popular wisdom often celebrates failure as the best teacher, and stories of heroic struggle are repeated so often that they have become almost [[hackneyed|hackneyed]].
In the same spirit, some claim that we learn our most valuable lessons from struggling with our limitations rather than from enjoying our successes.

I mostly disagree with this claim, because successes teach us what works and give us the confidence to keep learning, although struggle remains an important teacher when it eventually leads somewhere.
Successes provide models that others can copy, and they build the motivation needed to continue, even though struggle can sometimes produce discoveries that success never would.
First, successes teach valuable lessons because they show clearly what works and can be repeated.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
For public health workers like me, this success offers a practical lesson: clear rules, strong enforcement and public communication can change behavior quickly.
Similarly, Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
These successes are valuable precisely because they can be studied and [[emulated|emulate]], whereas a struggle often reveals only what does not work.
Knowing that one path failed is useful, but knowing exactly which path succeeded, and why, saves others years of wasted effort.
Health officials in other countries can study Vietnam's helmet law when designing their own road safety policies, which shows how a single success can teach far beyond its origin.
Second, success builds the confidence and motivation that make further learning possible.
Consider a student who repeatedly fails at mathematics.
Rather than learning from her limitations, she may decide that she is simply bad at the subject and stop trying, a response that teachers see often.
If she experiences a few small successes, however, she gains the confidence to attempt harder problems and to learn from her mistakes.
In my own teaching of young researchers, I have found that an early publication, even a modest one, often motivates them more than months of rejected drafts.
Constant struggle, in other words, can [[daunt|daunt]] people as easily as it strengthens them.
This shows that enjoying success is not a distraction from learning but often its foundation.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is that some of the greatest lessons have come from long periods of struggle.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Nevertheless, their struggle was valuable because it eventually produced success; years of difficult work became meaningful when the vaccines proved effective.
Without that success, the world might never have recognized what their research had taught, and their long struggle might have been forgotten.
Struggle and success are therefore [[complementary|complementary]], and the claim is wrong to rank one so clearly above the other.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that our most valuable lessons come from struggling with limitations rather than from enjoying successes.
Successes provide models to follow and build confidence, while even the most famous stories of struggle, such as the research behind mRNA vaccines, matter because they ended in success.
Rather than [[lionizing|lionize]] failure, we should learn from both our difficulties and our achievements.

essays.title: Boredom often reflects a lack of effort

paragraphs.text: People today have more books, courses and ideas available to them than at any time in history, many of them free.
Yet many still announce that they are bored, sometimes with a sense of self-satisfaction, as if boredom proved they were too sophisticated to be interested.

I largely agree with the claim that such boredom should be a source of embarrassment, and with the reason that it often arises from a lack of imagination and self-motivation, at least for people who have the freedom to choose their activities.

The claim holds because interesting work is almost always available, and the reason holds because curiosity can find value in ordinary situations, although boredom sometimes has causes beyond a person's control.
First, the claim is largely correct, because people with free time and access to information rarely lack opportunities to do something meaningful.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Its writers were not paid or ordered to contribute; they simply turned ordinary free hours into knowledge for millions of readers.
Similarly, retired doctors in Vietnam often volunteer at community clinics, using their spare time to serve patients rather than complain about having nothing to do.
When such opportunities exist, boasting about boredom is not a sign of sophistication but an admission of [[apathy|apathy]], which is why the claim is right to call it embarrassing.
Second, the reason is also persuasive, because curiosity can turn even dull situations into sources of interest.
Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold had killed bacteria on a culture plate, an event that many scientists would have dismissed as a ruined experiment.
His curiosity about this small accident led to penicillin, which became a usable drug when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
Likewise, in my own epidemiological work, routine data cleaning seemed tedious until I began asking why certain records were missing, a question that revealed real problems in reporting.
These examples suggest that boredom is often less a feature of the situation than a failure to ask questions, just as the reason claims.
An imaginative person treats an empty afternoon or a routine task as a question to explore, while an unimaginative one treats it as a [[vexation|vexation]] to endure.
Admittedly, not all boredom comes from a lack of imagination or motivation.
A factory worker doing the same task for ten hours a day, or a patient whose depression has drained her energy, may feel bored for reasons that are not her fault.
In such cases, telling the person to be more imaginative would be both unfair and unhelpful, and the reason clearly does not apply.
Nevertheless, the claim targets boredom expressed with self-satisfaction, and people in such difficult circumstances rarely boast about their condition.

This exception therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] the reason without undermining the claim: we should show compassion for boredom imposed by hard conditions, while still expecting those with freedom and resources to take responsibility for their own interest in the world.
In conclusion, I largely agree that self-satisfied boredom should be embarrassing and that it usually stems from a lack of imagination and self-motivation.
Meaningful opportunities are widely available, curiosity can find value in ordinary tasks, and only people bored by circumstances beyond their control deserve to be [[exonerated|exonerate]].
For most of us, then, the cure for boredom is not a more exciting world but a more curious and [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] mind.

essays.title: Boredom is a signal, not a shame

paragraphs.text: Almost everyone, from children in classrooms to adults in long meetings, has felt the heavy drag of boredom.
Some argue that, although people often express boredom with self-satisfaction, it should really be a source of embarrassment, because it arises from a lack of imagination and self-motivation.

I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, because boredom is often caused by people's circumstances and can serve as a useful signal, although self-satisfied boredom is sometimes a sign of laziness.

The claim is too harsh because boredom often reflects the environment rather than the individual, and the reason is weak because boredom can actually motivate change, even though some people do use boredom as an excuse.
First, the claim that boredom should be embarrassing is unfair, because boredom is frequently produced by environments that people cannot easily change.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.

Students in systems that rely heavily on rote preparation for tests, by contrast, often find school tedious, and their boredom reflects the [[monotony|monotony]] of the curriculum more than a lack of imagination.
Similarly, a worker who spends every day entering data into the same form is reacting reasonably to a dull job.
Blaming such people for being bored [[ascribes|ascribe]] to personal weakness what is really a problem of design.
The claim, therefore, places responsibility on the wrong party, since the cure for this kind of boredom is a better school or a better job, not personal shame.
Second, the reason is flawed, because boredom is not merely a lack of motivation; it often creates the motivation to change.
As a physician, I have met young doctors who felt bored by routine clinical work and, as a result, turned to research, public health or teaching.
Their boredom was not a failure of imagination but a signal that their talents needed a different outlet.
In clinical practice, persistent boredom and loss of interest can also be symptoms of depression, which no one should treat as a moral failing.
Attaching a [[stigma|stigma]] to boredom could even make such patients less willing to describe their symptoms and seek help.
These cases show that boredom often points to a mismatch between a person and an activity, and treating it as embarrassing would discourage people from listening to that signal.
Admittedly, some people do express boredom with a kind of [[affectation|affectation]], as if being uninterested made them seem superior.

Someone with free time and endless resources who declares everything "boring" may indeed be avoiding effort; after all, Wikipedia, written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history because ordinary people chose to use their spare hours.
Nevertheless, the problem in these cases is the attitude of superiority, not the experience of boredom itself.

This point narrows my disagreement but does not reverse it: we may criticize arrogance, but boredom as an experience deserves understanding rather than shame, because it often tells us something important.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that boredom should be a source of embarrassment and that it arises chiefly from a lack of imagination and self-motivation.
Boredom often reflects dull environments, it can push people toward more meaningful work, and only the self-satisfied pose of boredom deserves criticism.
Instead of feeling ashamed of boredom, we should ask what it is telling us about our schools, our jobs and ourselves.

essays.title: Empathy is the foundation of teaching

paragraphs.text: Most adults can still name one teacher who changed the direction of their lives.

When asked why, they tend to describe a teacher who understood them, which raises the question of whether understanding and empathy matter more than rigorous, demanding expectations in an effective teacher.
My position aligns more closely with the first view, because empathy allows teachers to reach students, although high expectations remain necessary once that trust is built.

Empathy helps teachers identify why students struggle, and it creates the trust that makes students willing to take on difficult work, while the second view correctly reminds us that standards still matter.
First, understanding and empathy are essential because they allow teachers to see the real reasons students fall behind.
Consider a rural student in Vietnam whose grades drop suddenly in her final year of school.
A demanding teacher might simply give her lower marks and warn her to work harder, but an empathetic teacher might discover that she is caring for a sick parent at night.
Only the second teacher can respond helpfully, perhaps by adjusting deadlines or connecting the family with support.
Medicine teaches the same lesson: a doctor who listens to a patient's fears often finds the real reason that treatment is failing, while one who simply repeats instructions does not.
This shows that empathy is not softness but a form of [[discerning|discerning]] attention; without it, even the highest expectations may be aimed at the wrong problem.
Second, empathy builds the trust that makes students willing to attempt challenging work.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Its approach suggests that well-trained teachers who know their students can guide learning without constant pressure from high-stakes exams.
Similarly, in my experience supervising young researchers, those who felt their questions were welcomed asked for help earlier and made fewer serious errors than those who feared criticism.
Students who trust their teachers are more likely to take intellectual risks, and that willingness is what allows real learning to [[burgeon|burgeon]].
Fear, by contrast, makes students [[reticent|reticent]], and a student who hides confusion cannot be helped.
Admittedly, the second view is right that empathy without high standards can leave students unprepared.
In medical training, a supervisor who [[condones|condone]] careless work out of kindness may put future patients at risk.
Nevertheless, rigor works best when it rests on understanding, because students accept demanding standards from teachers they believe care about them.
The best clinical teachers I have known were both exacting and kind, and their students worked hardest precisely because they did not want to disappoint them, not because they feared punishment.
This point therefore qualifies rather than reverses my view: rigor is an important tool for any teacher, but empathy is the foundation that makes it effective.
In conclusion, I believe that understanding and empathy are the most important qualities of an effective teacher, with rigorous expectations built on top of them.

Empathy helps teachers diagnose why students struggle and creates the trust that makes hard work possible, while demanding standards achieve their purpose only within a relationship of mutual trust and respect between teacher and student.
A teacher who begins with understanding can always raise the bar, but one who begins with demands alone may lose the student before learning even starts, however high the standards may be.

essays.title: Rigor is the mark of a great teacher

paragraphs.text: Students often rise or fall to the level that others expect of them.
This is the central issue in the debate over whether effective teachers should be defined mainly by understanding and empathy or by rigorous, demanding expectations.

My position aligns more closely with the second view, because high expectations push students to develop skills they would not otherwise reach, although empathy remains important in how those expectations are delivered.
Demanding teachers prepare students for real challenges and signal respect for students' abilities, while the first view rightly notes that rigor without understanding can discourage learners.
First, rigorous expectations are vital because they prepare students for the real demands of their future work.
In my training as an epidemiologist, my most demanding mentor returned my first analysis plan covered in questions about every assumption I had made.
At the time, the feedback felt harsh, yet it taught me to check my methods before reporting any result, a habit that now protects my research from serious errors.

Similarly, in medicine, the history of thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe around 1960, shows why future doctors must be held to [[exacting|exacting]] standards of evidence.
In fields where mistakes have real consequences, a teacher who accepts weak work out of sympathy does students no favor.
Kindness that lowers the bar may feel supportive in the classroom, but its costs appear later, when the stakes are much higher.
Second, demanding expectations communicate respect, because they show that the teacher believes students are capable of more.
Consider two teachers in a school serving poor neighborhoods.
One lowers the standards because she feels sorry for her students, while the other insists that they can master difficult material and offers extra practice until they do.
The second teacher's students are more likely to see themselves as capable, because her expectations tell them that their background does not limit their potential.
As a physician, I have seen the same effect with patients: those whose doctors expect them to manage their diabetes or tuberculosis treatment carefully often rise to that expectation.
Lowering standards out of empathy can therefore be quietly [[patronizing|patronizing]], whereas high expectations treat students as people who can grow.
Admittedly, the first view is correct that rigor without understanding can harm students.
A teacher who sets high demands but ignores a student's illness or family crisis may [[alienate|alienate]] that student entirely.
Nevertheless, empathy is most valuable as a way to deliver high standards, not as a replacement for them.

Finland, which requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a selective profession, shows that well-trained teachers can be both supportive and demanding about real learning, and it does not [[cosset|cosset]] students by lowering expectations.

This point refines my position: empathy shapes how a teacher applies rigor, but rigor remains the quality that most directly produces learning, because students rarely exceed the standards set for them.
In conclusion, I side with those who believe that rigorous and demanding expectations are the more important quality of an effective teacher.
High standards prepare students for real challenges and express respect for their abilities, while empathy matters chiefly as the means of helping students meet those standards.
The kindest thing a teacher can do, therefore, is to expect a great deal from every student and then provide the help needed to reach it.

essays.title: History needs disciplined creativity

paragraphs.text: Historical facts can look as fixed as the dates printed in a textbook.

Yet the claim here is that learning about the past, though often considered an objective pursuit, requires creativity, because we can never know the past directly and must reconstruct it by imaginatively interpreting accounts, documents and artifacts.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, as long as creativity is understood as disciplined interpretation that remains bound by evidence.
The claim holds because historians must decide what evidence means, and the reason holds because the surviving record is incomplete, although creativity without limits can turn history into fiction.
First, the claim is persuasive because even well-documented events require historians to interpret meaning, not merely record facts.
Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.

The basic facts are clear, but explaining why respected physicians ignored such evidence requires historians to imagine their professional pride, their beliefs about disease and the scientific culture of the time.

Similarly, Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, and historians still debate how far politics, personality and religion each shaped that outcome.
These cases show that the facts alone do not explain the past; historians must creatively connect them, just as the claim suggests.
Second, the reason is sound, because the evidence we have is partial, and gaps can only be filled through careful imagination.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.

To understand how he lived and worked, historians must interpret letters, unfinished paintings and the memories of others, then [[extrapolate|extrapolate]] a picture of a life that no single document fully describes.

My own work in epidemiology offers a parallel: when we reconstruct how an outbreak spread, we have only incomplete case reports, so we build models that imagine plausible pathways and then test them against the data.
Because the record is always incomplete, reconstruction is unavoidable, and reconstruction is a creative act.
Admittedly, creativity can be dangerous when it outruns the evidence.
Many popular stories about historical figures are [[apocryphal|apocryphal]], invented because they make the past more dramatic.
When writers fill gaps in the record with what they wish had happened, history becomes a tool for flattering the present rather than understanding the past.
Nevertheless, the solution is not to abandon creativity but to discipline it, by testing every interpretation against documents, artifacts and competing accounts.

In 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, a reminder that every field needs to check its own interpretations.

This danger therefore qualifies rather than undermines my agreement: history requires imagination, but imagination that is constantly checked, much as a scientist's hypothesis must be [[corroborated|corroborate]] before it is accepted.
In conclusion, I largely agree that learning about the past requires creativity and that this need arises because we can only reconstruct the past from limited evidence.
Historians must interpret the meaning of events, they must fill gaps in an incomplete record, and their creativity must remain tied to evidence to avoid producing fiction.
Good history, like good science, is neither pure fact nor pure invention but a [[judicious|judicious]] combination of the two.

essays.title: History needs rigor more than imagination

paragraphs.text: Every week, new books retell the past in surprising ways, and some of them read more like novels than like scholarship.

This has led some to claim that learning about the past requires creativity, because we can never know it directly and must reconstruct it by imaginatively interpreting historical accounts, documents and artifacts.
I mostly disagree with this claim and its reason, because the study of history depends far more on disciplined, evidence-based reasoning than on creativity, although interpretation does play a role.

The claim overstates the role of creativity because historical knowledge rests on verifiable evidence, and the reason confuses indirect knowledge with imagination, even though historians must sometimes fill gaps.
First, the claim is overstated, because much of what we know about the past is established by careful evidence, not creative invention.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
We know these facts not because historians imagined them but because medical records, government reports and testimony [[document|document]] them in detail.
Similarly, the date of the first powered airplane flight in 1903 is known through photographs, letters and witnesses, not through interpretation.
Even the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, will be remembered through its published records and freely available data rather than through anyone's imagination.
These examples show that the core of historical knowledge is factual and verifiable, so calling it a creative pursuit misrepresents how most of it is built.
Second, the reason is flawed, because knowing something indirectly does not mean we must know it imaginatively.
As an epidemiologist, I never observe the spread of a disease directly; instead, I infer it from case reports, laboratory tests and surveys.
That inference is systematic, using rules of evidence and statistics, and its conclusions can be checked by others, which is the opposite of free imagination.

Historians work in a similar way, comparing sources, dating artifacts and cross-checking accounts, and the best of them are valued for their [[meticulous|meticulous]] method rather than their [[fanciful|fanciful]] ideas.
Indirect knowledge, therefore, calls for rigorous inference, and the reason wrongly treats inference as if it were creativity.
If indirect knowledge required imagination, then much of modern science, which also studies things it cannot see directly, would be a creative art as well, a conclusion few scientists would accept.
Admittedly, there are parts of history where evidence is so thin that historians must use imagination.

Explaining why most physicians rejected Ignaz Semmelweis's evidence that hand washing reduced deaths from childbed fever, for instance, requires guessing at their motives, which no record fully reveals.
Nevertheless, even such interpretations are judged by how well they fit the evidence, and new studies regularly [[debunk|debunk]] creative accounts that cannot be supported.

This concession narrows my disagreement without reversing it, because such cases are the exception rather than the rule: creativity may suggest hypotheses, but evidence decides which ones become history, and that decision is [[empirical|empirical]] rather than creative.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that learning about the past fundamentally requires creativity and that our indirect access to the past makes imagination necessary.
Most historical knowledge rests on verifiable evidence, indirect knowledge calls for rigorous inference rather than invention, and creativity matters mainly where the record is incomplete.
The past may be out of reach, but it is best approached with the discipline of a scientist rather than the freedom of a novelist.

essays.title: Even generous acts carry some self-interest

paragraphs.text: People often praise a nurse who works an extra night shift without pay, or a stranger who returns a lost wallet, as models of pure generosity.
Yet if we look closely at why people help others, we usually find that the helper also gains something, even if it is only a feeling of pride.

I therefore largely agree with the claim that no act is done purely for the benefit of others, and I accept the reason that all actions are based on self-interest, as long as self-interest is understood broadly to include emotional rewards and personal values.
This essay examines the claim, then the reason, and finally the strongest objection, which comes from acts of genuine sacrifice.
First, the claim holds because even the most generous acts usually return some benefit to the person who performs them.
Consider Wikipedia, which was launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers.
These volunteers received no salary, yet many of them gained the satisfaction of sharing knowledge, the respect of other editors and a sense of belonging to a large project.

Similarly, in my own work as a physician in Vietnam, I have seen colleagues volunteer for weekend vaccination days; they truly wanted to protect children, but they also valued the gratitude of families and the [[approbation|approbation]] of their supervisors.
This shows that a benefit to others and a benefit to oneself are rarely separate, so it is hard to find an act that serves others purely.
Even when the helper's main goal is the welfare of others, a personal reward travels quietly alongside it.
Second, the reason itself is largely sound, because a person's motives are shaped by what that person values, and acting on one's values is a form of self-interest.

A pharmacist who refuses to sell antibiotics without a prescription may lose income, yet she acts this way because she does not want to feed antibiotic resistance, which makes drugs that once cured infections fail.
Her decision protects patients, but it also protects her own conscience and her professional reputation.

Likewise, a parent who saves money for a child's education often feels that the child's success is, in part, the parent's own success, and that pride is part of what keeps the parent saving year after year.
In each case, helping others satisfies a desire of the helper, which supports the reason that self-interest is [[inherent|inherent]] even in actions directed at others.
Admittedly, critics can point to acts of sacrifice in which the helper loses far more than he or she could ever gain.

Ignaz Semmelweis, for instance, had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply; yet most colleagues rejected his idea, so his [[pertinacious|pertinacious]] effort brought him rejection rather than reward.
Nevertheless, even Semmelweis was driven by a deep conviction that he was right, and defending that conviction mattered to him personally.
This objection therefore does not overturn my view, although it does show that the reason becomes weak if self-interest is stretched so far that it means any motive at all.
The claim is most [[cogent|cogent]] when we admit that motives are usually mixed rather than entirely selfish.
In conclusion, I largely agree that no act is done purely for others, because human motives almost always include some personal reward.
Volunteer work, professional choices and even costly sacrifices all reveal a helper who gains satisfaction, respect or peace of mind.
Recognizing this mixed nature of generosity should not make us [[cynical|cynical]]; instead, it suggests that societies can encourage helpful behavior by making sure that doing good also feels good.

essays.title: Some acts truly serve others first

paragraphs.text: [[Cynical|cynical]] observers like to say that every kind act hides a selfish motive, whether it is a wish for praise, a hope for future favors or simple guilt.
The claim that no act is done purely for others, together with the reason that all actions are based on self-interest, expresses this view in its strongest form.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, because although human motives are often mixed, many acts are chosen mainly for others at a real cost to the person who performs them.
I will first show that the claim ignores costly acts of service, then argue that the reason is circular, and finally concede that perfectly pure motives are rare.
First, the claim fails because there are clear cases in which people act for others while accepting serious losses themselves.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide, given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it despite pressure from its maker, and her refusal protected American families she would never meet.

Similarly, during the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, accepting daily hardship so that others would not face the same humiliation.
These people gained little personal comfort; in fact, they accepted inconvenience and risk, which suggests that some acts are done largely, if not purely, for the benefit of others.
If the claim were true, such sacrifices would be hard to explain, since the costs to these people clearly outweighed any benefit they could expect.
Second, the reason does not really support the claim, because it defines self-interest so broadly that it can never be proven wrong.
If a woman donates blood, the theory says she wants to feel good; if she donates anonymously and feels nothing special, the theory says she wants to avoid guilt.
Any motive at all can be relabeled as selfish after the fact, so the reason explains everything and therefore explains nothing.
As an epidemiologist, I would reject such a hypothesis in research, since a claim that no observation could ever [[refute|refute]] is not a finding but an assumption.
Thus the reason is [[specious|specious]]: it appears logical, yet it simply assumes the conclusion that it is supposed to prove, and so it cannot support the claim.
Admittedly, the strongest point on the other side is that motives are rarely simple, and many apparently generous acts do serve the helper.

Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet; this choice looked [[magnanimous|magnanimous]], but it also helped Lincoln govern by placing able critics inside his own team.
Nevertheless, the fact that an act benefits the actor does not mean that the act was based only on self-interest.

A physician who treats patients during an epidemic earns a salary, yet the salary hardly explains why she keeps working as her own risk of infection rises; she stays because her patients need her, not because the work serves her interests.
Mixed motives, then, weaken the idea of perfectly pure generosity, but they do not prove that self-interest drives every action.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that all actions spring from self-interest, even though I accept that entirely selfless acts are uncommon.
Costly acts such as Kelsey's refusal and the bus boycott challenge the claim, the reason relies on a definition that cannot be tested, and mixed motives do not amount to selfish ones.
A more accurate view is that people are capable of both self-interest and genuine concern for others, and healthy societies should [[bolster|bolster]] the second without denying the first.

essays.title: Cities reveal a society, but not alone

paragraphs.text: Anyone who walks through a busy city for a single afternoon can learn a great deal about the country around it: what people buy, how they travel and whom they trust.
The statement goes further, however, arguing that studying major cities is necessary to understand a society's most important characteristics.

I largely agree with this statement, because major cities concentrate a society's economic, political and cultural life, but I believe it holds true only if the study of cities is paired with attention to the countryside.
In this essay, I will discuss how cities reveal economic priorities, how they reveal social conflict and new ideas, and where the statement might not hold true.
First, the statement holds true because major cities show a society's economic character more clearly than any other place.
Singapore offers a striking case: its government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
A visitor who studies these housing estates quickly learns how much Singapore values home ownership, careful planning and an active role for the state.
Similarly, a researcher who walks through the crowded markets and new office towers of Ho Chi Minh City can see how quickly commerce now shapes daily life in Vietnam.
These examples show that cities act as a mirror in which the [[salient|salient]] priorities of a society become visible.
If one wants to know what a society values most, the way it builds and manages its largest cities is often the clearest evidence.
Second, major cities reveal the tensions and new ideas that shape a society, because large, [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] populations bring different groups into close contact.
The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, exposed the injustice of racial segregation in the United States.
Because the protest took place in a city, it was visible, organized and difficult to ignore, and it showed the rest of the nation that ordinary citizens could challenge unjust laws.
Likewise, during the Arab Spring of 2011, activists used smartphones and social media to organize quickly, revealing the frustrations of young, connected citizens.
Studying such urban events helps us understand not only what a society is but also what it is struggling to become, since tensions that stay hidden elsewhere become [[manifest|manifest]] in cities.

Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every case, because many societies are [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]], with large rural populations whose lives differ sharply from those of city dwellers.

In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, I have found that rural districts face different housing, water storage and health care problems than urban neighborhoods, so a city-based study would miss much of the picture.
Moreover, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 turned a country that had faced food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters, an achievement that depended on farmers.
Nevertheless, even these rural stories connect to cities, which supply many of the markets, policies and investments that shape village life.
This consideration shapes my position: cities are an essential starting point, but a [[myopic|myopic]] focus on them alone would produce an incomplete portrait.
In conclusion, I largely agree that studying major cities is necessary for understanding a society, provided that the countryside is not ignored.
Cities display a society's economic priorities, expose its conflicts and new ideas, and connect to rural life in ways that make them a natural place to begin.
Anyone who wants a full understanding, however, should treat the city as the first chapter of the story rather than the whole book.

essays.title: Cities are often the least typical places

paragraphs.text: Capital cities often appear on postcards, in news reports and in tourist guides as if they were the whole country, while the farms, small towns and fishing villages where many people live remain out of view.
This habit lies behind the statement that, to understand the most important characteristics of a society, one must study its major cities.
I mostly disagree with the statement, because major cities are often the least typical parts of a society, although I accept that they are useful places to observe power and change.
I will argue that cities can hide the majority's way of life, that they distort what researchers conclude about a society, and then consider the cases in which the statement does hold true.
First, the statement does not hold true for societies in which most people live and work outside large cities.
In Vietnam, for example, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
That transformation depended heavily on farming households, and a scholar who studied only Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City would miss the rural foundation of the country's recovery.
Similarly, the values of family, village and seasonal work that shape Vietnamese life are more visible in the countryside than in urban apartment towers.

Thus, in many societies, the most important characteristics are found where most people actually live, and regions that seem [[peripheral|peripheral]] when viewed from the capital may be central to national life.
Second, major cities can distort our understanding, because they attract unusual people and unusual resources.
As an epidemiologist, I know that data collected only from large urban hospitals often overstate access to care, since city residents can reach specialists that rural patients rarely see.
A policymaker who relied on such data might conclude that the health system works well for everyone, a conclusion that would be both [[erroneous|erroneous]] and harmful.
In the same way, the [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] culture of a capital city, with its foreign companies and international restaurants, may say more about global trade than about national character.

This shows that cities are a biased sample of a society, and studying them alone risks mistaking the exception for the rule; in epidemiology, we call this selection bias, and we work hard to avoid it.
Admittedly, the statement does hold true in some societies, especially those in which the city and the nation are nearly the same.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats, so studying its urban neighborhoods is, in effect, studying the entire society.
Nevertheless, Singapore is an [[anomaly|anomaly]]; most countries contain large regions, such as farming provinces and mountain districts, that differ sharply from their capitals.

Even where cities lead change, as in the Montgomery bus boycott, which helped end bus segregation in that city, the boycott revealed only one local part of an injustice that reached far beyond Montgomery.
These considerations shape my position: cities are valuable windows into a society, but they are only one window, and a [[judicious|judicious]] observer must look through several.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that major cities are the key to understanding a society, while granting that they reveal certain features clearly.
Cities can conceal the life of the rural majority and skew data, and only in unusual places such as Singapore do they truly represent the whole.
To understand a society well, we should study its villages, small towns and cities together, giving each the weight that its population and history deserve.

essays.title: Honest guidance is part of a school's duty

paragraphs.text: Choosing a field of study is one of the most expensive decisions a young person makes, measured in money, time and hope.
This raises the question of whether schools should step in when a student seems headed toward a field in which he or she is unlikely to succeed.

I largely agree that educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade such students, as long as dissuasion means honest, evidence-based advice rather than a ban that removes the student's right to choose.

I will explain how candid guidance protects students, how it protects the quality of important professions, and then address the most compelling challenge: that predictions of success are often wrong.
First, institutions should dissuade students from unsuitable fields because silence can cost those students years of effort.
Consider a medical student who repeatedly fails anatomy and physiology and struggles badly in every clinical rotation.
If the faculty say nothing, the student may spend several more years and a great deal of family money, only to fail the final licensing exam.

A [[candid|candid]] conversation in the second year, by contrast, could [[forestall|forestall]] that waste and help the student move into public health, laboratory science or another field that suits his strengths.
Similarly, a music school that sees a student's skills stall for several years helps the student more by saying so than by accepting another year's tuition.
In such cases, dissuasion is not cruelty but a [[prudent|prudent]] form of care that schools owe to the students who trust them.
Moreover, institutions have this responsibility because the public depends on the quality of the professionals they train.
Finland, for example, requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession.
By steering away candidates who are unlikely to teach well, such a system protects children from weak instruction and keeps the profession's standing high.
The same logic applies to medicine, where a doctor who lacks basic clinical [[acumen|acumen]] can harm patients, not merely himself.
When institutions accept every applicant and never warn the weakest ones, patients and schoolchildren eventually pay the price for that silence.
This shows that schools serve society as well as individual students, and honest dissuasion is part of that broader duty to the public.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that predictions of success are often wrong, and some of history's greatest achievers might have been dissuaded.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903, a result few advisers would have predicted.
Likewise, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Nevertheless, these cases argue for humility in giving advice, not for silence, because most students who struggle badly are not hidden geniuses.

A school that shares clear evidence, such as grades, skills assessments and job prospects, while admitting that no prediction is [[infallible|infallible]], respects both the student's freedom and its own duty to tell the truth.
In conclusion, I largely agree that schools should discourage students from fields in which they are unlikely to succeed, provided they do so honestly and without coercion.
Such guidance saves students from wasted years, protects the quality of vital professions, and can coexist with humility about the limits of prediction.
The goal is not to close doors but to make sure that students walk through them with open eyes and a realistic sense of what lies ahead.

essays.title: Inform students; do not steer them away

paragraphs.text: History is full of people who were told they would never succeed in the work they loved, only to prove their teachers wrong.
The claim that educational institutions should dissuade students from fields in which they are unlikely to succeed assumes that schools can reliably identify such students.
I mostly disagree with this claim, because schools predict success poorly and their discouragement can become a self-fulfilling prophecy; instead, they should inform students and let them choose.
I will discuss the weakness of predictions, the harm of biased dissuasion, and finally the strongest challenge to my view, which is the cost of failure.
First, institutions should not dissuade students because their judgments about future success are often unreliable, especially for students whose talents are unusual.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911 despite the [[daunting|daunt]] barriers women faced in science at the time.
Had her teachers judged her prospects by the expectations of her era, they might well have advised her to abandon science.
Teachers in her time could see only the obstacles in front of her, not the discoveries she would later make.
Similarly, the Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.

These cases show that early signs of "unlikely success" are often [[tenuous|tenuous]], especially when a person's talent does not fit familiar patterns, and an adviser's judgment often reflects the prejudices of the moment more than the student's true potential.
Second, dissuasion is harmful because it can create the very failure it predicts and reinforce existing prejudice.
Imagine a girl in a rural Vietnamese school who earns average marks in mathematics and is told that engineering is not for her.
She may stop trying, lose confidence and choose an easier path, and her teachers will later see her choice as proof that their judgment was correct.
Discouragement of this kind tends to fall most heavily on students from poor families or from groups already [[marginalized|marginalize]] in a field.
In Vietnam, I have seen bright students from poor provinces quietly lower their goals after a single discouraging comment from a teacher.
Therefore, a policy of dissuasion would not merely reflect unequal chances but would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] them, which runs against the purpose of education.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that letting students pursue hopeless goals wastes their time, their money and public resources.
In medical training, for instance, a student who repeatedly fails core examinations may spend years and take on large debts before leaving with nothing.
Nevertheless, the remedy for this problem is honest information, not active dissuasion.
A school can show the student his grades, the pass rates of similar students and the alternatives available, and then respect his decision, whether he chooses to persist or to change direction.
This approach answers the concern about waste while leaving the final choice where it belongs: with the student, who alone must live with the result.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that schools have a responsibility to steer students away from fields in which they seem unlikely to succeed.
Predictions of success are unreliable, discouragement can produce and deepen inequality, and the real problem of wasted effort is better solved by transparent advice.
Schools should be honest guides rather than [[arbiters|arbiter]] of who may dream, because the student who is told "no" today may be the one who changes the field tomorrow.

essays.title: Scandals create the urgency reform needs

paragraphs.text: Reformers can write reports for years without changing anything, yet a single shocking news story can move a [[complacent|complacent]] nation almost overnight.
This contrast explains why some people argue that scandals are useful because they focus our attention on problems in ways that no speaker or reformer ever could.
I largely agree with this claim, since scandals create a sense of urgency that ordinary advocacy rarely achieves, although their value depends on what happens after public attention fades.
I will show how scandals turn hidden harms into concrete stories, how they reach people whom reformers cannot, and then address the strongest objection: that scandals often fade or mislead.
First, scandals are useful because they turn abstract ethical concerns into concrete stories that the public cannot ignore.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
Principles of informed consent had been discussed for years, but it took a concrete case, with real victims, to make the public demand action.
When the study became public, the outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people, rules that still protect participants today.
In my own work as an epidemiologist, every study I design must pass such a review, a safeguard that exists largely because of that scandal.
This shows that a scandal can have a [[salutary|salutary]] effect, accomplishing in a short time what years of quiet ethical argument had not.
Second, scandals succeed where reformers fail because they reach people who would never read a reformer's arguments.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.
His evidence was strong, but evidence alone did not [[galvanize|galvanize]] his profession, and germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.

By contrast, when the sedative thalidomide caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe around 1960, the harm to children shocked the public, and the US passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.

The difference between these cases suggests that public attention, which scandals provide, is often the missing ingredient in reform; a reformer may supply the truth, but a scandal supplies the audience.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is that scandals can be [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] and misleading, focusing attention on the wrong problem or on none at all.
Smartphones and social media now spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a scandal may rest on rumor rather than fact.
In addition, public anger often fades before any law is passed, leaving the underlying problem untouched while the media move on to the next story.
Nevertheless, these risks show that scandals need reformers, not that scandals are useless.
The Tuskegee and thalidomide cases led to reform because experts were ready to turn outrage into rules; a scandal provides the energy, and careful advocates provide the direction.
In other words, scandals and reformers are partners, and the special contribution of a scandal is the attention that reformers cannot generate on their own.
In conclusion, I largely agree that scandals focus public attention in a way that speakers and reformers rarely can.
They make hidden harms concrete, reach audiences that arguments cannot, and, when guided by thoughtful advocates, produce lasting change despite their tendency to fade or mislead.
Societies should therefore treat each scandal as an opportunity: a brief moment of attention that must be used wisely before it passes.

essays.title: Lasting reform comes from patient reformers

paragraphs.text: Every few weeks, a new scandal fills the headlines, and every few weeks, it disappears, replaced by the next one.
Even so, some people claim that scandals are useful because they focus our attention on problems in ways that no speaker or reformer ever could.
I mostly disagree with this claim, because scandals produce brief and often distorted attention, whereas lasting reform usually comes from patient organizers who build public support over time.
I will discuss the power of sustained campaigns, the distortions that scandals create, and the strongest counterexample, the Tuskegee study, which shows what scandals can and cannot do.
First, the claim underestimates reformers, many of whom have focused public attention more effectively than any scandal.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
This organized protest kept attention on segregation far longer than a single shocking story could have, and it helped end bus segregation in that city.
Similarly, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, not on scandal.
These examples show that reformers can command attention, and that the attention they create runs deeper because it is tied to a clear goal.
A scandal, by contrast, usually tells people what to be angry about but not what to do next.
Second, scandals often focus attention in the wrong way, rewarding outrage rather than understanding.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a scandal can [[polarize|polarize]] the public before the facts are known.
As a physician, I have seen how a single frightening story about a vaccine side effect can make parents [[wary|wary]] of vaccination for years, even when careful studies show the vaccine is safe.
Months of patient reassurance from health workers can be undone by one viral post.

By contrast, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, a success that came from policy rather than scandal.
Thus scandals do not simply focus attention; they often distort it, while reformers can direct it toward practical solutions.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that some scandals have produced reforms that reformers alone had failed to achieve.

The Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent from 1932 to 1972, caused public outrage that led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, even this case shows that a scandal is a [[catalyst|catalyst]] rather than a cure.
The outrage would have faded without officials and researchers who translated it into specific, lasting rules, and those rules have shaped how studies like mine are reviewed ever since.
The Tuskegee case therefore qualifies my position, since scandals can sometimes open a door, but it does not support the claim that they accomplish what no reformer ever could.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that scandals focus attention better than any speaker or reformer.
Organized campaigns have held public attention longer, scandals tend to distort what the public sees, and even the strongest example of a useful scandal depended on reformers to succeed.

Rather than waiting for the next scandal, societies would do better to support the patient work of those who [[advocate|advocate]] for change every day, long before the cameras arrive and long after they leave.

essays.title: Fund cities, but not for that reason alone

paragraphs.text: From ancient Rome to modern Hanoi, great cities have long been the places where nations display their wealth and imagination.

This history supports the claim that governments must ensure their major cities receive the financial support they need to thrive, based on the reason that cities are where a nation's cultural traditions are preserved and generated.
I largely agree with the claim, but I accept the reason only in part: cities generate much of a nation's new culture, yet they are not the main place where traditions are preserved.
I will first evaluate the claim, then examine the reason, and finally consider the strongest objection, which is that urban funding may neglect rural citizens.
First, the claim is largely sound because well-funded cities produce benefits that spread across the whole nation.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Such sustained public investment gives citizens stable homes, a foundation on which work, family life and community can be built.
Similarly, in Vietnam, major hospitals in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City treat patients referred from many provinces, so funding these urban centers improves care for rural families too.
These cases show that when governments help cities thrive, the benefits rarely stay inside city limits.
Investment in major cities is therefore not a gift to urban residents alone but a service to the nation.
Second, the reason is partly true, because cities are where new cultural forms are most often generated, but it overstates their role in preservation.
Cities bring together artists, publishers, universities and audiences, and this mix [[engenders|engender]] new music, films and ideas at a speed that small towns rarely match.
However, many of Vietnam's oldest traditions, such as village festivals, folk songs and craft skills passed down within families, survive mainly in rural communities.
During fieldwork in rural districts, I have seen communities keep customs, such as ancestral rituals and seasonal farming ceremonies, that many city residents know only from television.

Thus the reason correctly identifies cities as cultural engines, but it ignores the countryside's role as a keeper of [[ingrained|ingrained]] traditions, which makes it a weaker support for the claim than it first appears.
Admittedly, the strongest objection to the claim is that directing funds to major cities may deepen the gap between urban and rural citizens.
When large budgets go to city metro lines and concert halls, rural clinics may lack basic equipment, and rural residents may feel [[marginalized|marginalize]] by their own government.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for balance, not for neglecting cities, which remain the country's main centers of trade, education and medicine.
A national budget can, for example, fund a city's metro line and teaching hospitals while still equipping the rural clinics that refer patients to those hospitals.

Governments should therefore ensure that major cities receive what they need, while keeping the overall distribution [[equitable|equitable]] so that rural communities do not pay the price of urban success.
In conclusion, I largely agree that governments should give major cities the support they need to thrive, though for broader reasons than the one offered.
Thriving cities spread benefits nationwide and generate new culture, but traditions are preserved largely in rural areas, and urban funding must not come at the countryside's expense.
A wise government, then, funds its cities as engines of the nation's future while honoring the villages that keep its past alive.

essays.title: Cities deserve fair support, not priority

paragraphs.text: When a government decides how to spend its money, it also decides whose lives matter most and whose voices it hears.

Some argue that governments must ensure their major cities receive the financial support they need to thrive, because it is primarily in cities that a nation's cultural traditions are preserved and generated.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason: cities deserve fair support, but they should not receive priority, and the reason misunderstands where culture actually lives.
I will first evaluate the claim, then challenge the reason, and finally concede what supporters of urban funding get right.
First, the claim is too strong because it treats the needs of cities as more urgent than those of the rest of the nation.
In my work on dengue control in Vietnam, I have seen rural districts struggle with too few staff and limited funds for mosquito control, while major city hospitals are far better supported.

Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, and the method has also been tested in Vietnam; programs like this need funding wherever the disease occurs.

Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths because it protected riders in every province, not only in the capital.
These cases show that a government's duty is to the whole nation, and a rule that cities must be funded first could [[undermine|undermine]] that duty.
Second, the reason is flawed, because cultural traditions are preserved at least as much in villages and small towns as in cities.
In Vietnam, many folk songs, craft skills and festivals have survived for generations in rural communities, where they are passed from parents to children.
Cities, by contrast, often allow a [[homogeneous|homogeneous]] global culture of shopping malls, chain restaurants and international films to [[supplant|supplant]] local customs.
A young person raised in a city apartment may know far more about foreign pop music than about the songs of his grandparents' village.
When rural communities lose funding for schools and cultural centers, the traditions they carry can disappear within a single generation.
Therefore, even if cities generate much new culture, the reason fails as a description of preservation, and it gives little support to the claim that cities deserve special funding.
Admittedly, supporters of the claim are right that cities are powerful engines of economic and cultural growth.
Singapore's government housing program, which now houses about 80% of the country's residents, shows how public investment in urban life can give a whole population stable homes.
Nevertheless, Singapore is a city-state, so its success says little about countries in which most people live outside major cities.
In such countries, money spent on a new urban concert hall may come from the budget for rural schools or clinics.
This concession therefore qualifies my position, since cities deserve adequate support, but it does not justify treating their needs as a national priority above all others.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that governments must guarantee their major cities whatever funding they need, and I reject the idea that cities are the primary keepers of culture.
National duties extend beyond city limits, traditions often survive best in rural communities, and the success of a city-state like Singapore cannot be generalized.
An [[equitable|equitable]] government should fund each region according to its needs, recognizing that a nation's culture and health depend on its villages as much as on its capital.

essays.title: Public funding lets art reach everyone

paragraphs.text: A public museum that anyone can enter, regardless of income, is one of the quiet achievements of modern society, and many such institutions depend on public money.
Such institutions raise the debate over whether government funding is necessary for the arts to flourish and be available to all, or whether it threatens the integrity of the arts.

I side mainly with the first view, because public money widens access and supports risky work that markets ignore, although I agree with the second view that funding must be protected from political control.
I will discuss how funding makes art available to all, how it allows unpopular art to flourish, and how the concern about integrity can be addressed.

First, government funding is necessary for the arts to be available to all people, because markets serve those who can pay, and private [[philanthropy|philanthropy]] often follows the tastes of wealthy donors.
Without public support, a farmer's child in a rural Vietnamese province may never see a professional theater performance, since touring companies earn little in poor areas.
Funded programs that bring music and theater to schools can give such children an experience that their families could not afford.
A useful parallel comes from science: the Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Public money in the arts can play the same role, turning cultural treasures from private goods into shared ones, which is the heart of the first view.
Moreover, public funding helps the arts flourish because it supports work whose value the market fails to recognize.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
An artist like him, working today, could use a public grant to keep painting rather than abandoning art for a [[mundane|mundane]] job.
Similarly, experimental composers and poets rarely attract buyers at first, and public support gives them time to develop.
Without such help, many of these artists would leave the arts before their work matured, and society would never know what it had lost.
This shows that flourishing art needs patience, and patience is something governments can provide when markets demand quick returns and safe choices.
Admittedly, the second view raises a real concern: whoever pays for art may try to control it.

History offers [[stark|stark]] warnings, such as when the Church forced Galileo in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, a reminder that powerful institutions can suppress ideas they dislike.
Nevertheless, this danger argues for careful design of funding, not for its removal.

When grants are awarded by independent panels of artists and critics rather than by politicians, artists can accept public money without surrendering their independence, much as university researchers accept public grants while still publishing results that criticize government policy.
In this way, the legitimate fear behind the second view can be [[mitigated|mitigate]], while the benefits stressed by the first view remain.
In conclusion, my position is closer to the first view: government funding is necessary for the arts to flourish and reach everyone.
Public support makes art available beyond the wealthy, sustains work the market overlooks, and, with independent oversight, need not threaten artistic integrity.
The real question is therefore not whether governments should fund the arts, but how they can do so while keeping a respectful distance from what artists create.

essays.title: State money can quietly shape the message

paragraphs.text: Artists have always needed money, but money rarely comes without expectations, whether it comes from a king, a church or a ministry of culture.

This tension lies at the center of the debate between those who believe government funding is necessary for the arts to flourish and be available to all, and those who believe such funding threatens the integrity of the arts.
I side mostly with the second view, because state money tends to shape what artists say, although I recognize that the first view rightly values public access.
I will explain how funding invites political control, how it rewards safe art over bold art, and what the first view gets right.
First, government funding threatens artistic integrity because those who control the money can control the message.
When the Church forced Galileo in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, it showed how a powerful institution can silence views it dislikes.
Artists who depend on state grants face a quieter version of the same pressure: they may become less [[candid|candid]] about the government that pays them.
No official has to issue an order; the artist simply learns which subjects are safe.
In many countries, publicly funded art has at times become propaganda, praising leaders and policies rather than asking difficult questions.

This shows that dependence on government can lead artists to [[expurgate|expurgate]] their own work before any official needs to ask, which is the most dangerous form of control because no one sees it.
Second, government funding tends to reward safe, committee-approved art rather than [[audacious|audacious]] work.
Grant applications must pass through a [[bureaucracy|bureaucracy]] of forms, budgets and review panels, which favors artists who write good proposals over those who create surprising art.

Vincent van Gogh, who sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, might well have struggled to win such a grant, since few people valued his work while he lived.

By contrast, Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history without government direction, showing that creative communities can flourish on their own energy.
Thus public funding may produce more art, but not necessarily freer or better art, because the art that wins grants is often the art that offends no one.
Admittedly, the first view is right that, without public support, many people would have little access to the arts.
A child in a poor rural district may never visit a museum unless public money pays for free entry or school trips.
Nevertheless, access can be expanded in ways that do not place artists under state control or make their income depend on official approval.
Governments can fund libraries, school programs and free museum days, while leaving decisions about what art to create to artists, private donors and audiences.
In this way, the legitimate goal of the first view can be met without accepting the risks that the second view identifies, which is why my position remains closer to the second view.
In conclusion, I side mostly with the view that government funding threatens the integrity of the arts.
Money from the state can shape artists' messages, it rewards cautious work over bold work, and it is not the only way to make art available to everyone.
Artists serve society best when they are free to [[antagonize|antagonize]] the powerful, and that freedom is easier to keep when their livelihood does not depend on the powerful.

bold and willing to take risks
a system of officials, rules and procedures
