essays.title: Regular renewal keeps organizations from stagnating

paragraphs.text: Leaders who stay in power for too long often begin to confuse their own comfort with the good of the organization they serve.
This concern underlies the claim that, in any field, those in power should step down after five years, based on the reason that revitalization through new leadership is the surest path to success.
I largely agree with the claim as a general rule, and I accept the reason with one qualification: fresh leadership usually revitalizes an enterprise, though it is not the only path to success.
I will first evaluate the claim, then examine the reason, and finally address the strongest objection, which is the loss of experience when capable leaders must leave.
First, the claim is largely justified because leaders who remain in power for many years tend to protect the [[status quo|status quo]] rather than adapt to change.

Kodak offers a clear warning: its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Leaders whose careers had been built on film may have had little reason to abandon the business that had made them successful.
Similarly, a university department led by the same head for twenty years may [[ossify|ossify]], ignoring new research areas simply because they fall outside that person's expertise.

These cases show that a fixed limit, such as five years, can prevent leaders from becoming [[complacent|complacent]] and force organizations to question old assumptions before those assumptions become costly.
Second, the reason is largely sound, because new leaders bring fresh perspectives that existing leaders find hard to adopt.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Such a change required leaders who were willing to break with the ideas of the past and accept the risks of trying something new.
In hospitals, too, a newly appointed director often notices wasteful routines that a long-serving director has come to accept as normal.

However, the word "surest" overstates the case: new leadership revitalizes many enterprises, but success also depends on skilled staff, resources and timing, so the reason supports the claim strongly but not absolutely.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that a strict five-year limit could remove capable leaders in the middle of long projects that depend on trust and continuity.

Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, and frequent changes in leadership could have [[impeded|impede]] that cooperation.
Nevertheless, this risk can be managed without abandoning the principle of renewal.
Organizations can ask an outgoing leader to remain as an adviser, or they can permit one renewal after an independent review of the leader's record.
Such flexibility keeps experience available while preserving the main benefit of the claim: no leader becomes permanent by default.
In this way, an organization can enjoy the stability of experience and the energy of new leadership at the same time.
In conclusion, I largely agree that those in power should step down after about five years and that new leadership is usually a powerful source of revitalization.
Long tenure encourages complacency, fresh leaders bring needed perspectives, and the loss of experience can be reduced through advisory roles and careful exceptions.
Organizations that build regular renewal into their rules are less likely to repeat Kodak's mistake of defending yesterday's success at the cost of tomorrow's.

satisfied with the current situation and unwilling to change

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason (fresh leaders revitalize, but 'surest' overstates it), and Body 3 concedes the loss of experience.

essays.title: Judge leaders by results, not years

paragraphs.text: Some of the greatest achievements in history required leaders who stayed long enough to see their work through, from long scientific projects to national reforms.
Yet some argue that in any field those in power should step down after five years, because the surest path to success is revitalization through new leadership.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, since a fixed limit ignores the needs of long-term projects and new leadership is only one of many sources of renewal.
I will first evaluate the claim, then examine the reason, and finally concede the real danger of leaders who stay too long and stop listening.
First, the claim is too rigid because many important enterprises take far longer than five years to succeed.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, required careful coordination among many research groups before it made the human DNA sequence freely available.

Similarly, testing Wolbachia mosquitoes, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, demanded patient work from teams that understood both the science and the local communities.
Forcing the leaders of such projects to step down on a fixed date, regardless of progress, would waste their hard-won knowledge and relationships.
These examples show that the right length of leadership depends on the task, so a single rule for every field is not [[tenable|tenable]].
A five-year limit treats a two-year marketing campaign and a twenty-year research program as if they required the same kind of leadership.
Second, the reason is weak because new leadership is neither the only nor the surest source of revitalization.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
He renewed his government's thinking not by leaving office but by inviting [[dissent|dissent]] into it.
In my own experience on research teams, projects improve most when a stable leader welcomes criticism from junior colleagues and outside reviewers, not when leaders change frequently.
A leader who stays but listens can renew an organization as effectively as a newcomer, without losing what has already been learned.
Revitalization, then, can come from new ideas, open debate and accountability, so the reason does not justify forcing every leader out after five years.
Admittedly, critics of my view can point to leaders who stayed too long and led their organizations into decline.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Similarly, a hospital director who has served for many years may resist new infection control practices simply because the old ones feel familiar.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure came from defending an old business model, and a new leader facing the same incentives might have made the same choice.

The [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] lesson is that organizations need regular, honest reviews of their leaders' performance, not an automatic departure date; this concession sharpens my position but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that all leaders should step down after five years and that new leadership is the surest path to success.

Long-term projects need continuity, renewal can come from open debate rather than turnover, and the danger of [[complacent|complacent]] leadership is better handled by accountability than by a fixed limit.
Organizations should judge leaders by their results and their openness to change, not by the number of years they have served, since a calendar cannot measure leadership.

essays.title: Breakthroughs grow from earlier achievements

paragraphs.text: Very few discoveries arrive out of nowhere; most are the last step in a long journey that many people began.

This observation supports the statement that, in any field of endeavor, it is impossible to make a significant contribution without first being strongly influenced by past achievements within that field.

I largely agree with the statement, because major contributions almost always build on earlier work, although I would replace "impossible" with "extremely rare," since some innovators make their mark by resisting the past.
I will show how past achievements make breakthroughs possible in medicine, how they guide inventors in technology, and where the statement might not hold true.
First, the statement holds true in medicine, where nearly every major advance rests on decades of earlier research.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year, but only because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Without that foundation, such a rapid response to the pandemic would have been impossible, no matter how talented the vaccine teams were.

Similarly, Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, but his [[nascent|nascent]] discovery became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed penicillin during World War II.
These cases show that even the fastest breakthroughs grow out of earlier achievements, just as the statement suggests, and the people who completed them depended on those who came first.
Second, the statement holds true in technology, where inventors learn from the successes and failures of those before them.
The Wright brothers achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Gliders already existed, and the brothers' success came from [[assiduous|assiduous]] study of how such machines behaved before they ever added an engine.
Likewise, GPS was built by the US military, and once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
In technology, therefore, past achievements act as [[precursors|precursor]] to new ones, and inventors who ignore them usually repeat old mistakes or waste time rediscovering what is already known.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every case, because some contributions come from people who reject the main ideas of their field.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, even though most colleagues rejected his idea.
Similarly, Galileo supported the idea that the Earth moves around the sun against the accepted thinking of his day, and in 1633 the Church forced him to recant.
Nevertheless, both men were trained thinkers who knew the ideas of their time well; their contributions were reactions to past achievements, not escapes from them.
This consideration shapes my position: being strongly influenced by the past does not always mean following it, since even [[iconoclasts|iconoclast]] must understand the ideas they challenge.
In conclusion, I largely agree that significant contributions depend on strong influence from past achievements, even if "impossible" is slightly too absolute.
Medical breakthroughs extend earlier research, technological inventions improve on earlier designs, and even rebels against tradition are shaped by what they rebel against.
For anyone hoping to contribute to a field, the practical lesson is clear: study the past deeply, but use it as a starting point rather than a limit.

a person who attacks accepted beliefs

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (medicine, technology), and Body 3 names cases where it seems not to (Semmelweis, Galileo) and explains how they refine the position.

essays.title: Fresh eyes can matter more than tradition

paragraphs.text: Progress often depends on [[mavericks|maverick]] who refuse to accept what everyone else believes.
This fact challenges the statement that, in any field, it is impossible to make a significant contribution without first being strongly influenced by past achievements within that field.

I mostly disagree with the statement, because many important contributions come from outsiders or from people who break with tradition, although I accept that most work in established fields builds on earlier achievements.
I will discuss how outsiders contribute, how strong attachment to the past can block progress, and where the statement does hold true.
First, the statement does not hold true for outsiders, who often contribute precisely because they are not shaped by a field's traditions.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their strength lay in their own experiments rather than in formal training in the engineering of their day, which left them free to test ideas that experts might have overlooked.

Similarly, Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, even though it broke with the long tradition of encyclopedias written by paid experts.
These examples suggest that significant contributions come not only from minds [[steeped|steeped]] in a field's history but also from fresh eyes and from people who simply ask new questions.
Second, strong influence from past achievements can actually prevent significant contributions, because it leads people to defend old ideas.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea.
Those colleagues were strongly influenced by the medical [[dogma|dogma]] of their time, and germ theory vindicated Semmelweis only years after his death.

Likewise, Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
In both cases, past achievements did not enable progress but [[stymied|stymie]] it, which contradicts the idea that strong influence from the past is a requirement for contribution.
Admittedly, the statement does hold true in many established fields, where new work is impossible without mastery of earlier findings.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year only because of decades of earlier basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Nevertheless, "many" is not "all," and the statement claims that strong influence is necessary in any field of endeavor.

In my own field of epidemiology, I learned methods from past research, but some of the most useful ideas I have seen came from colleagues trained in economics or computer science who questioned our habits.

This consideration shapes my position: knowledge of the past is often helpful, but strong influence from it is neither necessary nor always beneficial, and sometimes it is the very thing an innovator must overcome.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that significant contributions are impossible without strong influence from past achievements.
Outsiders have transformed fields they barely knew, attachment to past success has blocked progress, and even in fields that build on earlier work, fresh perspectives remain valuable.
The wisest innovators, then, are [[conversant|conversant]] with the past but not ruled by it, and they know when to set tradition aside.

essays.title: Protect wilderness, but share the benefits

paragraphs.text: Every generation inherits a natural world that it did not create and cannot fully replace.

As cities and farms expand, the question of whether nations should legally protect their last wilderness areas, even at the cost of economic gain, has become [[pressing|pressing]] in rich and poor countries alike.
I largely support this policy, as long as the laws are designed to share the benefits of protection with the people who live near these areas.

The likely consequences of such laws, namely the protection of irreplaceable resources, the prevention of serious health risks, and possible hardship for local communities, together shape this position.
First, preservation laws would protect resources whose value is often discovered only after they are gone, because wilderness, unlike a factory or a road, cannot be rebuilt once it is destroyed.
Consider a coastal province that clears its mangrove forests to build shrimp farms.

For a few years, the farms may generate income, but without the mangroves the coast loses its natural barrier against storms, and the cost of repairing flooded villages can quickly exceed the profits.
Similarly, a wetland drained for farmland may have been filtering a region's water supply, a service that is noticed only when it stops.

These cases show that the economic gain from development is frequently short-term, whereas the loss of wilderness is permanent; a law that preserves these areas therefore protects options that future generations may [[deem|deem]] priceless.
Moreover, preserving wilderness would reduce the health risks that follow when people push into untouched land.

In my work as an epidemiologist in Vietnam, I have seen how clearing forests and building new settlements brings people into closer contact with mosquitoes and wild animals, which can carry infections that local clinics are not prepared to treat.
Once such an outbreak begins, controlling it is far more expensive than preventing it, as the long struggle against dengue in Southeast Asia makes clear.

Thus, one consequence of the policy would be fewer opportunities for diseases to spread from wild areas to human communities, a benefit that rarely appears in the economic calculations used to justify development.
In Vietnam, where dengue already strains district hospitals each rainy season, adding new sources of infection would be a high price to pay for a short-term profit.
Admittedly, a strict ban on development could impose real hardship on poor regions that depend on land for their income.

Vietnam's own history illustrates the value of economic growth: after the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, poverty fell dramatically, and few would argue that this progress was unimportant.
Nevertheless, this consequence argues for designing the law carefully, not for abandoning it.
A government can pair protection with [[equitable|equitable]] support, for example by paying communities to guard forests or by developing eco-tourism that employs local guides.
In this way, the economic cost that critics fear can be [[mitigated|mitigate]] rather than ignored, so the concern [[qualifies|qualify]] my support for the policy without overturning it.
If such support is built into the law from the start, local people gain a reason to protect the forest rather than to clear it.
In conclusion, nations should pass laws that keep their remaining wilderness in its natural state, provided that these laws also address the needs of nearby communities.
Such laws would protect resources that cannot be replaced and prevent costly health threats, while their economic burden can be reduced through careful design.
When governments weigh short-term profits against permanent losses, the wiser choice is usually to preserve what cannot be rebuilt.

essays.title: A blanket wilderness ban harms people

paragraphs.text: Few people would argue against protecting nature, yet good intentions can produce poor laws when they leave no room for judgment.
The policy under discussion would require nations to keep any remaining wilderness in its natural state, even when development could bring economic gain.
Although some wilderness clearly deserves strict protection, I oppose this policy as stated, because a blanket rule would often harm the very people it is meant to serve.

Its probable consequences, namely trapping poor communities in poverty, encouraging illegal exploitation, and [[stymieing|stymie]] development that saves lives, shape my opposition, even though the value of irreplaceable ecosystems must be acknowledged.
First, a law that forbids all development of wilderness would keep many rural communities poor, because land is often the only resource they have.
Consider a mountain province where most families live on small farms beside a large forest.
If the government bans any road, mine or plantation in that forest, young people will find few local jobs and will continue to leave for the cities, while those who remain stay in [[penury|penury]].

Vietnam's experience after the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 shows the other path: once market incentives replaced central planning, a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically.
This contrast suggests that economic gain is not a minor concern to be set aside; for millions of people, it is the difference between hardship and a decent life.
Second, a rigid ban could [[undermine|undermine]] conservation itself, since rules that ignore local needs are often broken.
When a protected area offers villagers nothing but restrictions, illegal logging and hunting tend to increase, because people who feel excluded have little reason to obey distant laws.
In such cases, the forest may shrink faster under a ban than it would under a carefully managed plan that lets villagers share the income.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law offers a useful contrast: it raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months, partly because the rule was clear and obviously served riders' own interests.

This contrast shows that the success of a law depends on whether the people affected accept it; a policy that sacrifices their livelihoods without compensation is more likely to produce resentment and evasion than [[pristine|pristine]] forests.
Indeed, a law that people quietly ignore protects neither nature nor the communities that depend on it.
Admittedly, some wilderness areas are so valuable that no economic gain could justify their loss.
A rainforest may contain plants that become future medicines, and a unique wetland may shelter species found nowhere else on earth.
Nevertheless, this argument supports protecting the most important areas, not every remaining one.

A road built along the edge of a forest, for instance, may allow patients from remote villages to reach a district hospital in hours rather than days, and in my experience as a physician, such delays often decide whether a patient survives.
Weighing these benefits case by case is more [[judicious|judicious]] than a single rule that treats every hectare of wild land as untouchable.
Such decisions require weighing the value of each area against the needs of the people around it, which no blanket rule can do.
In conclusion, I disagree that nations should preserve all remaining wilderness regardless of the economic benefits of development.
Such a policy would keep poor communities poor, provoke illegal exploitation and block projects that improve health, even though the most valuable ecosystems do deserve strict protection.
A better law would rank wilderness areas by their value and allow carefully managed development elsewhere, so that both nature and people can thrive.

essays.task_note: Each body paragraph is a consequence of implementing the blanket law (poverty, illegal logging, blocked health access), and the essay explains how these push it toward case-by-case protection.

essays.title: Outside forces shape most behavior

paragraphs.text: Most of us like to believe that our choices are entirely our own.
However, the statement that people's behavior is largely determined by forces not of their own making challenges this comfortable belief.
I largely agree with the statement, although individuals still retain a meaningful, if limited, capacity to resist the forces around them.
Laws and social norms, as well as economic incentives, shape behavior far more than personal will does, yet people who defy their circumstances show where the statement reaches its limit.
First, the statement holds true because laws and social norms, which no individual creates alone, strongly shape everyday behavior.
Before 2007, many Vietnamese motorbike riders did not wear helmets, even though the risk of head injury was well known.
When a national law required helmets, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.

Similarly, in many countries, including Vietnam, antibiotics can be bought over the counter, so people take them for colds that do not need them, and this [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]] habit helps resistant bacteria spread.
In both cases, people largely did what the rules and available options encouraged, which suggests that behavior depended less on individual character than on the system around them.
Riders did not suddenly become more careful people; rather, the rules around them changed, and their behavior followed.
Second, economic forces beyond any person's control determine much of what people do and achieve.
Before Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, farmers worked under central planning, and the country faced food shortages.
Once market incentives were introduced, the same farmers produced so much that Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Likewise, a talented child born into [[indigence|indigence]] may leave school early to work, not because she lacks ambition, but because her family needs her income.
In my own clinical work, I have met patients who delayed treatment not out of carelessness but because a day at the hospital meant a day without wages.
These examples show that what looks like individual effort or laziness is often a response to incentives and constraints that people did not choose, which supports the statement.
Effort and ambition still matter, but they operate within limits that are set long before a person makes any choice.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for everyone, since some people act against the forces that surround them.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, defying a system that had long controlled their daily lives.
Nevertheless, even such courageous acts rarely arise from individual will alone.
The boycott lasted because residents acted together and supported one another, so each participant's choice was itself shaped by a community that no single person had created.

This case [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: people can resist outside forces, but they usually do so collectively and only under certain conditions, which is why I believe behavior is largely, though not entirely, determined from outside.
In conclusion, I largely agree that forces beyond our control shape human behavior, even if they do not dictate it completely.
Laws, social norms and economic incentives account for much of what people do, while acts of resistance reveal that individuals keep a limited but real freedom.
Recognizing this should make us more [[circumspect|circumspect]] before blaming individuals and more interested in changing the conditions that shape their choices.

words.meaning_here: careful; thinking before acting or judging

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 show where the statement holds (laws, norms, economic incentives) and Body 3 shows where it fails (the bus boycott) and how that qualifies the position.

essays.title: People can choose against their circumstances

paragraphs.text: Two people raised in the same poor neighborhood can lead completely different lives.
This simple observation raises doubts about the statement that people's behavior is largely determined by forces not of their own making.
Although outside forces clearly influence behavior, I largely disagree with the statement, because individuals repeatedly show that they can choose against their circumstances.
Acts of moral courage and achievements made despite disadvantage support this view, while the powerful effect of laws on behavior marks the area where the statement does hold some truth.
First, the statement fails to explain moral courage, which often requires people to act against strong outside pressure.
Around 1960, the sedative thalidomide was given to pregnant women in Europe and caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
In the United States, however, Frances Kelsey of the FDA refused to approve the drug, even though it was already in use abroad, and her decision spared American families the same tragedy.
Similarly, in Montgomery in 1955 and 1956, Black residents chose to walk rather than ride segregated buses for over a year, which helped end bus segregation in that city.
These [[intrepid|intrepid]] people lived among the same forces as everyone around them, yet they made different choices, which shows that behavior is not simply a product of circumstances.
Their courage came not from the forces around them but from a decision to resist those forces.
Second, many people achieve things that their backgrounds would never have predicted, which suggests that effort and choice matter a great deal.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Likewise, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
In my own field, I have worked with health workers in poor rural districts who, despite low pay and heavy workloads, chose to stay and serve their communities for decades.

If behavior were largely determined by outside forces, such [[anomalies|anomaly]] would be rare; in fact, history is full of them, because [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] people constantly turn limited opportunities into remarkable results.
Circumstances may make success harder, but they do not decide who will try.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in many everyday situations, where laws and incentives clearly change what people do.
When Vietnam required motorbike helmets in 2007, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
Nevertheless, this example shows that outside forces influence behavior, not that they determine it.
Each rider still decided whether to obey, and the law worked partly because most people understood that helmets protect their own lives.

In other words, external forces set the conditions under which people choose, but the choice itself remains theirs, so the statement goes too far when it calls those forces the main cause of behavior.
A force that people can choose to resist cannot be said to determine their behavior.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that forces outside our control determine how we behave.
Moral courage and achievement despite disadvantage show the power of individual choice, while the influence of laws reveals only that circumstances shape, rather than dictate, our actions.
Treating people as mere products of their environment may seem compassionate, but it [[slights|slight]] the dignity of those who choose to act differently.

words.meaning_here: exceptions that do not fit the usual pattern

essays.title: Free tuition rescues wasted talent

paragraphs.text: Talent is spread evenly across society, but opportunity is not.
For this reason, some argue that governments should offer a free university education to any admitted student who cannot afford the tuition.
I support this policy, provided that it is funded responsibly and linked to clear academic standards.
Its consequences for individual students and for society as a whole are largely positive, although its cost to taxpayers is a real concern that should shape how the policy is designed.
First, the policy would ensure that capable students are not lost simply because their families are poor.
Consider a gifted student from a farming village in the Mekong Delta who earns a place at a medical school in Ho Chi Minh City.
Without help, she might turn down the offer to support her family, and the country would lose a future doctor who might have served her home province.

History shows how much talent such barriers can waste; Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry despite the obstacles women faced, but many others in her position never had the chance to try.
Free tuition for admitted students who need it removes one major barrier, so that admission, rather than family wealth, decides who studies.
Over time, such a policy would also make universities more representative of the society they serve.
Moreover, the benefits of the policy would extend well beyond the students themselves, since educated citizens strengthen the whole society.
A poor student who trains as an engineer at public expense, for instance, may later design roads, water systems or bridges that serve an entire province.

Similarly, the publicly funded Human Genome Project made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, showing that public spending on knowledge can [[redound|redound]] to the benefit of everyone.
In my experience, physicians who grew up in rural areas are often the ones most willing to return and serve there.

In the same way, a government that pays for poor students' education is not offering charity but investing in future doctors, engineers and teachers whose work will [[augment|augment]] national prosperity.
Admittedly, the policy would be expensive, and taxpayers may object to paying for students who drop out or later leave the country.
A government with limited revenue might find that the cost of free tuition forces cuts to primary schools or rural clinics, which serve far more people.
Nevertheless, these risks can be reduced through sensible conditions rather than avoided by rejecting the policy.
Students could be required to maintain good grades, and those in fields such as medicine could agree to serve for several years in areas that lack professionals.

A program that [[stipulates|stipulate]] such conditions would keep its costs [[commensurate|commensurate]] with its benefits, which is why the cost concern shapes the design of my support rather than reversing it.
Such conditions would also make the policy easier to defend to taxpayers, who could see a clear return on their money.
In conclusion, I believe governments should pay the tuition of admitted students who cannot afford it, as long as the support comes with reasonable obligations.
Such a policy would rescue talent that poverty would otherwise waste and return its cost to society many times over, while conditions on students would keep its expense under control.
A nation that lets money, rather than merit, decide who studies is wasting its most valuable resource.

essays.title: Targeted aid beats free tuition

paragraphs.text: Good intentions do not always produce good policies.
The proposal that governments should offer a free university education to every admitted student who cannot afford tuition sounds generous, but its consequences deserve a careful look.
While I agree that poverty should never keep a capable student out of university, I oppose this policy as stated, because targeted grants and loans can achieve the same goal at a lower cost.
The policy's burden on public budgets and its weak incentives for students outweigh its benefits, even though its central aim, opening doors for poor students, is admirable.
First, free tuition would place a heavy burden on public budgets, often at the expense of more basic needs.
Consider a low-income country where many rural children still lack good primary schools and where district hospitals are short of staff.
If the government pays full tuition for every poor university student, it may have to cut the very services that help children reach university in the first place.
In my own field, I have seen how a small budget for disease surveillance can protect thousands of people, which makes me [[wary|wary]] of policies that spend heavily on a relatively small group.
Thus, one likely consequence of the policy is that money flows to the few who have already gained admission, while the many who never had a chance are left behind.
Second, free tuition can weaken students' incentive to choose their studies carefully and to finish on time.
When education costs nothing, some students may drift between programs or stay enrolled for years, because changing course or delaying graduation carries no financial penalty.

Singapore offers a useful parallel from another field: its government housing program houses about 80% of the country's residents, and most of them own their flats, so public support is combined with a personal stake.
A student who must repay part of the cost, by contrast, has a reason to choose a program carefully and to finish it.

Income-contingent loans follow the same [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] principle: students repay only when they earn enough, so poverty is no barrier, yet each student has a reason to take the investment seriously.
Thus, a policy that removes all cost may also remove the sense of responsibility that helps students succeed.
Admittedly, poor families are often [[leery|leery]] of debt, and some talented students might decline a place rather than borrow.
History reminds us how much is lost when talent is blocked; Marie Curie succeeded despite the barriers women faced in science, but countless others never had her chance.
Nevertheless, this concern supports generous grants for the poorest students, not free tuition for everyone who claims to need it.
A system that combines full grants for the poorest, partial grants for others and affordable loans for the rest can protect talent while keeping costs within reach.
Therefore, the risk of losing talent shapes my position by making me favor a mixed system, rather than leading me to accept the policy in its current form.
In this way, the goal of the policy is preserved while its most serious costs are avoided.
In conclusion, governments should help poor students attend university, but offering them free tuition is not the wisest way to do so.
The policy would strain public budgets and weaken students' incentives, and its main goal can be met through a [[judicious|judicious]] mix of grants and loans.
The real question is not whether to support poor students, but how to support them in a way that a country can sustain.

words.meaning_here: practical; focused on what actually works

essays.task_note: Bodies 1-2 are negative consequences of the policy (budget strain, weak incentives), Body 3 weighs the consequence of losing talent, and the essay explains how this leads to a mixed grant-loan system.

essays.title: Facts persuade best when stakes are high

paragraphs.text: In an age of endless opinion, many people long for arguments that rest on solid evidence.

This desire lies behind the claim that facts and statistics, rather than emotional arguments, are always the best way to persuade others, and behind the reason that facts are objective and therefore more persuasive.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, at least in matters where decisions affect many people, although emotion still plays a supporting role.
Facts persuade best in public decisions, their objectivity makes their influence last, and the limits of facts alone show why the claim needs a modest qualification.
First, the claim is largely correct when people must make important decisions for a community, because such decisions require [[empirical|empirical]] evidence that others can check.
In a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77%.
Such a figure gives health officials a concrete reason to adopt the method, and the same approach has also been tested in Vietnam.
Likewise, Vietnam's 2007 helmet law is easy to defend with data: helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
In both cases, statistics gave decision makers a [[cogent|cogent]] basis for action, which supports the claim that facts are the best tool of persuasion when much is at stake.
Emotional appeals may attract attention, but numbers like these are what justify spending public money.
Second, the reason behind the claim is sound, because the objectivity of facts allows them to be tested, shared and trusted by people who disagree.

The global campaign that eradicated smallpox, declared successful in 1980, relied on countries sharing data and vaccine; nations with very different political systems could cooperate because they trusted the same numbers.
By contrast, emotional appeals often fade once the feeling passes, and a skilled [[demagogue|demagogue]] can easily turn them to opposite ends.
In my own work, when I present dengue surveillance data to local officials, clear graphs often settle debates that hours of passionate discussion could not.
Because facts can be [[corroborated|corroborate]] independently, their power to persuade lasts longer and reaches further than subjective appeals, just as the reason suggests.
Objectivity, in short, is what makes facts a common language for people who share little else.
Admittedly, facts alone sometimes fail to persuade, especially when they threaten people's beliefs or pride.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea.
Nevertheless, this case shows the limits of a single presentation, not the weakness of facts.
Germ theory eventually vindicated Semmelweis, whereas the resistance of his critics, rooted in pride rather than evidence, is remembered only as a warning.
Therefore, the wisest persuaders lead with facts and use emotion only to help audiences care about them, which [[qualifies|qualify]] but does not overturn my agreement with the claim and its reason.
In conclusion, I largely agree that facts and statistics persuade better than emotional arguments, and that their objectivity explains why.
Evidence guides sound public decisions, survives scrutiny because others can verify it, and ultimately prevails even when it is first ignored.
The claim's only weakness is the phrase "in any situation," since even the strongest facts persuade best when they are presented with some understanding of the audience's feelings.

words.meaning_here: a leader who wins support by exploiting emotions

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates the reason that objectivity makes facts persuasive, and Body 3 concedes the Semmelweis case before qualifying the agreement.

essays.title: Facts need feeling to persuade

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has tried to change a friend's mind with a chart knows that numbers alone rarely win an argument.
Yet the claim holds that, in any situation, facts and statistics persuade better than emotional arguments, and the reason offered is that facts are objective while emotional appeals are subjective.
I disagree with both the claim and the reason, although I accept that facts are essential in technical and scientific decisions.
History shows that facts often fail to persuade on their own, the objectivity of facts does not guarantee that people accept them, and only in expert settings does the claim come close to the truth.
First, the claim is too broad, because in many situations facts alone have failed to persuade people.
In Vienna in 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Despite this clear evidence, most of his colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.

Similarly, the Montgomery bus boycott did not succeed by presenting statistics on segregation; it succeeded because residents' moral courage, sustained for over a year, [[galvanized|galvanize]] a community.
In my own work, I have found that villagers are more willing to remove standing water around their homes after hearing about a neighbor's child with dengue than after seeing case counts.
These cases show that persuasion depends not only on what is true but also on what feels [[salient|salient]] to an audience, so the claim's phrase "in any situation" cannot stand.
Facts, in other words, need a reason to be heard before they can persuade.
Second, the reason is also flawed, because what is presented as objective fact is not always reliable, and even reliable facts are received subjectively.

In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, showing that many "facts" presented with confident statistics were less reliable than they seemed.

Moreover, the same smartphones and social media that let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011 also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, which suggests that emotional stories often travel further than careful facts.
Because audiences judge facts through their fears, values and trust in the speaker, objectivity alone does not make an argument persuasive, and the reason therefore fails to support the claim.
Admittedly, in technical fields such as medicine, facts are indispensable, and emotional arguments can be dangerous.
Around 1960, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Nevertheless, even this case suggests that facts work best when people care about them.
The stricter drug-testing rules that the United States passed in 1962 probably owed as much to public horror at the harm done to babies as to the data themselves.
Thus, facts and emotion work as partners: facts establish what is true, while emotion often determines whether people act, which is why the claim's [[dichotomy|dichotomy]] between them is false.
A claim that ignores this partnership misunderstands how people actually change their minds.
In conclusion, I disagree that facts and statistics are always the best way to persuade, and I reject the reason that their objectivity makes them more persuasive.
Clear evidence has often been ignored, objective data are filtered through subjective judgment, and even in technical fields facts succeed most when people care about them.
The most effective persuaders therefore combine sound evidence with an [[articulate|articulate]] appeal to what their audience values.

words.meaning_here: a sharp division into two opposed parts

essays.task_note: Body 1 rejects the claim's 'in any situation', Body 2 shows the reason (objectivity) does not ensure persuasion, and Body 3 concedes the role of facts in technical fields.

essays.title: Effort, not gift, drives creative success

paragraphs.text: Behind almost every celebrated novel or film lie years of drafts that the public never sees.

This raises the question of whether success in creative fields such as painting, fiction writing and filmmaking comes mainly from hard work and perseverance or from innate talents that cannot be learned.
My position aligns more closely with the first view, because talent may open the door, but sustained effort is what turns potential into lasting work.

Creative skill is built through deliberate practice, perseverance carries artists through long periods of rejection, and although the second view rightly notes differences in natural ability, those differences matter less than discipline.
First, the view that success depends on hard work is more convincing because creative skill, like any other skill, is developed through deliberate practice.

The Wright brothers, though inventors rather than artists, offer a clear model of creative work: as bicycle makers without college degrees, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 only after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Similarly, a young filmmaker learns to frame a scene and pace a story by shooting, editing and reshooting many short films, not by waiting for inspiration.
These examples show that what looks like natural genius is usually the visible result of countless hours of [[assiduous|assiduous]] work, which supports the first view.
Talent may explain why some people begin with an advantage, but only practice explains how they reach a professional level.
Second, perseverance matters because creative success often arrives slowly, after long periods of rejection or neglect.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he kept painting, and he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
In a smaller way, I learned the same lesson in scientific writing: my first manuscripts came back with harsh reviews, and only by revising them again and again did I learn to write clearly.
Novelists, too, often collect many rejection letters before a publisher accepts their first book.
Without perseverance, Van Gogh would have left no body of work for later generations to admire, so even the most gifted artist depends on the will to continue when recognition is [[scant|scant]].
Perseverance is therefore not a minor virtue in creative work but the condition for everything else.
Admittedly, the second view captures something real, since people do differ in [[inborn|inborn]] abilities such as a musical ear or a strong visual memory.
Two students who practice drawing for the same number of hours may still progress at different speeds, and a few seem to grasp composition almost without instruction.
Nevertheless, [[nascent|nascent]] talent is only a starting point, not a destination.
Many gifted young writers never finish a novel, while less gifted but more disciplined ones publish book after book.

Because natural ability without effort produces little, whereas steady effort can [[offset|offset]] a modest gift, hard work remains the main requirement for creative success, even if talent gives some artists an early advantage.
Talent, in short, decides how fast an artist starts; hard work decides how far he or she goes.
In conclusion, I side with the view that creative success depends primarily on hard work and perseverance rather than on innate talent.
Practice builds creative skill, perseverance sustains artists through rejection, and natural ability, though real, cannot replace either one.
For aspiring artists, this is encouraging news, because the most important ingredient of success, unlike natural talent, is the one that lies within their own control.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the hard-work view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 credits the talent view for real differences in ability before explaining why discipline matters more.

essays.title: Exceptional art begins with innate talent

paragraphs.text: Millions of children take piano lessons, but very few become Mozart.

This gap lies at the heart of the debate over whether success in creative fields such as painting, fiction writing and filmmaking depends mainly on hard work and perseverance or on innate talents that cannot be learned.
My position aligns more closely with the second view, since effort is necessary but rarely produces exceptional creative work without an unusual natural gift.
The early appearance of extraordinary ability, the frequent failure of effort alone, and the fair point that talent must still be trained together explain why I favor the second view.
First, the second view is more convincing because exceptional creative ability often appears before any long period of training could explain it.

Mozart composed music as a young child, long before he could have practiced as much as adult professional musicians; his [[prodigious|prodigious]] gift was evident before hard work had time to shape it.
Similarly, most teachers of art or writing can recall a student whose first attempts already showed a sense of color, rhythm or story that classmates could not match after years of lessons.
Musicians speak of perfect pitch, the ability to name a note on hearing it, which some children show early and most adults cannot acquire even with training.
Such cases suggest that the highest levels of creative work depend on something [[inborn|inborn]], a quality that effort can refine but cannot create.
Hard work matters, but it builds on a foundation that some people simply possess and others lack.
Second, hard work alone often fails to produce creative success, which suggests that perseverance is not the deciding factor.
In every city, there are painters and novelists who work [[sedulously|sedulous]] for decades yet never produce anything that critics or audiences remember.

Even Vincent van Gogh, now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history, sold very few paintings during his lifetime; what eventually set him apart was not the amount of work he did but a way of seeing that no amount of effort could teach.

If success depended mainly on perseverance, the most persistent artists would be the most celebrated; since they often are not, the first view cannot explain the difference between competent work and [[sublime|sublime]] work.
Admittedly, the first view is right that talent without discipline usually fades.

The Wright brothers, though inventors rather than artists, achieved the first powered airplane flight only after years of careful experiments, and many gifted artists likewise need years of training before their work matures.
Nevertheless, effort works on the raw material that talent supplies, and it cannot replace that material.
Two filmmakers may study the same techniques for the same number of years, yet only one may possess the instinct for images that makes audiences remember a film.
Thus, hard work is a necessary condition for creative success, but innate talent is the main one, which is why the second view comes closer to the truth.
Hard work polishes the stone, but it cannot turn an ordinary stone into a diamond.
In conclusion, I side with the view that creative success depends mainly on innate talents that cannot be fully learned.
Extraordinary ability often appears early, effort alone often fails, and training, though essential, builds on a gift rather than replacing it.
Recognizing this does not [[disparage|disparage]] hard work; it simply acknowledges that the rarest creative achievements begin with something no amount of practice can supply.

words.meaning_here: of the highest excellence; inspiring awe

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the talent view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 grants the hard-work view that training is necessary before explaining why talent remains the main factor.

essays.title: Scrutinize new leaders, but do not obstruct

paragraphs.text: Trust is easy to give and hard to recover once it has been betrayed.
This is why some argue that in business, education and government it is always appropriate to remain skeptical of new leaders until they prove that they deserve trust.
I largely agree with the claim, as long as skepticism means careful scrutiny rather than hostility or a refusal to cooperate.

Unchecked authority can cause grave harm, and healthy scrutiny improves leaders themselves; the strongest challenge, that skepticism may paralyze a new leader, can be answered by distinguishing scrutiny from obstruction.
First, skepticism is appropriate because people in authority can cause great harm when no one questions them.

From 1932 to 1972, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and it continued for decades partly because the officials in charge were trusted rather than questioned.
By contrast, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, the sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and her caution protected American families.

These cases show that withholding automatic trust is not cynicism but a safeguard against [[credulous|credulous]] obedience, and that the cost of misplaced trust in authority can be [[grievous|grievous]].
History suggests that the leaders who most need scrutiny are often the ones who seem least to require it.
Moreover, scrutiny tends to make new leaders better, since leaders who know they are being watched have strong reasons to earn trust.

Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, presumably because he valued advisers who would question his decisions.
In my own experience, a new head of a research unit who presents her plans openly to doubtful colleagues usually earns lasting support, whereas one who demands loyalty from the start often loses it.
Such leaders tend to make fewer mistakes, because problems are raised before they become crises.
Thus, skepticism, when expressed through questions rather than resistance, is part of the process by which a leader becomes worthy of trust, as the claim implies.
A leader who welcomes such questions shows, in fact, one of the clearest signs of being worthy of trust.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that skepticism can paralyze a new leader, especially in a crisis that demands quick action.

Consider a newly appointed director of a provincial hospital during a dengue outbreak: if her staff refuse to follow her instructions until she has proven herself, patients may die while trust slowly builds.
Nevertheless, this objection targets obstruction, not skepticism.
The hospital staff can follow reasonable orders while still checking the results, asking questions and reporting problems.
In my own experience during dengue outbreaks, the most effective teams were those that acted quickly while openly discussing what was and was not working.

Skepticism of this kind does not delay action; it simply ensures that mistakes are noticed early, so the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] how skepticism should be expressed without undermining the claim itself.
The best response to the challenge, therefore, is not to abandon skepticism but to express it responsibly.
In conclusion, I largely agree that new leaders in business, education and government should face skepticism until they earn trust.
Questioning authority prevents serious harm and encourages better leadership, and the danger of paralysis disappears once skepticism is understood as scrutiny rather than resistance.
Leaders who deserve trust have nothing to fear from such [[prudent|prudent]] doubt, and those who do not deserve it will be discovered quickly.

words.meaning_here: too ready to believe or trust

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (skepticism paralyzes leaders in a crisis) and answers it by separating scrutiny from obstruction.

essays.title: Reflexive doubt stalls good leaders

paragraphs.text: Every leader starts as a stranger to the people he or she must lead.
According to the claim, in business, education and government it is always appropriate to remain skeptical of new leaders until they show that they are worthy of trust.

I disagree with the claim, because reflexive skepticism often blocks the very changes new leaders are chosen to make, although some caution is clearly [[warranted|warranted]] where leaders hold great power over vulnerable people.
Skepticism can stall necessary reform, trust offered early can encourage good leadership, and the case of abused authority, though serious, does not justify a universal rule.
First, automatic skepticism can stall the reforms that new leaders are often appointed to carry out.

When Vietnam launched the Doi Moi reforms in 1986, replacing central planning with market incentives, officials and farmers had to cooperate with new policies before anyone could prove they would work, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.

On a smaller scale, imagine a new school principal who wants to replace rote memorization with problem solving: if teachers [[balk|balk]] at every proposal until she proves herself, the reform may fail before it has a chance to work.
In such cases, insisting that leaders earn trust before receiving cooperation creates a [[paradox|paradox]], since they can prove themselves only if people are willing to follow them first.
Some trust must therefore come first, or no new leader can succeed.
Second, trust offered early often encourages leaders to behave well, whereas suspicion can create the very problems it fears.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers and extending trust to former opponents.
In my own work, a new team leader who was welcomed openly felt free to admit mistakes, while a colleague who faced constant doubt from the start became defensive and [[aloof|aloof]].
Similarly, a newly appointed hospital director who is given a reasonable period of support can learn the institution's problems before being judged on results.
These examples suggest that trust is not only a reward for good leadership but also one of its causes, so treating every new leader with suspicion can be [[counterproductive|counterproductive]].
Leaders, like everyone else, tend to rise or fall to the expectations placed on them.
The most compelling challenge to my view is that blind trust in authority has enabled terrible abuses.

From 1932 to 1972, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and the public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, this case argues for strong institutions that check every leader, not for personal suspicion of each new one.
Ethics review boards protect research participants whether or not a particular investigator seems trustworthy, which allows people to cooperate with leaders while rules guard against abuse.

Therefore, the danger of abused power shapes my position by placing caution in systems of oversight rather than in a habit of doubting every newcomer, which is why the word "always" makes the claim too sweeping.
In conclusion, I disagree that skepticism toward new leaders is always appropriate.
Reflexive doubt can stall reform and weaken good leadership, while the real danger of abuse is better handled by institutions than by personal suspicion.
Offering new leaders a measure of trust, backed by clear rules of accountability, gives them the chance to show what they can do before anyone decides whether they deserve it.

words.meaning_here: refuse or hesitate to go along
a situation that seems to contradict itself
having the opposite of the intended effect

essays.task_note: Body 3 takes the strongest challenge (Tuskegee and abused authority) and answers that institutions, not blanket suspicion, should provide the check.

essays.title: Shift class time to group work

paragraphs.text: Most important work today is done not by lone geniuses but by teams.

The claim under discussion holds that group assignments should replace a substantial amount of lecture-based instruction in colleges and universities, and the reason offered is that students must gain experience collaborating with peers to study a topic and reach a common goal.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, provided that lectures are reduced rather than eliminated.

Group work prepares students for collaborative careers, the reason is sound because collaboration can be learned only through practice, and the risk of uneven effort can be managed through careful course design.
First, the claim is persuasive because the work that graduates will actually do is increasingly collaborative.

The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, was an international effort that required many laboratories to divide tasks and share results before it could make the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Similarly, the global campaign that eradicated smallpox by 1980 depended on countries sharing data and vaccine rather than on any single expert.
In my own field, a single epidemiological study often requires clinicians, laboratory scientists, statisticians and field workers to coordinate their work.

If universities devote most class time to lectures, they prepare students for a world of solitary listening that hardly exists, whereas shifting a substantial part of instruction to group work would [[facilitate|facilitate]] their transition into professional life.
Collaboration is no longer an optional extra in professional life; it is the normal way serious work gets done.
Second, the reason behind the claim is sound, because collaboration is a skill that, like swimming, cannot be learned by listening to explanations.

In my own training as an epidemiologist, I learned more about study design from a group project analyzing a local dengue outbreak than from many lectures, since my teammates questioned my assumptions and forced me to explain my reasoning.
Likewise, students who must divide a task, resolve disagreements and meet a shared deadline learn to negotiate, listen and take responsibility, habits that no lecture can [[inculcate|inculcate]].

Thus, the reason does support the claim: if collaboration is vital, students need regular opportunities to practice it, and those opportunities require class time that only a reduction in lectures can provide.
Admittedly, group assignments can be unfair, since some students do most of the work while others contribute little.
Many students have experienced a project in which one [[indolent|indolent]] member received the same grade as the classmates who carried the group.
Nevertheless, this problem reflects poor design rather than a flaw in group learning itself.
Instructors can assign individual roles, ask each member to evaluate the others, and grade both the group product and each student's contribution.
In my experience, even a short weekly meeting where members report their progress makes free riding much harder.

Moreover, lectures still have a place for introducing foundational concepts, so the best approach is to [[amalgamate|amalgamate]] brief lectures with substantial group work, which qualifies but does not reverse my agreement with the claim.
In conclusion, I agree that group assignments should replace a substantial share of traditional lectures, and I accept the reason that collaboration is a vital skill.
Modern work depends on teams, collaboration is learned only through practice, and the risk of unequal effort can be reduced through careful design.
Universities that make this shift will graduate students who can not only understand a topic but also work with others to solve real problems.

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim, Body 2 evaluates whether the collaboration reason is true and supports the claim, and Body 3 concedes free riding before qualifying the agreement.

essays.title: Add group work; keep the lectures

paragraphs.text: A good lecture can give students in one hour what might take them days to piece together on their own.

The claim, however, holds that group assignments should replace a substantial amount of lecture-based instruction in colleges and universities, because students must gain experience collaborating with peers.
Although I accept that collaboration is a valuable skill, I disagree with the claim, and I find that the reason, while true, does not justify replacing a substantial amount of lecturing.

Lectures transmit foundational knowledge more efficiently than group work, collaboration can be practiced without sacrificing them, and the genuine importance of teamwork calls for a modest addition rather than a replacement.
First, the claim underestimates the value of lectures, because expert explanation is the most efficient way to teach the foundations of a field.
In medical school, students must master anatomy, physiology and pharmacology before they can reason about patients.

A skilled lecturer can explain in an hour how antibiotics work and why their overuse helps resistant bacteria spread, while a group of students working alone may spend days on the topic and still absorb misconceptions from one another.
Similarly, in mathematics or engineering, groups that lack a firm grasp of [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] principles often reach confident but [[erroneous|erroneous]] conclusions.
Thus, replacing a substantial amount of lecturing with group assignments risks leaving students with gaps in knowledge that later collaboration cannot fill.
Second, the reason is true but does not support the claim, since students can gain collaborative experience without giving up lectures.
Many universities already combine lectures with laboratory teams, student societies, internships and research projects, all of which require students to work toward a common goal.
The Wright brothers, for instance, learned to work as a team through years of shared experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, not through classroom assignments.
Even within a single course, a short group exercise after each lecture can give students practice in teamwork without replacing the lecture itself.

Because such opportunities exist outside lecture time, the importance of collaboration does not require universities to [[supplant|supplant]] lectures; the reason supports adding group work, not removing teaching that students still need.
In short, the reason identifies a real need but proposes the wrong remedy.
Admittedly, collaboration is vital in modern work, and students who never practice it may struggle after graduation.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, succeeded only because many teams shared their work.
Nevertheless, the scientists in that project had first mastered their own disciplines, presumably through years of traditional instruction.
Their collaboration was valuable precisely because each member brought deep, individually acquired knowledge to the team.
In my own training, the group projects I found most useful came only after lectures had given me the basic concepts of epidemiology and statistics.

This suggests that strong foundations are what make collaboration productive, so universities should add carefully designed group work to their courses without sacrificing the lectures on which effective teamwork depends.
Group work built on weak foundations, by contrast, often produces confident but shallow results.
In conclusion, I disagree that group assignments should replace a substantial amount of lecture-based instruction, even though I accept that collaboration matters.
Lectures build the foundations that group work needs, collaboration can be practiced in many other settings, and even large team efforts depend on individual expertise.
The wisest course is to [[bolster|bolster]] lectures with group work, not to sacrifice one for the other.

essays.task_note: Body 1 rejects the claim, Body 2 grants that the reason is true but shows it does not support replacing lectures, and Body 3 concedes that collaboration is vital.

essays.title: Breadth prepares specialists for real problems

paragraphs.text: Many of today's most urgent problems do not respect the boundaries between academic departments.
For this reason, some argue that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside his or her field of study.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as the requirement is limited in size so that students can still develop deep expertise in their chosen fields.

Complex problems demand knowledge from several disciplines, and broad study protects specialists from narrow thinking; the most compelling challenge, the cost to specialized training, can be met by keeping the requirement modest.
First, a broad education is valuable because real problems rarely fall within a single discipline.

Antibiotic resistance, for instance, is not only a biological problem: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so solving it requires knowledge of economics, law and human behavior as well as microbiology.
Likewise, the Wolbachia method, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, drew on both insect biology and public health research.
Such projects succeed only when each specialist understands enough of the others' work to cooperate effectively.
Graduates who have studied outside their own field are better able to understand and work with such [[disparate|disparate]] experts, which is exactly what the claim aims to achieve.
Without some exposure to other disciplines, specialists may not even know which questions to ask their colleagues.
Second, courses outside one's field protect students from the narrow thinking that can [[blight|blight]] even successful careers and companies.
In 1975, Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera, yet Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
A company whose leaders had received more [[eclectic|eclectic]] training in technology, economics and consumer behavior might have recognized the threat sooner.
In my own work on antibiotic resistance, some of the most useful insights have come from colleagues trained in economics or anthropology, who see patterns that clinicians overlook.
These examples suggest that [[myopic|myopic]] expertise can blind people to changes outside their own specialty, and that broad study helps students see connections that specialists alone may miss.
Breadth, in other words, is not a luxury but a form of protection against blind spots.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that required courses take time away from fields that already demand intense specialization.
Medical students, for example, must master an enormous amount of material, and an extra course in art history may seem like a distraction from learning to save lives.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for a limited requirement, not for abolishing breadth altogether.

Even physicians benefit from courses in ethics or history; the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, shows what can happen when technical expertise is separated from ethical reflection.

A requirement of a few well-chosen courses would preserve the depth that specialists need while giving them the perspective to use their expertise wisely, so the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my agreement rather than overturning it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to take a variety of courses outside their fields, provided the requirement is modest.
Broad study prepares students for problems that cross disciplines and guards against narrow thinking, while a limited requirement protects the depth that specialization demands.
In a world of complex problems, the most valuable graduates will be experts who can also see beyond their own field.

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (lost time for specialization, e.g. medical students) and answers it by limiting the requirement to a few courses.

essays.title: Breadth should be chosen, not required

paragraphs.text: Students arrive at university with limited time, limited money and, often, a clear sense of what they want to become.
Yet some argue that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside his or her field of study.
Although broad knowledge has real value, I disagree with this claim, because a universal requirement wastes scarce time and money and is not the best way to produce broad-minded graduates.

Such requirements impose real costs on students in demanding fields, breadth is better pursued through choice than through compulsion, and the strongest challenge, the interdisciplinary nature of modern problems, can be met through collaboration among specialists.
First, a requirement that applies to every student imposes significant costs, especially on those in long and demanding programs.

Medical students, for instance, must master anatomy, pharmacology and clinical skills in a crowded curriculum; adding required courses in unrelated subjects can extend their studies or force them to learn essential material less thoroughly.
For students from poor families, each extra semester also means more tuition and lost income, a burden that falls hardest on those who can least afford it.
Therefore, a universal requirement does not treat all students equally; it [[exacerbates|exacerbate]] the pressures on those whose programs are already the most [[onerous|onerous]].
Breadth is a worthy goal, but forcing it on every student ignores how unequal its costs can be.
Second, breadth is more meaningful when students pursue it by choice rather than by obligation.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, which shows how much people learn and share when they follow their own curiosity.
By contrast, students forced into required courses often treat them as obstacles, choosing the easiest options and forgetting the material soon after the final exam.
In my own medical training, the courses outside medicine that I remember best were those I chose myself, not those I was required to take.
A [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] course taken only to satisfy a rule adds little real breadth, whereas electives, reading and outside activities chosen freely can broaden a mind far more effectively.
Choice, not compulsion, is what turns exposure to a new field into genuine interest.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that many modern problems, from antibiotic resistance to climate change, demand knowledge from several disciplines.
The Wolbachia method of dengue control, which cut cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, required entomologists and public health researchers to work together.
Nevertheless, such success depended on specialists cooperating, not on each specialist having studied every field.
Similarly, the Human Genome Project brought together many teams, each with its own expertise, to make the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.

These cases suggest that interdisciplinary problems are best solved by deep experts who know how to collaborate, so the challenge supports training in teamwork rather than a requirement that every student study outside his or her field.
In conclusion, I disagree that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside his or her field.
Such a requirement burdens students in demanding programs, produces little real breadth when imposed, and is unnecessary for solving complex problems that teams of specialists can address together.

Universities should instead offer attractive electives and real opportunities for collaboration, which are a more [[viable|viable]] path for students to broaden their knowledge in ways that fit their goals.
