essays.title: A shared core curriculum makes schooling fairer

paragraphs.text: Every society must decide what its children should know before they become adults.
One way to make that decision is to require all students to follow the same national curriculum until they enter college.
I largely support this policy, as long as the shared curriculum sets a common core and still leaves teachers room to adapt how they teach it.
Its most important consequences would be greater fairness between rich and poor regions and a common foundation for higher study, although the risk of rigidity must be managed.
First, a national curriculum would make education fairer, because it would guarantee that a child's lessons do not depend on the wealth of her province.
Consider two students in Vietnam, one in a mountain village and one in Hanoi.
Without a shared standard, the village school might drop chemistry or foreign languages for lack of resources, and the gap between the two children would widen every year.
A required curriculum, by contrast, would oblige the state to supply qualified teachers and textbooks to both schools.
Similarly, a family that moves to another city for work could enroll its children in a new school without losing a year of progress.
These cases show that a common curriculum is not merely an administrative convenience; it is a tool to [[mitigate|mitigate]] the inequality that purely local choices would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]].
In a country with wide gaps between cities and rural provinces, this consequence alone is a strong reason to adopt the policy.
Second, a shared curriculum would give universities a reliable foundation on which to build, because every applicant would arrive with the same basic preparation.

In my experience teaching first-year students of public health, the hardest classes are those in which students arrive with [[disparate|disparate]] preparation: some have studied statistics, while others have never read a graph of data.
Lecturers then spend weeks on [[remedial|remedial]] lessons instead of advancing the course.
Likewise, a national curriculum would let a medical school in one city assume that applicants from every province have learned the same biology.
This shows that uniform preparation before college is a consequence that benefits higher education as much as the students themselves.
A national curriculum would therefore raise the starting point of every first-year class, allowing universities to spend their time on advanced work rather than on repairing gaps.
Admittedly, the policy could make schooling rigid if officials in the capital dictated not only what students learn but also how every lesson is taught.
A curriculum that changes slowly might [[ossify|ossify]], leaving students to memorize outdated facts while the world moves on.
Nevertheless, this danger depends on how the policy is implemented, not on the idea of a common curriculum itself.

Finland, for instance, requires its schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, so its well-trained teachers are trusted to adapt lessons to their students.
A nation that adopts a national curriculum can combine it with this kind of trust, fixing what students learn while letting teachers decide how to teach it and revising the content regularly.
Seen this way, rigidity is a risk to manage through design, not a reason to reject the policy outright.
In conclusion, requiring all students to study the same curriculum before college is a sound policy when the curriculum defines a core rather than a cage.
Its likely consequences, fairer opportunities across regions and a stronger foundation for higher education, outweigh the risk of rigidity, which careful design can reduce.
The policy is therefore worth adopting, provided that teachers are trusted and the curriculum is renewed as knowledge changes.

essays.title: One curriculum cannot fit every student

paragraphs.text: A shoe that fits one foot perfectly will pinch another.
The same problem arises when a nation requires every student, in every region and with every talent, to study an identical curriculum until college.
I oppose this policy as stated, although I accept that a small common core in reading, mathematics, and science is valuable.
A fully uniform curriculum would ignore students' different needs and make the whole school system slow to improve, and these costs outweigh its benefit of fairness.
First, one curriculum for all would ignore the [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] needs of students and communities, because what is useful in one place is often irrelevant in another.
Consider a teenager in the Mekong Delta who hopes to run his family's farm.
A curriculum designed in the capital might require him to spend years on advanced literature while offering nothing on soil, water, or small business, so he may lose interest and leave school early.
Similarly, a student with a gift for engineering would gain more from extra workshop hours than from a fixed list of courses shared with everyone else.
These cases show that a uniform requirement does not create equal opportunity; it simply treats unequal needs as if they were the same.
A policy meant to give every student the same chance would thus, in practice, fail the many students whose goals differ from the national average.
Second, a single national curriculum would make reform slow, because every change would have to pass through one central office.
Vietnam's own history offers a useful parallel.

Before the Doi Moi reforms of 1986, central planning directed the economy and the country faced food shortages; once market incentives replaced that system, Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Similarly, under a single national curriculum, a school that discovered a better way to teach mathematics would have to wait for national approval before it could change a single lesson.

Both examples suggest that systems controlled from a single center tend to [[ossify|ossify]], and a national curriculum would [[impede|impede]] the local experiments from which better teaching usually emerges.
These consequences, more than any abstract principle, explain why I oppose a fully uniform curriculum.
Admittedly, the strongest consequence in favor of the policy is fairness: without a shared standard, poor regions might offer weaker schooling than rich ones.
A child in a remote village could finish school without ever studying chemistry simply because no local teacher was qualified to teach it.
Nevertheless, this problem calls for a minimum standard and better funding, not for an identical curriculum in every classroom.

Finland, which makes teaching a respected and selective profession and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, shows that well-trained teachers may be a surer route to quality than central control.
Thus the concern for equity qualifies my position, leading me to accept a [[modest|modest]] common core, but it does not justify requiring the same curriculum for all.
The fairness that the policy promises can be secured at a far lower cost to students' freedom.
In conclusion, a nation should not require all students to study exactly the same curriculum until they enter college.
Such a policy would ignore students' varied needs and slow the reforms that schools require, while its main benefit, fairness, can be achieved through a small core and better-trained teachers.
A wise nation should set a floor for what every child learns, not a ceiling on what each child may explore.

essays.title: Guide students toward careers that pay

paragraphs.text: Few decisions shape a young person's future as strongly as the choice of a major.
Because that choice affects income for decades, some argue that schools and universities should actively encourage students to choose fields that lead to lucrative careers.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as encouragement means honest guidance rather than pressure that overrides a student's own interests.
Such encouragement corrects students' limited knowledge of the job market and directs talent toward fields that society needs, although the value of less profitable fields must not be ignored.
First, institutions should encourage lucrative fields because most students choose their major with very little information about future earnings.
In Vietnam, many families spend years of savings on a child's education, yet a seventeen-year-old often picks a major because a friend chose it or because its name sounds exciting.
If that student graduates into a crowded field with few jobs, the family's investment is lost, and the young graduate may feel [[crestfallen|crestfallen]] and adrift.
Similarly, a counselor who simply helps students [[ascertain|ascertain]] which fields are growing can prevent many such mistakes at almost no cost.
This shows that active encouragement is not an intrusion but a [[prudent|prudent]] correction of the information gap that students face.
Schools that stay silent about earnings are not neutral; they simply leave students to guess.
Moreover, the fields that pay well are often the fields that society most needs, so encouraging them serves the public as well as the individual.
Consider GPS, which was built by the US military; once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing, and delivery apps.
The engineers and programmers who build such services find well-paid work precisely because their skills create enormous public value.
Likewise, hospitals that compete to hire data analysts are signaling how urgently they need people who can make sense of patient records.
In a growing economy, a student guided toward nursing or software engineering is likely to find both a good salary and a chance to serve others.
In such cases, a lucrative career is a signal of social demand, and schools that guide students toward it help society meet that demand.
Encouragement of this kind aligns private success with public benefit.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that some of the most valuable work begins in fields that pay little and attract little attention.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed basic research on mRNA, yet that work allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year and earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Nevertheless, this example argues for balance, not for ignoring income.
Basic science is pursued by a small number of deeply committed people, whereas most students need [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] guidance to build a stable life.
Moreover, a student who earns a stable income can still support basic research as a donor, a taxpayer, or a volunteer.
Schools can therefore encourage lucrative fields as a default while still supporting the students whose passion leads them elsewhere, so the challenge qualifies my position without overturning it.
In conclusion, educational institutions are right to encourage students toward fields that offer good careers, provided that this encouragement informs rather than dictates.
Such guidance closes the information gap students face and steers talent toward fields that society values, while room remains for less profitable but important work.
The best schools will show students the numbers, explain what those numbers mean, and then let them make the final choice.

essays.title: Inform students, do not steer them

paragraphs.text: Salaries change faster than the courses students take to earn them.
For this reason, I doubt the claim that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study that will prepare them for lucrative careers.
I mostly disagree with this claim: schools should inform students about the job market, but they should not actively steer them toward money.
Such encouragement rests on unreliable predictions and neglects the public mission of education, and although it answers a real concern about income, it answers that concern in the wrong way.
First, institutions should not push students toward lucrative fields because no one can reliably predict which fields will stay lucrative.
Kodak is a clear warning.
Its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
A university that had urged students into film chemistry in the 1970s would have pointed them toward a shrinking industry.
Similarly, the high salaries of a booming field can prove [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] once too many graduates enter it or new technology replaces the work.
Even in medicine, the specialties that seem most profitable can change as health systems and technology evolve.
These cases show that encouraging students to chase current salaries can be [[myopic|myopic]], leaving them trained for a world that has already passed.
Encouragement based on today's salaries is therefore a weak foundation for a lifelong choice.
Second, the mission of educational institutions is to advance knowledge and serve the public, not merely to raise their graduates' incomes.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Its value lay not in the wealth of any participant but in the knowledge it gave to everyone.
Likewise, Finland makes teaching a respected and selective profession, showing that a society can attract talented people to public service by honoring its value.
Many of the doctors, teachers, and researchers on whom society depends could earn more elsewhere, yet their work is essential.
If universities [[exhort|exhort]] students to follow money, they will drain such fields of talent and [[undermine|undermine]] the public goods that education exists to create.
An institution that measures its success only by its graduates' salaries has forgotten why it was founded.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is that students and their families need income, and schools that ignore this need are being unrealistic.
In Vietnam, many families borrow money to pay for a child's education, and a graduate without a job cannot repay that debt.
Nevertheless, the answer is [[candid|candid]] information, not active encouragement toward one kind of career.
A school can publish employment and salary data for every major, invite graduates to describe their work, and teach practical skills such as statistics in every program.
This approach respects the real pressure of income while leaving the decision with the student, so the challenge refines my position rather than defeating it.
Students who receive honest data and still choose a modest salary are making an informed decision, which is exactly what education should make possible.
In conclusion, educational institutions should not actively steer students toward lucrative careers.
Such encouragement depends on forecasts that often fail and neglects the public purposes of education, while the legitimate concern about income is better met by clear information than by pressure.
Schools serve students best when they help them choose wisely, not when they quietly choose for them in the name of future income.

essays.title: Effective leaders must know when to yield

paragraphs.text: Politics has often been described as the art of the possible.
This idea lies behind the debate over whether effective political leaders must yield to public opinion and compromise, or whether they must remain consistently committed to fixed principles.
I side mainly with the first view: effective leaders must be willing to yield and compromise, although they should hold firm on a few core commitments.
Compromise lets leaders build the coalitions they need and correct policies that fail, while the second view correctly reminds us that some principles should never be traded.
First, the first view is closer to the truth because no leader can govern alone, and compromise is the price of the broad support that effective government requires.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet.
Rather than surrounding himself with loyal followers, he chose able critics, accepting their disagreement in exchange for their talent and influence.
Similarly, a health minister in any democracy must bargain with lawmakers to pass a budget, giving up some programs in order to protect others.
Such trade-offs disappoint some supporters, yet without them no budget would pass and no program would be funded.
These cases show that yielding is not weakness; it is how an effective leader turns [[contentious|contentious]] politics into actual decisions.
Compromise, in other words, is the means by which leaders gain the power to act at all.
Second, leaders who listen to public opinion can recognize when a policy has failed and change course.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 are a strong case.
The country had faced food shortages under central planning, and by replacing that system with market incentives, its leaders abandoned a long-held principle.
Vietnam then became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
By contrast, a leader who keeps an unpopular tax that is clearly harming families shows stubbornness, not strength.

This shows that the willingness to abandon a failing principle, which the first view defends, can be the very source of a leader's effectiveness, whereas an [[intransigent|intransigent]] government might have kept its people hungry.
Public opinion, after all, often reflects the daily experience of citizens who feel a policy's effects first.
Admittedly, the second view is right that some principles must not bend to public opinion.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and her firm stand spared American families that tragedy.
Nevertheless, Kelsey was a regulator applying scientific standards, not a political leader seeking a majority.
A regulator answers to evidence; a political leader must also answer to voters.
Political leaders face a different task: they must persuade millions of people, and a leader who never compromises will soon lose the power to protect any principle at all.
Thus the second view identifies a necessary limit, a small set of [[inviolate|inviolate]] commitments, but it does not describe what makes leaders effective from day to day.
In conclusion, I believe that effective political leaders must often yield to public opinion and compromise, even at the cost of principles they once held.
Compromise builds the support that governing requires and allows leaders to abandon failing policies, while the second view rightly reminds us that a few commitments should stay fixed.
The most effective leader, then, is [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] about means and firm only about the few ends that truly matter.

essays.title: Principle, not polls, makes leaders effective

paragraphs.text: A compass is useful only because its needle does not swing with every passing wind.

In the same way, many people believe that the most essential quality of an effective political leader is a steady commitment to particular principles and objectives, while others argue that leaders must yield to public opinion and compromise.
I side with the second view: effective leaders may adjust their methods, but they must stay committed to their core principles and goals.
Consistent commitment allows leaders to achieve long-term goals and to make unpopular but necessary decisions, and even the compromises that the first view praises depend on a fixed objective.
First, the second view is more convincing because important goals take years to achieve, and only leaders who stay committed reach them.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
Such an effort could succeed only because its leaders kept the same objective across many years and many countries, even when progress was slow.
Similarly, the Montgomery bus boycott lasted more than a year, and its leaders kept residents united until bus segregation in that city ended.
Their effectiveness came precisely from refusing to abandon their objective when the effort became costly.
These cases show that [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] commitment, rather than readiness to compromise, is what turns a goal into a result.
A leader who changed objectives whenever public enthusiasm faded would never have finished such a campaign.
Second, leaders who are committed to principle can make decisions that are unpopular at first but beneficial in the end.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets is a clear example.
Within months, helmet use rose from low levels to over 90%, and head injuries and deaths fell; a government that [[vacillated|vacillate]] at the first complaints would have lost those gains.
In my own work on antibiotic resistance, I have seen that a rule against selling antibiotics without a prescription means little unless officials enforce it steadily.
Officials who relax enforcement whenever pharmacies complain simply invite the overuse that spreads resistant bacteria.
This shows that effectiveness often requires a [[principled|principled]] leader to resist public opinion for a time, trusting that results will later win support.
Public opinion often follows success rather than leading to it.
Admittedly, the first view captures something real: leaders who refuse every compromise may achieve nothing.
Abraham Lincoln, for instance, appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Nevertheless, an [[expedient|expedient]] compromise on people or methods is different from abandoning principle.

Even Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms, which replaced central planning with market incentives, changed the method of running the economy in order to serve a constant goal: feeding the nation and reducing poverty.
In both cases, flexibility served a fixed objective, so the examples on which the first view relies actually [[corroborate|corroborate]] the second view.
Compromise is valuable, but only as a tool for reaching goals that remain fixed.
In conclusion, the most essential quality of an effective leader is steady commitment to clear principles and objectives, not a readiness to follow public opinion.
Such commitment allows leaders to pursue long-term goals and to make necessary but unpopular decisions, while the compromises that the first view praises succeed only when they serve a fixed purpose.
Leaders may change their route when the road is blocked, but they must not lose sight of their destination.

essays.title: Schools too often reward obedience over curiosity

paragraphs.text: Schools promise to open young minds, yet many students remember them mainly for exams.
This contrast lies behind the claim that formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits rather than set them free.
I largely agree with this statement when formal education rewards memorization and deference to authority, although it can liberate minds when it teaches students to question.
Formal systems often train students to accept established views and to value grades over curiosity, though the tools they provide can, in the right setting, set minds free.
First, the statement holds true because formal education often teaches students to defer to [[orthodox|orthodox]] views rather than to [[empirical|empirical]] evidence.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues, highly trained physicians, rejected his idea, which germ theory confirmed only years after his death.
Similarly, the Church, defending established teaching, forced Galileo in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
These cases show that institutions of learning can turn knowledge into [[dogma|dogma]], so that the most educated people become the least willing to see what is in front of them.
Training in a fixed body of knowledge, without training in how to doubt it, restrains rather than frees.
Second, the statement holds true because exam-centered schooling teaches students to value correct answers over curiosity.
When I prepared for medical school entrance exams in Vietnam, success meant memorizing model answers, and there was little time to ask why a disease spreads or whether a textbook might be wrong.
Several classmates who scored highly later found research difficult, because no exam had ever asked them to form their own question.

By contrast, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
This shows that formal schooling can [[stymie|stymie]] the habit of independent inquiry, while minds outside its routines may explore more boldly.
In this sense, the statement captures what many students in exam-driven systems actually experience.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold for every kind of formal education.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, and such work would have been impossible without serious scientific training.
Nevertheless, such successes arise when education teaches students to question, not merely to obey.
Finland, which relies far less on standardized testing than many countries, shows that schooling can be designed to encourage thinking rather than memorization.
In classrooms that reward questions as well as answers, students learn to treat knowledge as something to test rather than to memorize.
These cases qualify my position: formal education restrains minds not by its nature but by its common practices, which many systems have yet to change.
The statement, then, describes a common tendency rather than an iron law.
In conclusion, I largely agree that formal education tends to restrain minds and spirits, particularly when it rewards obedience and memorization.
It often [[inculcates|inculcate]] deference to authority and values grades over curiosity, although well-designed schooling shows that education can also free the mind.
Whether schools restrain or liberate depends less on their existence than on what they choose to reward: obedience or inquiry.

essays.title: Education gives the mind its tools

paragraphs.text: Freedom of thought is not simply the absence of rules; it requires tools.
For this reason, I question the claim that formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits rather than set them free.
I mostly disagree with this statement: although poorly designed schooling can limit curiosity, formal education usually gives people the knowledge and methods that make independent thinking possible.
Education provides the tools for original discovery and teaches the discipline of doubt, while the cases in which it restrains minds reflect bad teaching rather than education itself.
First, the statement does not hold because original thinking depends on knowledge that formal education supplies.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Her discoveries were not the product of untrained intuition; they required mastery of the methods that formal study in those sciences provides.
Similarly, the decades of basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, which made the COVID-19 vaccines possible in under a year, grew out of rigorous academic science.
A self-taught genius may appear now and then, but most discoveries come from people who first mastered what others had already found.
These cases show that education does not [[circumscribe|circumscribe]] creative minds; it gives them the materials with which to create.
Without such training, a curious mind has enthusiasm but few means of turning it into discovery.
Second, good formal education teaches students to doubt, which is the essence of a free mind.
In my training as an epidemiologist, I learned to ask how a study was designed before believing its result.
That habit matters, because in 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
A person without such training might accept every published finding as fact and be easily misled.
Courses in statistics and research methods exist precisely to teach this kind of doubt, and few people develop it without guidance.
This shows that formal education, at its best, makes people [[discerning|discerning]] rather than [[credulous|credulous]], which is the opposite of restraint.
A mind that can test claims for itself is far freer than one that must accept or reject them on faith.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in some cases, particularly when schooling rewards obedience to authority.
Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand washing with chlorinated lime sharply cut deaths from childbed fever on his Vienna ward, yet most of his highly trained colleagues rejected his idea.
Nevertheless, this failure came from a professional culture that valued status over evidence, not from education as such.
Indeed, it was germ theory, a product of later scientific study, that finally proved him right years after his death.
The Semmelweis case therefore qualifies my position: education can restrain minds when it hardens into [[dogma|dogma]], but the remedy is better education, not less of it.
Bad teaching can occur in any system, but it is a fault to correct rather than a reason to doubt education itself.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that formal education restrains our minds and spirits.
By supplying the knowledge behind discovery and the discipline of doubt, it usually frees people to think, while its failures reflect poor practice rather than its nature.
The real question is not whether to educate but how to educate so that students learn to question what they are taught.

essays.title: Questioning authority protects and improves society

paragraphs.text: Many of the rights people now take for granted were won by those who refused to accept official answers.
This history supports the statement that the well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
I largely agree with this statement, as long as questioning is based on evidence rather than on reflexive distrust of every institution.
Widespread questioning exposes abuses of power and drives social progress, although questioning without evidence can harm the very society it aims to protect.
First, the statement holds true because authorities that are never questioned can commit serious abuses.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
Only the public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Without such questioning, the study might have continued even longer.
Similarly, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, a sedative that caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and her doubts protected American families.
These cases show that questioning authority is not disloyalty; it is a society's main defense against the [[pernicious|pernicious]] effects of unchecked power.
In both cases, those who asked hard questions served their society better than those who simply obeyed.
Second, the statement holds true because social progress often begins when people refuse to accept unjust rules or official claims they have reason to doubt.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and 1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses.
Their collective challenge to local authority helped end bus segregation in that city.
No single critic could have achieved that result; it required many ordinary people acting together.
Likewise, Galileo's support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun challenged the Church, which forced him to recant in 1633, yet his questioning pointed science in the right direction.
In my own field, patients and advocates who questioned research practices have helped make clinical studies safer and more ethical.
When many people question authority together, their [[dissent|dissent]] creates pressure that leaders cannot easily ignore, and society improves as a result.
The statement holds true, then, because progress rarely comes from institutions that face no challenge.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when people question authority without evidence.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, as during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
A parent who distrusts every doctor, for instance, may refuse a safe vaccine because of a rumor spread online.
Nevertheless, the problem in such cases is not questioning itself but questioning that ignores evidence.
A good question asks for proof, while a rumor simply replaces one authority with another, less reliable one.

This consideration qualifies my position: a society benefits most when its people question authority in a [[judicious|judicious]] way rather than with blanket suspicion or [[credulous|credulous]] faith in rumors.
Informed questioning strengthens a society; uninformed suspicion weakens it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that a society's well-being is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
Such questioning exposes abuses like the Tuskegee study and drives progress such as the end of bus segregation in Montgomery, although questioning without evidence can do real harm.
The healthiest societies, therefore, teach their citizens not only to question but also to weigh the answers they receive.

disagreement with official or majority opinion
showing good judgment and careful thought
too ready to believe without evidence

essays.title: Societies need trust more than mass doubt

paragraphs.text: A society cannot function if every red light becomes a subject of debate.
This is why I am cautious about the statement that the well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
I mostly disagree: a society benefits when some people question authority on the basis of evidence, but it suffers when many people distrust legitimate authority as a habit.
Collective achievements depend on broad public trust, and widespread doubt allows misinformation to spread, although questioning by informed critics remains essential.
First, the statement often fails because many of a society's greatest achievements require most people to follow authority rather than question it.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
That success required millions of families to accept the vaccination their health authorities recommended; widespread doubt would have left pockets of infection.
Even a small share of refusals can allow an infection to survive and return.
Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 helmet law raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, a gain that depended on broad public compliance.
These cases show that trust in legitimate authority is not [[naïve|naïve]] obedience; it is a condition for collective well-being.
A society in which most people doubted every public health measure would have achieved neither result.
Second, when many people question authority by habit, misinformation can [[proliferate|proliferate]] and damage public health.
In my work on antibiotic resistance, I see how overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread.
Patients who doubt their doctor's advice often buy antibiotics on their own, and drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Likewise, social media, which helped activists organize during the Arab Spring of 2011, also spreads misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
In such an environment, a false rumor can reach thousands of people before any expert has a chance to respond.
This shows that habitual distrust of experts can [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] the very problems that authorities are trying to solve.
The statement ignores this cost, assuming that all questioning is healthy when much of it is merely uninformed.
Admittedly, the statement holds true when authority is abused, and in such cases questioning is a duty.

The Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent for four decades, and only public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Nevertheless, this outrage was a targeted response to documented wrongdoing, not a general suspicion of all authority.
Similarly, Frances Kelsey questioned thalidomide from within the US FDA, using evidence rather than rumor to refuse its approval.
Such cases refine my position: a society needs informed critics and institutions that respond to them, but it cannot afford a majority that doubts every expert by reflex.
The well-being of a society depends less on how many people question authority than on how well they question it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that a society's well-being grows when many of its people question authority.

Collective successes such as the eradication of smallpox depend on public trust, and habitual doubt helps misinformation spread, although evidence-based questioning remains vital when authority is abused.
A healthy society, therefore, needs a few [[discerning|discerning]] critics far more than it needs a nation of [[skeptics|skeptic]].

showing careful judgment based on evidence
a person who habitually doubts accepted claims

essays.title: Fix today's problems first, but watch tomorrow

paragraphs.text: A doctor treating a bleeding patient does not begin with advice about diet.
In much the same way, some argue that governments should focus on solving the immediate problems of today rather than on trying to solve the anticipated problems of the future.
I largely agree with this recommendation, particularly for governments with limited resources, as long as they do not ignore future threats that are already clearly visible.

Adopting it is advantageous when people face urgent hardship and when present needs are certain while future ones are not, but it is not advantageous when today's neglect will create a larger crisis tomorrow.
First, adopting the recommendation is advantageous in circumstances of urgent hardship, because a government that cannot [[alleviate|alleviate]] basic suffering loses both lives and legitimacy.
Vietnam in the 1980s illustrates this circumstance.

A country that had faced food shortages replaced central planning with market incentives through the Doi Moi reforms of 1986, became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and saw poverty fall dramatically over the following decades.
Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 helmet law addressed the immediate toll of road crashes, raising helmet use to over 90% within months and reducing head injuries and deaths.
These cases show that solving today's [[pressing|pressing]] problems is not short-sighted; it often lays the foundation for future prosperity.
A government that had ignored these problems in order to plan for distant risks would have failed the people it serves.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous when present problems are certain while future ones remain [[conjectural|conjectural]].
Consider a provincial health department facing a dengue season with a limited budget.

Spending that money now on proven control methods, such as releasing Wolbachia mosquitoes, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, protects people who are certainly at risk.
By contrast, spending the same funds on a disease that might emerge decades from now would mean accepting known harm for uncertain benefits.
Lives saved this season are a certain gain, while plans for a hypothetical disease may never be needed.
In such circumstances, focusing on immediate problems is the more [[prudent|prudent]] and more ethical use of scarce resources.
When resources are scarce, the certainty of a benefit should weigh heavily in a government's choices.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous when a visible future threat grows worse with each year of delay.

Antibiotic resistance is such a threat: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, and Alexander Fleming warned of this danger in his 1945 Nobel lecture.
Nevertheless, this threat is no longer only a future problem, since drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Hospitals in many countries already treat patients whose infections no longer respond to common drugs.
This case refines my position: governments should focus on present problems, but they must recognize that many so-called future problems have already begun and treat them as present ones.
Properly understood, then, a focus on immediate problems would still require governments to act against resistance now.
In conclusion, I largely agree that governments should give priority to the problems of today.
This focus is advantageous during urgent hardship and when present needs are certain, though it fails when a slowly growing threat is ignored until it becomes a crisis.
The wisest governments solve the problems in front of them while watching closely for those already on the horizon.

essays.title: Governments must invest in the future

paragraphs.text: The best time to dig a well is before the village is thirsty.
This old wisdom challenges the recommendation that governments should focus on solving the immediate problems of today rather than the anticipated problems of the future.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation: although emergencies sometimes demand full attention, governments are most valuable when they invest in problems that markets and individuals will not address in time.
Adopting it would be harmful when future threats grow worse with delay and when long-term investment creates future benefits, although it can be advantageous during an acute crisis.
First, adopting the recommendation would be disadvantageous in circumstances where a future problem becomes harder to solve every year it is ignored.
Antibiotic resistance is a clear case.

Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse would breed resistant bacteria, yet overuse and over-the-counter sales, common in many countries including Vietnam, have helped resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
A government that had acted on Fleming's [[prescient|prescient]] warning could have regulated antibiotic sales long before resistance became widespread.
Similarly, a city that postpones flood defenses to save money this year may pay far more when the river finally rises.
These cases show that a narrow focus on today's problems can be [[myopic|myopic]], allowing a manageable risk to grow into an [[intractable|intractable]] crisis.
The cost of waiting, in this circumstance, is measured in lives.
Second, the recommendation would not be advantageous because public investment in the future often produces benefits that no one could plan for today.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman.
A government focused only on immediate problems would have seen little reason to support such work.

Similarly, the publicly funded Human Genome Project made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, and GPS, built by the US military, later became the basis of everyday navigation apps.
These cases show that future-oriented spending is not a luxury; it is the source of tools that later solve immediate problems.
Had governments considered only immediate problems, the tools that later solved urgent crises would not have existed.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which focusing on immediate problems is advantageous, especially when people lack basic necessities.
When Vietnam faced food shortages, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 rightly addressed that urgent need first, and the country later became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Nevertheless, such emergencies are exceptions, and even Doi Moi was a structural reform whose benefits unfolded over decades rather than a short-term fix.
A government that treated every year as an emergency would never build the research, infrastructure, or institutions on which future security depends.
Thus this circumstance qualifies my position without reversing it: governments must answer emergencies, but they should not let urgent problems [[eclipse|eclipse]] important future ones.
Emergencies deserve attention, but they should not set the permanent priorities of government.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that governments should focus on today's problems at the expense of tomorrow's.

Delay allows threats such as antibiotic resistance to grow, and long-term investments such as basic research produce benefits that no short-term plan could deliver, although true emergencies deserve priority.
A government that thinks only of the present will soon find itself [[besieged|besiege]] by problems it could have prevented.

essays.title: Let talent and interest lead the choice

paragraphs.text: Students spend four years in college but may spend forty years in the careers that follow.

Given these stakes, some people believe that students should consider only their own talents and interests when choosing a field of study, while others believe that they should follow the availability of jobs.
I side mainly with the first view: talents and interests should guide the choice, although students should also be aware of the job market.
Students perform best in fields that suit them, and job forecasts are too unreliable to be the main guide, while the second view rightly reminds students that they must eventually earn a living.
First, the first view is closer to my position because students achieve more in fields that match their talents and interests.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Her persistence in a field that offered women little encouragement is hard to explain by job prospects; it reflected deep interest and talent.

Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
These cases show that genuine interest gives students the [[zeal|zeal]] to overcome obstacles that would [[daunt|daunt]] those who chose a field only for its jobs.
Students who love their subject also tend to keep learning long after graduation, which makes them valuable in any job market.
Second, choosing a field by job availability is risky because the job market changes faster than a student can complete a degree.
Kodak, once a profitable film company, was slow to embrace digital photography even though its own engineer had invented the digital camera in 1975, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Students who chose film chemistry for its secure jobs would have watched that security disappear.
In my own field, I have seen demand for epidemiologists rise and fall with each new outbreak.
Likewise, a student who enters a field only because it is hiring today may graduate into a market that no longer needs her.
This shows that job forecasts are too [[volatile|volatile]] to be the main basis for a decision that shapes a whole career.
Interest, by contrast, tends to last, and it keeps students learning even when the market shifts.
Admittedly, the second view is right that students cannot ignore the need to earn a living.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, even though he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Nevertheless, the lesson is not that students should abandon their talents, but that they should develop them in a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] way.
A student with a [[penchant|penchant]] for painting, for instance, might study graphic design or animation, fields that use the same talent and offer more jobs.
Thus the second view adds a useful condition to my position, yet interest and talent should still lead the choice, with the job market serving as a secondary check.
In conclusion, I believe that college students should choose their field mainly according to their talents and interests.
Such students perform better and are less exposed to unpredictable job markets, although the second view correctly warns that they must also consider how they will support themselves.
The best choice lies where a student's strengths meet a real need, but the search should begin with the student.

likely to change suddenly and unpredictably
a strong liking or natural tendency

essays.title: Jobs first, then choose by talent

paragraphs.text: Passion may inspire a student, but it does not pay the rent.
This tension underlies the debate over whether college students should consider only their talents and interests when choosing a field of study or base their choice on the availability of jobs.
I side mainly with the second view: job availability should be a central factor in the choice, although students should still choose among promising fields according to their abilities.
Considering jobs protects students from financial hardship and allows interests to develop through meaningful work, while the first view rightly stresses that talent matters for success.
First, the second view is more convincing because ignoring job availability can expose graduates to years of financial hardship.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, although he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
His talent was extraordinary, but it did not provide him a living while he was alive.
Similarly, in Vietnam many families borrow money to pay for a child's degree, and a graduate who cannot find work in a crowded field may leave the family in debt for years.
Talent determines what a person can do, but the market often determines whether anyone will pay for it.
These cases show that talent alone does not protect a person from [[penury|penury]], so choosing by interest alone is a gamble that few students can afford.
The second view simply asks students to take this risk seriously.
Second, interests are more [[malleable|malleable]] than the first view assumes, and they often grow from work rather than come before it.
Consider a student who enters nursing mainly because hospitals are hiring.
After a few years of caring for elderly patients, she may discover a [[latent|latent]] interest in geriatric care that she never knew she had.
In my own work, I have met many physicians who discovered their passion for public health only after years of clinical practice.
This shows that choosing a field with good job prospects does not mean giving up on interest; it often creates the conditions in which a lasting interest can form.
Waiting for a perfect passion before choosing a field can leave a student with neither passion nor a job.
Admittedly, the first view is right that talent and interest matter, because people who dislike their field rarely excel in it.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science, an achievement that only exceptional talent and devotion could explain.
Nevertheless, Curie's case is an exception, and most students have several talents that could fit more than one field.
A student who is good at both mathematics and biology, for example, can choose biostatistics, a field with steady demand, rather than a narrower path with few openings.
The [[judicious|judicious]] approach, therefore, is to identify fields with strong job prospects and then choose among them according to one's abilities.
Such an approach respects talent without making it the only factor, and it keeps students safe from the hardship that van Gogh endured.
In conclusion, I believe that college students should give job availability a central place when choosing a field of study.
Doing so protects them from financial hardship and allows interests to grow through work, while the first view reminds us that talent should guide the final choice among good options.
Students who balance the market with their own strengths are most likely to find careers that are both secure and satisfying.

essays.title: Flexible laws, fixed principles

paragraphs.text: A rule written for one era can become an [[anachronism|anachronism]] in the next.
This risk explains the view that laws should be flexible enough to take account of various circumstances, times, and places.
I largely agree with this statement, as long as flexibility applies to the details of laws while basic rights remain fixed for everyone.
Laws must change as knowledge advances, and they must fit the conditions of each place, although flexibility can be misused to justify unequal treatment.
First, the statement holds true because laws must change over time as society learns from experience.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Without the ability to change, drug law would have remained exactly as weak as it was before the tragedy.
Similarly, the outrage over the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
These cases show that a legal system that could not be [[revamped|revamp]] in response to new evidence would leave people exposed to dangers that society had already recognized.
Flexibility over time is therefore not a weakness in law but a sign that it can learn.
Second, the statement holds true because laws work best when they fit the conditions of a particular place.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets was designed for a country where motorbikes fill the roads.
It raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, whereas the same law would matter far less in a country where most people drive cars.

Likewise, the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives suited to Vietnam's situation, and a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
Rules about land, water, and transport, for example, naturally differ between a crowded delta and a mountain province.
This shows that laws designed for local conditions are more [[efficacious|efficacious]] than rules copied without regard to context.
A law that ignores where it will be applied risks being either useless or harmful.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when flexibility becomes an excuse for treating some people worse than others.
Segregated buses in Montgomery reflected local practice, and it took a boycott in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride those buses to help end that practice.
Nevertheless, this danger argues for limits on flexibility, not for rigid laws.
Equal treatment and informed consent should be [[inviolate|inviolate]] everywhere, while rules on matters such as traffic, trade, and drug approval can vary with time and place.
Those principles exist precisely to prevent local custom from overriding human dignity.
This consideration qualifies my position: laws should be flexible in their details but firm in the principles they protect.
Flexibility in the service of justice is a strength, whereas flexibility that excuses injustice is a failure of law.
In conclusion, I largely agree that laws should be flexible enough to reflect different circumstances, times, and places.
Laws must evolve as society learns and must suit local conditions, although flexibility should never extend to basic rights such as equal treatment.
A good legal system, like a good physician, adjusts its treatment to each case without abandoning its core principles.

never to be broken or infringed

essays.title: Laws work when they apply to everyone

paragraphs.text: A law that bends for everyone protects no one.
This concern makes me doubt the statement that laws should be flexible enough to take account of various circumstances, times, and places.
I mostly disagree with this statement: although laws must sometimes be revised, their force depends on applying the same rules consistently to everyone.
Consistent laws produce reliable results and protect vulnerable people from unequal treatment, while the need for change is better met through formal reform than through flexible application.
First, the statement often fails because laws achieve their goals only when people know that the rules apply to everyone without exception.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
If police had excused riders on short trips or in hot weather, many people would have claimed an exception, and the law's benefits would have faded.

Similarly, a hospital rule on hand washing works only if every doctor follows it, a lesson Ignaz Semmelweis demonstrated in Vienna in 1847, when washing with chlorinated lime sharply cut deaths from childbed fever on his ward.
Doctors who considered themselves exceptions would have kept spreading infection from patient to patient.
These cases show that [[lax|lax]] or flexible enforcement can [[undermine|undermine]] even a well-designed law.
Clear and uniform rules, by contrast, leave little room for excuses.
Second, flexibility is dangerous because it allows those in power to treat some people worse than others.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, treating these men as exceptions to basic medical ethics.
Likewise, bus segregation in Montgomery reflected local practice until Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helping end the practice in that city.
In each case, a rule that should have protected everyone was set aside for a particular group.
In my own work, research ethics rules matter precisely because they apply to every study, whatever its location or sponsor.
This shows that when laws bend to local circumstances, [[marginalized|marginalize]] groups often suffer first, so firm and uniform protections are essential to an [[equitable|equitable]] society.
A flexible law is easily bent by whoever holds power in a given place.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in one important sense: laws must change over time as society learns.
After thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, the US passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Nevertheless, this change came through a new law passed by legislators, not through officials deciding case by case how strictly to apply the old one.
Indeed, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA protected American families precisely by refusing to approve thalidomide rather than making an exception for it.
This consideration refines my position: laws should be revised openly when evidence demands it, but between revisions they should be applied with [[unequivocal|unequivocal]] consistency.
Such openness allows laws to improve while keeping their meaning clear to every citizen.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that laws should be flexible enough to vary with circumstances, times, and places.
Consistent laws produce reliable results and protect vulnerable people, while legitimate change should come through formal reform rather than flexible application by individual officials.
Laws may evolve, but at any given moment they must mean the same thing for everyone.

essays.title: Heroes reveal what a society values most

paragraphs.text: Every society tells stories about the people it admires, and those stories are rarely chosen by accident.
The question, then, is whether such heroes offer the clearest window into a society's character.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, as long as we examine not only official heroes but also the people ordinary citizens actually admire.
Heroes expose a society's priorities, they reveal its highest ideals, and even their limits tell us something about the society that chose them.
First, the claim holds because the people a society celebrates show what it rewards and what it ignores.
Consider Ignaz Semmelweis, who in 1847 had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime.
Deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, and only years after his death, when germ theory proved him right, did medicine begin to honor him.
Similarly, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, but today he is [[lionized|lionize]] as one of the greatest painters in history.
In both cases, the shift from neglect to praise reveals how a society's character changed: it came to value evidence over authority and originality over convention.
This shows that examining whom a society chooses as its heroes, and when it chooses them, is a powerful way to understand its character.
Second, the reason behind the claim is also sound, since heroes embody the ideals that a society hopes its members will follow.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, but Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it.
Americans came to admire her, and in 1962 the country passed stricter drug-testing rules, turning her caution into law.
Likewise, the Black residents of Montgomery who refused for over a year to ride segregated buses are now honored for their courage and their commitment to equality.
These figures are admired not for wealth or fame but for [[principled|principled]] action, which suggests that heroes do reveal a society's highest ideals.
A society that honors a cautious regulator, rather than the company that sold a dangerous drug, tells us that it values the safety of its children above profit.
Admittedly, heroes are sometimes chosen by governments or advertisers rather than by the people, and in that case they may reflect propaganda more than character.
A state may [[venerate|venerate]] a soldier or a business leader simply because that figure serves its political goals, while citizens privately admire someone else.
Nevertheless, even manufactured heroes are revealing, because they show what those in power want the public to value.

In my work as a physician in Vietnam, for instance, official awards show which doctors the health system wants to promote, while patients reserve their deepest respect for those who listen carefully and give [[candid|candid]] explanations; each choice is revealing.
This gap does not overturn the claim; it qualifies it.
To understand a society well, we must look at both its official heroes and the role models its people choose for themselves.
In conclusion, the heroes and role models a society embraces offer one of the best guides to its character, provided that we look beyond official lists.
They reveal what the society rewards, they embody its highest ideals, and even the distance between official and popular heroes tells us something [[salient|salient]] about it.
Studying heroes carefully, then, is less about worshipping individuals than about reading the values of the people who admire them.

words.meaning_here: celebrate and treat as a great hero
based on firm moral rules rather than self-interest
honor with deep, almost religious respect
honest and direct, without hiding unpleasant facts

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim (heroes expose priorities), Body 2 evaluates the reason (heroes embody highest ideals), and Body 3 concedes that official heroes can be propaganda before qualifying the thesis.

essays.title: Character shows in practice, not in heroes

paragraphs.text: It is easy to praise courage and honesty; it is much harder to practice them.
This difference lies at the heart of the claim that a society's heroes are the best guide to its character.

Although heroes do say something about a society, I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, because a society's character is better revealed by how it treats ordinary and vulnerable people than by whom it admires.
The claim overlooks the gap between admiration and conduct, the reason confuses ideals with character, and the value of heroes as evidence is real but limited.
First, the claim is flawed because a society can celebrate noble heroes while tolerating deeply unjust practices.
In the twentieth century, the United States honored leaders who spoke of liberty and equality.

Yet from 1932 to 1972, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and only public outrage finally led to rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Similarly, a country may build monuments to its soldiers while an [[obdurate|obdurate]] bureaucracy leaves wounded veterans waiting years for basic care.
In both cases, the society's heroes said little about its real character, which became visible only in how it treated the weak.

Therefore, examining heroes is not the best way to understand a society: a visitor who studied only America's celebrated heroes during those decades would have formed a far kinder picture of the country than the facts justified.
Second, the reason is only partly true: heroes may reveal a society's highest ideals, but ideals are not the same as character.
In Vietnam, physicians are traditionally respected, and the dedicated doctor is a familiar role model.
At the same time, overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics are [[pervasive|pervasive]], helping resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Similarly, many societies praise teachers in speeches while paying them too little to stay in the profession.
Such [[discrepancies|discrepancy]] between ideals and conduct show that a society's character, like a person's, is measured by habits, not by aspirations.
Therefore, even if the reason is accurate, it does not support the claim that heroes are the best guide to character.
Admittedly, heroes are not meaningless, and in some cases they reflect a society's actual behavior quite well.
The Montgomery bus boycott, in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, is honored today, and that honor reflects real changes in American life.
Nevertheless, heroes are at best a clue, and a clue becomes [[tenuous|tenuous]] evidence when it is not checked against conduct.
Admiration for the boycott matters precisely because it was matched by changes in how people were actually treated.
By contrast, a city could build statues of the boycott's leaders while keeping its schools segregated, and the statues alone would mislead an observer.
Heroes, then, are useful only when read alongside laws, institutions and daily habits.
On their own, they tend to flatter a society rather than describe it.
In conclusion, while heroes and role models tell us what a society hopes to be, they are not the best way to understand what it is.
The claim ignores the gap between admiration and action, the reason mistakes ideals for character, and heroes become reliable evidence only when conduct confirms them.
To judge a society [[judiciously|judicious]], we should watch how it treats its patients, its poor and its minorities, not just whom it places on a pedestal.

essays.title: Reframing challenges fuels long-term effort

paragraphs.text: Few people reach their goals without setbacks, and how they interpret those setbacks often decides what happens next.
Some argue that seeing a challenge as a chance for growth is helpful, while others warn that such reframing distracts from the work of solving the problem.
My position aligns more closely with the first view, as long as the growth mindset supports concrete action rather than replacing it.

Viewing challenges as opportunities sustains effort over time and turns failure into useful lessons, and although the second view rightly warns about emergencies, the first remains the wiser habit for most situations.
To begin with, the first view is persuasive because people who see a challenge as a chance to grow are more likely to keep trying.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, spent years experimenting with gliders and even built their own wind tunnel.
Each failed glider could have [[daunted|daunt]] them, but instead it taught them something, and in 1903 they achieved the first powered airplane flight.
Similarly, Marie Curie faced the barriers women met in science at the time, yet she won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry.
Her persistence shows how a hostile environment can become a reason to work harder rather than to quit.
Neither would likely have continued if every setback had seemed [[futile|futile]].
This shows that viewing difficulty as growth is not a luxury but a source of the [[assiduous|assiduous]] effort that hard problems demand.
Moreover, reframing a challenge as an opportunity helps people and institutions learn from failure instead of hiding it.
Early in my career, a dengue study I worked on recruited far fewer patients than planned.
Rather than treating this as a personal defeat, our team treated it as a lesson, redesigned recruitment with local health workers, and ran a much stronger study the next year.

On a national scale, Vietnam faced food shortages before its 1986 Doi Moi reforms replaced central planning with market incentives; the country then became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
In both examples, the challenge was used as a reason to change, not merely endured.
This shows that the growth view does not compete with effective action; it often [[engenders|engender]] it.
Admittedly, the second view has merit in acute situations, where reflection can indeed take attention away from the task at hand.
When I am treating a patient in shock, I should not be thinking about how the experience will make me a better doctor; every thought must go to the patient's blood pressure and breathing.
Nevertheless, this objection applies to the moment of crisis, not to how one approaches challenges overall.
After the emergency, the same team that focused narrowly on the patient benefits from reviewing what went wrong and what it learned.
Thus, the second view describes a [[prudent|prudent]] limit on when to reflect, not a reason to abandon the growth view altogether.
Indeed, the growth view works best precisely when it separates the time for action from the time for reflection.
In conclusion, I side mainly with those who see challenges as opportunities for growth, provided that this outlook leads to action.
Such a view sustains effort through repeated failure, converts setbacks into lessons, and needs to be set aside only briefly during true emergencies.
The most effective people, it seems, focus fully on a crisis while it lasts and then ask what it has taught them.

essays.task_note: The thesis sides with the first view, Bodies 1-2 support it, and Body 3 grants that the second view is right in acute emergencies before explaining why the first view is closer to the truth overall.

essays.title: Face the problem first, reflect later

paragraphs.text: When a house is on fire, the wise owner looks for the exit, not for the meaning of the flames.
This image captures the debate over whether people should reimagine challenges as chances for personal growth or keep their attention on the challenges themselves.
Although reflection has value, my position aligns more closely with the second view: reframing a difficulty as a growth opportunity often takes the focus that people need to solve it effectively.

Hard problems demand concentrated attention, the growth frame can make people too comfortable with problems they should fix, and the benefits of reflection are best kept for after the challenge has passed.
First, I favor the second view because serious challenges reward people who concentrate on the problem rather than on themselves.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 because health workers around the world focused on concrete tasks: vaccinating people and sharing data and vaccine across countries.
Their attention stayed on the virus and the next village, not on their own development.
Similarly, in an emergency department, a doctor managing a patient in shock must think only about breathing, circulation and the next intervention.
Any thought about what the case means for her career would only slow her hands.
In both cases, success depended on [[unalloyed|unalloyed]] focus on the task: reflection could wait, but the patient and the outbreak could not.
In short, when a challenge is real and urgent, reimagining it as personal growth competes for the very attention it requires.
Second, the growth frame can make people tolerate problems that they ought to fix.
Consider a district hospital where antibiotics are often given without clear need.
If the staff describe rising resistance merely as "a learning experience," they may grow [[complacent|complacent]] and delay the strict prescribing rules that would actually slow it.
Meanwhile, more patients would carry infections that no longer respond to common drugs.
Likewise, a student who fails an exam and tells himself it was "good for growth" may feel better without changing the study habits that caused the failure.
Comforting language can [[mitigate|mitigate]] the pain of a challenge while leaving its cause untouched.
Therefore, the second view rightly warns that reframing can replace action rather than support it, since growth that is not tied to correcting the problem is merely comfort.
Admittedly, the first view captures something true: over a long career, people who learn from hardship often grow stronger.
The Wright brothers treated years of failed glider experiments as lessons and achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Nevertheless, their success came from the [[meticulous|meticulous]] work of testing gliders in a wind tunnel they built themselves, not from telling themselves that failure was good for them.

Likewise, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of little-noticed basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, steady work rather than a hopeful reframing of neglect.
Growth, in other words, is usually a by-product of solving problems well, not a goal that should compete with solving them.
This is why I welcome reflection after a challenge but remain [[wary|wary]] of it during one.
In conclusion, while the idea of growth through hardship is appealing, I side with those who believe it can drain the focus needed to face a challenge.
Urgent problems require full attention, the growth frame can breed comfort instead of change, and even famous success stories rest on focused work rather than on reframing.
The best approach is to solve the problem first and to reflect on its lessons once the fire is out.

essays.title: Moving among places teaches us to connect

paragraphs.text: Most of us feel at ease with people who speak, eat and think as we do.
The question is whether we learn to connect with others better by traveling and living in many places or by staying in one community and knowing it deeply.
I side mainly with the first view, as long as the traveler stays long enough in each place to engage with its people rather than make [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] visits.
Living in different places exposes us to unfamiliar ways of life, challenges the assumptions we absorb at home, and, although rootedness offers a real kind of depth, builds a wider ability to relate.
To begin with, the first view is convincing because living among different people teaches us perspectives we would never meet at home.
When I worked with colleagues on health projects in Sub-Saharan Africa, I learned that many patients there explained illness through family and community rather than through individual symptoms.
Adapting my questions to that view helped me [[elicit|elicit]] far more useful histories from patients.
Without that experience, I would have kept asking questions that made sense only in my own culture.
Similarly, a nurse who has worked in both a crowded city hospital and a remote mountain clinic tends to understand patients from very different backgrounds.
Such experiences make us more [[discerning|discerning]] listeners, slower to judge and quicker to ask.
This shows that moving among places develops the ability to relate to people unlike oneself, which is the hardest kind of connection.
Moreover, traveling and living elsewhere challenges the [[insular|insular]] assumptions that a single community can quietly teach us.
Many medical students in Vietnam assume that the way medicine is practiced in their own teaching hospital is the only way.
After a training period abroad, they often return more open to other approaches and better at working with foreign colleagues.
In the same way, a manager who has worked in offices in several countries usually leads an international team more smoothly than one who has never left headquarters.
She has already learned, for example, that a silent colleague may be showing respect rather than disagreement.
When people see that their habits are only one option among many, they become less quick to judge and more able to cooperate.
Therefore, living in numerous places strengthens the very skills that connection requires.
Admittedly, the second view is right that deep roots allow a kind of understanding that a newcomer cannot easily match.
A village health worker who has lived in one commune for decades knows each family's history, and patients trust her in ways they would not trust a visiting doctor.
She is often the first person a frightened mother calls at night.
Nevertheless, this deep understanding usually applies to people who share her background, and it may not help her relate to strangers or outsiders.
A migrant worker from another province or a foreign researcher may find her warm toward her neighbors but unsure how to approach newcomers.
Rootedness, then, builds strong ties within a group, whereas mobility builds the broader capacity to connect across groups.
In a [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] world where we constantly meet people unlike ourselves, the second capacity matters more.
In conclusion, I believe that traveling to and living in many places generally does more to improve our ability to relate to others than staying in one place.
Mobility exposes us to unfamiliar perspectives and loosens rigid assumptions, while rootedness, valuable as it is, mainly deepens bonds with people already like us.
The ideal, perhaps, is to live in several places but to stay long enough in each to belong, not merely to visit.
