essays.title: Deep roots build deeper human connection

paragraphs.text: Knowing many people is not the same as knowing people well.

This distinction is central to the debate over whether our ability to connect with others grows more from traveling and living in many places or from staying in one community and understanding it deeply.
While travel has real benefits, my position aligns more closely with the second view, because lasting connection depends on trust, and trust grows mainly through time spent in one place.

Long residence builds the trust that real connection requires, frequent moving tends to produce shallow relationships, and travel's genuine strength, exposure to difference, is valuable only when it rests on deeper roots.
First, I favor the second view because connecting with people depends on trust, which is earned slowly within a community.
In Vietnam, community health workers who have lived for decades in the same commune often know which families are [[leery|leery]] of vaccinating their children and why.
Because neighbors trust them, they can persuade parents in ways that a visiting specialist never could.

Similarly, a method such as releasing Wolbachia mosquitoes, which has been tested in Vietnam, depends on residents accepting it, and acceptance comes most easily through local leaders who understand the community.
In my own work, the most effective field staff are rarely the best-traveled ones; they are the ones whom villagers have known for years.
Deep knowledge of a place lets a person understand not only what people say but also what they fear and value.
This shows that rootedness builds the most meaningful kind of connection.
Second, constantly moving from place to place often leaves relationships too brief to mature.
Consider a consultant who works in a different country every year.
She may become [[affable|affable]] and skilled at small talk, but she rarely stays long enough to see a colleague through illness or to be trusted with a difficult secret.
By contrast, the Montgomery bus boycott lasted over a year because Black residents who knew and relied on one another kept supporting each other day after day.
Their trust in one another had been built over years of shared life in the same city.
Such [[solidarity|solidarity]] is hard to build among people who are always leaving; a traveler may know many people, but few of them would make such sacrifices for her.
Therefore, while numerous moves may widen one's circle, they often make each connection [[ephemeral|ephemeral]].
Admittedly, the first view is right that travel can break down prejudice and help people relate to those who are different from them.
A doctor who has practiced in both Vietnam and Sub-Saharan Africa may understand patients from many cultures better than one who has never left home.
Experience abroad can show a person that her own habits are not universal.
Nevertheless, this benefit depends on the traveler first knowing how to build trust somewhere, a skill learned through staying.

Exposure to difference teaches tolerance, but tolerance is not the same as connection, and without the patience developed by belonging to one community, travel may produce only an [[urbane|urbane]] surface that hides shallow relationships.
Indeed, the travelers who connect best are often those who once belonged deeply to a home community and carry that skill with them.
In conclusion, although travel broadens our view, I believe the ability to connect with others is better cultivated by living in one place and understanding it deeply.
Rootedness builds trust, constant movement keeps relationships brief, and even the real benefits of travel depend on skills learned at home.
Those who wish to connect widely would do well to learn first how to belong somewhere, because the skill of belonging travels well.

essays.title: Screens are crowding out real social practice

paragraphs.text: Walk into any café in Hanoi, and you will likely see groups of young friends sitting together, each looking at a separate screen.
This familiar scene raises the question of whether young people's heavy use of smartphones and tablets has damaged their social skills.
I largely agree with the claim and partly agree with the reason, although the harm comes less from the devices themselves than from how much time they consume.

Heavy device use reduces the face-to-face practice that social skills require, online platforms do encourage curated rather than honest self-presentation, and the real benefits of these devices limit but do not erase the harm.
First, the claim is largely true because social skills develop through practice, and screens take away much of that practice.
As a teacher of medical students, I have noticed that many young trainees find it hard to hold eye contact or to tolerate a patient's silence while taking a history.
Several have told me that they are far more comfortable texting than speaking with strangers.
One student admitted that she rehearsed even simple greetings in her head before entering a patient's room.
Similarly, parents often report that children who spend hours on tablets struggle to wait their turn or to read the emotions of others at school.
These skills are learned only through repeated, sometimes awkward, real conversations, and no app can provide the immediate feedback of a frown, a pause or a laugh.
When devices [[supplant|supplant]] those conversations, young people's social development suffers, just as the claim states.
Second, the reason is also partly sound: online platforms reward people for presenting edited versions of themselves.
A teenager on social media quickly learns that carefully chosen photos and clever captions earn more approval than honest admissions of doubt or sadness.
Over time, she may come to treat friendship as a performance and feel uneasy in [[candid|candid]], unscripted conversations.
Likewise, a young man who spends every evening in online games may form close ties with his teammates while knowing little about the classmates who sit beside him.

Such habits [[undermine|undermine]] the honesty and attention on which real relationships depend, and young people who grow used to controlling how they appear may find the unpredictability of real conversation threatening.
This shows that the reason identifies a genuine mechanism, even if it is not the only one.
Admittedly, portable devices also help young people connect, and for some they are a lifeline.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, activists used smartphones to organize quickly, and shy or isolated teenagers today often find supportive friends online whom they would never meet in their own towns.
For such teenagers, an online community can be the first place where they practice speaking up.
Nevertheless, these benefits depend on moderate use, whereas the claim concerns extensive use.
A teenager who spends most evenings scrolling, for instance, has little time left for the unplanned conversations through which empathy grows.
When devices fill most of a young person's free time, even good online contacts cannot replace the [[nuance|nuance]] of a face-to-face conversation.
The benefits therefore qualify my agreement rather than reverse it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that young people's extensive use of portable devices has hurt their social skills, and I accept the reason with some reservations.
Heavy use reduces real practice, online platforms reward edited personalities, and the genuine benefits of devices appear mainly when use is moderate.
The [[salutary|salutary]] lesson is not to ban these devices but to protect enough screen-free time for young people to learn the slow art of real conversation.

essays.title: Devices change social skills, not destroy them

paragraphs.text: Every new technology, from the printing press to the telephone, has been accused of ruining the young.
Today the accusation falls on smartphones and tablets, which, critics [[aver|aver]], have damaged young people's social skills by encouraging fake online lives.
Although heavy use can cause harm, I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, since these devices more often change how young people socialize than weaken their ability to do so.

Devices help young people practice real social skills such as cooperation, most online relationships extend rather than replace offline ones, and the harm that does occur comes from excessive use, not from the devices themselves.
First, the claim is overstated because portable devices often help young people practice important social skills.
During the Arab Spring of 2011, activists, many of them young, used smartphones and social media to organize quickly.
That task required persuasion, coordination and trust among strangers, skills that no one can exercise alone.

Similarly, Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history, which shows that people working online must negotiate, disagree politely and cooperate on a huge scale.

These are genuine social skills: persuading an unseen audience, settling a dispute over a shared article or coordinating a group across a city demands as much social judgment as a conversation at the dinner table.
This shows that the claim mistakes a change in the setting of social life for a decline in social ability.
Second, the reason is weak because most young people's online relationships are not artificial at all.
My younger cousins in Hanoi spend hours messaging the same classmates they sit beside at school, sharing jokes, planning weekend meetings and comforting one another after exams.
When a friend is sad, a late-night message often leads to a face-to-face meeting the next day.
Likewise, students who move abroad for university use video calls to stay close to their parents and friends at home, and those relationships are anything but fake.
In my own family, a group chat with cousins scattered across Vietnam keeps us closer than occasional holiday visits once did.

Online contact, in these cases, [[augments|augment]] honest relationships rather than replacing them with false ones; the online and offline worlds of most young people are woven together, not set against each other.
The reason therefore treats an [[aberrant|aberrant]] pattern as if it were the norm.
Admittedly, extensive use can harm social development, especially when screens replace sleep, play and family meals.
Many parents notice that children who spend most evenings on tablets become irritable and withdrawn, and some young people do build misleading online personas that make honest conversation harder.
Nevertheless, these harms result from the amount of use and the absence of limits, not from the devices themselves.
A teenager who chats with friends on her phone for an hour and then joins her family for dinner faces little risk.

This concession therefore narrows my position rather than reversing it: the problem is excessive, unsupervised use, which parents and schools can [[mitigate|mitigate]] through clear limits without condemning the technology.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that portable devices have hurt young people's social skills, and I reject the idea that they do so mainly by encouraging artificial relationships.
Devices often help young people practice cooperation, their online ties usually extend real friendships, and the genuine harms stem from excess rather than from the tools.
Instead of [[deriding|deride]] a whole generation's habits, adults would do better to teach balance and to model it themselves.

essays.title: Fewer options often lead to better decisions

paragraphs.text: A restaurant menu with fifty dishes can leave a hungry diner staring at the pages long after a simpler menu would have produced a satisfying meal.
This common experience raises the question of whether decisions are better made when one has only a limited number of options.
I largely agree with the claim and the reason, at least for complex or frequent decisions, provided that the limited options are chosen carefully.
Limited options make good decisions faster and more consistent, too many options do strain rational judgment, and although narrowing choices can exclude the best one, this risk can be managed.
First, the claim holds because a well-designed short list of options often produces better decisions than an open field.
In many hospitals, antibiotic guidelines restrict doctors to a few recommended drugs for common infections.
Such limits counter the overuse of antibiotics, which in many countries, including Vietnam, helps resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Similarly, a busy emergency team that follows a short protocol for chest pain acts faster and more consistently than one that considers every possible test.

In both settings, fewer choices reduce the room for error and for habits that serve the individual rather than the patient: a doctor choosing among three proven drugs is less likely to make a costly mistake than one choosing among thirty.
This shows that a limited set of options can lead to decisions that are not only quicker but also better.
Second, the reason is largely sound: as options multiply, rational comparison becomes harder.
Consider a patient asked to choose among twenty health insurance plans, each with different fees and coverage.
Overwhelmed by details, she may [[vacillate|vacillate]] for weeks, pick the plan a friend chose, or simply give up.
Likewise, a graduate student with dozens of possible research questions may spend a year comparing them and then rush the one she finally picks.
Rational choice requires weighing options on the factors that matter, and the human mind can hold only a handful of such factors at once.
Therefore, as the reason suggests, a [[plethora|plethora]] of options often pushes people toward shortcuts and [[capricious|capricious]] decisions: they do not choose better, only more randomly.
Admittedly, limiting options can exclude the very choice that matters most.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Had Kodak kept digital photography on its short list, its story might have ended very differently.
Nevertheless, Kodak's failure came from removing a promising option for the wrong reason, not from having a short list.

The lesson is that options should be limited [[judiciously|judicious]], by experts acting on evidence rather than on existing interests, and the short list should be reviewed regularly so that a promising new option can always be added.
Under that condition, the risk of narrowing choices is smaller than the cost of drowning in them.
In conclusion, I largely agree that decisions are usually better when options are limited and that too many choices make rational judgment harder.
Short lists make decisions faster and more consistent, an excess of options strains reasoning, and the risk of excluding the best choice can be reduced by narrowing options carefully.
The goal, then, is not to have as few options as possible but to have the right few, chosen by people who understand the decision.

essays.title: More options, used well, yield better choices

paragraphs.text: For centuries, people have struggled for the freedom to choose their work, their leaders and their beliefs.
It may seem strange, then, to argue that decisions are better when options are limited, yet that is exactly what the claim suggests.
Although too many choices can be tiring, I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason, since more options usually improve decisions when people have a clear way to compare them.
Wider choice allows better outcomes, difficulty in choosing is not the same as irrationality, and the real benefits of limited options apply mainly to urgent, standardized situations.
First, the claim is mistaken because limiting options often prevents people from finding the best solution.

Under central planning, Vietnam faced food shortages, but after the Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced that system with market incentives, the country became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Similarly, Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace the digital camera that its own engineer had invented, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
In both cases, a narrow set of options proved [[deleterious|deleterious]], whereas in Vietnam a wider range of choices, once producers could respond to market incentives, opened the path to success.
This shows that, far from being better, limited options can trap decision makers in poor outcomes.
Second, the reason is flawed: more options make decisions harder, but not less rational.
In my work as an epidemiologist, choosing a study design involves many options, from simple surveys to randomized trials.
Rather than being [[stymied|stymie]] by choice, my colleagues and I list the criteria that matter, such as cost, time and strength of evidence, and compare each design against them.
Without a range of designs, we would often be forced to use a method poorly suited to the question.
Likewise, a careful car buyer facing dozens of models can first remove those beyond her budget and then compare the few that remain.
Difficulty, in other words, can be managed by a [[cogent|cogent]] method, and the extra effort often yields a better choice.
The reason therefore confuses effort with irrationality and does not support the claim; indeed, comparing options carefully is the essence of a rational decision.
Admittedly, there are situations in which limited options lead to better decisions.
An emergency doctor treating a patient in cardiac arrest follows a short protocol, because weighing every possible drug would waste precious minutes.
Similarly, a pilot facing an engine failure relies on a short checklist rather than on fresh reflection.
Nevertheless, such cases are [[exigent|exigent]] and highly standardized, and they make up only a small part of the important decisions people face.
Even these protocols were written by experts who first compared many options before selecting the best few.
Thus, limiting options is a useful tool for speed, but it works only because someone has already done the harder work of choosing among many.
Outside such moments, the choices that shape a life, such as a career, a city or a research question, benefit from a wide field.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that decisions are better with limited options or that more options undermine rational decision making.
Wider choice can unlock better outcomes, a sound method turns difficulty into careful reasoning, and limited options help mainly when time is short.
Instead of fearing choice, we should learn the [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] skill of narrowing options wisely ourselves, so that freedom and good judgment work together.

essays.task_note: Body 1 evaluates the claim (wider choice unlocks better outcomes), Body 2 evaluates the reason (difficulty is not irrationality), and Body 3 concedes that limited options help in urgent, standardized situations.

essays.title: Pressure to share is eroding privacy

paragraphs.text: A generation ago, a family photo stayed in an album at home; today it may be seen by thousands of strangers within minutes.
This change lies behind the claim that, because people increasingly feel compelled to share personal details online, the right to privacy is eroding.
I largely agree with the claim, especially where social and professional pressure makes sharing feel less like a choice than a requirement.

Online sharing has become a social expectation, shared information is collected and combined in ways people cannot control, and the strongest challenge to this view, that sharing is voluntary, overlooks how compelled it has become.
First, the claim holds because sharing personal details online has become a [[pervasive|pervasive]] expectation rather than an option.
Young professionals in Vietnam, like those elsewhere, are often expected to maintain online profiles listing their education, employers and even family events.
A job applicant with no online presence may seem suspicious, so many people share far more than they would like.
Similarly, a teenager who refuses to post photos may be left out of the group chats where friendships now unfold.
Even doctors are now often expected to keep public profiles so that patients can rate them online.

When the cost of silence is exclusion, the choice to keep information private becomes merely [[nominal|nominal]], and a right that can be exercised only at the price of one's career or friendships is a weak right indeed.
The pressure to share, therefore, steadily weakens privacy, just as the claim suggests.
Moreover, once details are shared, people lose control over how they are used, which weakens privacy further.
As an epidemiologist, I have seen patients post their diagnoses and test results in online support groups to seek advice.
Those posts can later be found by employers or neighbors, and a single post about a mental illness or HIV status can attach a lasting [[stigma|stigma]] to the writer.
Likewise, location tags on ordinary photos can reveal where a person lives and when the house is empty.
Each piece of shared information may seem [[innocuous|innocuous]], but together they form a detailed portrait that others can exploit.
Therefore, privacy is eroding not only through what people share but also through what others can assemble from it.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that sharing is voluntary, and a right that one gives up freely is not eroded but exercised.
No law forces anyone to open a social media account, and many people enjoy sharing their lives with distant friends and relatives.
Nevertheless, a choice made under strong social and economic pressure is not fully free, and the claim itself rightly speaks of people feeling "compelled."

Research ethics teaches the same lesson: after the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, the United States required ethics review boards, recognizing that consent must be informed and free.
By the same logic, sharing under pressure cannot be counted as a free surrender of privacy, so the challenge, though serious, does not overturn the claim.
In conclusion, I largely agree that the growing pressure to share personal details online is wearing away the right to privacy.
Sharing has become a social requirement, shared data can be combined and misused, and the argument that sharing is voluntary ignores how much pressure lies behind it.
Protecting privacy will therefore require not only stronger laws but also social norms that allow people to [[abstain|abstain]] from sharing without penalty.

essays.title: Privacy is threatened, but not by sharing

paragraphs.text: Privacy is often discussed as if it were a single object that people either keep or lose.
The claim that privacy is eroding because people feel compelled to share their personal details online treats it this way and blames the problem on users themselves.

Although privacy is under pressure, I mostly disagree with the claim, because the main threat comes from data collected without people's active sharing, and the right to privacy itself is in many ways growing stronger.

Much personal data is gathered without anyone choosing to share it, legal protections for privacy have expanded, and the most compelling challenge, that oversharing exposes people, confuses losing information with losing a right.
First, the claim misidentifies the cause, since much personal information is collected without people deciding to share it.
GPS was built by the US military, and once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Every trip a person takes with such an app can leave a record of her location, even if she never posts a word online.
Similarly, a patient's records may pass between clinics, laboratories and insurers without the patient ever being asked.
Fitness watches, smart televisions and store loyalty cards gather similar data silently.
In these cases, privacy is weakened by collection, not by a compulsion to share, and even a person who never opens a social media account cannot escape it.
This shows that blaming users' sharing habits [[deflects|deflect]] attention from the companies and institutions that gather most data.
Second, the right to privacy, as a legal and ethical principle, has in many areas become stronger rather than weaker.
After the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Today, in my own research in Vietnam, every study must explain to participants how their data will be stored and protected.
Likewise, a hospital that once left paper files open on desks now typically limits electronic records to the staff who need them.
A right is measured by the protections that defend it, and those protections have [[burgeoned|burgeon]]; in research, at least, the people whose data are used have never been better protected.
Therefore, the claim that the right itself is eroding is [[tenuous|tenuous]] at best.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is that people who share intimate details online expose themselves to real harm.
A careless post about one's health or family can be copied and shared by strangers within hours, and once it spreads, it becomes almost impossible to retract.
Nevertheless, this harm involves losing control over particular information, not losing the right to privacy itself.
A person who reveals her diagnosis online still has the legal right to keep her medical records confidential.
Those protections apply whether or not she chooses to post anything.

The challenge therefore shows that individuals should share more carefully, but it does not prove that the right is disappearing; if anything, it reveals why that right must be [[buttressed|buttress]].
In conclusion, while privacy faces serious pressure, I mostly disagree that people's compulsion to share is wearing away the right to it.
Most data are collected rather than volunteered, legal protections have grown, and oversharing harms individuals without abolishing their rights.
If we want to protect privacy, we should focus less on scolding users and more on regulating those who collect data [[surreptitiously|surreptitious]].

bank: Ignaz Semmelweis (Vienna, 1847) had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime; deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate; penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II. In his 1945 Nobel lecture Fleming warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.

Antibiotic resistance today: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe; Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
The Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent; the public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.

Wolbachia mosquitoes: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms (1986) replaced central planning with market incentives; a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
In 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, revealing how often single findings mislead.
GPS was built by the US military; once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helped end bus segregation in that city.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, as during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.

concepts.sentence: Students who choose a topic themselves tend to approach it with alacrity, whereas those pushed through an imposed syllabus often do the bare minimum.

synonyms.note: requiring great care and effort; close to 'demanding'
severe and without warmth; more negative
of conditions or regimens: harsh and frugal

concepts.sentence: A teacher who returns a draft covered in comments may seem harsh, yet such exacting feedback often produces the most lasting gains.

synonyms.note: willing to obey rules or requests
too ready to believe what one is told
self-satisfied, so no drive to question

concepts.sentence: A classroom that rewards only rote recall produces credulous graduates who accept any confident claim, which is precisely the habit higher education should break.

synonyms.note: by persistent repetition; 'inculcate X in students'
fill with a quality; note the grammar: 'imbue students with X'
improve morally or intellectually; the object is the person

concepts.sentence: The aim of early schooling is not merely to transmit facts but to inculcate habits of inquiry that persist long after the facts are forgotten.

synonyms.note: noun: a formal speech or text of high praise

concepts.sentence: Praise works best when it is specific: a coach who commends a player's footwork, rather than simply saying 'good job,' shows her exactly what to repeat.

concepts.concept: Correcting or reprimanding (graded mild to severe)
concepts.sentence: Ignoring a student who plagiarizes does not make the behavior disappear; a teacher who quietly admonishes him signals that standards matter without humiliating him.

synonyms.note: built into the nature of something; also used for things, not only people
belonging to the essential nature; common with 'motivation' and 'value'
caution: deeply fixed through time or habit, not from birth

concepts.sentence: Even prodigies need training, since an inborn aptitude for music remains latent unless years of instruction draw it out.

synonyms.note: find out for certain; stresses certainty

concepts.sentence: Tying salaries to test scores assumes that a single exam can accurately gauge what a teacher contributes, an assumption that ignores where the students started.

synonyms.note: control by rules; does not mean 'forbid'

concepts.sentence: Few would argue that research should be wholly unregulated; the real question is how tightly governments should circumscribe it without stifling discovery.

synonyms.note: funds set aside by a legislature
deck headword: coffer; means the treasury that funding comes from

concepts.sentence: When the public coffers are stretched thin, every subsidy for the arts competes directly with funding for clinics and school meals.

synonyms.note: rich sense of thriving, beyond income

collocations: the general welfare of its citizens
concepts.sentence: A nation's greatness is better reflected in the well-being of its ordinary citizens than in the prizes its scientists bring home.
Mandatory volunteering may serve a worthy end, but it erodes the very autonomy that makes civic service meaningful.

synonyms.note: conceal faults to protect a reputation
hide one's true motives; often intransitive ('officials dissembled')
speak evasively to avoid the truth

concepts.sentence: During a public-health emergency, officials may briefly withhold unverified data, but a pattern of concealment soon breeds the distrust that undermines compliance.
A leader who accedes to every swing in polling data will never complete the unpopular reforms whose benefits arrive only years later.

synonyms.note: mutual courtesy between groups; the climate that makes agreement possible

concepts.sentence: Legislative progress usually depends less on grand ideals than on finding enough common ground for rival parties to concur on a modest first step.

synonyms.note: can imply weakness or being too easily influenced
formal sense: capable of being molded

collocations: the letter versus the spirit of the law
concepts.sentence: A sentencing law malleable enough to consider a defendant's circumstances can deliver justice that a rigid, one-size-fits-all statute cannot.

synonyms.note: protected from harm; legal or sacred tone

concepts.sentence: Once a pristine wetland is drained for a shopping center the loss is permanent, whereas the economic gain could often be had elsewhere.

synonyms.note: shrewd and prudent in political choices
convenient in the short term; implies sacrificing principle

concepts.sentence: Politicians who chase quixotic ideals often accomplish nothing, while their pragmatic colleagues pass imperfect laws that nonetheless improve lives.

synonyms.note: caution: open to more than one interpretation, not simply 'unknown'

concepts.sentence: Almost all basic research has indeterminate consequences at the outset; demanding certainty before funding would have blocked the early studies of bacterial immunity that later yielded CRISPR gene editing.

synonyms.note: harmful in a gradual, hidden way

concepts.sentence: Some technologies prove deleterious only decades later, as the slow damage done by leaded gasoline illustrates.

synonyms.note: beneficial, often in an unwelcome way ('a salutary lesson')
effective at producing a result; not merely 'good'
caution: harmless rather than actively helpful

concepts.sentence: Moderate oversight can be salutary for science itself, since the public trusts research more when it knows dangerous experiments are reviewed.

synonyms.note: just beginning to develop; used of fields and ideas

concepts.sentence: Novel ideas often come from outsiders precisely because they have not yet learned which questions are considered closed.
Fleming's discovery of penicillin was fortuitous, but only a trained eye would have noticed that the mold had killed the surrounding bacteria.
Each advance in genetics has made heredity seem more intricate, not less: the single 'gene for' a trait has given way to networks of thousands of interacting variants.

synonyms.note: reinforce; same as bolster, more formal

concepts.sentence: A single striking study proves little until independent teams corroborate its results with different samples and methods.

synonyms.note: widespread, usually of something bad ('rife with')

concepts.sentence: Smartphones are now so ubiquitous that the question is no longer whether young people use them but how.
An online friendship can be genuine, but for many teenagers it becomes an ersatz substitute for the harder work of face-to-face conversation.

synonyms.note: deck headword: aesthetic; value as beauty or art

concepts.sentence: A song enjoyed by millions may still lack lasting merit, while a difficult novel may be valued for centuries.

synonyms.note: clear and simple; usually of prose style

concepts.sentence: Clarity is a virtue in an argument, but demanding that every poem be immediately intelligible would rule out much of the best poetry ever written.

synonyms.note: meant for a small inner circle

concepts.sentence: Much modern art first struck audiences as opaque; Stravinsky's Rite of Spring provoked an uproar at its 1913 premiere, yet it is now a concert-hall staple.

synonyms.note: overused to the point of meaninglessness

concepts.sentence: An artist who merely imitates the masters produces derivative work; one who studies them and then breaks their rules may produce something new.
Folk festivals in rural villages often preserve a nation's heritage more faithfully than urban museums, which display traditions rather than live them.

synonyms.note: make impure by adding inferior elements

concepts.sentence: When a ministry dictates which themes an artist may address, state funding begins to compromise the integrity of the very work it pays for.
Cities nurture new cultural forms because their heterogeneous populations bring traditions into contact and friction.
Before public arts councils existed, the munificence of a few wealthy patrons decided which composers prospered and which starved.

synonyms.note: deck headword: fecund; prolific generation of ideas

concepts.sentence: In fields such as design, imagination outweighs knowledge only when enough knowledge disciplines it into something feasible.
Talent may open the door to a creative career, but only assiduous practice sustains one over decades.
A principled leader who refuses to trade away civil rights for a short-term bump in the polls may lose an election but win the verdict of history.

synonyms.note: deck headword: vacillate; switching back and forth

concepts.sentence: Voters rarely trust a leader whose positions vacillate with every news cycle, because they cannot predict what he will do next.

synonyms.note: combined effect greater than the parts
unity of purpose within a group

concepts.sentence: The most productive research consortia run on collaboration: no single laboratory has the samples, skills, and funding to answer a global question alone.
Healthy competition sharpens performance, but a leader who is merely combative treats colleagues as rivals and drives talented staff away.

synonyms.note: proven honesty, esp. in public office

concepts.sentence: Probity matters in public office not because leaders must be saints but because a single exposed lie can destroy the trust that every policy depends on.

synonyms.note: deck headword: eminent; distinction in a field

concepts.sentence: Young people chasing instant renown on social media may gain thousands of followers but rarely build the skills that sustain a career.

synonyms.note: bold; can be admiring rather than critical

concepts.sentence: Risk-taking is not the problem; impetuous risk-taking, without any estimate of what could go wrong, is.

synonyms.note: wary of risks; considers all sides

concepts.sentence: A judicious investor does not avoid risk altogether; she accepts it only after weighing the plausible worst case.
Term limits can revitalize an organization, but forcing out a capable leader after exactly five years may sacrifice hard-won expertise for mere novelty.

synonyms.note: generous, esp. toward rivals or the less powerful

concepts.sentence: Even if volunteers feel good when they help, that warm feeling does not make their act any less magnanimous, since the benefit to others is real.

synonyms.note: eager to acquire wealth or things

concepts.sentence: A corporation may grow by pursuing profit alone, but an acquisitive culture that ignores pollution eventually pays in lawsuits and lost trust.
Group identity offers belonging, but it can also demand conformity, pressuring members to adopt views they have never examined.

synonyms.note: challenge the truth or integrity of

concepts.sentence: A society in which citizens freely question authority catches its leaders' mistakes early, before they harden into disasters.

synonyms.note: odd in behavior; not necessarily principled

concepts.sentence: Many celebrated scientists began as mavericks, as Barry Marshall did in the early 1980s when his claim that bacteria cause stomach ulcers was widely dismissed.

synonyms.note: a perfect example of a quality

concepts.sentence: The heroes a society celebrates reveal its ideals: a culture that lionizes billionaires values wealth, whereas one that honors nurses values care.
Tabloids that denigrate public figures for minor slips make it harder to recognize genuine heroism when it appears.

synonyms.note: attractive on the surface but without value

concepts.sentence: In an age of curated online profiles, an ostentatious lifestyle can attract more attention than quiet competence.
Convenience does not automatically weaken character; a person can rely on a washing machine and still be self-reliant in the decisions that matter.

synonyms.note: deck headword: warranted; give good reason for

concepts.sentence: A worthy goal cannot warrant every means; no cure for a disease would justify testing it on unwilling patients.

concepts.concept: Relevance (of the past to the present)
concepts.sentence: History is germane to modern policy not because events repeat exactly but because human motives such as fear and greed recur.

synonyms.note: belonging to a much earlier period
deck headword: anachronism; out of its time
neutral: of the past, not necessarily useless

concepts.sentence: Some knowledge does become obsolete, yet the reasoning that produced it, such as the habit of testing claims against evidence, rarely does.
Remaining wary of a new leader's promises is sensible, but treating every newcomer as a suspect can poison a team before it has even begun.

synonyms.note: based on facts rather than feelings

concepts.sentence: Facts may be objective, but the choice of which facts to present rarely is, so even a statistics-heavy argument is never fully dispassionate.
The best test of an argument may not be whether it converts opponents, since even a cogent case can fail against listeners committed to their views.

synonyms.note: deck headword: tenable; cannot be defended
plausible on the surface but wrong

concepts.sentence: The reasoning that a fact may someday be revised, so all facts should be mistrusted, is fallacious: it confuses provisional with unreliable.
Progress in medicine has often come when clinicians with divergent assumptions were forced to test their claims against the same data.

synonyms.note: expert judge, esp. in the arts or taste

concepts.sentence: Expert critics notice technical flaws that ordinary viewers miss, but the connoisseur's judgment is not the only one that counts for art made for the public.
A neophyte may ask the naïve question that experts stopped asking years ago, and occasionally that question exposes a hidden assumption.

synonyms.note: deck headword: predisposed; make more likely

concepts.sentence: Poverty does not dictate a child's future, but it engenders constraints, such as hunger and unstable housing, that make some outcomes far more likely.
